paragraphs.text: Since we are about to write on the book of the Gospel which Saint Luke set out with a somewhat fuller arrangement of the Lord's deeds, we think we should first explain its style, for it is historical. Divine Scripture does strip worldly wisdom of its learning, because that wisdom rests more on an elaborate show of words than on the reason of things. Yet if anyone looks in the divine Scriptures even for the things the worldly think admirable, he will find them.

The philosophers of this world thought three things the most excellent of all, namely that wisdom is threefold: natural, moral or rational. We were able to notice these three already in the Old Testament too. What else do those three wells signify, one of vision, another of abundance, the third of the oath, but that this threefold virtue was present in the patriarchs? The well of vision is the rational one, because reason sharpens the sight of the mind and cleanses the eye of the soul. The well of abundance is the ethical one, because when the foreigners, who stand for the vices of the body, gave way, Isaac found the living water of the mind; for good morals flow out pure, and goodness itself, generous to the people, overflows for others while it is more sparing toward itself. The third is the well of the oath, that is, of natural wisdom, which grasps both what is above nature and what belongs to nature; for what is affirmed and sworn, as it were, with God as witness also embraces divine things, since the Lord of nature is called as witness to its truth. And what do Solomon's three books, one the Proverbs, another Ecclesiastes, the third the Song of Songs, show us but that holy Solomon was skilled in this threefold wisdom? In Proverbs he wrote of rational and ethical matters; in Ecclesiastes of natural matters, because all that is established in this world is vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, for the creation was subjected to vanity; and in the Song of Songs of moral and rational matters, because when love of the heavenly Word is poured into our soul and the holy mind is joined to the rational by a kind of fellowship, wonderful mysteries are revealed.

And what wisdom do you think the evangelists lacked? Although all of them are full of the various kinds, each nonetheless excels in a different one. For truly natural wisdom is in the book of the Gospel written according to John. No one, I dare say, has seen the majesty of God with such loftiness of wisdom and opened it to us in his own words. He passes beyond the clouds, passes beyond the powers of the heavens, passes beyond the angels, and finds the Word in the beginning and sees the Word with God. Again, who has followed out each thing in human terms more morally, setting forth for us precepts for living, than Saint Matthew? And what is more rational than that wonderful linking which Saint Mark thought should be placed right at the beginning: "Behold, I send my messenger," and "The voice of one crying in the wilderness"? He did this both to stir wonder and to teach that man ought to please God by humility, self-denial and faith, just as that holy John the Baptist climbed to immortality by these steps: his clothing, his food, his message.

Saint Luke, for his part, kept a kind of historical order and revealed to us more of the miracles among the Lord's deeds, yet in such a way that the narrative of his Gospel embraced the virtues of every kind of wisdom. For what could be more excellent for natural wisdom than his revealing that the Holy Spirit was also the creator of the Lord's incarnation? He teaches natural things, then, if the Spirit creates. That is why David too, teaching natural wisdom, says: "Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created." He teaches moral things in the same book, when in those beatitudes he teaches me conduct: how I should love my enemy, how I should not strike back or return the blow of one who beats me, how I should do good, and lend with no hope of getting it back and yet with the repayment of a reward; for the reward follows more readily the one who does not expect it. He also taught rational things, when I read that "whoever is faithful in the least is faithful also in the greater." What more shall I say of natural things, since he taught that the powers of the heavens are moved and that the only-begotten Son of God is the Lord of the sun, at whose passion darkness fell in the daytime, the earth was darkened, and the sun withdrew?

Therefore all the primacy that worldly prudence falsely claims for itself is truly possessed by spiritual wisdom. This is all the more so because, if we may venture something more boldly, our faith itself, the very mystery of the Trinity, could not exist without this threefold wisdom, unless we believe that the Father is the natural one, who begot for us the Redeemer; that the Son is the ethical one, who, obedient to the Father even unto death according to his humanity, redeemed us; and that the Spirit is the rational one, who poured into human hearts the reason for worshipping the Godhead and governing one's life. Let no one think that we have made any difference of power or might, since by that slander one could also attack Paul. For he made no difference when he said: "There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but the same God, who works all things in all." For the Son also works all things and in all, as you have elsewhere: "Christ is all and in all." The Holy Spirit works too, because "one and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each as he wills." There is therefore no difference in their works, no distinction, where in the Father, in the Son and in the Holy Spirit alike there is a fullness of power second to none.

Let us, then, consider these things carefully as we read, so that in the passages themselves they may shine out more clearly for us. For whoever seeks finds, and to whoever knocks it will be opened. Diligence opens for itself the door of truth, and so let us obey the heavenly precepts. It was not said idly to man, as to none of the other living creatures: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread." For the earth was commanded by God to supply fodder to those animals that are by nature irrational, but to man alone, so that he might exercise the reason he has received, a course of life in toil is prescribed. Man is not content with the fodder of the other animals; the fruit-bearing tree given to all in common for food is not enough for him, but he seeks out for himself the delights of varied banquets, fetches delicacies from lands across the sea, sweeps delicacies from the waves. He ought not, then, to refuse to seek his living by labor, if for eternal life he undergoes a brief labor. So if anyone entering these contests of sacred discussion strips off the anxiety of this life, exposed as it is to error, and, stripped of malice, an athlete of piety, his soul's limbs, as it were, anointed with spiritual oil, takes up the contests of truth, he will without doubt earn the everlasting prizes of the sacred crowns. For good labors bear noble fruit, and the more the contests, the more excellent the crown of virtues.

But let us return to our subject. We said that this book of the Gospel was arranged in a historical style. Indeed, we see that, compared with the others, more ample care has been spent on describing events than on setting out precepts. And the evangelist himself, in the manner of historians, took his beginning from a narrative: "There was," he says, "in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah," and he follows out that story in full order. That is why those who have held that the four forms of living creatures revealed in the Apocalypse are to be understood as the four books of the Gospel want this book to be represented by the figure of the calf; for the calf is a priestly victim. And this book of the Gospel fits the calf well, because it began with priests and ended with the Calf who, taking on himself the sins of all, was sacrificed for the life of the whole world; for he is that priestly Calf. Indeed, he is both calf and priest: priest, because he is our propitiation, for we have him as our advocate with the Father; calf, because he washed us and redeemed us by his own blood. And it is fitting that, since we said the book of the Gospel according to Matthew is moral, an opinion of this kind should not be passed over; for morals are properly called human.

Many, however, think that our Lord himself is represented in the four books of the Gospel by the four forms of the living creatures, because he is at once man, lion, calf and eagle: man, because he was born of Mary; lion, because he is strong; calf, because he is a sacrifice; eagle, because he is the resurrection. And so the form of a living creature is represented in each book in such a way that the course of each book appears to suit the nature, the power, the grace or the miracle of the creature assigned to it. Although all these are in all of them, still there is a certain fullness of a particular virtue in each. One described more fully the birth of the man, and also instructed human conduct with fuller precepts. Another began by expressing the divine power: that, King from King, Strong from Strong, True from True, he despised death with living power. The third put the priestly sacrifice first and set out the very sacrifice of the calf in a fuller style. The fourth expressed the miracles of the divine resurrection more abundantly than the rest. One, therefore, is all, and one is in all, as we have read: not unlike himself in each, but true in all. But now let us take up the very text of the Gospel.
BOOK ONE

"Since," he says, "many have undertaken to set in order a narrative of the things." Most of our affairs, like those of the ancient Jews, take shape from the same kinds and causes, correspond in the like use and outcome of similar examples, and agree in their beginning and end. Among that people many prophesied, filled with the divine Spirit, while others promised to prophesy and then betrayed their profession with a lie. These were false prophets rather than prophets, like Hananiah son of Azzur. But the people had the grace of discerning spirits, so as to know whom they ought to count among the prophets and whom, like a good money-changer, they ought to reject: those in whom corrupt metal showed its dross rather than the splendour of true light shining back. In the same way now, in the New Testament, many have tried to write gospels, and the good money-changers did not approve them. Out of them all they judged that only one should be chosen, the one arranged in four books.

Another gospel is indeed in circulation which the Twelve are said to have written. Basilides even dared to write a gospel, which is called the gospel according to Basilides. Another gospel is also in circulation, titled according to Thomas. I know of another written according to Matthias. We have read some of these so that they may not be read. We read them so as not to be ignorant of them; we read them not to hold on to them but to reject them, and to know what kind of writings these are in which those grand men lift up their hearts. The Church has four books of the gospel and abounds in evangelists throughout the whole world. The heresies have many gospels but do not have one. Many have tried, but they were left without the grace of God. Many have even taken from the four books of the gospel whatever they thought suited their poisonous assertions and crammed it into one. So the Church, which has one gospel, teaches one God. But those who assert that the God of the Old Testament is one God and the God of the New another have made out of many gospels not one God but many.

"Since many," he says, "have undertaken." Those who undertook were certainly those who could not complete. So Saint Luke bears even richer witness that many began and did not finish, when he says that very many had undertaken. Whoever undertook to set things in order undertook it by his own labour and did not finish. The gifts and grace of God require no effort. When grace pours itself in, it waters the writer's mind so that it does not run short but overflows. Matthew did not "undertake," Mark did not undertake, John did not undertake, Luke did not undertake. The divine Spirit supplied an abundance of words and of every matter, and they finished what they had begun without any struggle. And so he rightly says: "since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative of the things which have been fulfilled among us," or "which abound among us."

What abounds fails no one, and no one doubts what has been fulfilled, since its effect establishes faith and its outcome makes it plain. So the gospel has been fulfilled. It abounds for all the faithful throughout the whole world, waters the minds of all and strengthens the soul. Therefore one who is founded on the rock and has taken up the whole fullness of faith and the firm support of constancy rightly says "which have been fulfilled among us." For those who describe the Lord's saving deeds, or who fix their minds on his wonders, tell the true from the false not by signs and prodigies but by the word. What could be more reasonable than this? When you read of deeds that are beyond man, you should believe that they belong to a higher nature. But when you read of things that belong to human conduct, you should believe that they are the sufferings of the body he took on. So our faith is founded on word and reason, not on signs.

"Just as they handed them down to us," he says, "who from the beginning saw for themselves and were ministers of the word." This way of speaking does not seem fitting, since it would make us believe that the word was ministered rather than heard. But what is meant here is not a spoken word but the substantial Word, the one who became flesh and dwelt among us. So let us understand not an ordinary word but that heavenly Word whom the apostles served. Yet we also read in Exodus that the people saw the voice of the Lord, and a voice is certainly not seen but heard. What is a voice but a sound, which is not seen by the eyes but perceived by the ear? But Moses, with the loftiest insight, wanted to declare that the voice of God is seen, for it is seen by the gaze of the inner mind. In the gospel, however, what is seen is not a voice but the Word, which is far more excellent than a voice. That is why Saint John the evangelist also says: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard and which we have seen, which we have looked upon with our eyes and our hands have examined, concerning the Word of life: the life appeared, and we have seen it and bear witness and proclaim to you the life which was with the Father and appeared to us." You see, then, that the Word of God was both seen and heard by the apostles. They saw the Lord not only according to the body but also according to the Word. Those who saw the glory of the Word with Moses and Elijah saw the Word. These saw Jesus, for they saw him in his glory. Others, who could see only the body, did not see him, for Jesus is seen not with bodily eyes but with spiritual ones.

Indeed the Jews, who saw him, did not see him. Abraham saw him, for it is written: "Abraham saw my day and rejoiced." So Abraham saw him, though he certainly did not see the Lord in the body. But whoever saw him in the spirit saw him in the body. Whoever saw him in the body and did not see him in the spirit did not see, even in the body, what he was looking at. Isaiah saw him, and because he saw him in the spirit, he saw him in the body too. So he says: "He had no form nor comeliness." The Jews did not see him, for their foolish heart was blinded. He himself also testifies that the Jews could not see him, when he says: "Blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel!" Pilate did not see him. Those who shouted "Crucify, crucify him!" did not see him, for if they had seen, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty. So whoever saw God saw Emmanuel, that is, saw God with us. But whoever did not see God with us could not see the one whom the Virgin bore. Indeed, those who did not believe in the Son of God did not believe in the Son of the Virgin either.

What, then, is it to see God? Do not ask me. Ask the gospel, ask the Lord himself, or rather listen to him saying: "Philip, whoever has seen me has also seen the Father who sent me. How can you say, 'Show us the Father'? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?" Certainly a body is not seen in a body, nor a spirit in a spirit. Only that Father is seen in the Son, and only this Son is seen in the Father. Unlike beings are not seen in one another. But where there is unity of operation and power, the Son is seen in the Father and the Father in the Son. "The works that I do," he says, "he also does." Jesus is seen in his works, and in the Son's works the Father too is perceived. Whoever saw that Galilean mystery saw [?], for no one but the Lord of the world could change the elements. I see Jesus when I read that he smeared the blind man's eyes with clay and gave him back his sight. I recognize in him the one who formed man from clay and poured into him the breath of life and the light of sight. I see Jesus when he forgives sins, for no one can forgive sins but God alone. I see Jesus when he raises Lazarus, and those who saw it did not see. I see Jesus, and I also see the Father, when I lift my eyes to the sky, turn them to the seas, or bring them back to the earth. For his invisible things are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made.

"Just as they handed them down to us who from the beginning saw and were ministers of the word." There is a twofold virtue in the perfect man: contemplation and action. The holy evangelist credits the apostles with both. They not only saw, he says, but were also ministers of the word. Contemplation belongs to seeing and ministry to action. The end of contemplation is action, and the beginning of action is contemplation. To use the apostles' own example: Peter and Andrew heard the voice of the Lord saying, "I will make you fishers of men," and without any delay they left the oar and followed the Word. That was contemplation. But action does not come at once with contemplation. There was still no action, only contemplation, when Peter says: "Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you." There was the intent to suffer, but not yet the act. Still, there was already action in his fasts, in his vigils and in his contempt for bodily pleasures, for this is the action of a Christian. Contemplation and action are not present together in all things. A person may be acting in one matter while still only contemplating in another. Peter himself had long accomplished much by apostolic power. Yet afterwards, when the Lord said to him "Follow me," he took up his cross, followed the Word and undertook the act of suffering. But grant that in Peter, Andrew, John and the other apostles contemplation and action were evenly balanced:

sometimes, though, there is more in contemplation than in action, or more in action than in contemplation. We see this in the gospel in the difference between holy Mary and Martha. One was listening to the Word, while the other was busy with serving. Martha stood and said: "Lord, do you not care that she has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me." And he said to her: "Martha, Martha... Mary has chosen the best part, which will not be taken from her." So in one of them zeal for contemplation abounded, and in the other the ministry of action. Yet each had zeal for both virtues. Martha would not have undertaken the service if she had not heard the Word, and her action is a sign of contemplation. Mary gained so much grace from the perfection of both virtues that she anointed Jesus' feet, wiped them with her hair and filled the whole house with the fragrance of her faith. Sometimes, too, there is very great contemplation but empty action. Suppose someone applies his mind to medicine and learns all the rules of healing, but does not carry out its duties. Because the action is empty, the contemplation turns out empty as well. In some people, again, action is at times richer and contemplation thinner. Suppose someone receives the sacraments of saving baptism but will not apply his mind to learning the precepts of the various virtues. It often happens that through neglect of contemplation he loses the fruit of action. So we must seek the fullness of both virtues, which the apostles were able to attain. Of them he says: "who from the beginning saw and were ministers." By "they saw" we are to understand their contemplation of divine knowledge, and by "they were ministers" their action is made known.

"It seemed good to me," he says. What he declares seemed good to him need not have seemed good to him alone. It did not seem good by human will only, but as it pleased the one of whom he says, "Christ, who speaks in me." Christ works so that what is good may seem good to us as well, for he calls those on whom he has mercy. So anyone who follows Christ, when asked why he chose to be a Christian, can answer: "It seemed good to me." In saying this he does not deny that it seemed good to God, for the will of men is prepared by God. That God is honoured by a saint is itself God's grace. Indeed very many wanted to write a gospel, but only four were received, those who were found worthy of divine grace.

"It seemed good to me also," he says, "having followed all things carefully from the beginning, in order." No one will doubt that this book of the gospel is fuller than the others. And so he claims for himself not what is false but what is true. He even earned from the holy apostle Paul a testimony to his diligence. This is how Paul praises Luke: "whose praise," he says, "is in the gospel throughout all the churches." Truly praiseworthy is the one who deserved to be praised by so great a teacher of the Gentiles. So he says he has followed not a few things but all things. Having followed all things, he chose to write not all things but a selection from all. He did not write everything, but he followed everything. For as it says, "if all the things that Jesus did were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself could contain them." You notice that he deliberately passed over even things that others had written. In this way a different grace would shine out in each gospel, and each book would stand out for certain wonders of mysteries and deeds of its own. The soldiers of Christ divided his garments among themselves, and this will be explained more fully in its place.

The gospel is written to Theophilus, that is, to one whom God loves. If you love God, it is written to you. If it is written to you, accept the evangelist's gift. Keep this pledge from a friend carefully in the inner chambers of your soul. Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, look at it often and examine it frequently. Faithfulness is the first thing owed to a pledge, and diligence follows faithfulness, so that moth or rust may not consume the pledges entrusted to you. Whatever has been entrusted to you can be consumed. The gospel is a good pledge, but take care that neither moth nor rust consumes it in your soul.

The moth consumes it if you believe wrongly what you have read rightly. The heretic is a moth. Photinus is a moth, and Arius is your moth. Whoever separates the Word from God tears the garment. Photinus tears the garment when he reads: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was." The garment is whole if you read: "and the Word was God." Whoever separates Christ from God tears the garment. Whoever reads "And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God" tears the garment, unless he also knows Christ. Eternal life is not to know the Father alone as truly God, but also to know Christ as true God. True from true, God from God: that is everlasting life. To know Christ without faith in his divinity or in the sacrament of his body is a moth. Arius is a moth, and Sabellius is a moth. The spirit of the wavering suffers these moths. The spirit that does not believe that Father and Son are one in divinity suffers these moths. Whoever divides the one into separate substances tears what is written: "I and the Father are one." The spirit that does not believe that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh suffers this moth, and is itself a moth, for that is the antichrist. But those who are of God hold fast to the faith, and so they cannot suffer the moth that divides the garment. For everything that is divided against itself cannot last, like the kingdom of Satan.

There is also a rust of the soul. It forms when the keen edge of religious contemplation is coated with the filth of worldly desires, or when the purity of faith is discoloured by a cloud of faithlessness. Greed for property is rust of the mind. Carelessness is rust of the mind. Craving for honours is rust of the mind, if one's highest hope in this present life is placed in them. So let us turn to divine things and sharpen our minds and exercise our love. Then we can keep that sword which the Lord tells us to buy by selling our garment always ready and bright, as though stored in the sheath of the mind. The soldiers of Christ must always have at hand spiritual weapons, mighty through God for pulling down strongholds. Otherwise, when the commander of the heavenly army comes, he may be offended by the rust of our years and separate us from the company of his legions.

"There was," he says, "in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. His wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. They were both righteous, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without reproach."

Divine Scripture teaches us that we ought to praise not only the character of those who deserve praise but also their parents. In this way an inheritance of spotless purity, as if handed down, stands out in those we wish to praise. What else does the holy evangelist intend here than to show the nobility of Saint John the Baptist through his parents, his miracles, his character, his office and his passion? In the same way Hannah, the mother of Saint Samuel, is praised. In the same way Isaac received from his parents a nobility of piety, which he left to his descendants. So Zechariah was a priest. He was not only a priest but of the division of Abijah, that is, noble by descent among the foremost.

"And his wife," he says, "was of the daughters of Aaron." So Saint John's nobility comes down not only from his parents but also from his ancestors. It was not exalted by worldly power but made venerable by a succession in religion. The forerunner of Christ needed to have ancestors like these. Then his preaching of faith in the Lord's coming would be seen not as something conceived suddenly, but as received from his ancestors and instilled by the very law of nature.

"They were both," he says, "righteous, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without reproach." What do they say to this who look for excuses for their sins? They think a man cannot live without frequent sins, and they use the verse written in Job: "No one is clean from filth, not even if his life lasts but a single day; on earth his months are numbered by him." We must answer them by first asking them to define what it means for a man to be without sin: whether it means never to have sinned at all, or to have stopped sinning. If they think that being without sin means having stopped sinning [?], I agree with them too, for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. But some correct their old error and change their way of life so that they refrain from sin. If they deny that such people abstain from wrongdoing, I cannot agree with their opinion. For we read that the Lord so loved the Church that he would present her to himself glorious, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but holy and spotless. The Church was gathered from the Gentiles, that is, from sinners. So how can she be spotless when she comes from the spotted? First, by the grace of God, because she has been washed clean of sin. Then, because by a settled habit of not sinning she abstains from wrongdoing. So she was not spotless from the beginning, for that is impossible for human nature. She is spotless through the grace of God and through her own character. Because she no longer sins, she comes to be seen as spotless.

It was not idly that he called them righteous before God, walking in the commandments and ordinances of the Lord. In these words he included both the almighty Father and the Son. The holy evangelist also declares that it was the Son who gave the law and laid down the commandments. He rightly says "righteous before God," for not everyone who is righteous before men is also righteous before God. Men see one way and God another: men look at the face, God at the heart. So it can happen that someone seems righteous to me because of a goodness put on for the public, yet is not righteous before God. That happens when his righteousness does not come from a simple mind but is feigned to win favour, for a man cannot detect what is hidden in it. The perfect praise, then, is to be righteous before God. That is why the apostle speaks of one "whose praise is not from men but from God." Blessed indeed is the one who is righteous in God's sight. Blessed is the one of whom the Lord deigns to say: "Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no guile." The true Israelite is one who sees God, knows that he is seen by God, and lays bare to him the secrets of his heart. He alone is more perfect who is approved by the one who cannot be deceived. The judgments of the Lord are true, but the judgments of men are often mistaken. They frequently give the credit of righteousness to the unrighteous, and they either persecute the righteous man with hatred or stain him with lies. But the Lord knows the ways of the spotless. He does not take the praiseworthy for a sinner or the sinner for praiseworthy, but judges each person by the reckoning of what he has deserved, for he is judge alike of mind and of deed. Divine judgments measure the merit of the righteous by the disposition of the mind, not by how some deed turns out. Often a good mind is disfigured by a deed that turns out badly, or a wicked thought is veiled by the fair appearance of some deed. But even what you have done well cannot be approved by God's judgment if your intention was bad. For it is written: "Justly shall you pursue what is just." If it were not possible to do what is just unjustly, it would never have been said: "Justly shall you pursue what is just." The Saviour himself certainly taught us that what is just can be done unjustly, when he said: "When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you," and "When you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites." Mercy is good, and prayer is good, but they can be done unjustly. That happens if someone gives to a poor man out of vanity, so as to be seen by others.

So the holy evangelist says not only that they were righteous before God and walked in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord. He also says that they walked without reproach. This agrees wonderfully with the prophetic saying that holy Solomon used in Proverbs: "Provide good things always before God and before men." So there is no reproach where goodness of mind and goodness of deed agree. Often a harsher righteousness provokes the reproach of men.

Notice carefully how well the very distinction between the words fits and how fitting their order is. "Walking," he says, "in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord." The commandment comes first and the ordinance second. When we obey the heavenly commandments, we walk in the Lord's commandments. When we judge, and judge fittingly, we are seen to keep the Lord's ordinances.

This, then, is complete praise, for it takes in family, character, office, deed and judgment. Family is seen in the ancestors, character in fairness, office in the priesthood, deed in the commandment, and judgment in the ordinance.

"Now it happened that while Zechariah was serving as priest before the Lord God in the order of his division, according to the custom of the priesthood, the lot fell to him to enter the temple of the Lord and offer incense. And the whole people was praying outside at the hour of incense."

Holy Zechariah seems to be designated here as high priest. As we read, the priests always went into the first tabernacle to carry out their ministries, but he entered the temple at only one time of the year: into the second, once a year, the high priest alone, and not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the sins of the people. This is the high priest who is still sought by lot, because the true one is still unknown; for one who is chosen by lot is not grasped by human judgment. That one, then, was being sought, and another was being prefigured. The true priest for ever was being sought, to whom it is said: You are a priest for ever. He would reconcile God the Father to the human race not by the blood of victims but by his own blood. But then blood was shed in figure and the priest was ordained in figure; now, since the truth has come, let us leave the figure and follow the truth. Then, indeed, there were turns of service, but now there is perpetuity. There was, therefore, and surely there was, one in whose stead those turns were being served.

So the priest who was to enter the temple was chosen by lot. If, then, no witness could be brought in under the type, what else was signified but that a priest would come whose sacrifice would not be shared with the others, who would not sacrifice for us in temples made with hands, but would empty out our sins in the temple of his own body? So the priest was sought by lot. Perhaps this is also why the soldiers cast lots for the Lord's garments: since the Lord was preparing to offer sacrifice for us in his own temple, the casting of lots around him too would fulfil the precept of the law. That is why he says: I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it. Surely this was so that he himself might be the one who was both awaited by the Old Testament and seen to be chosen by God's command. And so the lot also fell on the apostle Matthias, lest the election of an apostle seem to depart from the command of the old law.

And there appeared to him an angel standing at the right of the altar of incense. It is not without reason that an angel is seen in the temple, since the coming of the true priest was now being announced and the heavenly sacrifice, at which angels would minister, was being prepared. And it is well said that he "appeared" to the one who suddenly caught sight of him. Divine scripture has a particular custom, with regard either to angels or to God, of saying that what cannot be foreseen "appears"; thus you have: God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre. For one who is not sensed beforehand, but is seen in a sudden sight, is said to appear. Things perceptible to the senses are not seen in the same way as he whose being seen depends on his will, whose nature it is not to be seen, and whose will it is to be seen. For if he does not wish it, he is not seen; if he wishes it, he is seen. God appeared to Abraham because he willed to; to another he did not appear, because he did not will to. Stephen too, while he was being stoned by the people, saw heaven opened; Jesus too was seen standing at the right hand of God, and was not seen by the people. Isaiah saw the Lord of Hosts, but another could not see him, because he appeared to whom he pleased.

And why do we speak of human beings, when we have read even of the heavenly virtues and powers themselves that no one has ever seen God? And he added what is beyond the heavenly powers: the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself made him known. So either it must be granted, if no one has ever seen God the Father, that it was the Son who was seen in the Old Testament, and then let the heretics stop assigning a beginning from the Virgin to him who was seen before he was born of the Virgin. Or else it certainly cannot be refuted that the Father, or the Son, or indeed the Holy Spirit (if there is in fact a vision of the Holy Spirit), is seen in a form that the will has chosen, not one that nature has fashioned, since we have learned that the Spirit too was seen in a dove. And so no one has ever seen God, because no one has beheld the fullness of divinity that dwells in God; no one has grasped it with mind or eyes, for "seen" must be referred to both. Indeed, when it is added, the only-begotten Son has himself made him known, it is the vision of minds rather than of eyes that is meant. For a form is seen, but power is made known; the one is grasped by the eyes, the other by the mind.

But why should I speak of the Trinity? The seraph appeared when he wished, and Isaiah alone heard his voice. The angel appeared, and he is present now too, but he is not seen; for it is not in our power to see, but in his power to appear. Yet even if we have no power of seeing, there is the grace of deserving, so that we may be able to see. And so he who had grace merited the opportunity; we do not merit the opportunity, because we do not have the grace of seeing God.

And what wonder is it if in the present age the Lord is not seen except when he wishes? Even in the resurrection itself it is not easy to see God, except for those who are pure in heart. And so: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. How many he had already counted blessed, and yet he had not promised them the ability to see God! If, then, those who are pure in heart will see God, surely others will not see him; for neither will the unworthy see God, nor can one who has not wished to see God see him. Nor is God seen in a place, but by a pure heart. God is not sought with bodily eyes, nor bounded by sight, nor held by touch, nor heard in speech, nor perceived in his approach. When he is thought to be absent, he is seen, and when he is present, he is not seen. Indeed, not even all the apostles saw Christ. And so he says: I have been with you so long, and still you have not known me! For whoever has known what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, has seen both Christ and the Father. For now we no longer know Christ according to the flesh, but according to the spirit; for the Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord. May he in his mercy deign to fill us with all the fullness of God, so that he may be seen by us. This, then, is why the angel appeared to Zechariah at the right of the altar of incense: he appeared when he willed, and did not appear as long as he did not will.

He appeared at the right of the altar of incense because he was bringing the token of divine mercy; for: The Lord is at my right hand, that I may not be moved; and elsewhere: The Lord is your protection upon your right hand. And would that an angel might stand by us too as we burn incense on the altars and offer sacrifice, or rather show himself to be seen! For do not doubt that an angel stands by when Christ stands by, when Christ is sacrificed; for Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Nor should you fear that your heart may be troubled by the sight of an angel. We are indeed troubled and taken out of our usual state of mind when we are dazzled by the encounter with some higher power; but the same angel who meets us will be able to strengthen us, just as he strengthened Zechariah in mind, who had been troubled before, saying: Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for behold, your prayer has been heard. And your wife Elizabeth will bear a son, and you shall call his name John; and he will be a joy to you, and many will rejoice at his birth.

God's benefits are always full and overflowing; they are not confined to a meagre number but heaped up in a rich abundance of good things. So it is here: first the fruit of prayer, then a son born to a barren wife, then the gladness of many and greatness of virtue. A prophet of the Most High is also promised; indeed, lest there be any doubt, even the name of the child to come is specified. Since so many gifts were flowing beyond what he had prayed for, it is not undeserved that silence is the penalty for his distrust, which we shall explain later. There is a festal joy at the birth and begetting of saints; for a saint is not only a grace to his parents but also the salvation of many. Hence we are admonished in this passage to rejoice at the birth of saints.

Parents too are admonished to give thanks no less for the birth of their children than for their merits; for it is no small gift of God to give children to carry on the race, heirs to succeed them. Read how Jacob rejoiced in the birth of twelve sons; a son is given to Abraham; Zechariah is heard. The fruitfulness of a parent, then, is a divine gift. So let fathers give thanks because they have begotten, sons because they have been begotten, mothers because they are honoured with the rewards of marriage; for children are the wages of their service. Let the earth flourish in God's praise because it is tilled, the world because it is known, the Church because it is increased by the number of a devoted people. And it was not idly that marriage was joined by God's command at the very beginning of Genesis; it was so that heresy might be destroyed. For God so approved marriage that he joined it, and so rewarded it that divine kindness granted children to those whom barrenness had denied them.

And he will be great before the Lord. Here he declared greatness not of body but of soul. Before the Lord there is greatness of soul, greatness of virtue; there is also smallness of soul and childhood in virtue. For we reckon the ages of the soul just as we do those of the body, not by the measure of time but by the quality of virtue. So a perfect man is said to be one who is free of the error of childhood and, through maturity of mind, does not feel the slipperiness of youth; but a little one is one who seems not yet to have made any progress in virtue. Hence the passage in Jeremiah, when the Lord had compassion on Ephraim as he wept and begged pardon for his own sins: From my youth, he says, Ephraim is my beloved son, a child in delights. For if he had not been a child in delights, he would never have sinned. And he rightly said both, "in delights" and "a child"; for a child is one who does not sin: Behold my child, whom I have chosen. So he who had been so formed by the Lord as to know nothing of error sinned through delights. Therefore, if he had not been a child in delights, and if he had advanced in the age of virtue to the perfect man, he would never have fallen so as to need to ask pardon for his sins, when he ought rather to have hoped for the rewards of merit. Our Lord too seems to express this in the Gospel when he says: Do not despise one of these little ones. But let more be kept for its proper place. So the little one is the opposite of the great. And if, according to the apostle, the little child is under the elements (for when we were little children, we were under the elements of this world), then the great one is above the elements of the world.

So John will be great, not in strength of body but in greatness of soul. Indeed, he did not extend the borders of any empire, nor did he set his heart on triumphs crowned with the glories of war; but, what is greater, preaching in the desert, he suppressed men's luxuries and the wantonness of the body by great strength of soul. Little, then, in the world, but great in the spirit. Indeed, as a great man, not captivated by the allurements of life, he did not change the constancy of his judgment out of a desire to live.

And he will be filled, he says, with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb. There is no doubt that this promise of the angel was true, since holy John, before he was born, while still in his mother's womb, showed the grace of the Spirit he had received. For though neither his father nor his mother had worked any wonders before, he, leaping in his mother's womb, proclaimed the good news of the Lord's coming. For so you have it that when the mother of the Lord came to Elizabeth, she said: Behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the infant leapt in my womb. He did not yet have the spirit of life, but he had the spirit of grace. Indeed, elsewhere too we have been able to observe that the grace of sanctification can precede the substance of life, when the Lord says: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you and appointed you a prophet to the nations. For the spirit of this life is one thing, the spirit of grace another. The former takes its beginning at birth and its end at death; the latter is not confined by times or ages, is not extinguished by death, is not shut out by a mother's womb. So too holy Mary, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied; Elisha, when dead, raised a man's corpse by the touch of his body; and Samuel after death, according to the testimony of scripture, did not keep silent about things to come.
And he will be filled, he says, with the Holy Spirit; for one to whom the Spirit of grace is present lacks nothing, and one into whom the Holy Spirit is poured has a fullness of great virtues.

Indeed, he says, he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. We need no testimony that holy John turned the hearts of very many. In this both the prophetic and the gospel scriptures support us: The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. And the baptisms thronged by the people show that no small progress was made among a converted people, because when John is believed, Christ is believed. For the forerunner of Christ preached not about himself but about the Lord.

And so he will go before in the sight of the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. These are rightly joined, for there is never power without the spirit nor the spirit without power. And perhaps it says "in the spirit and power of Elijah" because holy Elijah had both great power and grace: power to turn the minds of the people back from faithlessness to faith, the power of abstinence and patience, and the spirit of prophecy. Elijah was in the desert, John was in the desert; the one was fed by ravens, the other by the scrub of the wild, and trampling on every allurement of pleasure he chose frugality and despised luxury. The one did not seek the favour of King Ahab, the other spurned that of Herod; the one divided the Jordan, the other turned it into a saving bath; this one keeps company with the Lord on earth, that one appears with the Lord in glory; this one is the forerunner of the Lord's first coming, that one of his second. The one, after three years, watered the parched earth with rain, and this one, after three years, drenched the soil of our body with the shower of faith. Do you ask what the three years are? Behold, he says, these three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. For a mystical number was due, so that salvation might be restored to the peoples: one year was in the patriarchs (indeed, there was then such a harvest of men as there has not been since upon the earth), another in Moses and the other prophets, the third in the coming of the Lord our Saviour. Behold, he says, the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense. And that householder who planted the vineyard sent collectors for the fruit not once but repeatedly: first he sent servants, a second time other servants, and the third time he sent his son.

So John came in the spirit and power of Elijah, for the one cannot exist without the other, as will also be found in what follows, when it is said: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. But perhaps this example may seem beyond us and beyond the apostles. For under Elijah, too, when the river was divided, the flowing back of the river's waters to their source (as scripture said: The Jordan was turned back) signifies the mysteries of the saving bath that were to come, through which those who are baptized are restored from malice, as little children, to the first beginnings of their nature. What of the fact that the Lord himself promised his apostles that the power of the Spirit would be given them, saying: You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you? Then in what follows: Suddenly, it says, there came a sound from heaven, as of the Spirit borne along with great force. "With great force" is well said, because all their power is by the Spirit of his mouth. And that is the power which the apostles obtained from the Holy Spirit.

Rightly, too, will holy John go before the face of the Lord, for he was forerunner in his birth and forerunner in his death. And perhaps this mystery is still celebrated in our life today. For a certain power of John runs ahead into our soul when we are preparing to believe in Christ. It prepares the ways of our soul for faith and makes straight paths for our journey out of the winding track of this life, so that we do not slip on the bends of error. Thus every valley of our soul can be filled with the fruits of virtue, and every height of worldly minds can bow down before the Lord in humbler fear, knowing that nothing frail can be lofty.

And Zechariah said to the angel: How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days. And the angel answered him, saying: I am Gabriel, the angel who stands before the Lord, and I have been sent to announce these things to you. And you will be silent and unable to speak until the day when all these things come to pass, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.

The priest's unbelief is condemned by silence, and the faith of the prophets is approved by an oracle. Cry out, he says. And I said: What shall I cry? All flesh is grass. You see the command of the one who orders, the compliance of the one who obeys, the disposition of the one who asks, the oracle given to the one who obeys. For one who asks what he should cry has believed, and because he believed, he prophesied. But Zechariah, because he did not believe, could not speak, but kept making signs to them and remained mute. The mystery is not one man's alone, nor is the silence one man's alone.

The priest is silent, the prophet is silent. Unless I am mistaken, in one man the voice of the whole people was struck dumb, because in one man, Moses, the whole people used to speak to the Lord. The ceasing of the sacred rites and the silence of the prophets is the muteness of the prophet and the muteness of the priest. I will take away, he says, the mighty power, the prophet and the counsellor. And truly he took away the prophets, from whom he took away the Word that used to speak in the prophets. And truly he took away power from those whom the power of God had left; he took away the counsellor from those whom the Angel of great counsel turned away from; he took away the voice, because the voice belongs to the Word, not the Word to the voice. For unless that Word works in us, there is no sound of a voice. John is the voice, for he is the voice of one crying in the desert; Christ is the Word. This Word works, and so, where it ceased to work, the tongue, as it were the tongue of the soul, suddenly became mute, lacking breath, and fell silent. For the Word of God has passed over to us, and in us it is not silent. Indeed, the Jew can no longer say what the Christian can say: You seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me.

And he kept making signs to them. So Zechariah remained mute and kept making signs to them. What is a sign made by nodding but a bodily action without words, trying to indicate a wish without expressing it, a kind of mute speech of the dying when the voice has been stifled by approaching death? Does not the Jewish people seem to you like him? It is so devoid of reason that it cannot give an account of its actions; set at the final expiry of its living hope, it has lost the voice it had, and by the motion of a faltering body seeks to convey the sign of a word, not the word itself. A mute people, then, without reason, without the Word. For why should one who does not know sound seem to you more mute than one who does not know the mystery? There is certainly a voice of works and a cry of faith, as we read: Your brother's blood cries out to me. And he cries out who cries in his heart by day. So he who has lost the cry of the heart has lost that of the tongue; for how can one who does not keep the clear articulation of faith keep that of words? Moses, too, had said before that he could not speak; but after he spoke, he received the word and displayed the brightness of good works. So, just as Moses was a type of the people and a type of the law, so also Zechariah was silent.

We must therefore consider how each detail corresponds: the Word is in the womb, the law in silence; John is named and Zechariah speaks; the Word is brought forth, the law is set free. But the setting free of the law is the unfolding of the Word, and so he who has uttered the Word speaks, even if he did not speak before. Zechariah is ordered by an angel to be silent; by an angel the voice of the Jews is suppressed. For this is the command not of human but of divine power: that one who has not believed Christ shall not speak to God. And so let us believe, that we may speak; let the Jew believe, that he may be able to speak. Let us speak mysteries in the Spirit; let us understand the meaning of the ancient sacrifices and the riddles of the prophets. He is mute who does not understand the law; he is mute who does not understand the sequence of the divine scriptures; for our voice is faith. And so: In church I would rather speak five words with my mind, to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue; for tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers.
After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and she hid herself for five months, saying: Why has the Lord done this for me in the days when he looked on me to take away my reproach among men?

The saints take great care for modesty, so that there is often shame even in what they pray for. We notice this here in holy Elizabeth, who certainly longed to have children, and yet hid herself for five months. What reason could she have for hiding, except shame? Every duty has its prescribed age. What is fitting at one time is unfitting at another, and a change of age often changes the nature of each act. Marriage itself also has certain prescribed times, when it is seemly to devote oneself to having children: while the years are vigorous, while there is hope of raising children, while begetting is in keeping with common example and intercourse is still eagerly pursued. But when ripe old age has come on, and one's age is better suited to bringing children up than to producing them, it is shameful to carry the signs of intercourse, however lawful, to be weighed down with a burden belonging to another age, and to have one's belly swell with fruit out of its season. The old are shut out by their very age, and a just shame at incontinence calls them back from doing the works of marriage. Even the young generally plead the wish for children, and think that the heat of their age must be excused by the desire for offspring. How much more shameful, then, for the old to do what the young are ashamed to admit! Indeed, even young men who temper their hearts with sobriety through the fear of God often renounce the works of youth once they have had offspring.

And why be surprised at this in human beings, when even beasts declare by a kind of silent action that what they seek is to beget, not the lust of coupling? For once they have felt their womb grow heavy and the seed received into the field of generation, they no longer indulge in mating or in the wantonness of lovers, but take on the care of a parent. Human beings, however, spare neither what they have conceived nor God: they defile the one and provoke the other. "Before I formed you in the womb," he says, "I knew you, and in your mother's womb I sanctified you." To restrain your wantonness, you see, as it were, the hands of your Maker forming a human being in the womb. He is at work, and you pollute the secret place of the sacred womb with lust? Either imitate the beasts or revere God. But why speak of beasts? The earth itself often rests from the work of bearing; and if, through people's impatient greed, it is kept busy with seed sown again and again, it punishes the farmer's shamelessness and turns its fertility into barrenness. So even in the elements and in beasts there is a kind of natural shame at never ceasing from the work of begetting.

Rightly, then, holy Elizabeth blushed at the grace, even though she was conscious of no fault. For though she conceived by her husband—it is not lawful to believe that any human being is born otherwise—she still blushed at bearing a child at her age. And yet she rejoiced that she was rid of reproach; for it is a shame for women not to have the rewards of marriage, since this is their only reason for marrying. So she consoles herself that this reproach has been taken away at the cost of a shame of her own—the shame, as I said, that she felt because of her age. From this it can be understood that they no longer came together in conjugal intercourse; for a woman who did not blush at intercourse in old age would not have blushed at giving birth. And yet she blushes at the burden of motherhood as long as she does not know the mystery of religion.

She who hid herself because she had conceived a son began to glory because she was bearing a prophet; she who had blushed before now blesses, and she who had doubted before is made firm: "For behold," she says, "as soon as the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the infant in my womb leapt for joy." So she cried out with a loud voice when she perceived the Lord's coming, because she believed that her child was a holy birth. For there was no cause for shame once the birth of a prophet confirmed that this offspring had been given, not sought.
BOOK TWO.

"Now at that same time the angel Gabriel was sent by the Lord to a city of Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary." The divine mysteries are indeed hidden, and, as the prophet says, no one can easily know the counsel of God. Yet from the other deeds and precepts of our Lord and Saviour we can understand that this too was a matter of very carefully weighed counsel: that the one chosen above all to bear the Lord was a woman betrothed to a man. But why was she not made pregnant before she was betrothed? Perhaps so that it could not be said that she had conceived in adultery. And Scripture rightly states both things, that she was betrothed and that she was a virgin: a virgin, so that she might be seen to have had no union with a man; betrothed, so that she might not be branded with the disgrace of violated virginity, as a swelling womb would have seemed to display the mark of corruption. The Lord preferred that some should doubt his birth rather than his mother's chastity—for he knew how delicate a virgin's modesty is, and how easily the good name of chastity slips—nor did he think that belief in his birth should be built on injury to his mother. So holy Mary's virginity is preserved, unblemished in chastity and equally inviolate in reputation. For the saints ought to have a good report even from those outside; and it was not fitting that virgins living under an evil reputation should be left the cover of an excuse, on the ground that even the Lord's mother had seemed to be defamed.

And what blame could have been laid on the Jews, or on Herod, if they had seemed to persecute one born of adultery? And how could he himself have said, "I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it," if he had seemed to begin with an offence against the law, since the law condemns childbirth by an unmarried woman? Moreover, the husband is brought in as a weightier witness to her chastity, since he could have both resented the injury and avenged the disgrace, had he not recognized the sacred mystery. What of the fact that Mary's words also gain greater credibility, and every motive for lying is removed? For an unmarried woman who was pregnant would seem to have wanted to cover her fault with a lie. An unbetrothed woman had a motive for lying; a betrothed one had none, since for women childbirth is the reward of wedlock and the grace of marriage.

There is also no slight reason in this: that Mary's virginity should deceive the prince of this world, who, seeing her betrothed to a man, could not suspect the birth. That it was a plan to deceive the prince of this world is shown by the Lord's own words, when the apostles are ordered to keep silent about Christ, when those healed are forbidden to boast of their cure, when the demons are commanded to be silent about the Son of God. That it was a plan, as I said, to deceive the prince of this world, the Apostle too has declared, saying: "But we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which none of the princes of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty"—that is, they would never have brought about my redemption by the Lord's death. So he deceived for our sake; he deceived in order to conquer; he deceived the devil when he was tempted, when he was questioned, when he was called the Son of God, so that he never acknowledged his own divinity. Yet he deceived the prince of this age still more. For although the devil sometimes doubted, as when he said, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down," he nevertheless recognized him, however late, and departed from him. The demons too recognized him, when they said: "We know who you are, Jesus, Son of God. Why have you come before the time to torment us?" And they recognized that he had come because they knew beforehand that he would come. But that the princes of this age did not recognize him, what stronger proof can we give than the Apostle's statement: "For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty"? The malice of demons easily detects even what is hidden; but those who are taken up with the vanities of this age cannot know divine things.

The evangelists divided the task well between them: St Matthew presents Joseph being warned by an angel not to send Mary away, and there the evangelist bears witness that they had not come together; here, in Luke, Mary herself confesses it, when she says to the angel: "How shall this be, since I do not know a man?" St Luke himself also declared her a virgin, saying, "and the virgin's name was Mary." The prophet taught it, saying, "Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb." Joseph indicated it, since he wished to send her away when he saw her pregnant, whom he had not known. And the Lord himself made it plain as he hung on the cross, when he said to his mother, "Woman, behold your son," and then to the disciple, "Behold your mother." Both of them, too, the disciple and the mother, bore witness to it, for from that hour the disciple took her into his own home. Surely, had they come together, she would never have left her own husband, nor would her husband, a just man, have allowed her to depart from him. And how could the Lord have ordered a divorce, when it is his own teaching that no one ought to put away his wife except for the cause of fornication?

St Matthew beautifully taught what a just man ought to do who has discovered his wife's disgrace: he should keep himself unstained by murder and pure from adultery; for he who is joined to a harlot is one body with her. So everywhere in Joseph the grace and character of a just man are preserved, so that the witness may be honoured; for the mouth of the just knows no lie, and his tongue speaks judgment, and his judgment speaks truth. Nor should it trouble you that Scripture often calls her his wife; for what is declared is not the taking of her virginity but the witness to the marriage, the celebration of the wedding. After all, no one sends away a woman he has not taken; and so the man who wished to send her away was acknowledging that he had taken her.

Nor should it trouble you that the evangelist says, "He did not know her until she had borne a son." This is either an idiom of Scripture—as you have elsewhere: "Even until you grow old, I am." Did God cease to be after they grew old? And in the psalm: "The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet." Will he not sit there afterwards?—or else it is because one who pleads a case thinks it enough to say what pertains to the case and does not seek what is superfluous; it is enough for him to establish the case he has taken up and to set aside an incidental one. So the one who had undertaken to prove the incorrupt mystery of the incarnation did not think he should pursue further the evidence for Mary's virginity, lest he be thought a defender of the virgin rather than a herald of the mystery. Certainly, when he showed Joseph to be a just man, he made it clear enough that Joseph could not have violated the temple of the Holy Spirit, the mother of the Lord, the womb of the mystery.

We have learned the course of the truth; we have learned the plan. Let us learn the mystery too. Rightly was she betrothed and yet a virgin, because she is a type of the Church, which is spotless and yet married. A virgin conceived us by the Spirit; a virgin bears us without groaning. And perhaps holy Mary was married to one and filled by another for this reason: that the individual churches too are filled by the Spirit and by grace, yet are joined to the outward form of a priest in time.
"And the angel came in to her and said: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women. But when she saw him, she was troubled at his coming in."

Learn the virgin from her conduct; learn the virgin from her modesty; learn the virgin from the oracle; learn her from the mystery. It is the way of virgins to tremble, to be afraid whenever a man comes in, to be wary whenever a man speaks to them. Let women learn to imitate her resolve of chastity. Alone in the inner rooms, where no man could see her, the angel alone found her; alone without companion, alone without witness, so that she might not be corrupted by any base address, she is greeted by an angel. Learn, virgin, to avoid wantonness in speech: Mary was wary even of an angel's greeting. "Yet she was pondering," it says, "what sort of greeting

this was"—and so with modesty, because she was afraid, and with prudence, because she marvelled at a new form of blessing, one never read anywhere, never heard before. This greeting was reserved for Mary alone; for she alone is rightly called full of grace, who alone obtained a grace that no other woman had deserved: to be filled with the Author of grace. So Mary blushed, and Elizabeth blushed too; and therefore let us recognize the difference between the modesty of a married woman and that of a virgin. The one blushed for a reason; the other out of modesty. In a married woman a measure of modesty is observed; in a virgin the grace of modesty is increased.
"And the angel of the Lord said to her: Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with God. And behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus."

"He will be great." The angel also said of John that he would be great; but John was great as a man, this one is great as God. For great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no end. And John was truly great, for among those born of women there is no greater prophet than John the Baptist. Yet he has one greater than himself, for he who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he. John, then, is great. But John, great before the Lord, drank neither wine nor strong drink, whereas this one eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners. Let John, who had no power by nature, gather merit through abstinence; but Christ, who had by nature the power to forgive sins, why should he avoid those whom he could make better than the abstinent?

At the same time, in a mystical sense, he does not disdain the table of those to whom he is going to give the sacrament. So this one eats and that one fasts, a type of each people: in the one the people fasts, in the other it is fed. But Christ fasted too, so that you would not shirk the precept; and he ate with sinners, so that you might see his grace and recognize his power. John, then, is great too; but his greatness has a beginning and has an end, whereas the Lord Jesus is himself both the end and the beginning, himself the first and the last. Nothing is before the first; nothing beyond the last.

Do not let the pattern of human generation lead you into error, so that you think he is not first because he is a Son. Follow the Scriptures, and you cannot go astray. The Son is called first. We also read that the Father alone "has immortality and dwells in light unapproachable," as you have read: "and to the immortal, the only God." But the Son is not first before the Father, nor is the Father alone without the Son. If you deny one, you assert the other; follow both, and you confirm both. He did not say, "I am earlier and I am later," but, "I am the first and I am the last." The Son is first, and therefore coeternal; for he has a Father with whom he is eternal. I dare to say, "The Son is first, but he is not alone"—and I say it rightly, and I say it devoutly. Why do you prick up your ears for impiety, you heretics? You have fallen into the snares you set. The Son is first and is not alone: first, because he is always with the Father; not alone, because he is never without the Father. It is not I who say this; he himself said: "And I am not alone, for the Father is with me." The Father is alone because there is one God; the Father is alone because the Godhead of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is one alone, and what is one is alone. The Father alone, the Only-begotten alone, the Holy Spirit alone: for the one who is the Son is not also the Father, nor is the one who is the Father also the Son, nor is the one who is the Holy Spirit also the Son. The Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another; for we read: "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate." The Father is alone, because there is one God, from whom are all things; the Son is alone, because there is one Lord, through whom are all things. The Godhead makes him "alone"; generation testifies to both Father and Son, so that the Son is never seen without the Father, nor the Father without the Son. So the Father is not alone, since he is not alone immortal; nor does he alone dwell in unapproachable light, for no one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, who sits at the right hand of the Father. And yet some dare to say that the light in which the Father dwells is unapproachable to him. Is the light, then, greater than the Father? And what light can be unapproachable to one to whom the Father is not unapproachable, who is himself the true light and the begetter of the eternal light, of which it was said: "He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world"? Consider whether that is not the unapproachable light in which the Father dwells and the Son dwells too, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father.

Rightly, then, "great"; for the power of God is poured out far and wide, the greatness of the heavenly substance stretches far and wide. The Trinity has nothing prescribed, nothing circumscribed, nothing measured out, nothing measured off. It is not enclosed by place, not grasped by opinion, not confined by estimation, not altered by age. The Lord Jesus did indeed give greatness to men; for their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world—yet not to the ends of the universe, not to the ends of heaven, not beyond the heavens. But in the Lord Jesus all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, and he is before all, and in him all things hold together. Look at heaven: Jesus is there. Gaze at the earth: Jesus is present. Ascend in word to heaven, descend in word to the underworld: Jesus is present. For if you ascend into heaven, Jesus is there; if you descend into the underworld, he is present. Today, as I speak, he is with me, within this point of time, within this moment; and if a Christian is speaking now in Armenia, Jesus is present; for no one says "Lord Jesus" [?] except in the Holy Spirit. If you penetrate the depths in thought, there too you will see Jesus at work; for it is written: "Do not say in your heart, Who has ascended into heaven? (that is, to bring Christ down), or, Who has descended into the abyss? (that is, to bring Christ back from the dead)." Where, then, is he not, who has filled things heavenly, infernal and earthly? Rightly, then, is he great, whose power has filled the world, who is everywhere and will be for ever, because of his kingdom there will be no end.

"And Mary said to the angel: How shall this be, since I do not know a man?" Here Mary seems not to have believed, unless you pay careful attention; for it is not right that she who was chosen to bear the only-begotten Son of God should seem to have been unbelieving. How could it be—granting that the mother's prerogative is preserved, to whom more deference was certainly due; but as her prerogative was greater, so greater faith too had to be reserved for her—how, I say, could it be that Zechariah, who had not believed, was condemned to silence, while Mary, if she had not believed, was exalted by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit? But Mary ought neither to have disbelieved nor to have presumed so rashly—neither to disbelieve the angel nor to lay hold of divine things. For it was not easy to know the mystery hidden from the ages in God, which not even the higher powers could know. And yet she did not refuse faith, did not decline the task; rather, she adapted her will to it and pledged her obedience. For when she says, "How shall this be?" she did not doubt that it would come about, but asked in what manner it would come about.

How much more measured is this answer than the words of the priest! She says, "How shall this be?" He answered, "How shall I know this?" She is already dealing with the matter itself; he still doubts the message. He who denies that he knows denies that he believes, and seeks, as it were, yet another guarantor for his faith; she professes that she will do it, and does not doubt that what she asks how it can come about is to come about. For so you have it: "How shall this be, since I do not know a man?" A generation so incredible and unheard of had to be heard first in order to be believed. That a virgin should give birth is a sign of a divine mystery, not a human one. And so he says, "Take a sign for yourself: behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son." Mary had read this, and so she believed it would happen; but how it would happen she had not read before, for the manner of it had not been revealed even to so great a prophet. So great a mystery of the command was to be uttered not by the mouth of a man but by that of an angel. Today for the first time it is heard: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you"; and it is heard and believed.

Then she says, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word." See her humility, see her devotion. She calls herself the handmaid of the Lord, she who is chosen to be his mother, and she was not lifted up by the sudden promise. At the same time, by calling herself a handmaid, as one who would do what she was bidden, she claimed for herself no prerogative from so great a grace; for since she was to bear one meek and humble, she too had to show humility. "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word." You have her obedience; you see her desire. For "Behold the handmaid of the Lord"

is readiness for service; "let it be to me according to your word" is the conceiving of a desire. How quickly, then, Mary believed, even in a matter of such unequal elements! For what is so unequal as the Holy Spirit and a body? What so unheard of as a virgin pregnant, against the law, against custom, against modesty, which a virgin holds most dear? Zechariah, however, disbelieved not because of unequal elements but because of old age; for the elements themselves were suited to each other. Birth from a man and a woman is the normal course, and ought not to seem incredible where nature agrees. For since age belongs to nature, and not nature to age, it often happens that age hinders nature; yet it is not unreasonable that the lesser cause should yield to the greater, and that the stronger prerogative of nature should override the limit set by age, the lesser factor. Add to this that Abraham and Sarah had a son in old age, and that Joseph was a son of old age. If Sarah is rebuked because she laughed, he is more justly condemned who believed neither the oracle nor the precedent. But Mary, when she says, "How shall this be, since I do not know a man?" does not seem to have doubted the fact, but to have asked about its manner. For it is clear that she believed it would come about, since she asked how it would come about. Hence she also deserved to hear: "Blessed are you who believed." And truly blessed, for she surpassed the priest. When the priest had refused to believe, the virgin corrected the error. Nor is it surprising that the Lord, when he was about to redeem the world, began his work with Mary, so that she through whom salvation was being prepared for all should be the first to draw the fruit of salvation from her own child.

And she was right to ask how it would come about; for she had read that a virgin would give birth, but she had not read how a virgin would give birth. She had read, as I said, "Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb"; but how she would conceive the angel first declared in the Gospel.
"And Mary arose in those days and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah, and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth."

It is natural for everyone that those who ask for faith should give grounds for it. So when the angel announced hidden things, he gave an example to support faith: he announced to the Virgin Mary that an elderly and barren woman had conceived, to show that God can do whatever pleases him. When Mary heard this, she set out into the hill country. She did not go as one who disbelieved the oracle, or was unsure of the message, or doubted the example. She went joyful in her desire, devout in her duty, and hurrying for joy. For where would she, already full of God, hasten but to the heights?
