The grace of the Holy Spirit knows nothing of slow efforts.

You too, holy women, should learn the care you ought to show to kinswomen who are with child. Before this, Mary had stayed alone in the innermost rooms of the house. Yet virginal modesty did not keep her from going out in public, the roughness of the mountains did not hold back her eagerness, and the length of the journey did not stop her from her duty. The virgin went with haste into the hill country. Mindful of her duty and heedless of hardship, strong in affection and not held back by her sex, she left her home and set out.

Learn, virgins, not to run around other people's houses, not to linger in the streets, and not to strike up conversations in public. Mary was slow to leave home and quick when out in public. She stayed with her kinswoman for three months. She had come for the sake of duty, and she held to that duty. She stayed three months, not because someone else's house delighted her, but because she did not like to be seen often in public.

You have learned Mary's modesty, virgins; now learn her humility. The kinswoman came to her relative, the younger to the elder. She not only came but also greeted her first, for the more chaste a virgin is, the more humble she ought to be. Let her know how to defer to her elders. Let her who professes chastity be a teacher of humility. Here there is a reason of devotion and also a rule of doctrine. For we must observe that the superior comes to the inferior so that the inferior may be helped: Mary came to Elizabeth, Christ to John. Later, too, the Lord came to baptism in order to sanctify John's baptism. The benefits of Mary's coming and of the Lord's presence are also shown at once: as soon as Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting, the infant leaped in her womb, and she was filled with the Holy Spirit.

See the distinction, and the exact force of each word. Elizabeth heard the voice first, but John felt the grace first. She heard in the order of nature; he leaped because of the mystery. She sensed the coming of Mary, he the coming of the Lord: the woman sensed the woman, and the child the child. The women speak of the grace; the children work within, taking up the mystery of devotion for their mothers' benefit. So by a double miracle the mothers prophesy by the spirit of their little ones. The infant leaped, and the mother was filled. The mother was not filled before the son. Rather, when the son had been filled with the Holy Spirit, he filled his mother too. John leaped, and Mary's spirit also leaped. When John leaped, Elizabeth was filled. Yet we know that Mary was not filled with the Spirit; rather, her spirit leaped, for the Incomprehensible was working incomprehensibly in the mother. And the one is filled after conceiving, the other before.
Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?

The Holy Spirit knows his own words and never forgets them. Prophecy is fulfilled not only by the wonders of events but also by the exactness of its words. Who is this fruit but the one of whom it was said: "Behold, sons are the inheritance of the Lord, the fruit of the womb is the reward"? That is, the sons are the inheritance of the Lord, and they are the reward of that fruit which came forth from Mary's womb. He is the fruit of the womb and the flower of the root. Isaiah prophesied well of him, saying: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from the root." For the root is the family of the Jews, the rod is Mary, and the flower of Mary is Christ. Like the fruit of a good tree, he grows in us as our virtue advances: now he flowers, now he bears fruit in us, now he is renewed by the resurrection that brings the body back to life. "And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?"

She does not say this as if she did not know. She knows that it is the grace and work of the Holy Spirit that the mother of the prophet should be greeted by the mother of the Lord for her child's benefit. Rather, she says it because she recognizes that this is a gift of divine grace and not a reward for human merit: "Why is this granted to me?" That is: "What great good has come to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? I find no merit of mine in it. Why is this granted to me? By what righteousness, by what deeds, for what merits? These are not the usual courtesies between women, that the mother of my Lord should come to me. I sense a miracle. I recognize a mystery: the mother of the Lord is pregnant with the Word and full of God."
For behold, as soon as the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy.

"And blessed are you who believed." You see that Mary did not doubt. She believed, and so she obtained the fruit of faith. "Blessed," she says, "are you who believed." But you too are blessed, who have heard and believed. For every soul that believes both conceives and brings forth the Word of God and recognizes his works. Let the soul of Mary be in each of you, to magnify the Lord; let the spirit of Mary be in each of you, to rejoice in God. According to the flesh Christ has one mother, but according to faith Christ is the fruit of all. For every soul receives the Word of God, provided that it is spotless and free from vices and keeps its chastity with unblemished modesty.

So any soul that has been able to become such magnifies the Lord, just as Mary's soul magnified the Lord and her spirit rejoiced in God her Savior. For the Lord is magnified, as you have also read elsewhere: "Magnify the Lord with me." This is not because the human voice can add anything to the Lord, but because he is magnified in us. For Christ is the image of God. So if the soul does anything just and devout, it magnifies that image of God in whose likeness it was created. And while it magnifies that image, it is itself raised higher by a kind of share in its greatness, so that it seems to reproduce that image in itself through the bright colors of good deeds and through imitating its virtue. Mary's soul magnifies the Lord and her spirit rejoices in God because, devoted in soul and spirit to the Father and the Son, she worships with loving devotion one God, from whom are all things, and one Lord, through whom are all things.

Mary's prophecy follows, and the better the person, the fuller the prophecy. Nor does it seem to be without purpose that Elizabeth prophesies before John's birth and Mary before the Lord's birth. For the first beginnings of human salvation are already spreading. Sin began with women, and so good things also begin with women. In this way women, too, may put aside womanly ways and renounce weakness. The soul, which has no sex, may then imitate the chastity of Mary, who knows no error, with devout zeal.

"And Mary stayed with her three months and returned to her home." Holy Mary is fittingly shown both to have done her duty and to have kept a mystical number. For she did not stay so long only because they were family, but also for the benefit of so great a prophet. At her first arrival there was such progress that the infant leaped in the womb at Mary's greeting, and the infant's mother was filled with the Holy Spirit. How much, then, do we think holy Mary's presence added over so long a time? "And Mary stayed with her three months." So the prophet was anointed and trained in his mother's womb like a good athlete, for his strength was being prepared for a very great contest. Mary stayed just as long as it took Elizabeth to complete her time for giving birth. If you look carefully, you will find this expression used nowhere except at the births of the righteous. Thus the days were fulfilled for Mary to give birth; the time was fulfilled for Elizabeth to give birth; the time of life was fulfilled when holy men departed from the course of this life. The life of the righteous has fullness, but the days of the wicked are empty.

So Elizabeth gave birth to a son, and her neighbors rejoiced with her. The birth of the saints brings joy to many, because it is a common good; for righteousness is a virtue shared by all. So at the birth of a righteous man a sign of his future life is given in advance. The grace of virtue that will follow is marked out and foreshadowed by the rejoicing of the neighbors. The time the prophet spent in the womb is fittingly described, so that Mary's presence would not go unmentioned. But the time of his infancy is passed over in silence, because he was strengthened in his mother's womb by the presence of the Lord, and so he knew none of the hindrances of infancy. That is why in the Gospel we read nothing about him except his birth and the oracle, his leaping in the womb, and his voice in the wilderness. For he passed through no stage of infancy. While still in his mother's womb, beyond nature and beyond his age, he began from the measure of the full stature of the fullness of Christ.

"And his mother answered and said: No, but he shall be called John. And they said to her: There is no one among your kindred who is called by this name. So they made signs to his father to ask what he wanted him to be called. And he took a writing tablet and wrote, saying: His name is John. And they all marveled. And at once his tongue was loosed and his mouth was opened, and he spoke, blessing God." It was an admirable choice of the holy

evangelist to note first that many thought the infant should be called by his father's name, Zacharias. This shows you that the mother did not reject the name as unworthy. Rather, the Holy Spirit had poured into her what the angel had earlier foretold to Zacharias. Since Zacharias was mute, he could not tell his wife their son's name, but Elizabeth learned by prophecy what she had not learned from her husband. "His name is John," she says. That is: "We are not giving a name to one who has already received a name from God. He has his own name, which we have recognized, not one we have chosen." The saints have this privilege by their merits, that they receive their name from God. So Jacob is called Israel because he saw God. So our Lord Jesus was named before he was born, and it was not an angel but the Father who gave him his name. For he says: "My son Jesus shall be revealed with those who shall rejoice with him, who have been left, for four hundred years. And after these years my son Christ shall die, and the world shall be turned back." You see that angels announce what they have heard, not what they have taken upon themselves. Nor should you wonder that a woman declared a name she had not heard, since the Holy Spirit, who had given the angel his message, revealed it to her. Nor could she who had prophesied Christ fail to know the Lord's forerunner.

The evangelist rightly adds that no one in her kindred was called by this name. This lets you understand that the name belonged to the prophet, not to the family. Zacharias, too, is asked by signs. Unbelief had taken away his speech and his hearing, so what he could not say with his voice he said with his hand and with letters. For he wrote, saying: "His name is John." Here, too, the name is not given but confirmed. And rightly his tongue was loosed at once, because faith untied what unbelief had bound. Let us also believe, then, so that we may speak, and so that our tongue, bound by the chains of unbelief, may be loosed by the voice of reason. Let us write mysteries by the Spirit if we wish to speak. Let us write the forerunner of Christ not on tablets of stone but on the fleshly tablets of the heart. For whoever speaks John prophesies Christ. Let us speak John, and let us speak Christ too, so that our mouth also may be opened. In so great a priest, the reins of wavering faith held that mouth in check, as if he were a beast without reason.

"And Zacharias his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying." See how good God is and how ready to forgive sins. He not only restores what was taken away but also grants what was not hoped for. The man who was mute until recently now prophesies. For this is God's greatest grace: that those who had denied him confess him. So let no one lose confidence. Let no one who is aware of past sins despair of God's rewards. God knows how to change his sentence, if you know how to correct your sin. "And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High."

He did well, while prophesying about the Lord, to turn his words to the prophet. In this way he showed that this too was a gift of the Lord. Otherwise, while publicly listing the Lord's gifts, he might seem ungrateful for keeping silent about the gifts he had received and recognized in his son. But perhaps some may think it an irrational lapse of mind that he speaks to an eight-day-old infant. But if we hold [?], we surely understand that the child, once born, could hear his father's voice, since he heard Mary's greeting before he was born. The prophet knew that a prophet has other ears, opened by the Spirit of God and not by bodily age. The child who had the feeling to leap for joy had the sense to understand.

Notice also how briefly Elizabeth prophesies and how fully Zacharias does. Both spoke filled with the Holy Spirit, but order is kept, so that a woman should be more eager to learn divine things than to teach them. Nor do we easily find any woman who prophesied more fully than the mother of the Lord. Even Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, ended the words of her song very quickly. And when she spoke at greater length together with her brother, she did not escape punishment for her words.
Now it came to pass in those days that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered in a census.

Since we are about to speak of the Saviour's birth, we do not think it out of place to ask at what time he was born. For what has a secular registration to do with the Lord's birth, unless we are to notice that here too there is a divine mystery? While a secular registration is put forward, a spiritual one is carried out, made not to the king of the earth but to the King of heaven. This registration is one of faith, a census of souls. For the old census of the synagogue was abolished, and a new census of the Church was being prepared, one that would not exact torments but take them away, and that already, spiritually and in the figure of the people, was entering its names to Christ. Here it is not tracts of land that are assessed but minds and souls; boundaries are not recorded but extended; no age is set apart, but every age is enrolled. No one is exempt from this census, for every age brings its gift to Christ: crying infants confess him by martyrdom, and children still in the womb bear witness to him by leaping for joy. Fear nothing harsh in this census, nothing cruel, nothing grim; faith alone sets its seal on each person. Do you want to hear Christ's census-takers? They are commanded to make their count without rods, to seek out the people not by terror but by grace, to put away the sword and to possess no gold. By such census-takers the world was won.

So that you may know, then, that the census was not Augustus's but Christ's, the whole world is ordered to register. When Christ is born, all register; when the world is shut in, all are in danger. Who, then, could demand the registration of the whole world except the one who held dominion over the whole world? For the earth and its fullness belong not to Augustus but to the Lord, the world and all who dwell in it. Augustus did not rule the Goths, he did not rule the Armenians; Christ ruled them. Certainly those who produced martyrs for Christ received Christ's census-taker. And perhaps that is why they are defeating us, as present events show: because the one whom they confessed by offering their blood, the Arians made the subject of a dispute about his origin.

"This," it says, "was the first registration." Yet histories tell us that many parts of the earth had often been registered before. This, then, is the first registration not of nations but of minds, in which all register because no one is left out; they are summoned not by a herald's voice but by a prophet's, who foretold long before: "Clap your hands, all you nations; shout to God with a voice of joy, for God Most High is awesome, a great king over all the earth." Then, so that you may know it is a census of righteousness, Joseph and Mary come to it, that is, the righteous man and the virgin: he who was to keep the Word, she who was to bear him. Where do the righteous man and the virgin register, if not where Christ is born? For "every spirit that confesses that [?] Christ has come in the flesh is from God." And in a deeper sense, where is Christ born if not in your heart and in your breast? For "the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart."

It is fitting, too, that he added the governor's name, in order to mark the sequence [?] of time. "This first registration," he says, "took place when Quirinius was governor of Syria," so that the evangelist seems to have written in a sort of consul for this book by way of a date. For if consuls are written into deeds of purchase, how much more ought the time to be written into the redemption of all! So you have everything customary in contracts: the name of the one holding supreme power there, the day, the place, the cause. Witnesses too are usually called; and these Christ also called to his birth and his generation according to the flesh, to seal the gospel, when he said: "You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem." "And it came to pass that while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn."

Saint Luke has briefly set out how, when, and where Christ was born according to the flesh. But if you ask about his heavenly generation, read the Gospel of Saint John, who began from heavenly things and came down to earthly ones. There you will find when he was, how he was, and what he was, what he had done, what he was doing, and where he was; where he came, how he came, at what time he came, and why he came. "In the beginning," he says, "was the Word": there you have when he was. "And the Word was with God": there you have how he was. You have also what he was: "And the Word," he says, "was God"; what he had done: "All things were made through him"; what he was doing: "He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world"; and where he was: "He was in this world"; where he came: "He came to his own"; how he came: "The Word became flesh." As for when he came, John bears witness about him, saying: "This is the one of whom I said, He who comes after me has been set before me, because he was before me." Why he came, John himself testifies: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world." If, then, we have come to know both generations, and have grasped the office of each and the reason for which he came, namely that by taking on himself the sins of a perishing world he, who could not be conquered, might abolish in himself the stain of sin and the death of all, it follows that now Saint Luke the evangelist should also teach us and show us the ways of the Lord as he grew according to the flesh.

No one should be troubled that we said John's infancy was passed over by a deeper design, while we maintain that Christ's infancy has been described. For it is not everyone who can say: "To the weak I became weak, to win the weak; I have become all things to all." Nor can it be said of anyone else that "he was wounded for our iniquity and made weak for our sins." So he was a little one, he was an infant, so that you could become a perfect man; he was wrapped in swaddling clothes, so that you might be freed from the snares of death; he was in a manger, so that you might be at the altars; he was on earth, so that you might be among the stars; he had no other place in that inn, so that you might have many mansions in heaven. "Though he was rich," it says, "he became poor for your sake, so that by his poverty you might become rich." That poverty, then, is my inheritance, and the Lord's weakness is my strength. He chose to be in need himself so that all might have abundance. The tears of that crying infancy wash me clean; those tears have washed away my sins. So, Lord Jesus, I owe more to your sufferings, by which I was redeemed, than to your works, by which I was created. It would have been no gain to be born, had it not been a gain to be redeemed.

But let no one confine the whole form of the Godhead within the condition of the body. The nature of the flesh is one thing; the glory of the Godhead is another. For your sake there was weakness; in himself, power. For your sake, poverty; in himself, riches. Do not judge by what you see, but recognize that you are redeemed. You see that he is in swaddling clothes; you do not see that he is in heaven. You hear the infant's cries; you do not hear the lowing of the ox that recognizes its Lord. For "the ox knew its owner, and the donkey its master's manger" (or rather, I should say, "crib," as the translator wrote; for to me a difference of word matters nothing where there is no difference of sense). For if their orator, speaking of those who chase the trappings of speech, denies that the fortunes of Greece depend on whether he used this word or that, and holds that it is the matter that must be considered; if their very philosophers, who spend whole days in disputation, used Latin and accepted words less than terms of their own; how much more ought we to disregard words and look to the mysteries, in which plainness of speech wins out, because the miracles of the divine works, adorned with no fine speech, shone with the light of their own truth? Indeed, the holy mangers fed that rational donkey not with the gloss of dainties but with the sap of natural nourishment.

This is the Lord, this the manger, by which a divine mystery was revealed to us: that the Gentiles, living without reason like cattle at their mangers, were to be fed with the abundance of sacred nourishment. So the donkey, which is the figure and type of the Gentiles, recognized its master's manger. And so it says: "The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing." Is he proved God by slight signs, that angels serve him, that magi worship him, that martyrs confess him? He comes forth from a womb, but he shines from heaven; he lies in an earthly inn, but he is alive with heavenly light. A wife gave birth, but a virgin conceived; a wife conceived, but a virgin brought forth. For Saint Matthew taught us no small mystery, which Saint Luke thought he should pass over in silence because it had already been fully set out, believing he would be rich enough if, out of everything, he claimed for himself the Lord's manger.

This little one, then, whom you in your unbelief regard as worthless, the magi coming from the East followed over so great a distance; falling down, they worship him, call him king, and confess that he will rise again, offering from their treasures gold, frankincense, and myrrh. What are these gifts of true faith? Gold for a king, incense for God, myrrh for one who has died. For the one is the emblem of a king, the other the sacrifice due to divine power, the third the honor of burial, which does not corrupt the body of the dead but preserves it. Let us also, brothers, who hear and read these things, bring out such gifts from our own treasures; for "we have a treasure in earthen vessels." If, then, even in yourself you ought to judge what you are not from yourself but from Christ, how much more in Christ ought you to consider not what is yours but what is Christ's!

So the magi offer gifts from their treasures. Do you want to know how good their merit is? The star is seen by them, and where Herod is, it is not seen; where Christ is, it is seen again and shows the way. So this star is the way, and the way is Christ, because according to the mystery of the incarnation Christ is the star; for "a star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise up out of Israel." Indeed, where Christ is, there the star is too; for he himself is "the bright morning star." So he marks himself out by his own light.

Take another proof. The magi came by one way and return by another; for having seen Christ and understood Christ, they certainly go back better than they came. There are two ways: one that leads to destruction, the other that leads to the kingdom. The one is the way of sinners, which leads to Herod; the other way is Christ, by which we return to our homeland. For here our stay is only temporary, as it is written: "My soul has long been a sojourner." Let us therefore beware of Herod, who holds worldly power for a time, so that we may obtain an eternal dwelling in the heavenly homeland.

These rewards are offered not only to the chosen but to all, since "Christ is all and in all." For you see that it was not without purpose that Abraham, from among the Chaldeans, who are reckoned most skilled in numbers, believed God, or that the magi, though they devote their efforts to winning the favor of the divine by magical arts, believed in the Lord's birth on earth. Not without purpose, I say, but so that testimony to the holy religion and an example of the fear of God might be drawn from the hostile nations.

Yet who are these magi, if not those who, as a certain history teaches, are descended from Balaam, by whom it was prophesied: "A star shall rise out of Jacob"? These, then, are heirs no less of his faith than of his line. He saw the star in the spirit; they saw it with their eyes and believed. They had seen a new star that had not been seen since the creation of the world; they had seen a new creation, and they sought the grace of the new man not only on earth but also in heaven, according to what Moses set down prophetically: "A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise up out of Israel." And they recognized that this was the star that signifies one who is man and God. They worshiped the little child; certainly they would not have worshiped him if they had believed him to be only a little child. So the magus understands that his arts are coming to an end, and do you not understand that your gifts have come? He confesses one who is not his own, and do you not recognize the one promised to you? He believes against his own interest, and do you not think you should believe for your own sake?

So the magi announce that a king has been born. Herod is troubled; he gathers the scribes and chief priests and asks where the Christ is to be born. The magi announce only a king; Herod asks about the Christ; so he confesses that the very king he asks about is the Christ. Then, when he asks where he was to be born, it is plainly shown that he had been foretold; for no one could have been sought who had not been announced. O senseless Jews, you do not believe that he has come whom you see; you do not believe that he has come whom you say is to come! "Report to me," he says, "so that I may come and worship him." Herod is indeed plotting, yet he does not deny God, since he speaks of him as one to be worshiped. Then he orders the infants to be killed. To whom else but God was such a victim owed? Infancy, though lacking understanding, nonetheless confesses the God for whom it is slain. We have touched on these few things from Matthew so that it might be clear that the time of his infancy was by no means empty of the works of the Godhead. And if the age of the flesh was incapable of action, it was surely God who exercised that age of the flesh in works of divinity, who also made the shepherds in that region keep watch, guarding their flock through the watches of the night.

See the beginning of the rising Church: Christ is born, and the shepherds began to keep watch, so as to gather into the Lord's fold the flocks of the Gentiles, who had lived like cattle before, lest they suffer any attacks from spiritual beasts amid the darkness spread by the night. And well do the shepherds keep watch, for the Good Shepherd forms them. The flock, then, is the people; the night, the world; the shepherds are the priests. Or perhaps he too may be a shepherd to whom it is said: "Be watchful and strengthen," because the Lord appointed not only bishops to guard the flock but also assigned angels. "Behold, an angel of the Lord stood before them."

See how divine care builds up faith. An angel instructs Mary, an angel Joseph, an angel the shepherds. It is not enough for one to be sent once; for "on the word of two or three witnesses every word stands." "And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will."

Rightly is the company of angels called a host, for they were following the commander of their army. To whom, then, would the angels give praise if not to their Lord, as it is written: "Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels"? So the prophecy was fulfilled. The Lord is praised from the heavens and seen on earth, of whom Saint Mark says that "he was with the wild beasts, and the angels ministered to him," so that in the one you may recognize the mark of his mercy, in the other the sign of his divine power. That he endures wild beasts is for your sake; that he is proclaimed by angels is his own. "And they said: Let us see this word that has come to pass, as the Lord has shown us. And they came in haste."

You see the shepherds hurrying; for no one seeks Christ sluggishly. You see that the shepherds believed the angel; you too believe the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, the angels, the prophets, the apostles. See how precisely Scripture weighs the force of each word. "They hurry," it says, "to see the word." For when the Lord's flesh is seen, the Word is seen, who is the Son. Do not think this a small example of faith, or the shepherds persons of little worth. Surely the less they are worth in learning, the more precious they are in faith. The Lord did not seek out schools crowded with bands of the wise, but simple common folk, who did not know how to dress up or embellish what they had heard; for simplicity is what is sought, not ambition. Nor should you think the shepherds' words to be despised as worthless. From the shepherds even Mary gathers faith; by the shepherds the people are gathered to reverence for God; for "they wondered at the things told them by the shepherds."

"But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Let us learn the holy Virgin's chastity in all things: she, modest no less in speech than in body, pondered the proofs of faith in her heart. If Mary learns from shepherds, why do you refuse to learn from priests? If Mary keeps silent before the apostolic precepts, why do you, after the apostolic precepts, desire to teach rather than to learn? Learn that the fault lies in the person, not in the sex; for the sex is holy. Indeed, Mary did not receive a precept; she gave an example.

So the child is circumcised. Who is that child, if not the one of whom it was said: "A child is born to us, a son is given to us"? For he was made under the law, so that he might win those who were under the law.

I would explain what it means to be presented to the Lord in Jerusalem, had I not already done so in my commentary on Isaiah; for one circumcised from vices was judged worthy of the Lord's gaze, because "the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous." You see that the whole sequence of the old law was a figure of what was to come (for circumcision too signifies the cleansing of sins). But because the frailty of human flesh and mind, through an inclination and desire to sin, is entangled in inextricable vices, the future cleansing of all guilt was prefigured by the eighth day of circumcision, in the age of the resurrection. For this is the meaning of: "Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord"; for in the words of the law the virgin birth was being promised. And he is truly holy, because he is spotless. Indeed, the words repeated by the angel in the same way declare that it is he who is marked out by the law: "for that which shall be born," he says, "shall be called holy, the Son of God." For no intercourse with a man opened the hidden places of the virgin womb, but the Holy Spirit poured spotless seed into an inviolate womb. For of all born of woman the Lord Jesus alone is holy in every respect, who by the newness of his spotless birth did not feel the contagion of earthly corruption and by his heavenly majesty drove it away.

For if we follow the letter, how is every male holy, when it is well known that many have been most wicked? Was Ahab holy? Were the false prophets holy, whom fire, avenging the insult to heaven, consumed at Elijah's prayers? But he is the holy one whom the devout precepts of the divine law marked out as the figure of the mystery to come, because he alone was to open the hidden womb of the holy Church, the virgin, with spotless fruitfulness, to bring forth the peoples of God. He alone, then, opened the womb for himself. Nor is this surprising; for he who had said to the prophet, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and in your mother's womb I sanctified you"—he, then, who sanctified another's womb so that a prophet might be born, is the one who opened his own mother's womb so that he might come forth spotless.

"And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel." The Lord's birth receives testimony not only from angels and prophets, from shepherds and parents, but also from elders and the righteous. Every age and both sexes, and wondrous events, build up faith: a virgin conceives, a barren woman gives birth, a mute man speaks, Elizabeth prophesies, a magus worships, one shut in the womb leaps for joy, a widow confesses, a righteous man waits. And rightly righteous, for he sought not his own favor but the people's: he himself longed to be freed from the chains of bodily frailty, but waited to see what was promised; for he knew that "blessed are the eyes" that would see.

"Now," he says, "let your servant depart." See the righteous man, shut up as it were in the prison of his bodily frame, wishing to be released so that he may begin to be with Christ; for "to depart and be with Christ is far better." But whoever wishes to be released, let him come into the temple, let him come into Jerusalem, let him wait for the Lord's Christ, let him take the Word of God into his hands and embrace him with the arms, as it were, of his faith. Then he will be released, so that he who has seen life will not see death.

You see that the Lord's grace was poured out abundantly on all at his birth, and that prophecy was denied to unbelievers, not to the righteous. Behold, Simeon too prophesies that the Lord Jesus Christ has come for the fall and rising of many, to distinguish the deserts of the righteous and the wicked, and, as a true and just judge, to decree punishments or rewards according to the character of our deeds.

"And a sword," he says, "will pierce your own soul too." Neither the letter nor history teaches that Mary departed this life by suffering bodily death; for it is not the soul but the body that is pierced by a material sword. And so it shows Mary's wisdom, by no means ignorant of the heavenly mystery. For "the word of God is living and powerful and sharper than any sharpest sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow"; it searches out the thoughts of the heart and the secrets of souls, because all the things of the mind lie naked and open to the Son, whom the secrets of the conscience do not deceive.

So Simeon prophesied; a married woman had prophesied, a virgin had prophesied; a widow ought to prophesy as well, so that no state of life and neither sex would be lacking. And so Anna is introduced, such in the years of her widowhood and in her character that she may well be believed worthy to announce that the Redeemer of all had come. Since we have described her merits elsewhere, when we were exhorting widows, we do not think they need repeating here, as we are hastening on to other things. Yet it was not without purpose that he stated the eighty-four years of her widowhood, for seven twelves and two forties seem to signify a sacred number.

"And when he was twelve years old." From his twelfth year, as we read, the beginning of the Lord's teaching is taken; for this was the number owed to those who would preach the gospel and proclaim the faith. And not without purpose does he, who according to the flesh was being filled with the wisdom and grace of God, become forgetful of his parents according to the flesh and is found in the temple after three days, as a sign that after three days of his triumphant passion he who was believed dead would rise again and present himself to our faith on the heavenly throne and in divine honor.

"Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" There are two births in Christ: one from the Father, the other from his mother. The one from the Father is the more divine; the one from his mother is the one that comes down into our toil and our needs. So the things that happen beyond nature, beyond his age, beyond what is usual should not be credited to human abilities but referred to divine powers. Elsewhere his mother urges him on to a mystery; here his mother is rebuked, because she still asks for what is human. But since here he is described as twelve years old, and there he is shown already having disciples, you see that his mother had learned from her son, so that she asked for a mystery from him when he was grown, she who had marvelled at a miracle when he was younger.

"And he came to Nazareth and was subject to them." For what should the teacher of virtue do but fulfil the duty of filial devotion? And are we surprised that he defers to the Father, when he submits to his mother? This submission certainly comes not from weakness but from devotion, however much the serpent of faithlessness, sent out from its dark lairs, may raise its head and spew poison from its snake's breast. When the Son says that he was sent, the heretic calls the Father greater, so as to call the Son imperfect, since he can have someone greater, and so as to claim that one who is sent needs the help of another. Did he also need human help, then, that he served under his mother's authority? He deferred to a human being, he deferred to a handmaid (for she herself says, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord"), he deferred to one who only seemed to be his father: and are you surprised that he deferred to God? Or is it devotion to defer to a human being, but weakness to defer to God? At least judge divine things by human ones, and recognize what love is owed to a father. The Father honours the Son: do you not want the Son to honour the Father? The Father declares with a voice from heaven that he is well pleased in the Son: do you not want the Son, clothed in the garment of human flesh, speaking with a human voice and with human feeling, to say that the Father is greater? For if "great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no end," then surely a greatness that has no end can have no increase either. So why should I not accept with reverent ears that the Son obeyed the Father in taking a body, when I reverently accept that the Father defers to the Son?

Learn rather the precepts that are for your own good, and recognize the examples of filial devotion. Learn what you owe your parents, when you read that the Son does not differ from the Father in will, in work, or in time. Although they are two in persons, they are one in power, and that heavenly Father certainly went through no labour in begetting. But you owe your mother the wound to her modesty, the loss of her virginity, the danger of childbirth; you owe your mother long months of sickness, long months of peril. For her, poor woman, the danger is greatest at the very moment her prayers bear fruit, and when she has brought forth what she longed for, she is released from labour but not from fear. Why should I speak of the years fathers spend on their children's advancement, of fortunes multiplied for others to use, of seed sown by the farmer to benefit generations to come? Should not at least obedience be given back in return for these? Why should an undutiful son find his father's life too long, and a shared inheritance too small, when Christ does not shrink from having co-heirs?

"The word of God came upon John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness." The Son of God, about to gather the Church, first works in his humble servant. So Saint Luke rightly wrote that the word of God came upon John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness, so that the Church would begin not from a man but from the Word. For she herself is the wilderness, because "the children of the desolate are more than those of her who has a husband." Accordingly it is said to her, "Rejoice, you barren one," and, "Exult, O wilderness," because she was not yet cultivated by any works of a people newly come, and those trees that could bear fruit did not yet show any crown of their merits. Not yet had he come who would say, "But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord"; not yet was that heavenly vine supplying fruit to its branches through a kind of grafting of its words. So the word came, so that the land that had been a wilderness might produce fruit for us; the word came, and the voice followed. For the word works first within, and the service of the voice follows. That is why David also says, "I believed, and therefore I have spoken."

He believed first, so that he could speak. And the word came so that the holy Baptist John might preach repentance. That is why many take Saint John as a type of the law, because the law could denounce sin but could not forgive it. For the law calls back from error everyone who was following the way of the Gentiles, holds him back from crime, and urges him to repent so that he may obtain grace. "The law and the prophets were until John," but John was the forerunner of Christ. So the law is the forerunner of the Church, and repentance the forerunner of grace. Saint Luke, then, did well to be brief, declaring John a prophet by saying that the word of God came upon him. He had no need to add anything else, for no one who abounds in the word of God needs anything more to point him out. So he said one thing and made everything plain.

Saint Matthew and Mark, however, chose to show that he was a prophet by his clothing, his belt and his food, saying that he had a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and that he ate locusts and wild honey. For the forerunner of Christ would not let the hides of unclean beasts go to waste, and by the very sign of his clothing he indicated that Christ would come, who would take upon himself the sins of the unclean Gentiles, woven together out of beastliness and filth because of the ugliness of our deserts, and on that trophy of the cross would strip off the garment, as it were, of our flesh.

And what does the girding with a leather belt mean, except that this flesh, which used to weigh down the mind, after the Lord's coming began to be not a hindrance but a girdle? For, as David says, "we have hung our instruments on the willows," and, as the Apostle says, we have no confidence in the flesh, yet we have confidence in the body: not in pleasures, but in sufferings. So affection, fervent in spirit, grows strong, and we are girded for every act of obedience to the heavenly commandments, intent with devotion of mind and unencumbered in the readiness of the body.

His food too points to his prophetic office and announces a mystery. For what could be more pointless as an ordinary human occupation than hunting for locusts, and what could be fuller of meaning as a prophet's mystery? For the more useless locusts are for producing fruit, the more worthless for any use, the harder to catch, the more erratic in their leaping and the shriller in their noise, the more fittingly they serve as a figure of the Gentile people, who, with no useful labour and no fruit of their work, without weight and without a voice, uttered only the sound of complaint and did not know the word of life. This people, then, is the food of the prophets; for the more numerous the people that is gathered, the more abundant the use of the prophetic mouth becomes. The grace of the Church is also prefigured in the wild honey, which was not found within the hive of the law as the offspring of the Jewish people, but was scattered through the fields and leaves of the forest of the Gentiles' wandering, as it is written: "We found it in the fields of the forest."

And he ate wild honey, announcing that the peoples would be filled with honey from the rock, as it is written: "And with honey from the rock he satisfied them." So too the ravens fed Elijah in the wilderness with food brought from elsewhere and with drink they had procured, as a sign that the peoples of the nations, filthy with the foul colour of their deserts, who once sought their food among stinking corpses, would now supply the prophets from their own resources with nourishment brought from outside. For the food of the prophets is the accomplishing of God's will, as the Lord himself declared when he said, "My food is to do the will of him who sent me."

"The voice of one crying in the wilderness." John, the forerunner of the Word, is rightly called a voice. For John himself, when asked, "What do you say about yourself?" replied, "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness." That is why he says, "He who comes after me has been placed before me": because the voice, which is lesser, goes first, and the Word, which is greater, follows. That is also why he chose to be baptized by John, because among human beings the word is consecrated by the voice of a teacher. And perhaps that is why Zechariah got his voice back, because he spoke out the Voice.

Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruits, then, worthy of repentance, and do not begin to say, "Abraham is our father." For I tell you that God is able from these stones

…to raise up children to Abraham," the malice of the Jews does seem to be rebuked. Spotted with the venom of a harmful mind, they work at the gliding of serpents and at earthly lairs, and not at any mystery of divine knowledge. Yet when it is said, "Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" it is shown that by God's mercy a certain prudence has been poured into them, so that they do penance for their sins and fear the terror of the coming judgment with a far-sighted devotion. The comparison to vipers, then, refers to the present generation, not to their line of descent. Or perhaps, in keeping with what is written, "Be wise as serpents," they are shown to have a natural prudence: they see what will profit them and ask for it of their own accord, but they do not yet give up what is harmful.

And so they are warned to claim for themselves the distinction of good works rather than the nobility of birth, since descent gives no privilege unless an inheritance of faith goes with it. By God's will that inheritance was to pass to the Gentile peoples, and he revealed this in prophetic words, saying: "God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham." God can indeed change and transform different natures; yet since the mystery profits me more than the miracle, in the words of Christ's forerunner I ought to recognize nothing so much as the building of the rising Church. It is built not of rough rock but of living stones, and it has risen into a dwelling place for God and into the pinnacle of a temple through the conversion of our souls. For God was preparing to soften the hardness of our minds and to raise up worshippers of true religion from stones of stumbling. What else were they taken for but stones, those who served stones, and were surely like the things they made? So the prophecy foretells that faith will be poured into the stony hearts of the Gentiles, and the oracles promise that through faith they will become children of Abraham, though through hardness of mind a stony habit of senseless and irrational nature had grown into them. The apostle compared to living stones men made firm by the strength of faith, as it is written: "You too, like living stones, are built up into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices." Far more deeply, then, does the prophetic voice here seem to compare to stones men who had so lost the sense of a human mind that, while they thought some divine reason dwelt in stones, they themselves were turned into the nature of stones, not in the use of their bodies but in the disposition of their minds. Indeed, those who sprang from Abraham according to the flesh are called both rulers of Sodom and whitewashed walls. So it is likeness of conduct rather than the line of ancestors that lays claim to the privilege of birth. Moreover, so that you may know that men were compared to stones, the prophet also compared men to trees, adding:

"For even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees." The image was changed so that, through that progression of comparison, a gentler advance of man may now be understood. For those who were before shapeless for use, bare of adornment, barren of fruit and incapable of progress are now represented in the form of trees. Graced by a kind of rational gift of nature, trees are fit for use, lovely to look on and rich in fruit; they rise up in their tops, spread out in their branches, fill with fruit and are clothed with leaves. Would that we could imitate the usefulness of fruitful trees, and, as our merits grow, being grounded in the root of long humility, lifted high above the ground and comely to see, might raise up full-grown crowns of fruitful works, so that the axe of the gospel husbandman may not cut down the root of a wild trunk! For "woe is me if I do not preach the gospel" — but that is the apostle's voice — woe is me if I do not weep for my sins; woe is me if I do not rise at midnight to give thanks to you; woe is me if I deal deceitfully with my neighbor; woe if I do not speak the truth. Already the axe is at the root. Let him who can bear the fruit of grace bear it; let him who owes it bear the fruit of penance. The Lord is at hand to seek fruit, to give life to the fruitful and to expose the barren. It is three years since he came, and he could find no fruit among the Jews: may he find it in us! He is about to order the fruitless trees cut down, so that they may not take up the ground. But let those who as yet have no fruit strive to bear it in the time to come. That good tiller of the field will intercede for us who are unfruitful, for us who bear no fruit, that time may be given and patience extended, in case we too may yet be able to bear some fruit for God.

Holy John the Baptist also gave a fitting answer to each class of men: one answer to all, and then to the tax collectors, that they should not exact more than is appointed; to the soldiers, that they should not make false accusations or seek plunder. He taught that pay is fixed for military service precisely so that a soldier, while looking for his keep, may not go about as a robber. But these and other precepts belong to particular callings. Mercy is for common use, and so it is a common precept, necessary to every calling and every age and owed by all. Neither tax collector nor soldier is exempted, neither farmer nor townsman, rich or poor: all alike are warned to give to the one who has nothing, for mercy is the fullness of the virtues. And so the pattern of perfect virtue is set before everyone, that they should not hold back their clothing and their food. Yet in mercy itself a measure is kept according to the means of the human condition, so that no one strips himself of everything, but shares what he has with the poor.

"As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether perhaps he was the Christ, he answered, saying: I baptize you with water for repentance." John, then, saw the secrets of the heart. But let us consider whose grace this is. Paul shows how the secrets of the heart are laid bare to the prophets, when he says: "The secrets of his heart will be disclosed, and falling on his face he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you." So it is the gift of God, who reveals, not the power of man; and the one who sees is helped more by a divine favor than by a natural faculty. And what does this questioning of the Jews achieve, except to prove that Christ has come according to the Scriptures? For he who was awaited was there, and surely it was the very one awaited who came, not one who was not awaited. Yet what could be more foolish than that one who is supposed to be present in another should not be believed in himself? They thought he would come through a woman, and they do not believe that he came through a virgin. What birth according to the flesh was more worthy of God than that the spotless Son of God should keep the purity of a spotless birth even in taking up a body? And surely the sign of the divine coming was set in the childbearing of a virgin, not of a woman.

"I," he says, "baptize you with water." He quickly proved that he was not the Christ, since he worked by a visible ministry. For since man consists of two natures, that is, of soul and body, the visible is consecrated by visible things and the invisible by an invisible mystery: the body is washed by water, and the sins of the soul are cleansed by the Spirit. We do one thing and invoke another, though the sanctifying power of the Godhead also breathes upon the font itself; for the whole cleansing is not the water. But these cannot be separated from each other, and so the baptism of repentance was one thing and the baptism of grace is another: the latter is from both, the former from one only. For since sins are common to mind and body, the purification also had to be common to both. And holy John did well: showing that he had understood what they were thinking in their hearts, and yet, as if he had not understood, avoiding the odium of claiming majesty, he declared not in word but in deed that he was not the Christ. For it is the work of man to do penance for sins; it is the gift of God to fulfill the grace of the mystery.

"But one mightier than I is coming." He did not make a comparison, as though he were calling Christ merely mightier than himself — for there could be no comparison between the Son of God and a man — but because there are many mighty ones. For the devil too is mighty: "no one can plunder the goods of the strong man unless he first binds the strong man." So there are many mighty ones, but none mightier except Christ. Indeed, so far was he from making a comparison that he added: "whose sandals I am not worthy to carry." By this he showed that the grace of preaching the gospel had been conferred on the apostles, who are shod for the gospel.

Yet he seems to say this because John often represented the Jewish people. Hence some refer to this his saying, "He must increase, but I must decrease," meaning that the Jewish people had to become less and the Christian people had to increase in Christ. Moses too represented the people, but he wore not the Lord's sandals but those of his own feet. The apostles, perhaps, were shod with sandals not belonging to their own feet, whereas Moses is commanded to loose the sandals from his own feet, so that the step of his soul and mind, freed from the bonds of bodily ties, might walk the spiritual road. The apostles had put off bodily sandals when they were sent out without sandals, without staff, without bag, without belt; but they did not at once carry the Lord's sandals. Perhaps they began to carry them after the resurrection, for before it they were warned not to tell anyone of the Lord's deeds. Afterward, indeed, they are told: "Go into all the world and preach the gospel," so that, bearing the footprints of the gospel preaching, they might carry the whole story of the Lord's deeds throughout the world. The wedding sandal, then, is the preaching of the gospel. But we shall explain something about this more fittingly elsewhere.

"He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire." "His winnowing fan is in his hand": by the sign of the winnowing fan the Lord is declared to have the right to judge between merits. For when grain is winnowed on the threshing floor, the full is separated from the empty and the fruitful from the worthless, as if by the weighing of a breathing breeze. By this comparison, then, the Lord is shown to distinguish on the day of judgment the solid merits and fruits of virtue from the fruitless lightness of empty boasting and meagre deeds, and to place men of more perfect merit in the heavenly dwelling. For he is the more perfect fruit who has been found worthy to be conformed to him who, like a grain of wheat, fell to the ground so as to bear much fruit in us — he who is hostile to chaff and no friend to empty merits. And so a fire will burn before him, not harmful by its own nature, since it burns up the evils of wickedness and heaps up the splendor of goodness.

"Now it came to pass, when all the people had been baptized, and Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, that heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove, and a voice came from heaven: You are my Son; in you I am well pleased." The Lord, then, was baptized not because he wished to be cleansed, but to cleanse the waters, so that, washed by the flesh of Christ, which knew no sin, they might have the power of baptism. And so whoever comes to the washing of Christ lays down his sins. Holy Luke the Evangelist has made a fine summary of what the others said, and has left it to be understood, rather than stated, that the Lord was baptized by John. The reason for the Lord's baptism the Lord himself declares, saying: "Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness."

Since, then, God in his divine favor has granted so much for the building of his Church that, after the patriarchs, the prophets and the angels, the only-begotten Son of God came down and came to the washing, do we not recognize that it was truly and divinely said of the Church: "Unless the Lord builds the house for himself, those who build it labor in vain"? Nor is it surprising if man cannot build, since he cannot guard: "Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain." So much from a psalm. Yet I too dare to say that a man cannot set out on a road unless he has the Lord going before him. Hence it is written: "You shall walk after the Lord your God," and: "A man's steps are directed by the Lord." Indeed, he was the more perfect who understood that he could not walk without the Lord: "Teach me your ways," he says. And to come to the history — for we ought not merely to take in the plain sequence of events, but also to measure our own actions by the example of what is written — the people went out of Egypt. They did not know the way that led to the holy land. God sent a pillar of fire so that by night the people might learn the way. He also sent a pillar of cloud by day, so that they might turn aside neither to the left nor to the right. But you, O man, are not such as to deserve a pillar of fire as well; you do not have Moses, you do not receive a sign. For now, since the Lord's coming, faith is required and signs are hidden away. Fear the Lord and trust in the Lord, for "the Lord will send his angels round about those who fear him, and will deliver them." You see, surely, that everywhere the power of the Lord works together with human efforts, so that no one can build without the Lord, no one can guard without the Lord, no one can begin anything without the Lord. And so, according to the apostle: "Whether you eat or drink, do all things to the glory of God," "in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." For in two epistles he has commanded you to act, in one place in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in another to the glory of God, so that you may know that the glory of the Father and of the Son is the same and their power is the same, and that the Father and the Son do not differ in anything concerning their divinity, since they do not differ in protecting us. David, then, has taught me that no one builds a house or guards a city without the Lord.

Moses has also taught me that no one but God made the world, for "in the beginning God made heaven and earth." He has also taught that God made man by his own work, and did not set him there idly: "God formed man from the slime of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life," so that you may perceive a certain activity of God in the building of man, after the manner of bodily work. He has also taught that God made woman too: "God cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and he slept; and he took one of the ribs from his side and filled up flesh in its place. And the Lord God built the rib which he took from Adam into a woman." Not in vain, as I have said, does Moses present God as working on Adam and Eve as if with bodily hands. God commanded the world to be made, and it was made, and Scripture shows the work of the world completed by a single word. But when it comes to man, the prophet was at pains to show you, in a way, the very hands of God at work.

These works of God, so carefully wrought, compel me to understand in them something more than I read. In my perplexity the apostle came to my aid, and by the divine Spirit he revealed to me what I did not understand — what was meant by "bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh, and she shall be called woman, because she was taken from her husband" — when he said: "This is a great mystery." What mystery? That "the two shall be one flesh," and that "a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife," and that "we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones." Who is this man for whose sake the woman is to leave her parents? [?] The Church leaves her parents, gathered as she is from the Gentile peoples, to whom it is said in prophecy: "Forget your people and your father's house." For the sake of what man, if not perhaps the one of whom John says: "After me comes a man who was before me"? From his side, as he slept, God took a rib. For he it is who slept and took his rest and rose again, because the Lord sustained him. What is his rib but power? For when the soldier opened his side, at once there came out water and blood, which was poured out for the life of the world. This life of the world is the rib of Christ; this is the rib of the second Adam. For "the first Adam became a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit": the last Adam is Christ, and the rib of Christ is the life of the Church. We, then, are "members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones." And perhaps this is the rib of which he said: "I perceive that power has gone out from me." This is the rib that came out of Christ and did not diminish his body; for it is not a bodily rib but a spiritual one, and the Spirit is not himself divided, but "distributes to each one as he wills." This is Eve, the mother of all the living. For if you understand "you seek the living among the dead," you understand that those are dead who are without Christ, who have no share in life; for this is what it is not to share in Christ, since Christ is life. The mother of the living, then, is the Church, which God has built with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, fitted together, grows into a temple.

Let God come, then, and build the woman — the one a helper for Adam, this one for Christ; not because Christ needs help, but because we seek and long to reach the grace of Christ through the Church. Even now she is being built, even now she is being formed, even now the woman is being shaped, even now she is being created. That is why Scripture used a new word, because "we are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets." And even now a spiritual house is rising into a holy priesthood. Come, Lord God, build this woman, build the city. Let your Servant come too; for I believe you when you say: "He shall build my city."

Behold the woman, the mother of all; behold the spiritual house; behold the city that lives forever, because it does not know how to die. For she is the city of Jerusalem, which is now seen on earth but will be caught up higher than Elijah — for Elijah was only one man — and will be carried beyond Enoch, whose death is not found. He was caught up so that wickedness might not change his heart; but she is loved by Christ as glorious, holy, spotless, without wrinkle. And how much better it is that a whole body should be taken up than that he was taken up! For this is the hope of the Church. She will certainly be caught up; she will be taken up, she will be carried over to heaven. See, Elijah was caught up in a chariot of fire; the Church will be caught up. Do you not believe me? Believe Paul at least, in whom Christ spoke: "We shall be caught up," he says, "in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord."

To build her, then, many are sent: the patriarchs are sent, the prophets are sent, Gabriel the archangel is sent, countless angels are dispatched, and a multitude of the heavenly host praises God, because the building of this city was drawing near. Many are sent to her, but Christ alone builds her. Yet he is not alone, for the Father is present; and though he builds alone, he does not claim for himself alone the grace of so great a building. It is written of the temple of God which Solomon built, in which there was a type of the Church, that there were seventy thousand who carried loads on their shoulders and eighty thousand stonecutters. Let those angels come, let the stonecutters come; let what is superfluous in our stones be cut away and what is rough be smoothed; let those who carry on their shoulders come too, for it is written: "They shall be carried upon shoulders."

He came, then, to John — for you have learned the rest. He came to John's baptism; but John's baptism was a repentance for sins. And so John tries to prevent him, saying: "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me? Why do you come to me, who have no sin? For the one who has sin must be baptized; but why should the one who has committed no sin seek the washing of repentance?" "Let it be so now," he says — that is, while the Church is being built — "it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." What is righteousness but mercy? "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor: his righteousness endures forever." He has given to me, poor as I am; he has given to me in my need a grace I did not have before; so "his righteousness endures forever." What is righteousness but to be the first to begin what you want another to do, and to encourage others by your example? What is righteousness, if not that, having taken flesh, he should not shut out the feeling and service of the flesh as God would, but should conquer the flesh as man, so as to teach me to conquer? For he taught me how I may bury to sin, and renew in virtue, the filth of guilty flesh, compacted as it is of earthly vices. O truly divine foresight in the very humility of the Lord!

For the lower the humility, the more divine the providence. By the bitterness of the injuries he suffered, God is revealed; and by using remedies, he who needed no remedies is proved to be God. For what could be so divine a way of drawing the peoples as this: that no one should shun the washing of grace, since Christ did not shun the washing of repentance? Let no one say he is free of sin, since Christ came to the remedy for sins. If Christ washed for us — or rather, washed us in his own body — how much more ought we to wash away our own sins? By what work, then, by what mystery is he more clearly proved to be God, though he is God in all things, than by this: that throughout the whole world, wherever the human race is spread, across the separations and stretches of distant regions, in one moment and in one body God abolished the deceit of the ancient error and poured out the grace of the heavenly kingdom? For one was plunged into the water, but he raised up all; one went down so that we might all go up; one took on himself the sins of all, so that in him the sins of all might be cleansed. Purify yourselves, then, as the apostle says, since he who had no need of purification purified himself for us. So much concerning us.

Now let us consider the mystery of the Trinity. We say that there is one God, but we confess the Father and we confess the Son. For although it is written, "You shall love the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve," the Son denied that he was alone, saying, "But I am not alone, for the Father is with me." Nor is he alone now, for the Father bears witness that he is present. The Holy Spirit is present, for the Trinity can never be separated from itself. Then the heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove. How, then, can the heretics say that he who is not alone on earth is alone in heaven? Let us pay attention to the mystery. Why like a dove? Because the grace of the washing requires simplicity, so that we may be simple as doves. The grace of the washing requires peace, which in the ancient type a dove once brought to that ark which alone was untouched by the flood. He whose type that dove was, and who has now deigned to descend in the form of a dove, has taught me; he has taught me that in that branch and in that ark there was a type of peace and of the Church, because amid the very floods of the world the Holy Spirit brings fruitful peace to his Church. David also taught it, who, discerning the sacrament of baptism by the prophetic Spirit, said: "Who will give me wings like a dove?"

So the Holy Spirit came; but mark the mystery. He came to Christ, for all things were created through him and hold together in him. But see how kind the Lord is: he alone submitted himself to injuries, and he alone did not seek grace. And where did he build the Church? "I will ask the Father," he says, "and he will give you another Advocate, to be with you for ever, the Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him." Rightly, then, did the Spirit show himself in a body, since in the substance of his divinity he is not seen.

We have seen the Spirit, though in bodily form; let us see the Father as well. But since we cannot see him, let us hear him; for God in his kindness is present and will not abandon his temple. He wishes to build up every soul, he wishes to shape it for salvation, he wishes to carry living stones from earth to heaven. He loves his temple; let us love him too. If we love God, let us keep his commandments; if we love him, let us know him, for whoever says that he knows him and does not keep his commandments is a liar. For how can anyone love God who does not love the truth, since God is truth? Let us hear the Father, then, for the Father is invisible. But the Son too is invisible according to his divinity, for no one has ever seen God. Since the Son, then, is God, he is certainly not seen in that respect in which he is God; but he chose to show himself in a body, and because the Father did not bear a body, the Father chose to prove to us that he is present in the Son, saying: "You are my Son; in you I am well pleased." If you want to learn that the Son is always present with the Father, read the words of the Son, who says: "If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present." If you are looking for the Father's testimony, you have heard it from John. Believe him to whom Christ entrusted himself to be baptized, him to whom the Father commended his Son with a heavenly voice, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

Where are the Arians, who are not pleased with the Son in whom the Father is well pleased? It is not I who say this, nor has any human being spoken it; for God did not speak through a man, nor through angels or archangels, but the voice sent from heaven by the Father himself set its seal on it. Then elsewhere the same Father repeats it, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him"—listen, that is, to him when he says, "I and the Father are one." So whoever does not believe the Son does not believe the Father. The Father is a witness concerning the Son; if there is doubt about the Son, the Father's testimony is not believed. Moreover, when he says, "in whom I am well pleased," he is praising in the Son not what belongs to another but what is his own. For what does "in whom I am well pleased" mean, if not "all that the Son has is mine," just as the Son said, "All that the Father has is mine"? For the power of an undivided divinity makes no distinction between the Father and the Son, but shares one authority between the Father and the Son. Let us believe the Father, whose voice the elements made to resound; let us believe the Father, whose voice the elements obeyed. The world has believed in the elements; let it believe in human beings. It has believed in lifeless things; let it believe in human beings. It has believed in mute things; let it believe in those who speak. It has believed in things that have no understanding; let it believe in those who have been given understanding so that they might know God.
BOOK THREE.

"And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years of age, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph." Since we are about to speak of the genealogies, we see that there is some difference between the one in the Gospel according to Matthew and the one in this Gospel, whose interpretation we have in hand. It is not credible that holy men could have said things contrary to one another, especially about the deeds of the Lord our Saviour. So let us show, with all the care we can, that they did not say things that disagree.

First of all, no one should be troubled that it is written, "who was supposed to be the son of Joseph." He was rightly "supposed" to be so, because he was not his son by nature. He was supposed to be so because Mary, who had been betrothed to her husband Joseph, had given birth to him. For so you have it: "Is not this the son of Joseph the carpenter?" We have said above why the Lord our Saviour willed to be born of a virgin, why of a betrothed woman, and why at the time of the census. It seems fitting also to explain why he had a carpenter for a father. By this figure he shows that his Father is the one who, as maker of all things, founded the world, as it is written: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." Human things are not to be compared with divine ones, yet the figure holds good. The Father of Christ works by fire and spirit. Like a good craftsman of the soul, he hews away our vices on every side. He is quick to lay the axe to barren trees, skilled in cutting away what is small and keeping what is tall for the roof-beams. He softens rigid minds with the fire of the Spirit, and he shapes the whole human race for various uses through different kinds of service.

Mary conceived Christ of the Holy Spirit, and Joseph seems to have had no part in the Lord's begetting. So why is Joseph's lineage described rather than Mary's? We might be in doubt about this, if the custom of the Scriptures, which always seeks out the man's origin, did not instruct us. For so you have it: Perez was the son of Judah, prince of the tribe. He begot Hezron, and Hezron begot Ram, and Ram begot Amminadab, and Amminadab begot Nahshon, and Nahshon begot Salmon, and Salmon begot Boaz, and Boaz begot Obed, and Obed begot Jesse, and Jesse begot David. It is the man's person that is looked to, for even in the senate and in the other councils of cities, it is the man who lays claim to the dignity of his family. How unseemly it would be to set aside the man's origin and look for the woman's! Then the one who was to be preached to the peoples of the whole world would seem to have had no father.

Let us also show that elsewhere a genealogy is traced in a different order, so that here too the evangelists, who followed the ancient order, may not seem to disagree. For so you have it: "There was a man of Arath, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeremiel, the son of Heli, the son of Ozi." You see that in the ancient way an account of origins is woven both from fathers to sons and from sons to fathers. You see that everywhere a family is traced through the generations of its men. So do not wonder that Matthew ran through the order of generations from Abraham down to Joseph, and Luke from Joseph up to Adam and to God. Do not wonder that it is Joseph's origin that is described. Born according to the flesh, he had to follow the custom of the flesh, and since he came into the world, he had to be described in the world's manner. This is all the more so because Mary's origin is also contained in Joseph's. Joseph was a just man, so he certainly took a wife from his own tribe and his own homeland, and as a just man he could not act against what the law prescribed. For so you have it: "Each of the children of Israel shall keep to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers, and they shall not pass from tribe to tribe; and every daughter who possesses an inheritance among the tribes of the children of Israel shall be the wife of one of the people and of the tribe of her father." So at the time of the census Joseph went up, being of the house and homeland of David, to be registered with Mary his wife. Since she registers as being of the same house and the same homeland, she certainly shows herself to be of the same tribe and the same homeland.

Elizabeth is also introduced as Mary's kinswoman. The first reason is that all Jews are kin, as the apostle taught when he said, "For I could wish that I myself were accursed for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites." So they were kinswomen because both were Israelites, and they were kinswomen also because both were of the tribe of Judah. You have learned that Mary was of the tribe of Judah; learn that Elizabeth was too. For "Mary arose in those days and went into the hill country with haste, to a city," it says, "of Judah, and entered the house of Zechariah." Moses prescribed that each should live among their own tribe. So since she lived in a city of Judah, she was certainly of the tribe of Judah, especially since there were priests in Elizabeth's family, whose portion is God. And how beautiful it is that these two should be seen to be kin according to the flesh, since they were not without the fellowship of spiritual kinship according to God! The one bore the forerunner of Christ, the other bore Christ. The one conceived of the Holy Spirit, the other, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied.
