Moreover, the holy apostle says that the man is the head of every woman, and the divine law says that the two are in one flesh. Those who were one flesh and one spirit could hardly be seen to have a divided homeland and tribe. Add to this that the angel Gabriel foretold of the Lord that "the Lord will give him the throne of his father David." It is certain, therefore, that Mary too descended from David's line. At the same time, we also learn that it makes no difference in what order the line of generations is set out, since the road can be travelled in either direction.

It seems we should explain why St Matthew began to list Christ's genealogy from Abraham, while St Luke carried it from Christ up to God. But first, St Matthew began the order of generations from Abraham, yet he did not write "The book of the generation of Abraham." Instead he wrote "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham." I think we must by no means pass over why he did so, and why he named these two above all. These most faithful founders of the line are not chosen without purpose. We are meant to understand that even in a fleshly genealogy it is above all a spiritual succession that is sought. For these are the two men to whom the divine promises came down.

The first is Abraham. Before the law of Moses and before there was a Jewish people, he left what was his own and came to know God. He earned the testimony of faith, because he believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. He also received an oracle from God, who said to him: "Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house into the land that I will show you. I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, and you shall be blessed. I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you, and in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed." You see, then, that the gathering of the nations and the assembly of the holy Church were first promised to this man by a divine oracle. That is why he, who first earned the pledge of a Church to be founded, had to be named as a founder of the line.

David too is rightly declared a founder of the line, because he received an answer, confirmed by an oath, that Christ would come from him according to the flesh. For so it is written: "The Lord swore the truth to David, and he will not repent of it: Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon my throne." And elsewhere: "Once have I sworn by my holiness that I will not lie to David; his seed shall endure for ever, and his throne shall be like the sun before me." And in Chronicles: "When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, who shall come from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house, and I will set up his throne for ever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me, and I will not take my mercy away from him, as I took it away from those who were before you." Through Isaiah too the same Lord God revealed the Lord's lineage, saying: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from the root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding." And further on: "There shall be the root of Jesse, and he who shall rise to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope." And elsewhere: "A child is born to us, a son is given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulders, and his name shall be called Angel of Great Counsel. For I will bring peace upon the rulers, and health to him. Great is his power, and of his peace there is no end, upon the throne of David and in his kingdom." In Aquila's translation of this passage too, we see that the promise was made not as if about a man, but about one who was more than a man. For he translated it: "A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and his measure is upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, my counsellor, strong, mighty, Father of the age, Prince of peace. His discipline is fulfilled, and of his peace there is no end, upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom."

Clear oracles show that all these things fit Christ, and that the fruit of the divine power cannot be diverted to the credit of Solomon, who was David's son. Solomon's end is known beyond doubt, for Solomon's kingdom and peace came to an end, as the readings from the books of Kings show. Christ alone is the one whose kingdom has no end. Again, Solomon ruled over no nations, but Christ gathered the Church from the nations. Finally, Solomon was born and came to the throne while David was still alive. But the one who is promised is shown as one who will rise up after David's death, as you have it: "When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up from your seed one who shall come from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house, and I will set up his throne for ever." Did Solomon reign for ever? He reigned for only forty years. "I will be a father to him," it says, "and he shall be a son to me." Who is God's own Son, if not the one to whom it was said, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you"? "And I will not take my mercy away from him, and I will keep him faithful in my house and in his kingdom for ever." We know from the sequence of the divine readings that Solomon in fact went seriously astray. Perhaps this happened so that people would not go astray and believe that the promise had come down to him. For he built a temple to the idol Astarte for love of a woman, and the Lord was angry with Solomon. So he began to reign while David was still alive. For so you have it: when David was told that Solomon was reigning, the king bowed down on his bed and said, "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who has given me today one of my seed sitting on my throne, and my eyes see it." And he went astray and gave offence. If so, you see that the sequence of the promise pledged Christ.

That is why the evangelist chose these two founders of the line. The one received the promise about the gathering of the peoples, the other obtained the oracle about the begetting of Christ. So although David comes later in the order of succession, he is listed before Abraham in the Lord's genealogy. To have received a promise about Christ is greater than to have received one about the Church, since the Church itself exists through Christ. So one is the head of the line according to the flesh, the other the head of the line according to the spirit; one by the gift of offspring, the other by the faith of the peoples. For the one who saves is greater than the one who is saved. That is why he is called the son of David: "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David." He had to be called first the son of the man to whom a son was promised. Yet the apostle says that Christ was promised to Abraham too: "The promises were made to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say 'and to seeds,' as of many, but as of one: 'and to your seed,' which is Christ." So to one belongs the special claim of descent, and to the other a primacy. To David was granted that Jesus should be called his son. To Abraham, as head of the family and of the nations, is kept the privilege that the Lord's genealogy should begin with him. For Scripture too had to declare the author of faith to be the author of the divine lineage.

Hence Luke also thought that Christ's origin should be traced back to God, because God is the true begetter of Christ. He is so either as Father, by true generation, or as the giver of the mystic gift, by the regeneration of the washing. So Luke did not begin to describe his genealogy at the start. He did so only after he had told of his baptism, because he wished to show God, through baptism, as the author of all things. He declared that Christ too came down from God in the order of succession, weaving everything together so as to show him to be the Son of God by nature, by grace, and according to the flesh. And what clearer sign of divine generation could there be than this: about to speak of the genealogy, he first set down the Father himself saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased"?

Here too some people like to raise questions. Matthew counted forty-two generations from Abraham to Christ, but Luke counted fifty. And Matthew described the line as descending through some persons, Luke through others. Here you can already prove what we said. Matthew wove into the order of generations some ancestors of the Lord's line, and Luke others. Yet both marked out Abraham and David as founders of the line, ahead of the rest.

Matthew thought the line should be traced through Solomon, but Luke through Nathan. This seems to show that Christ's family was both royal and priestly. We should not take this to mean that one account is truer than the other. Rather, each agrees with the other with equal faithfulness and truth. For even according to the flesh he truly belonged to a royal and a priestly family: a king descended from kings, a priest descended from priests. The oracle, however, speaks not of fleshly things but of heavenly ones. For the King rejoices in the strength of God, and judgement is given to him by the Father, who is King. And he is a priest for ever, as it is written: "You are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." So each kept faith well. Matthew showed that the descent ran through kings. Luke traced the line of generations from God to Christ through priests, and so declared it the holier. At the same time, the figure of the calf is also signified here, in that Luke thinks the priestly mystery must be kept everywhere.

Do not be surprised that there are more generations from Abraham to Christ according to Luke and fewer according to Matthew, since you admit that the line was traced through different persons. It may be that some men lived long lives, while the men of the other line died young. We see many old men living alongside their grandchildren, while other men die as soon as they have had sons.

We also notice that St Matthew records that Jacob, the father of Joseph, was the son of Matthan. But Luke writes that Joseph, to whom Mary was betrothed, was the son of Heli, and that Heli was the son of Melchi. How can one man have two fathers, Heli and Jacob? And how can he have two paternal grandfathers, Matthan and Melchi? If you follow the matter through, you will find that, according to the rule of the old law, two brothers had different sons by one wife, sons born of the same mother. For it is recorded that Matthan, who was descended from Solomon, had a son Jacob and died while his wife was still alive. Melchi later took her as his wife, and by her Heli was born. Heli's brother then died without children, so Heli in turn joined himself to his brother's wife and had a son, Joseph. Joseph is called the son of Jacob according to the law, since by the ordinance of the old law a brother raised up offspring for his dead brother. So he was called the son of two men, though he was not begotten by both. He became the son of one by begetting and of the other by law. In this rule of the law, offspring that would last for ever was promised to us for the dead. But the Jewish people did not understand this. They took it according to the letter and spoiled the grace of the oracle. For there was another brother who would raise up offspring for his dead brothers, a brother not by blood but by the purity of grace. And so perhaps it says, "A brother does not redeem; shall a man redeem?" For it was not a brother by blood, but the Lord and mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who spread abroad the grace of the resurrection. There is, however, another interpretation of this verse, which we shall give in its proper place.

It does not seem unreasonable that St Matthew thought the generations should be divided into groups of fourteen, the mystic number doubled: from Abraham to David, from David to the exile in Babylon, and from the exile in Babylon to Christ. In this he also marked the turns of change. For from Abraham to David the Jewish people were without kings, since lawful kingship began with David. After that the whole Jewish nation was ruled by kings, and their kingdoms remained intact until the exile. After the exile, the nobility of a degenerating people, now cut down, sank toward its setting. As for the fifty generations from Abraham that Luke thought should be woven together, it is clear enough that the grace of a mystic number is kept there too. For ten and seven are both mystic numbers, and each, repeated three times, signifies a mystery. And Pentecost, whose grace Luke followed, and the forty, whose grace Matthew followed, have shown a mystic number more than enough.

Many also wonder why Matthew thought he should include in the Lord's genealogy a mention of Tamar, a woman of ill repute, as it seems to them. They also wonder why he mentioned Ruth, and why that woman too who was Uriah's wife and, after her husband was killed, passed into marriage with David. They wonder all the more because he nowhere mentions the holy women Sarah, Rebecca and Rachel. For so you have it: "Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, Jacob begot Judah and his brothers, and Judah begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar." It was not without purpose, then, that the evangelist put in this woman's name, and it seems we should treat her separately for now.

First, if you look at the truth, this woman was not so much disreputable as righteous. She did not seek the use of passing lust; she desired the gift of offspring. For it was a disgrace to have no children, and the civil laws even imposed penalties for it. Judah had promised her to his son, but he had long put off the marriage they had agreed. Because the promise was delayed, the bridegroom died. Before Christ's coming the grace of virginity and of widowhood had not yet blossomed. Grieving that she had been left without children, she devised a trick out of the desire for offspring and forestalled Judah with a plan: after she learned that his wife had died, she dressed herself up and presented herself to him. You see that the woman's conduct is approved at every point. She did not steal another woman's bed. She was not dressed as a harlot out of a harlot's desires. She was not chasing wandering lust. Long cheated by her father-in-law's promises, she wished by a disguised trick to obtain the fruit of offspring from the family she had chosen. So who was the more chaste? She who waited so long for what was promised, or he who could not resist a love that was offered? She who did not flee from her bridegroom's family, or he who took her for a harlot? She who did not grant even an hour of her body to those who wanted to lie with her, or he who began from a desire for wantonness and, through the woman's chastity, brought it to the grace of offspring? She who had no children and feared that the delay of marriage would shut out her time to conceive, she who chose a man of mature gravity, or he who fell in love with the youth of a younger woman? Indeed, he admitted it himself, saying, "Tamar is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah." So she wished to test the very man who had demanded chastity of her. Indeed, she never knew a man again afterwards, and after their union she put on the garment of widowhood. But he, who had demanded years of chastity from the girl, could not hold out for a single hour. He cast off his mourning, changed his clothes, cut his hair, left the funeral pyre, and climbed into bed as a lover.

But we do not defend her in order to accuse him. Rather, let us excuse them both. Yet it is not we who excuse them, but the mystery that the fruit of that union expressed. For the woman bore Perez and Zerah as sons; she bore twins. So it was not without purpose that Matthew named them both, although only Perez was needed for the record. For Perez begot Hezron, Hezron begot Ram, and so on one by one in order. Isaac had two sons and Jacob had several, yet Scripture mentions only the one son of each whom the Lord's line of descent required. Why then did it record both of these, unless there is a mystery in both of them?

We have dealt with the moral sense: she did not ply a harlot's trade but chose the gifts of fruitfulness. Let us now deal with the historical sense and examine the mystical, for it cannot be without a mystery that she received a ring, a necklace and a staff. No common person is she who deserves to receive an ornament, a seal and authority: the seal of deeds, the ornament of the breast, the emblem of royal freedom. So, to begin with the history: when Tamar was giving birth, you have read that one of the children put out a hand from her womb, and the midwife took hold of it and tied a scarlet thread on it, saying, “This one will come out first.” But when the child drew his hand back into his mother's womb, his brother came out at once. And the midwife said, “Why has the hedge been broken through for you?” And she called his name Perez. And after him came out his brother, on whose hand was the scarlet thread, and she called his name Zerah. You see how many riddles disclose the mystery: the hand put out first, the scarlet thread tied on, the hand drawn back, the midwife's double saying, that one would come out first and the other would break through the hedge.

Why did one put out his hand from the womb, while the other went ahead at the moment of birth, unless it is because through the mystery of the twins the twofold life of the peoples is described, one according to the law, the other according to faith, one according to the letter, the other according to grace? Grace comes before the law, faith before the letter. And so the type of grace put out his hand first, because the working of grace came first. It was present in Job, Melchizedek, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who lived by faith without the law; for Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. Melchizedek too, going before, showed the grace of the holy sacrifice in figure. For the holy patriarchs, who came before the law, were free from the bonds of its precepts and shone with the free grace of the gospel, the same grace as ours.

The younger of these brothers is the second order of godliness; for the first is in the patriarchs, the second in the kings and priests. Both kinds of life are according to God. For those too who served a devout and godly service according to the law of Moses are not without a share in grace and honor; but the fruit of godliness came first in the founders rather than in the heirs. For Zerah came first, whose name means “the rising”; for the light of godliness is the brightness of the true rising, of him, that is, who said, “The Rising is my name,” whose ray of light first shone in the patriarchs. For they were the first to put forth the action of their life in this world, and in their hand our action too was prefigured, as of a fuller body, while we were still held in a kind of womb of nature that was bringing us to birth. But the observance of the law was set in between like a hedge, and in a way the life of the forefathers seems to have been cut off. Of this, in a type, that midwife, perhaps justice, who received us as we were sent forth from the womb of mother nature, is reported to have said, “This one will come out first.” And truly that order of godliness was wonderful, for it was impressed not by Moses, nor by any man, nor through a man, but by a gift of wisdom pouring itself in of its own accord.

The first discipline of godliness, then, is according to the gospel, because we believe through the cross and blood of Christ. Abraham saw his day and rejoiced; Noah foresaw with spiritual understanding his grace prefigured in the type of the Church; Isaac did not refuse to take his place in the sacrifice; Jacob worshiped him when he prevailed over him; Isaiah saw the redness of his garments — for the life of the prophets too is according to the gospel. In his blood, amid the destruction of the world, Rahab, a harlot in type, the Church in mystery, pointed to the future sign of salvation for all. She does not refuse union with many strangers, and the more people she is joined to, the more chaste she is: an immaculate virgin, without wrinkle, unblemished in modesty, common to all in love, a chaste harlot, a barren widow, a fruitful virgin. A harlot, because she is visited by many lovers with the allure of love yet without the defilement of sin — for whoever is joined to a harlot is one body with her. A barren widow, who could not bear while her husband was absent — the husband came and begot this people and this multitude. A fruitful virgin, who has borne this multitude with the fruit of love, without the indulgence of lust.

But to return to the history: what do the words of the midwife mean, when she says, “This one will come out first,” unless that he bore the type of him who, though later by bodily birth, was first in power and truth and claimed for himself the primacy over all? Hence John too says, “After me comes a man who ranks ahead of me.” What does it mean that she tied a scarlet thread on his hand, unless that he was a type of him who by the sign of his cross and the shedding of his blood shed light on human action? So after he drew back his hand, his brother came out, as though a breach had been made in the hedge — the one whom the Apostle called, as it were, the middle wall of the hedge or partition — and he took his name from the breach, for Perez means “division.” Hence also

…he calls them Pharisees, because they separated themselves from association with the many. But it would have been far happier and far better if the hedge had not been broken through, but had remained one and the same and undivided. This could have happened if the service of the life that came after had been in keeping with the life that first put out its hand, that is, first displayed its conduct. It would have been much better if the circumcised people had been willing to imitate the life of their forebears. Then there would have been one hedge, one wall, one building of those who came first and those who followed. But because the weakness of the later life could not live up to that first conduct of life, a breach was certainly made in its hedge or wall, which had been built according to God, and a middle wall, as it were, was set up between them, so that the hedge, that is, the lasting and unbroken building of good character, was broken down. For a hedge is what surrounds a fruitful field and keeps the thief from breaking in. It encloses what is cultivated and shuts out what is wild. A wall also encloses a house, and if the wall stands, the house is safe. Accordingly he says, “I will take away its wall, and it shall be plundered.”

Let us pray that this may remain intact. Let it be the enclosure of our house, the spiritual house that is within us; for it cannot be built by man, but only by the living God, who says: "And I set an enclosure around it." So those who destroyed the enclosure destroyed their salvation. Let the enclosure remain, then; let this hedge remain. Do you want to know how useful a hedge is? "Hedge your ears with thorns and thistles, and do not listen to a wicked tongue"; for that hedge protects you from guilt.

So the Lord Jesus, who afterwards came into the light according to the flesh, restored the defence of that ancient hedge and refashioned us to the conduct of our forebears and the ancient simplicity of faith. This is why the prophet said of him: "You shall be called the builder of the hedge." For he took away that barrier which divided the unity of mind and body and the course of a simple life, and he himself became our peace, who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of the hedge. The apostle explains this wall as the enmities in the flesh. These enmities the Lord took away; he restored peace and abolished the law of commandments expressed in decrees, so as to create the two in one new man. By this the apostle means not only the outer and the inner man but also Jew and Greek, so that Christ might be all and in all. For the Lord took away the superstition of the sabbath, of the bodily sabbath, and so to speak broke down the dividing wall of the law. By the difficulty of its decrees that wall kept us from the piety that is according to God, because under the law of Moses it was neither easy nor even possible for the Gentiles to serve as soldiers of God, since the empty superstition of the Jews held back the pure devotion of the Gentiles from taking up its observance. What then? Is the law useless? Far from it. It is useful for unbelievers and necessary for the weak, to restrain those who slip and wander by the severity of a saving precept and to confine them by close attention to observances. And the law is good, because it is spiritual. It is not good, then, for one who does not consider it spiritual, who has become small and lowly of mind and so could not see what is above the law, namely the majesty of Christ. Isaiah, lofty of mind, looking as it were over that wall, certainly saw that majesty, the glory of God, which is seen on the mountains, not on the hills.

And so the Church has taught us in the Song of Songs that this wall could not stand in the way of our Lord Jesus Christ, nor of the one who followed Christ, saying: "The voice of my brother! Behold, he comes leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills. My brother is like a roe or a young stag on the mountains of Bethel. Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking in through the windows, peering through the lattices. My brother answered and said to me: Arise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove, for behold, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. The flowers have appeared in the land, the time of pruning has come, the voice of the turtledove has been heard." The flowers are the apostles; the time of harvest is the fruit of Christ; the voice of the turtledove is the voice of the Church. Rightly, then, did the Son of God, once he saw that men were earthbound, not climbing toward the heights but hemmed in by bodily narrowness (for there was none who did good, not even one), deign to come down to earth himself, to take away that wall of the law, that is, a kind of heavy mass and superstition of bodily understanding, which as it were weighed down and overshadowed the hearts of the peoples. Better, then, an enclosure than a wall. Indeed, a whitewashed wall is not good, and it was not idly said to the chief of the priests, because he was preserving the obstacles of the dividing wall. The Lord Jesus removed that wall as a harsh service, so as to pour in a clearer observance of religion, so that no longer the one race of the Jews, shut in as it were by a bodily prescription of the law, but all nations might be called to the worship of God through the gospel.

So the two twins are two twin lives, two twin services, such that the first is better than the one that follows. And therefore what is better has been restored. Who would deny that the gospel surpasses the law? Yet the law is good if you raise your mind above the letter, for the letter kills. But what grace would this story have unless we saw the light of so great a mystery? For the holy apostle taught us to seek the hidden truth within the simplicity of the story, and to carry its meaning over into certain discussions that cannot be understood according to the letter, when he wrote: "Tell me, you who read the law, have you not heard the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. The one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, but the one by the free woman according to the promise. These things," he says, "are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants." And further on: "But the Jerusalem above is free."

Let us then strive with loftiness of mind toward that Jerusalem which the dividing wall could not cut off and divide. For that wall of the Old Testament, as understood in a bodily sense, has been broken down; the slave woman has been cast out, the free woman is kept. From the free woman we are free; for the Church is free, the synagogue has been cast out, since the Jewish people was in slavery. The yoke of slavery has been removed, which pressed down the necks, so to speak, of our souls, so that we could not look out beyond the wall of our former life. We have a good and light yoke, which, by the reins of peace and the bonds of grace, lifts up rather than presses down those who are joined to it. This is the Lord, whose type went before in Zerah, because the Lord Jesus, from the tribe and seed of that Zerah, was born according to the flesh not only of a woman but also under the law, to redeem those who were under the law at the price of his own blood. His figure therefore went before on the hand of that Zerah, to promise us that he was to come who would recall the way of the old life and restore in the last Adam the freedom he had granted to the first Adam, so that the human race might now be without the law of slavery.

If, then, we have learned that Tamar was recorded among the Lord's ancestors because of a mystery, we should judge that Ruth too was by no means passed over without a similar reason. The holy apostle seems to have had her in mind when, foreseeing in the Spirit that the call of the foreign nations would be celebrated through the gospel, he said that the law is not laid down for the just but for the unjust. For how did Ruth, a foreigner, marry a Jew? And why did the evangelist think that her marriage, which the order of the law forbade, should be mentioned in the genealogy of Christ? Did the Saviour, then, not descend from a lawful line? It seems unseemly, unless you return to the apostle's statement that the law is not laid down for the just but for the unjust. For she was a foreigner and a Moabite, and the law of Moses forbade such marriages and excluded Moabites from the assembly; for so it is written: "Moabites shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, to the third and fourth generation, and for ever." How, then, did she enter the assembly, unless because, holy and spotless in her conduct, she was placed above the law? For if the law is laid down for the ungodly and for sinners, then surely Ruth, who went beyond the limit set by the law, entered the assembly, became an Israelite, and deserved to be counted among the ancestors of the Lord's line, chosen for kinship of mind, not of body, is a great example for us, because in her went before a figure of all of us who have been gathered from the Gentiles to enter the Church of the Lord. Let us then imitate her, so that, as she by her conduct earned this privilege of being admitted into their fellowship, as the story teaches, we too, because of the excellence of our conduct and with our merits supporting us, may be enrolled in the Church of the Lord.

For when in earlier times, in the days of the judges, famine pressed hard on the Israelites, a man went from Bethlehem, a city of Judah, in which Christ was born, to live in the country of Moab with his wife and two sons; the man's name was Elimelech, the woman's Naomi. Her sons took Moabite wives, one named Orpah and the other Ruth, and they lived there about ten years and died. The woman, left behind by her two sons and bereft of her own husband, learned that God had visited Israel, and preparing to return home, she began to urge her sons' wives to go back to their own homes. One agreed, but Ruth stayed with her mother-in-law. When her mother-in-law said to her, "See, your sister-in-law has already gone back to her people and to her gods; you too go back with your sister-in-law," Ruth answered: "Far be it from me to leave you and return to my god, for wherever you go I will go with you, and where you live I will live. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. And where you die I will die, and where you are buried I will be buried." And so the two of them came to Bethlehem. When Boaz, the great-grandfather of David, came to know her character, her holiness toward her mother-in-law, her devotion to her dead husband, and her reverence toward God, he chose her as his wife according to the law of Moses, so as to raise up seed for his dead kinsman.

It is worth noticing, too, that she was found in a field full of harvest gathering sheaves, as it is written, and saving the produce for her mother-in-law, and that she did not go after a young man but followed a mature man. So she deserved to hear: "For you are a woman of virtue," and: "For you have made your last kindness better than your first"; for the last kindness, that of the Church gathered together, surpasses the former. We say this briefly here because we have set it out more fully in the books I wrote On the Faith. He who was far off drew near, because he who was nearest withdrew, and by receiving the woman he acquired the shoe of the nearer kinsman. For it was the custom that the nearest kinsman, if he did not wish to take his kinswoman in marriage, would loosen his shoe and give way to another. In this lies no small mystery, since he who took the foreign woman as a type received the power of preaching the gospel.

That this marriage was a type is attested by the blessing of the elders, who said: "May the Lord make the woman who enters your house like Rachel and like Leah, who built up the house of Israel, and may you do mightily in Ephrathah and have a name in Bethlehem. And may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, through the offspring the Lord will give you from this young woman." And Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife, and she bore Obed, the father of Jesse, the grandfather of David. Rightly, then, did Saint Matthew, who through the gospel was to call the Gentiles to the Church, record that the Lord himself, the author of the gathering of the Gentiles, took a descent from foreigners according to the flesh, so that even then there might be a sign that this line would bring forth the one who calls the Gentiles. Him we were all to follow, gathered from among the foreigners, leaving behind our ancestral ways and saying to the one who called us to the worship of the Lord, for example to Paul or to any bishop: "Your people are my people, your God my God." So Ruth, like Leah and Rachel, forgetting her people and her father's house, loosed the bond of the law and entered the Church.

The one who does not receive the Church loosens his shoe. And to Moses it is said: "Loosen the shoe from your feet," so that he himself would not be thought to be the bridegroom of the Church. Only he who is the true bridegroom does not loosen it. And therefore John says: "The strap of whose shoe I am not worthy to loosen." So this too is a type, and she built up the house of Israel.

How fitting it was that she should be named in the Lord's lineage is shown by the expression of a deeper mystery, in which it was prophesied that Christ would be born of her line in Ephrathah, when it is said: "May the Lord grant you to do mightily in Ephrathah and to have a name in Bethlehem." For what is that might but the one that gathered the peoples of the Gentiles through Christ? And what is that name but the one Bethlehem acquired by becoming the homeland of the Lord when he was born according to the flesh? Hence it was said in prophecy: "And you, Bethlehem of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will govern my people Israel." We see, then, that in the mention of these women history, character and mystery all agree.

Yet while defending Tamar and Ruth I do not deny that sinners too are counted among the ancestors of the Lord's line. Saint Luke, wishing to avoid mentioning them, followed a different order of succession, and thought that neither Ahab nor Jechoniah nor, finally, the wife of Uriah should be named, so as to set out an unblemished series of a priestly line. But just as the reasoning behind his plan holds good, so too the plan of Saint Matthew is not at odds with sound reason. For since he was proclaiming that the Lord, who was to take on the sins of all, was born according to the flesh, subject to injuries and liable to suffering, he thought that the Lord should not be declared exempt even from this act of devotion: that he did not refuse the injury of a stained origin either. At the same time, the Church was not to be ashamed of being gathered from sinners, since the Lord was born of sinners. Finally, he wished the benefit of redemption to begin even with the Lord's own ancestors, so that no one would think that a stain of origin could be an obstacle to virtue, nor boast insolently of the nobility of his family, nor, being more bashful, blush at the crimes of his parents, since he is given the means of overshadowing his origin with the flower of virtue.

Or was not holy David, though much about him is a figure of mystery, all the more exalted because he recognised that he was a man and believed that the sin he had committed in taking the wife of Uriah should be washed away with tears of repentance, showing us that no one ought to trust in his own virtue? For we have a great adversary, who cannot be conquered by us without God's favour. And you will often find grave sins in illustrious and blessed men, so that you may recognise that, being men, they were open to temptation, and so that they would not be believed to be more than men because of their outstanding virtues. David, carried away by presumption in his own virtue, had said: "If I have repaid those who rewarded me with evil," and elsewhere: "But I said in my abundance: I shall never be moved." He at once recorded that he had suffered the penalty for this insolence, saying: "You turned your face from me, and I was troubled." If he, the founder of the Lord's line, incurred offence for his insolence, how much more must the rest of us sinners, who have no privilege of merits to support us, fear the rock of insolence, on which good things suffer shipwreck. This is all the more so since so great a man is for us the author both of teaching and of example, who thought he should sing afterwards a kind of recantation to win back the Lord's favour, saying: "Lord, my heart is not lifted up, nor are my eyes raised too high," and: "The Lord is at my right hand, that I may not be shaken." For he knew that when he trusted in himself, he fell. Indeed he showed that there is nothing else in man except that he knows God; for so you have it: "What is man that you have made yourself known to him, or the son of man that you take account of him?" If, then, David condemns insolence and puts on humility, it is right that this lesson in pursuing humility should be drawn from the story of Uriah's wife.

And yet, if Solomon, that man of peace, was born of her, let us see whether there may not be a mystery in this: that once he was removed from the scene who earlier, by his marriage, laid claim to the people of the Gentiles, the Church married another husband, the true David. For Christ was called David, being given the name of his forefather, as it is written: "I have found David my servant." To him the Church was married, and, filled with the seed of the Word and the Spirit of God, she brought forth the body of Christ, that is, the Christian people. She is therefore the woman who, while her husband lives, is bound to the law, and so her husband died, so that she would not be an adulteress if she were with another man. So there is mystery in the figure and sin in the history; the guilt came through a man, the sacraments through the Word. Since we have spoken of this story more fully elsewhere, it seems we should pass over it quickly here. And rightly did holy David write the mystical fiftieth psalm about this story, on account of his marriage to Bathsheba, saying: "Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin." If the friend of God acknowledges his iniquity and that his sin stands in the way of his merits, if he even confesses that he has sinned against God, why should you blush to confess your crime, when it is the contriving of a crime, not its confession, that is shameful?

So, since David did not pass over the story of Bathsheba in his psalms, so as to teach us in it either a mystery or the practice of perfect repentance, we rightly see that she was not passed over in the Lord's genealogy either. For David himself, who took her as his wife, is declared a forerunner of the Lord's line according to the flesh. His special merit, as we have said, was to see the rise of the Church in this mystery and to receive the oracle that Christ would be born of his line. One thing he said refers to the Church: "Behold, we heard of her in Ephrathah; we found her in the fields of the forest." The other refers specifically to the promise of the Lord's body, revealed in a most plain oracle, when it is said: "Of the fruit of your body I will set upon my throne." Yet do not be careless of so great a promise, for it was not given without a condition, but: if you keep the covenant and observe the testimonies of the Lord, which he promises he will speak in the gospel, the possession of the eternal throne will lie open to you too. So much for the wife of Uriah.

As for Ahab, whose wife was Jezebel, the matter is clear enough. As for Jechoniah, Jeremiah is a sufficiently reliable witness that he was guilty of the gravest offence, so much so that he even took from him the name he had. And so the man called Jehoiakim in the books of Kings is named Jechoniah by Jeremiah, who says: "Jechoniah has been cast aside like a vessel; there is no use in him, and therefore he and his seed have been thrown out. O land, land, hear the word of the Lord: write this man down as disowned, for none of his seed shall rise to sit on the throne of David as a ruler again in Judah." For while he reigned the Babylonians laid waste Judea, and afterwards no one of his seed was ever able to obtain the kingdom in Judea. For afterwards the people, released from captivity, were under priests and tetrarchs. Hence there were tetrarchs right up to the birth of Christ, and as far as history teaches, not even they preserved the dignity of the royal line.

For it is reported by those who have handed it down to us, whether by inference, or teaching in good faith, or establishing the truth, that Idumaean bandits broke into Ascalon, a city of Palestine, and from the temple of Apollo, which stood near the walls, carried off among other captives Antipater, the son of a certain Herod, a temple servant; his father was too poor to ransom him. This Antipater, then, trained in the learning and rites of the Jews, became a friend of Hyrcanus, king of Judea, and Hyrcanus sent him as his envoy to Pompey. Because he gained success from that embassy, he used the favour it won him to aim at a share of the kingdom. After Antipater was killed out of envy at his good fortune, his son Herod was later, under Antony, appointed by decree of the senate to reign over the Jews; his son was Herod, and the other tetrarchs. We have thought it worth translating this from the Greek histories so that it may be clear that Herod, who had no kinship with the Jewish race, sought the kingdom by fraudulent deceit. Indeed, conscious of his low birth, and so that no question might be raised against his descendants on the basis of the old records, he burned their records, thinking that if he removed the evidence from public view, no other testimony could make it clear that he did not descend from the stock of the patriarchs or of the early proselytes. But, as with most human schemes, he could not forestall the discovery and investigation of the truth.

Yet so that this may not count against us, who say that Christ is of a true and royal line and that the Lord's lineage was traced through true and noble kings, let us consider the matter. When an illegitimate offshoot seized the kingdom, the order of descent, not of power, preserved the succession of his nobility; yet we have not accepted Christ himself as a king according to worldly honour. How, then, is it said: "Of the fruit of your body I will set upon my throne"? How does the angel also say of him that the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob? How is he promised a reign and yet not shown to reign? Or how does the prophet say that none of Jechoniah's seed will reign? For if Christ reigned, and Christ is of the seed of Jechoniah, the prophet lied, and the oracles lied too. But there it is not denied that Jechoniah would have descendants from his seed; and so Christ is of his seed, and the fact that Christ reigned is not contrary to the prophecy. For he did not reign with worldly honour, nor did he sit on Jechoniah's throne; he reigned on the throne of David.

But since Jeconiah himself sat on David's throne, how are we to resolve the saying that Jeconiah's descendants will not sit on David's throne, when both seem to have had the same throne? We too cannot deny that it was David's throne. Yet the throne of King David on which Christ sat is not the same one on which Jeconiah sat. Indeed, no one else of David's line could sit on his throne except Christ, because David's seed is eternal in no one else but Christ, as God himself revealed when he said: “Once for all I have sworn by my holiness that I will not lie to David: his seed shall endure for ever, and his throne like the sun before me.” Whom, then, does he mean here? Certainly not Solomon, not Rehoboam, not Nathan, but the one of whom alone he can say: “I will set his hand upon the sea and his right hand upon the rivers. He will call upon me, ‘You are my Father,’” and: “I will establish his seed for ever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven.” Solomon certainly did not sit on this throne, nor Rehoboam, nor Jeconiah. Do you want to know who sat on it? It is the one of whom the angel says to Mary: “Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” If you do not believe the angel, at least you will believe the Lord himself when he says: “You say that I am a king.” Did he too lie, then, in saying that he reigned, when he did not reign on earth? How is Scripture to be explained, when it says that he reigns yet does not show him reigning?

We have come to a sheer drop in the argument; we are stuck on a shoal and tossed about in a kind of shipwreck of the truth. Let us therefore wake Christ; let us question him, and let him answer. Let us question the Scriptures. We find that the Lord's kingdom is not of this world, for he himself said: “My kingdom is not of this world.” He who says that his kingdom is not of this world shows that it is above the world. So his kingdom both was and was not: it was not in this world, it was above this world. There was, then, another kingdom of the true David, which Christ alone received; and there was another seed of David, which endures for ever, from which Christ alone was born, who alone is the true son of David, and who alone also received his name, as it is written: “I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him.” What precedes this makes clear that it is said not of David the prophet but of the Lord, for it is written: “I have laid help upon one who is mighty, and I have exalted one chosen from my people”; for Christ alone is mighty, Christ alone is chosen. For the seed of the saints lies more in faith than in descent; and so the Apostle says: “Those who are of faith, these are the sons of Abraham.”

We think we should not pass over this point either: from the time of David down to Jeconiah, that is, down to the captivity, there were seventeen kings of Judea, yet St Matthew gave fourteen generations; and again, from Jeconiah down to Joseph, though the generations counted man by man come to twelve, he afterwards stated that fourteen generations had been set down. For this is what you have: “So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ fourteen generations.” First we must recognize what we said earlier, that there can be more successions and fewer generations; for some may live longer and beget children later, or indeed have no offspring at all. So the periods of the kings are not the same as those of the generations. That is why Matthew passed over those whom he did not consider to belong to the line of descent. For if his aim had been to describe the succession of kings, we would reasonably be troubled as to why, when the books of Kings and Chronicles agree that after Joram reigned Ahaziah, then Joash and Amaziah, and that Uzziah succeeded Amaziah, St Matthew passed over those three kings, Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah, and placed Jehoshaphat after Joram. But he placed him there not in the succession of kings but in the line of descent; indeed, he stated that he was recording generations. It may have happened that Joram fathered a child rather late and that Jehoshaphat came to the throne later, and so Joram succeeded his father in descent, though he did not succeed him in power.

As for the evangelist's seeming to count twelve generations after Jeconiah, if you pay careful attention you will be able to find the reckoning of fourteen generations here too. For twelve are counted down to Joseph, not down to Christ; the thirteenth is Christ, from Joseph. Yet it makes no difference whether the falsehood lies in two generations or in one; but even here you will find no Caphareus, no rock on which the truth is shipwrecked. For history shows that there were two Joachims, that is, two Jeconiahs: one born before the deportation, the other at the very time of the deportation, that is, father and son. So the father, who succeeded Josiah, was counted among the earlier generations; the son, who succeeded his father, that is, Josiah's grandson, among the later ones. The books of Kings show that there were two, for it is written thus: “And Pharaoh made Joachim son of Josiah king over Israel, to reign in Judea in place of Josiah his father, and changed his name to Joachim when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.” To this it adds: “And the rest of the words of Joachim and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the words and in the days of those who reigned in Judea? And Joachim slept with his fathers, and Joachim his son reigned in his place. Joachim was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem; his mother's name was Mesola. And all that his father had done in the sight of the Lord, he did as well. And in his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against Jerusalem.” You see, then, that Josiah's son was one man and his grandson another: the son was the one to whom Jeremiah gave a name, the grandson the one who was called by his father's name. And St Matthew rightly chose not to differ from the prophet, naming him Jeconiah rather than Joachim. At the same time, as we said above, he set forth more fully the fruit of the Lord's loving-kindness, since the Lord did not seek nobility of descent in every case, but fittingly chose to be born of captives and sinners, he who came to proclaim release to captives. So the evangelist did not suppress either of them, but indicated both, since each was called Jeconiah. Thus, once the younger Jeconiah is added, fourteen generations are counted. So much for Matthew.

Luke, for his part, did well. Since he could not include the many sons of Jacob, lest he seem to wander outside the line of descent in a superfluous series, he nevertheless judged that the names of the patriarchs should by no means be left out, though borne by others, that is, by men who lived much later; and he chose before the rest Joseph, Judah, Simeon and Levi. For we recognize that in the patriarchs whose descendants these were there were four kinds of virtue: in Judah, that is, the earlier one, the mystery of the Lord's passion was prophesied in a figure; in Joseph an example of chastity went before; in Simeon, the avenging of outraged honour; in Levi, the office of the priest. In Nathan too we observe the dignity of prophecy expressed, so that, since Christ Jesus alone is all things [?], different kinds of virtue might go before him in each of his ancestors as well.

Nor should mention of righteous Noah have been left out of the Lord's line of descent, so that, since the [?] of the Church was being born, he might be seen to have placed first, as the founder of his own line, the man who had founded the Church beforehand in a type. And what shall I say of Methuselah, whose years are counted beyond the flood? Since Christ alone is the one whose life felt no aging, it was fitting that in his ancestors too he should be seen not to have felt the floods. And is not Enoch a clear sign both of the Lord's loving-kindness and of his divinity, in that the Lord did not undergo death and returned to heaven, an ancestor of whose line was caught up into heaven? From this it is clear that Christ too could have avoided dying, but did not wish to, so that his death might benefit us. Enoch, indeed, was caught up so that wickedness might not change his heart; but the Lord, whom the wickedness of the world could not change, returned by the majesty of his own nature to the place from which he had come. The murderer of his brother is, of course, passed over in silence; for it was not reasonable to count among the Lord's ancestors the man who had struck down his brother, since the Lord [?] his servants, so as to grant them the honour of the name of brothers. Nor is it without purpose that Seth was not passed over, whom Adam received as a later offspring, so that, since there are two generations of the people, it might be signified in a type that the Lord Jesus Christ was to be counted in the later rather than the earlier generation.

Now as for Adam himself, who according to the Apostle bore the figure of Christ, what could have been more beautifully fitting than that the most holy line of descent should begin from the Son of God and lead back to the son of God? That the one who was created should go before in figure, so that the one who was born might follow in truth; that the one made in the image of God should lead the way, for whose sake the Image of God would come down? And if we examine the mystery of the first sin: Adam tasted of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, deceived by the devil and persuaded by Eve, so that Christ, before he knew evil, might choose the good for us and, persuaded by the Church, might bring to nothing the snares of the dread serpent, as it is written: “For before the child knows good or evil, he does not trust in wickedness, so as to choose what is good”; and: “Before he knows how to call father or mother, he will take the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria.” For this is the child whose cradle the Magi filled with the spoils of the East, because the nation that before Christ was unbelieving, now that its faith was changed, offered to the Lord as triumphal booty the spoils stripped from its idols.

These matters concerning the genealogy of Christ, brother, are not unknown to you, but I thought they should be followed up at greater length, so that no one who went over them in the Gospel with too little attention might be somewhat unsettled. The holy evangelists, hastening on to greater miracles and more divine deeds of the Lord, thought these things should be touched on briefly rather than spread out at length. So, after the manner of those who think it enough to point out to people who do not know the roads certain markers, as it were, of the route and its paths, we gather up the paths of the spiritual way (whether with a successful outcome for the truth I shall see; certainly with faith as our devout guide) and press on into the hidden depths of the mysteries. We fear that someone, on reading these things, might, as the proverb says, be “like a boy with a sword,” not knowing in his infancy how to handle powerful weapons, and might receive a wound through his lack of foresight rather than salvation from his reading. For the weak are wounded by their own weapons, and one who does not know how to carry arms cannot use them well. And so in matters of faith a mature man is required, in whom infancy does not crawl along the ground of knowledge, in whom no feeble age, lacking the senses of mystical understanding, totters; an age that, having lost the strength of youth, no longer seeks the crown of the glorious contest, and like an aging eagle, which once used to snatch up a hare or a goose in its talons, but now, worn out by age, seeks the unfledged young of smaller birds, like those who cannot take more solid food.
BOOK FOUR.

I think the work we have completed on the Lord's genealogy was not out of place. It was certainly not fruitless to linger a while over the Lord's ancestors. Think of people setting out to cross a great sea by sailing along the coast. Like us, they lack the confidence to take the shorter course over deep water, and they often stop to visit fields and cities along the shore, charmed by the beauty of the places. How much more, then, should we, set on so vast a deep, a deep not of the elements but of heavenly deeds, choose the nearer harbours and love to put in often, so that no one, worn out by the tedium of a long voyage, finds himself unable to hold back the nausea of disgust. Certainly, if anyone has noticed the treacherous flaws of an unsafe vessel, the books offer him frequent harbours: he may lower the sails of his ears and drop the anchor of his reading. Whoever puts in to harbour is not thought to have abandoned the ship, but to have finished the course.

In many places, perhaps, the very charm of the spot will invite the traveller to stop. Consider Ulysses, as the stories tell of him. (The prophet too said, "The daughters of the Sirens shall dwell there"; and even if the prophet had not said it, no one could rightly object, since Scripture has also mentioned the giants and the valley of the Titans.) After ten years of exile, in which war was waged at Troy, and ten more years of wandering, Ulysses was hurrying home. Yet the Lotus-eaters could hold him back with the sweetness of their fruit, the gardens of Alcinous could delay him, and finally the Sirens, luring him with the song of their voices, had almost brought him to that famous shipwreck of pleasure. That would have happened if he had not stopped up his companions' ears with wax against the sound of the alluring song. If all this could hold back Ulysses, how much more fitting it is for religious men to be charmed by wonder at heavenly deeds! Here we are not to taste the sweetness of fruit, but that bread which came down from heaven. We are not to gaze at the vegetables of Alcinous, but at the sacraments of Christ, for "let the one who is weak eat vegetables." So our ears are not to be shut but opened, so that the voice of Christ can be heard. Whoever has taken it in will not fear shipwreck. He need not be tied to the mast with bodily ropes like Ulysses; his soul must be bound to the wood of the cross with spiritual bonds, so that it is not moved by the lures of wantonness and does not turn the course of nature aside into the danger of pleasure.

The story is coloured with poetic inventions. It tells of certain maidens who lived on a rocky seashore. If their sweet voices drew any sailors to turn their ship aside for the pleasure of their ears, the maidens led them onto hidden shoals, tricked them with a treacherous anchorage, and destroyed them in a wretched shipwreck. The tale is put together for show and painted over with an elaborate comparison, so that the sea, the women's voices and the shallow shores are all invented. But what sea is more abrupt than the world, so treacherous, so changeable, so deep, so stormy with the blasts of unclean spirits? What does the figure of the maidens mean, if not the lure of unmanly pleasure, which weakens the constancy of the mind it has captured? And what are those shoals, if not the rocks that wreck our salvation? Nothing is so hidden as the danger of worldly delight. While it soothes the soul, it overwhelms its life, and it dashes the mind's understanding against rocks of the body.

Rightly, then, our Lord Jesus trains us by his fasting and by the desert against the lures of pleasure. The Lord of all allows himself to be tempted by the devil so that in him we might all learn to conquer. Let us notice, then, that the evangelist did not idly describe three things that the Lord set in their order. There are three things that serve the needs of human salvation: the sacrament, the desert, the fast. For no one is crowned unless he has competed according to the rules, and no one is admitted to the contest of virtue unless he has first been washed from every stain of sin and consecrated by the gift of heavenly grace.

So the Lord came to the washing, so that the grace of the mystery might be proved to us both by sight and by sense. The Law was proclaimed with heaven and earth as witnesses. But here heaven is no longer called as a witness; it performs the witness's office itself, when the voice of God is carried down from heaven. This is so that you might believe that the mystery of the Godhead, hidden for ages in God, is greater than the Law. At the same time, so that no doubt in your mind may make you stumble over the mystery of faith, invisible things are shown to you working visibly.

The Lord came to the washing, for he became all things for your sake. To those under the Law he was circumcised as though under the Law, though he himself was not under the Law, so that he might win those who are under the Law. He joined those who were without the Law in the fellowship of a meal, so that he might win those who lived without the Law. To the weak he became weak through the suffering of his body, so that he might win them. In the end he became all things to all: poor with the poor, rich with the rich, weeping with those who weep, hungry with the hungry, thirsty with the thirsty, lavish with those who have plenty. He is in prison with the poor man, he weeps with Mary, he feasts with the apostles, he thirsts with the Samaritan woman, he hungers in the desert. He hungered so that the food the first man had tasted by his transgression might be cancelled by the Lord's fast. To our peril Adam satisfied his hunger for the knowledge of good and evil; to our profit this man took hunger upon himself.

"Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the devil." It is fitting to recall how the first Adam was cast out of paradise into the desert, so that you may notice how the second Adam returned from the desert to paradise. See how the old judgements are untied at their own knots, and God's blessings are restored along their own tracks. Adam came from virgin earth, Christ from a Virgin. The one was made in the image of God; this one is the image of God. The one was set above all irrational animals; this one above all living things. Through a woman came folly, through a Virgin wisdom; death came through a tree, life through the cross. The one, stripped of spiritual things, covered himself with the cast-off leaves of a tree; this one, stripped of worldly things, did not desire the coverings of the body. Adam was in the desert, Christ was in the desert. For he knew where he could find the condemned man, whom he would call back to paradise once his error was undone. But Adam could not return clothed in worldly coverings, and no one can live in paradise unless he is stripped of guilt. So he put off the old man and put on the new, so that, since divine decrees cannot be undone, it was the person rather than the sentence that was changed.

But Adam lost the way he had been given in paradise because he had no guide. How then could he, without a guide, find the lost way again from the desert, where temptations are many, the climb to virtue is hard, and the slide into error is easy? The nature of virtue is like that of trees. While they are still small, rising from the earth toward the heights, and growing in the youth of their tender leaves, they are exposed to the poison of a savage tooth and can easily be cut down or burned. But once a tree has set itself on a deep root and lifted itself up with lofty branches, it is sturdy, and the bites of wild beasts, the arms of country folk and the storms of the various winds will try it in vain.

What guide, then, should he appoint against so many lures of the world and so many tricks of the devil? For he knew that our struggle is first against flesh and blood, and then against powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Should he appoint an angel? But an angel too has fallen, and legions of angels have barely helped individual men. Should he send a seraph? A seraph too came down to earth, into the midst of a people of unclean lips, and cleansed the lips of only one prophet by applying a coal. Another guide had to be sought, one whom we could all follow. Who could be so great a guide, able to help everyone, except the one who is above all? Who could set me above the world, except the one who is greater than the world? Who could be so great a guide as to lead male and female, Jew and Greek, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free under one leadership, except Christ alone, who is all and in all?

For there are many snares wherever we go. The devil sets snares in the body, snares in the Law, snares on the pinnacles of temples and on the ledges of walls; snares in philosophers, snares in desires (for "the eye of a harlot is a snare for the sinner"); a snare in money, a snare in religion, a snare in the pursuit of chastity. For the human mind is swayed by the slightest things, and is often pushed this way and that by the cunning of the one persuading it. The devil sees a religious man who honours God with reverence, treats what is holy as holy, and would admit no insult to it. He trips him up in his very religion, making him disbelieve that the Son of God truly took on this flesh of ours, this body of ours, this frailty of our limbs. Yet the suffering belonged to the body, and the Godhead remained untouched by injury. So guilt arises out of religion, for "every one who denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God." He sees a man of pure and unblemished chastity, and he urges him to condemn marriage, so that he may be cast out of the Church and, by his very zeal for chastity, be cut off from the chaste body. Another has heard that there is "one God, from whom are all things," and he worships and reveres him. The devil lies in wait for him and shuts his ears, so that he does not hear that there is "one Lord, through whom are all things." So by excessive piety he drives him into impiety: while he separates the Father from the Son, he also confuses Father and Son, and thinks that the one is a single person rather than a single power. And so, not knowing the measure of faith, he falls into the misery of faithlessness.

How then shall we escape these snares, so that we too can say, "Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we are set free"? He does not say, "I broke the snare"; David did not dare to say that. He says, "Our help is in the name of the Lord." He wanted to show from where the snare would be undone, and to prophesy that the one who would break the snare laid by the devil's deceit would come into this life.

But the snare could not be broken better than by showing the devil some prey. Then, as he hurried toward the prey, he would be caught in his own snares, so that I could say, "They prepared snares for my feet, and they themselves fell into them." What could that prey be, except a body? So this trick had to be played on the devil: the Lord Jesus would take a body, and a corruptible body, a weak body, so that he could be crucified in weakness. If it had been a spiritual body, he would not have said, "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." Listen, then, to both voices, the voice of the weak flesh and the voice of the willing spirit. "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me": this is the voice of the flesh. "Yet not what I will, but what you will": here you have the devotion and the strength of the spirit. Why do you reject the Lord's condescension? It was condescension that he took my body; it was condescension that he took on my injuries and my weaknesses. The nature of God certainly could not feel these, since even human nature has learned to despise them, or to bear and endure them. So let us follow Christ, as it is written: "You shall walk after the Lord your God and cling to him." To whom shall I cling but to Christ? As Paul said, "Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit with him." Let us then follow in his footsteps, so that we may return from the desert to paradise.

See by what roads we are led back. Now Christ is in the desert. He drives man on, instructs him, shapes him, trains him, and anoints him with spiritual oil. [?] When he saw that man had grown stronger, he led him through sown and fruitful fields. This was when the Jews complained that his disciples were plucking ears of grain from the crop on the Sabbath, for he had already placed his apostles in cultivated land and in fruitful work. Later, at the time of his passion, he set him in paradise. For this is what you read: "When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he entered with his disciples." The prophet teaches in the Song of Songs that a garden is better than a fruitful field, when he says, "A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride, a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed; your shoots are a paradise." For this is the pure and spotless virginity of the soul, which no terror of punishment, no lure of worldly pleasure and no love of life can draw away from the faith. Finally, this evangelist, more than the others, testifies that man was called back by the Lord's power. He alone presents the Lord saying to the thief, "Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise."

So Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, is driven into the desert. He goes by design, to challenge the devil, for if the devil had not fought, Christ would not have won the victory for me. He goes as a mystery, to free that Adam from exile. He goes as an example, to show us that the devil envies those who strive for better things, and that this is when we must be most on our guard, so that the weakness of our mind does not abandon the grace of the mystery.

"Forty days": you recognize a mystical number. You remember that for that many days the waters of the deep were poured out. By a fast of that many days the prophet was sanctified, and the kindness of a clearer sky was poured back. By a fast of that many days holy Moses earned the receiving of the Law. For that many years the fathers, living in the wilderness, received the bread of angels and the gift of heavenly food, and they were not allowed to enter the promised land until they had completed the time of the mystical number. By a fast of that many days the Lord's entrance into the Gospel is opened to us. So whoever wishes to gain the glory of the Gospel and the fruit of the resurrection must not break the mystical fast. Moses in the Law and Christ in his Gospel, with the authority of both Testaments, laid it down as the faithful contest of virtue.

But what does it mean that the evangelist noted that the Lord was hungry, when we see nothing of the kind stated about the fasts of Moses and Elijah? Is the endurance of men stronger than God? No. He who could not hunger for forty days showed that what he hungered for was not food for the body but salvation. At the same time he was provoking the adversary, who was already afraid, having been wounded by the forty days' fast. So the Lord's hunger is a holy trick. The devil, fearing something greater, was already on his guard; but, enticed by the appearance of hunger, he would tempt him as a man, and so the triumph would not be prevented. Learn this mystery too: [?] it was the single judgement of the Holy Spirit that Christ should offer himself to be tempted by the devil.

"And the devil said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.'" We are taught that the devil has three chief weapons with which he usually arms himself to wound the human mind: the first is gluttony, the second boasting, the third ambition. He began where he had already conquered. And so I begin to conquer in Christ where I was conquered in Adam, provided that Christ, the image of the Father, is my example of virtue. Let us learn, then, to beware of gluttony and to beware of self-indulgence, for it is a weapon of the devil. The snare is laid when the table of a royal banquet is spread, which often makes the mind lose its constancy. For we must avoid the snare not only when we hear the devil's words, but also when we see his abundance. You have learned the devil's weapon, then: take up the shield of faith and the breastplate of abstinence.

But what is meant by the opening of his speech, "If you are the Son of God," unless he knew that the Son of God was to come? But he did not think he had come in this weakness of the body. He is both probing and tempting: he professes to believe in God and tries to make a fool of the man.

But look at Christ's weapons, with which he won the victory for you, not for himself. By his majesty he showed elsewhere, through the changing of one nature into another, that stones can be turned into bread. Yet here he teaches you that nothing should be done at the devil's bidding, nor for the sake of displaying your power. At the same time, learn in this very temptation the devil's crafty cunning. He tempts in order to probe, and probes in order to tempt. The Lord, on the other hand, deceives in order to conquer, and conquers in such a way as still to deceive. For if he had changed the nature of the stone, he would have revealed himself as the Creator. So he answered in a middle way, saying, "It is written that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God."

You see what kind of weapons he uses to defend man against the attack of spiritual wickedness, fenced in and fortified against the provocations of gluttony. He does not use his power as God (for what good would that have done me?). Instead, as a man, he calls on the help that is common to us all: intent on the food of divine reading, he neglects the hunger of the body and gains the nourishment of the heavenly word. Intent on this, Moses did not long for bread; intent on this, Elijah did not feel the hunger of his long fast. For whoever follows the word cannot long for earthly bread, since he receives the substance of the heavenly bread. There is no doubt that divine things surpass human things, and spiritual things surpass bodily ones. So whoever longs for true life waits for that bread which strengthens human hearts by its imperceptible substance. At the same time, by saying "Man does not live by bread alone," he shows that it was a man who was tempted, that is, the nature he took from us, not his divinity.

Next comes the weapon of boasting, by which people easily fall into sin. For when men want to boast of the glory of their virtue, they come down from the place and position their merits had earned. "And he led him," it says, "to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple."

That is what boasting is like: while each person thinks he is climbing higher, he is pushed down lower by claiming lofty deeds for himself. "And he said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.'"
Truly a devilish voice, which tries to cast the human mind down from a higher rank of merit! For what is so characteristic of the devil as to urge each person to throw himself down?

So learn, you too, to conquer the devil. The Spirit drives you: follow the Spirit. Do not let the lure of the flesh call you back. Filled with the Spirit, learn to despise pleasures. Fast, if you want to conquer. It follows that the devil will think he must tempt you through another person. Christ, as the stronger, is tempted face to face; you are tempted through a person. And it is the devil's word when someone says, "You are strong: eat and drink, and stay as you are." Do not trust yourself. Do not be ashamed to need the safeguards that Christ did not need. Yet he did not neglect them, so as to teach you, saying, "Take care that your hearts are not weighed down with wine and drunkenness." Paul was not ashamed, who said, "I strive in this way, not as one beating the air." The apostle was indeed not beating the air, but he was striking the powers of the air. "But," he says, "I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be found disqualified."

At the same time the devil reveals his own weakness and malice, for the devil can harm no one unless that person throws himself down. Whoever leaves heavenly things behind and chooses earthly ones runs into a kind of voluntary headlong fall from a life that is slipping away. At the same time, since the devil saw that his weapon had been blunted, he who had subjected all men to his own power began to judge that this was more than a man. But the Lord again judged that not even the things prophesied about him should be done at the devil's bidding. Keeping the authority of his own divinity, he met the devil's cunning in such a way that, since the devil had put forward an example from the Scriptures, he was defeated by examples from the Scriptures. For God has power to conquer, but for me it is Scripture

that conquers. Learn here also that Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, and often prepares a snare for the faithful out of the divine Scriptures themselves. This is how he makes heretics, how he guts the faith, how he attacks the laws of piety. So do not let a heretic catch you because he can produce some examples from the Scriptures, and do not let him claim authority because he seems learned. The devil too uses the testimony of the Scriptures, not to teach but to entrap and deceive. He notices someone devoted to religion, distinguished in virtues, mighty in signs and works. He sets the snare of boasting for such a man, to puff him up with pride, so that he trusts not in piety but in boasting, and does not credit God but claims the credit for himself. That is why the apostles commanded demons not in their own name but in the name of Christ, so that they would not seem to claim anything for themselves. So Peter heals the paralytic, saying, "In the name of Jesus of Nazareth, rise and walk." Learn from Paul too to flee boasting. "I know a man," he says, "whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows, who was caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. Of such a man I will boast, but of myself I will not boast, except in my weaknesses."
