So here too the devil, because he sensed that Christ was strong, holds out boasting, which deceives even the strong. But the Lord answered, "You shall not tempt the Lord your God." In this you recognize that Christ is both Lord and God, and that Father and Son are of one power, as it is written, "I and the Father are one." So if the devil holds up "one" against you, answer him that it is written, "I and the Father are one." Mark the word "one," so that you do not divide the power; mark the word "one," so that you do not separate the Father and the Son. "And the devil led him again onto a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time."

It is fitting that worldly and earthly things are shown "in a moment of time." This expresses not so much the speed of the sight as the frailty of a power that is doomed to fall. For all those things pass away in a moment, and the world's honour has often departed before it has even arrived. What in the world can be lasting, when the ages themselves do not last? Here we are taught to despise the gusts of empty ambition, because every worldly rank is subject to the devil's power,

fragile in its use and empty in its fruit. But how is it that here the devil gives power, when elsewhere you read that all power is from God? Can anyone serve two masters, or receive power from two? Is this then a contradiction? Not at all. But see that all things are from God. For the world is not without God, since the world too was made through him; yet although it was made by God, its works are evil, because the world lies in the evil one. The ordering of the world is from God, the works of the world from the evil one. So too the ordering of powers is from God, but the ambition for power is from the evil one. Indeed, "There is no power," he says, "except from God, and those that are from God are ordained" — not given, but ordained — and "whoever resists the power," he says, "resists the ordinance of God." Here too, although the devil says that he gives power, he does not deny that all these things were permitted to him for a time. So the one who permitted it ordained it, and power is not evil; the one who uses power badly is. Do you want, then, not to fear the power? Do good, and you will have praise from it. So power is not evil, but ambition is. Indeed, the ordering of power is from God to such a degree that whoever uses power well is God's minister. "He is God's minister," he says, "to you for good." So the fault lies not in the office but in the officeholder; nor can God's ordinance be displeasing, but only the conduct of the one who administers it. To draw an example from heavenly things down to earthly ones: the emperor confers an honor and is praised for it. But if anyone uses that honor badly, the fault is not the emperor's but the judge's. Crimes have their own culprit: it is not power that entangles each person, but his own conduct in office.

What then? Is it good to use power, to strive for honor? It is good if it is conferred, not seized. Yet even this good must be distinguished. For one use is good in the world, another belongs to perfect virtue; for it is good that the pursuit of knowing the Godhead be hindered by no occupations. Although there are many goods, there is only one eternal life. "And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent." And so, since the fruit of eternal life is the greatest, and God alone is the rewarder of eternal life, let us worship God alone, our Lord, and serve him only, so that he alone may reward us with the richest fruit. Let us flee everything that is subject to the devil's power, lest, like a wicked tyrant, he use the power he has received with cruelty against those whom he finds within his kingdom.

So power is not from the devil, though it is exposed to the devil's snares. Nor is the ordering of powers evil on that account, because the powers are exposed to evil. For it is good to seek God, yet certain twists and errors creep into the very search. If the seeker turns aside into sacrilege through a perverse interpretation, the seeker's offense turns out worse than if he had not sought at all. Yet the fault is not in the seeking but in the seeker; it is not the search that is exposed to evil, but the disposition of the one who seeks. And if the one who seeks God is often tempted because of the frailty of the flesh and the narrowness of the mind, how much more exposed is the one who seeks the world! Ambition is all the more pernicious for this very reason, that it is a kind of flattering little go-between for high office; and often those whom no vices delight, whom no luxury could move and no avarice overthrow, ambition makes into criminals. For it has charm in public and danger at home, and in order to rule others it first serves. It bows in servility so as to be rewarded with honor, and while it wants to be loftier, it becomes lowlier, since in power itself what is preeminent belongs to another; for it commands through the laws, yet is a slave to itself.

Someone will perhaps say that only one who has done evil is afraid; yet the one who sails the sea is more afraid. By contrast, one who stands on the unmoving ground of dry land does not usually fear shipwreck; but if he boards the moving element, he becomes exposed to more frequent dangers. Flee, then, the sea of the world, and you will not fear shipwreck. Although the blasts of blowing winds often beat upon the tops of trees, yet with their roots firmly set there is no fall; but at sea, when the winds rage, even if not all are shipwrecked, all are in danger. So too, when the adverse blasts of spiritual wickedness blow, no one is safe either on the sand or on the open sea, and the ships of Tarshish are often shattered by a violent wind.

So much for the moral sense. As for the mystical order, you see the chains of the ancient error loosed in their own footsteps, so that first the snare of gluttony, second that of compliance, and third that of ambition might be undone. For Adam was enticed by food, and, having passed over through a pliant judgment to the place of the forbidden tree, he also incurred the crime of rash ambition in aspiring to likeness with God. And so the Lord first loosed the bonds of the old injury, so that, having shaken off the yoke of captivity, we might learn to conquer sins with the protection of the Scriptures.

If the Lord Jesus did not desire what was his own, why should you seek what belongs to others? If the Creator of all things despised the glory of the world through the virtue of embracing poverty, why do you disdain what you were born to and covet what is not owed you? Why do you demand things which cannot last long for your use, but will last long for your punishment? Beware of snares, beware of deceits. And precisely because the crafty devil shakes the whole world with his deceit in order to overthrow man, and fights with every allurement of the world, you must guard all the more against his blandishments. It was not food that swayed Eve, nor forgetfulness of the commandments that left her defenseless; it was the enticing ambition for a promised honor that deceived her. Had she been willing to worship the Lord alone, she would not have sought what was not owed her. And so a remedy is given to blunt the weapon of ambition: that we serve the Lord alone. For religious devotion is free of ambition.

"And when every temptation was ended, the devil departed from him until a time." These three kinds of vice are shown to be the sources of nearly all sins; for Scripture would not have said that every temptation was ended unless these three contained the material of all offenses, whose seeds must be guarded against at their very origin. The end of temptations, then, is the end of desires, because the causes of temptations are the causes of desires. And the causes of desires are the pleasure of the flesh, the appearance of glory, and the greed for power. How religious it seems not to refuse to live with a Christian woman! But frequent temptation comes from it. If the devil sees people intent on God, he makes suggestions in order to deceive them; so however confident you are in your resolve, beware of temptation, knowing your nature. If you remember, Paul too prescribed that these three be guarded against, pointing out that there are three kinds of sin, and, free of them, he awaited the crown of righteousness. "For we were never," he says, "in a word of flattery, nor on a pretext of greed — God is witness — nor seeking glory from men." And so he conquered the devil and sought the crown.

You see, then, that the devil himself is not persistent in his efforts. He usually yields to true virtue. And although he does not cease to envy, he is afraid to press on, because he shrinks from being triumphed over too often. So when he heard the name of God, he "departed," it says, "until a time"; for afterward he came, not to tempt, but to fight openly.

So divine Scripture teaches you that your struggle is not against flesh and blood but against spiritual snares. You see the greatness of the Christian man, who contends with the rulers of the world and, though placed on earth, fights with strength of soul against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. For we do not contend for earthly things, that we should do battle on earth; rather, since spiritual prizes are set before us — the kingdom of God and the inheritance of Christ — spiritual obstacles must first be overcome. A crown is set before us; contests must be undergone. No one can be crowned unless he has conquered, and no one can conquer unless he has first fought. The fruit of the crown itself is greater where the labor is greater; for narrow and strait is the way that leads to life, but broad and spacious is the way that leads to death. And so we ought by no means to fear temptation; for it is the cause of victory and the material of triumphs.

That rich man who felt no temptation in the world is in torment in the underworld, while the poor man Lazarus, who was so afflicted and worn down by poverty and disease that his sores were licked by dogs, gained through the hardship of this wretched life the crown of eternal glory. For many are the tribulations, not of just anyone, but of the righteous. Indeed, those whom the Lord loves he often chastens. Peter was tempted so that he denied; he denied so that he might weep. And what shall I say of the rest? Job, surely, was approved by God; but though he was approved, he was not yet a victor. His devotion had been proved, yet he did not have the prize of virtue, and so he is offered up to be tempted, that he might be made more glorious.

In that contest, too, it matters that you observe the stages. The devil does not have just one weapon; he keeps hurling darts, so as to conquer either by reward or by weariness. First he wounds through greed, second through family affection, third through health; for he fights with wounds of mind and body alike. The very variety of the temptations also corresponds to the variety of those who contend. The rich man is pressed by the loss of what he covets, the father by the loss of his children, the man by pains, the body by sores. How many these weapons are! That is why the Lord chose to have nothing he could lose, and so he came here poor, that the devil might have nothing to take away. Do you want to know how true this is? Hear the Lord himself saying: "The prince of this world comes, and finds nothing in me." Nor did he wish to be the father of a few, so that he might be the father of all — and it would be in vain to tempt with bodily sores one who despised all the sufferings of the body — and at the same time to show us that an unstained victory was due to him once the enemy of the body had been driven off. But Job, as a man, is tempted with what was his own, Christ with what is public; from the one his patrimony is taken away, to the other the kingdom of the world is offered. Nor is the devil wholly without guile, since he was afraid to provoke the Son of God: the one he tempts with injuries, the other with rewards. Job says like a humble servant: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away"; Christ, conscious of his nature and of the divine plan, smiles at having his own things offered to him. And to return to Job: messenger presses upon messenger, wounds are doubled, yet the brave athlete is not disturbed in mind. A wife is brought in, the lure of the first deception; Christ, born of a virgin, had no wife liable to error. Friends are brought in to overwhelm him with wicked counsel as he resists; but in all that happened to him Job never sinned with his lips in the sight of God.

For when he curses the day, saying, "Let the day perish on which I was born," and further on, "And let him curse it who cursed that day, who is ready to overpower the great sea monster," this belongs to prophecy, because our Lord Jesus Christ overpowered the devil as the monster of this stormy world; and he desires the day of his fleshly birth to perish, so that his day may be counted in regeneration. "Let the worldly day perish," he says, "so that the spiritual day may dawn." So holy Job, in his temptation, was speaking mysteries; for he who was conquering the world was seeing Christ.

Let us, then, not fear temptations, but rather glory in temptations, saying, "When we are weak, then we are strong"; for that is when the crown of righteousness is woven. But perhaps that crown is suited to Paul; we, however, since there are many crowns, ought to hope for one or another. In the world the laurel is a crown, and the shield is a crown. But for you a crown of delights is set before you: "For a crown of delights will overshadow you." And elsewhere: "With the shield of his good will he will surround you"; and the one whom the Lord loved he crowned with glory and honor too. So he who wills to give a crown suggests temptations; and whenever you are tempted, know that a crown is being prepared. Take away the contests of the martyrs, and you have taken away their crowns; take away their torments, and you have taken away their beatitudes.

Was not Joseph's temptation the consecration of his virtue? Was not the injury of prison the crown of his chastity? How could he have gained a share in the kingdom in Egypt, had he not been sold by his brothers? That this was done by God's will, so that the righteous man might be proved, he himself showed when he said: "So that it might come about, as today, that a great people should be fed." We ought not, then, to fear the temptations of the world as evils, since good rewards are won through them; rather, considering the human condition, we should pray that we may undergo only such temptations as we are able to bear.

"And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee." Here is fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah, who says: "The region of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and the rest who dwell on the coast, and those along the sea and beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles — the people who sat in the shadow of death have seen a great light." For who is the great light but Christ, who enlightens every man coming into this world? Then he took the book, to show

that he himself is the one who spoke in the prophets, and to refute the sacrileges of the faithless, who say that the God of the Old Testament is one and the God of the New another, or who say that Christ had his beginning from the virgin. For how did he begin from the virgin who, before the virgin, was saying: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me"? You see the Trinity, coeternal and perfect.

The Scripture of the Law speaks of him as God and man, perfect in both; it speaks also of the Father and of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is shown to be a fellow worker when he descended upon Christ in bodily form like a dove, when the Son of God was baptized in the river and the Father spoke from heaven. What greater testimony, then, do we seek than that he declared with his own voice that it was he who spoke in the prophets? He is anointed with spiritual oil and heavenly power, so that he might water the poverty of the human condition with the eternal treasure of the resurrection, turn back the captivity of the mind, enlighten the blindness of souls, and proclaim the year of the Lord, spread over endless ages — a year that knows no return to the round of labor, but grants men continuous fruit and rest. And he stooped to every service so far that he did not even disdain the office of reader; while we were impious, who, looking at his body, denied the faith in his divinity that ought to have been gathered from the miracles of his works.

"Amen, I say to you, that no prophet is accepted in his own country." Envy is plainly exposed here, which, forgetting the love owed to one's fellow citizens, turns the causes of love into bitter hatred. At the same time, by this example and saying alike, it is made clear that you wait in vain for the help of heavenly mercy if you envy the fruits of another's virtue. For the Lord scorns the envious, and he turns the miracles of his power away from those who persecute divine gifts in others. For the deeds of the Lord's flesh are a pattern of his divinity, and his invisible things are shown to us through the things that are visible.

Not without reason, then, does the Savior explain why he performed no miracles of power in his own country, lest anyone perhaps think that our affection for our country ought to be less. For he who loved all could not fail to love his fellow citizens; but those who envy have disowned themselves from the love of their country, for love is not jealous, is not puffed up. Yet his country is not without a share in divine benefits. For what greater miracle is there than that Christ was born in it? See, then, what evil envy brings. Because of envy a country is judged unworthy to have its citizen work in it, though it was worthy to have the Son of God born in it.

"In truth I say to you, there were many widows in the days of Elijah." Not that the days belonged to Elijah, but they were days in which Elijah worked; or else because he made day for those who saw in his works the light of spiritual grace and were turned to the Lord. And so heaven was opened to those who saw the eternal and divine mysteries, and was shut when there was famine, because there was no abundance of the knowledge of God.

But I have written more fully about this when I wrote about widows. "And there were many lepers in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian." Clearly this saying of the Lord instructs us for our salvation and urges us to zeal in revering God, since no one is shown to have been healed and freed from the disease that stains the body except one who sought healing with religious devotion. For divine benefits are conferred not on those who sleep but on those who keep watch. And with a well-chosen example for comparison the arrogance of envious fellow citizens is beaten back, and the Lord's deed is shown to agree with the ancient Scriptures. For in the books of Kings too we read that a Gentile, Naaman, was freed from the stains of leprosy by the prophet's word, while leprosy of body and mind alike was consuming very many Jews; indeed, the history records that those four men who, driven by famine, were the first to make their way into the camp of the king of Syria were lepers. Why, then, did the prophet not cure his brothers, not cure his fellow citizens, not heal his own people, while he healed strangers — healed those who had no observance of the Law and no fellowship in religion — unless because the remedy depends on the will, not on the nation, and the divine gift is won by prayers, not conferred by right of birth? Learn to ask for what you wish to obtain; the benefits of heavenly gifts do not attend the disdainful.

But although the simple explanation shapes our moral disposition, the grace of the mystery is not hidden either. For just as later things are derived from earlier ones, so also earlier things are confirmed by later ones. I said in another book that in that widow to whom Elijah was sent a type of the Church was foreshadowed. It is fitting that the people should follow the Church. That people was gathered from foreigners; that people was formerly leprous, formerly stained, before it was baptized in the mystic river; the same people, after the sacraments of baptism, washed clean of the stains of body and mind, began to be no longer leprous but an unstained virgin without wrinkle. Rightly, then, Naaman is described as great in the sight of his master and admirable in countenance, since in his type salvation was declared to the Gentiles to come. On the advice of a holy girl, who had come as a captive into the enemy's power when the strength of her fellow citizens was broken, he was urged to hope for salvation from the prophet, and he was healed not by the command of an earthly king but by the generosity of divine mercy.

Why is he told to immerse himself a mystic number of times? Why is the river Jordan chosen? "Are not," he says, "the Abana and the Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than the Jordan?" But in anger he preferred them; on reflection he chose the Jordan. For anger does not know the mystery; faith knows it. Learn the grace of saving baptism: the one who went down a leper came up one of the faithful. Learn that spiritual sacraments are signified: a remedy for the body is sought, and one for the mind is gained; the flesh is washed, and the heart is washed. For I see that the leprosy of the mind was cleansed no less than that of the body, since after baptism, with the filth of his former error wiped away, he declares that he will not offer to foreign gods the sacrifices he promises to the Lord.

Learn also the precepts of fitting virtue: he proved his faith who refused rewards. Learn from both teachings, of words and of deeds, what you should follow. You have the Lord's command and the prophet's example: to receive freely, to give freely, and not to sell the ministry but to offer it. For the grace of God is not appraised at a price, nor is profit sought in the sacraments, but the service of the priest.

Yet it is not enough that you yourself do not seek profit; the hands of your household must also be restrained. Nor is it only demanded that you keep yourself alone chaste and unstained; for the apostle did not say "you alone," but "keep yourself chaste." What is required, then, is not only your own purity from this kind of trafficking, but also that of your household. For a priest must be blameless, ruling his own household well, having his children in submission with all chastity. "But if anyone does not know how to rule his own household, how will he take care of the church?" So instruct your household, exhort them, watch over them; and if a servant deceives you — for I do not exclude human weakness — once caught, let him be dismissed after the prophet's example. Leprosy quickly follows a shameful wage, and money wrongly gained stains body and soul. "You have taken money," he says, "and with it you will acquire fields and vineyards and olive groves and flocks; and the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your seed forever." You see that the heir's succession is condemned for the deed of its author; for the guilt of selling a mystery cannot be expiated, and the vengeance of heavenly grace passes on to descendants. Thus the Moabites and others shall not enter until the third and fourth generation — that is, to interpret it more simply, until the succession of many generations should wipe out the guilt of their ancestors.

But since those who sinned against God through the error of idolatry appear to have been punished to the fourth generation, the sentence by which Gehazi's seed is condemned forever by prophetic authority for his desire for gain certainly seems harsher — especially since our Lord Jesus Christ has granted forgiveness of sins to all through the washing of regeneration — unless you are to understand it as a seed of vices rather than of descent? For just as those who are children of the promise are reckoned as good seed, so those who are children of error are reckoned as bad seed. For the Jews too are of their father the devil, not by succession of the flesh, of course, but of crime. So all the covetous, all the avaricious, possess Gehazi's leprosy along with their riches, and with their ill-gotten wages they have amassed not so much an estate of possessions as a treasury of crimes, with eternal punishment and short-lived fruit. For while riches are perishable, the punishment is everlasting, since neither the avaricious nor the drunkard nor the idolater shall possess the kingdom of God.
And when they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath, and they rose up and drove him out of the city.

The Lord had foretold the sacrileges of the Jews long before through the prophet. In a verse of a psalm he had declared what he would suffer once he had taken a body, saying: "They repaid me evil for good." In the gospel he teaches that this was fulfilled. For while he was spreading his benefits among the peoples, they were heaping injuries on him. Nor is it any wonder that they lost salvation, since they drove the Saviour from their borders. For the Lord is a teacher of conduct, and by his own example he taught his apostles to become all things to all men. He does not reject the willing or bind the unwilling. He does not resist those who drive him out, and he does not fail those who ask. So elsewhere, when the Gerasenes could not bear his mighty works, he left them as weak and ungrateful.

At the same time, understand that the suffering of his body was not forced on him but voluntary, and that he was not seized by the Jews but offered himself. For when he wills, he is taken; when he wills, he slips away; when he wills, he is hanged; when he wills, he is not held. Here too he had gone up to the brow of the hill to be thrown down, and behold, he came down through the midst of them, for the minds of the raging men were suddenly changed or struck dumb. The hour of his passion had not yet come. Indeed, he still preferred to heal the Jews rather than destroy them, so that when their fury came to nothing they might stop wanting what they could not accomplish. You see, then, that what he did here belongs to his divinity, and that his being taken there belongs to his will. For how could a few hold him when a whole people could not? But he did not want the sacrilege to be the act of many. He wanted to turn the odium of the cross back on those who were guilty of it, so that he would be fastened to it by a few but would die for the whole world.

And in the synagogue there was a man who had an unclean spirit, and further on: And rising from the synagogue he entered the house of Simon and Andrew. And Simon's mother-in-law was gripped by a high fever.

See the clemency of the Lord and Saviour. He is not moved by indignation, offended by their crime, or wounded by their injury, and he does not desert Judea. Instead, forgetful of the injury and mindful of mercy, he soothes the hearts of that faithless people, now by teaching, now by setting free, now by healing. And Saint Luke did well to put first the man freed from the spirit of wickedness and to place the healing of a woman after it. For the Lord had come to cure both sexes. The one who was created first ought to be healed first, but she who had sinned more from fickleness of mind than from depravity was not to be passed over.

That the works of the Lord's healing began on the sabbath signifies that the new creation began where the old creation had once ceased. It showed from the very beginning that the Son of God is not under the law but above it, and that the law is not abolished but fulfilled. For the world was made not through the law but by the word, as we read: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm." So the law is not abolished but fulfilled, so that man, who was already falling, might be renewed. Hence the apostle too says: "Strip off the old man and put on the new, who is created according to Christ." And he did well to begin on the sabbath, to show that he himself is the Creator, who was weaving works into works and carrying on the work he had already begun. When a builder sets out to renovate a house, he does not begin removing the old from the foundations but from the roof. So he first sets his hand where he had earlier left off.

Then he begins with lesser things in order to reach greater ones. Even men can free someone from a demon, though only by the word of God. But to command the dead to rise belongs to divine power alone.

Nor should it trouble anyone that in this book the devil is presented as the first to speak the name of Jesus of Nazareth. Christ did not receive his name from the devil; an angel brought it from heaven to the Virgin. But it is like the devil's impudence to be the first among men to seize on something and to bring it to them as if it were new, so as to strike them with terror of his power. Indeed, in Genesis too he was the first to name God to man. For so you have it: "And he said to the woman: Why has God said that you should not eat of every tree?"

Both, then, were deceived by the devil and healed by Christ. Follow the rest, learn the mysteries of the gospel reading, and recognize in the healing of the two the sacrament of the salvation of all. For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all are made alive. Who is the man in the synagogue who had the unclean spirit of a demon, if not the Jewish people? Bound as if in the coils of a serpent and knotted in the snares of the devil, they defiled their feigned bodily purity with the filth of the mind within. And it was fitting that the man with the unclean spirit was in the synagogue, because the synagogue had lost the Holy Spirit. The devil had come in where Christ had gone out. At the same time this shows that the devil's nature is not wicked, but his works are evil. For by his higher nature he confesses as Lord the one he denies by his deeds. Both his wickedness and the depravity of the Jews appear in this: he so clouded the people with blindness of a mad mind that the people deny the one whom the demons confess. O heirs worse than their master! He tempts the Lord by word, they by deed. He says, "Cast yourself down"; they set upon him to cast him down.

If we weigh these things more deeply, we must understand here the healing of both soul and body, with the soul, which was struggling against the serpent's snares, being set free first. For the soul would never be overcome by the body unless it had first been tempted by the devil. The soul drives, quickens and governs the body, so how could it be carried off captive into the body's enticements unless it too were bound in the chains of some higher power? Indeed, Eve did not hunger before the cunning of the serpent tempted her. Therefore the medicine of salvation had to work first against the very author of sin.

Perhaps, too, the mother-in-law of Simon and Andrew is a type of our flesh, which lay sick with the various fevers of sin and burned with the immoderate enticements of diverse desires. I would not say that the fever of love is any less than the fever of heat. The one inflames the mind, the other the body; for lust is our fever, because desires are fiery. Hence the apostle too says: "If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn." Luxury is our fever, anger is our fever. Though these are vices of the body, they wrap fire around the bones and assail the mind, the soul and the senses. It is the flesh that the devil's craft solicits first. A fine field, a garment, a necklace: these are the serpent's persuasion. The favour of honours, the heights of power, the delight of banquets, the beauty of a harlot: these are the devil's snare, a kind of alluring voice of spiritual wickedness. Through the enticement of the flesh, which a sort of feminine fickleness quickly softens, it casts the mind too down from its place. For the mind does not desire a woman's beauty before the eye of the body does. Indeed, what you have not seen you will not love. But once the flesh has desired, the steadfastness of the mind, which suffers along with it, gives way, and the mind is bent by its partnership in that love, for the two are in one flesh. And so death creeps in through the accomplishment of sin, with the devil tempting and the flesh

persuading. Yet the fever of the mind is more violent than that of the body, and so the health of the body is often scorned for the pleasure of the mind, and people do not keep away from danger. So it does not seem out of place to recall how Theotimus could not restrain himself. He was suffering from a serious disease of the eyes and loved his wife. His physician forbade him to have intercourse, but he could not bear his desire and was carried away by the force of his lust. He knew full well that he would lose his eyes, and before he came together with his wife, in the very heat of burning desire and as they prepared for their usual intimacy, he said: "Farewell, dear light." So lust burns hotter than fever, and it hurls us down and inflames us more grievously.

But when someone has come to his senses after the madness, the eye of his inner conscience is opened, repentance for the deed follows, and each person blushes at the shameful things of his own crime. Then God is feared, and the sinner wants to hide himself but cannot. Then the flesh is blamed and the devil accused, the one as the procuress of vices, the other as the author of error. The ugliness is laid bare, for every secret is naked before God. The secrets of shameful deeds are not veiled by those fig leaves, that is, by bodily covering or worldly boasting. And everyone, with a mind conscious of sin, dreads God's judgment, saying: "Who will make the mountains fall on me? In what clefts of the rocks shall I hide myself when he comes to shatter the earth?" Then the flesh produces thistles and thorns for the soul: the bites of cares and the burning of anxieties, which the soul has put around itself through the desires of the flesh. For the soul is nailed, as it were, to bodily pleasures, and once it has clung to them, sunk in earthly desires, it can hardly fly back up to the height from which it came down without God's favour. It is now held fast, bound in the snares of its own deeds and in thrall to the enticements of worldly delights.

This, then, is the Adam and this the Eve whom the Lord came to set free. The one was made in the image of God; the other received the strength of her husband. As long as she was subject to the stronger, they shared in one spirit a single will that was pleasing to God, and, placed in God's paradise, they worked to gain the nourishment of heavenly life. But after the flesh began to urge something different and not to keep its proper law, they became exiles from paradise and, because of their sin, fell back into this lower and sunken place. Let no one think it unfitting that Adam and Eve should be taken as a type of soul and body, since they are taken as a type of Christ and the Church. For when the apostle said that the two are in one flesh, he added: "This is a great sacrament, but I speak of Christ and the Church." If this can hold a mystery of God on high, it can much more hold a mystery of our own soul.

But the soul clings fast; it is nailed down and taken captive. Set burning by bodily fevers, it falls sick through its fellow-suffering with the flesh. A physician must be sought. But who is great enough to heal the sores of a wounded mind? What man is great enough to help others when he cannot help himself? Who could give life back to others when he himself cannot escape death? For all died in Adam, because through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all men, in whom all sinned. His fault, then, is the death of all. Then saints were sent, and prophets were sent to speak the oracles of God, and they could achieve nothing. Let us look, then, for a physician among the angels or archangels. But how can they protect me from sinning, when an archangel himself could not keep from sin? How could an angel call me back to paradise, when Satan himself and his angels could not keep the place they had been given? And getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked them to put out a little from the land.

After the Lord had given many people various kinds of healing, neither the time nor the place could hold the crowd back in their eagerness to be healed. Evening came on, and they followed. The lake lay before them, and they pressed on. And so he got into Peter's boat. This is the boat that in Matthew is still being tossed about and in Luke is filled with fish, so that you may recognize both the beginnings of the Church, tossed about, and its later abundance. For the fish are those who sail through this life. There Christ is still asleep for the disciples; here he gives commands. For he sleeps for the fearful and keeps watch for the perfect. But you have heard how Christ sleeps, when he says through the prophet: "I sleep, and my heart keeps watch."

Saint Matthew was right to think that the sign of eternal power, when he commands the winds, should not be passed over. For this is not human teaching, as you heard the Jews say, "By a word he commands the spirits"; it is the mark of heavenly majesty. The troubled sea is calmed, the elements obey the command of the divine voice, and things without sense receive the sense to obey. In this the mystery of divine grace is revealed: the waves of the world grow calm, and the unclean spirit is quieted by a word. The one does not cancel the other; both are celebrated. You have a miracle in the elements and a lesson in the mysteries.

Because Saint Matthew had already touched on those things, Saint Luke chose for himself the boat in which Peter fished. The boat that has Peter is not troubled; the one that has Judas is troubled. Though the disciples sailed in it with many merits, the treachery of the betrayer still tossed it about. Peter was in both boats, but he who is firm in his own merits is troubled by another's. Let us beware, then, of the faithless; let us beware of the betrayer, lest many of us be tossed about because of one. This boat, then, is not troubled, for in it prudence sails, faithlessness is absent, and faith blows like a breeze. How could it be troubled when he in whom the Church has its foundation was in command of it? There, then, is turmoil, where faith is small; here is security, where love is perfect.

Further, though others are told to let down their nets, to Peter alone it is said: "Put out into the deep," that is, into the depths of reasoning. For what is as deep as to see the depth of riches, to know the Son of God, and to profess his divine birth? The human mind cannot grasp it by inquiry with full reason, yet the fullness of faith embraces it. For though I am not permitted to know how he was born, I am not permitted to be ignorant that he was born. I do not know the order of his generation, but I acknowledge the authority of his generation. We were not present when the Son of God was born of the Father, but we were present when the Father called him the Son of God. If we do not believe God, whom do we believe? For everything we believe, we believe either by sight or by hearing. Sight is often deceived; hearing is a matter of faith. Or is the person who makes the claim being questioned? If good men said it, we would think it wicked not to believe. God asserts it, the Son proves it, the sun confesses it by fleeing, the trembling earth testifies to it. Peter leads the Church into these depths of reasoning, so that on one side she may see the Son of God rising again, and on the other the Holy Spirit flowing forth.

And what are the nets of the apostles that they are told to let down, if not the interweaving of words, the folds, as it were, of speech and the recesses of reasoning, which do not let go those they have caught? And nets are fitting instruments for apostolic fishing, for they do not kill what they catch but keep it alive. They draw it up from the deep into the light and carry those who were tossed about from the lowest depths to the heights.

There is also another apostolic kind of fishing, and in this kind the Lord tells Peter alone to fish, saying: "Cast a hook and take the first fish that comes up." This is indeed a great spiritual lesson. It teaches Christian men that they ought to be subject to the higher authorities, so that no one should think that the decree of an earthly king can be set aside. For if the Son of God paid the tax, who are you, so great, that you think it need not be paid? He who possessed nothing paid the tax. But you, who chase after worldly gain, why do you not acknowledge the duty you owe the world? Why do you carry yourself above the world with arrogance of mind, when wretched greed makes you subject to the world?

So the didrachma is paid. It was the price of our redemption and of our body, foreshadowed in the law and paid in full in the gospel. It was not found in the fish's mouth for nothing, for by your mouth you will be justified. Our confession is the price of immortality for us, because, as it is written, with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

And perhaps this first fish is the first martyr, who has in his mouth the didrachma, that is, the price of the tax. Our didrachma is Christ. So that first martyr, Stephen, had a treasure in his mouth when he spoke of Christ during his suffering. But let us return to the passage before us and learn the humility of the apostles.

"Master," he says, "we have toiled all night and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the nets." I too, Lord, know that it is night for me when you do not give the command. No one has yet given in his name; it is still night for me. I have cast the net of my voice through Epiphany and still have caught nothing. I cast it by day. I wait for you to command; at your word I will let down the nets. O empty presumption! O fruitful humility! Those who had caught nothing before now enclose a great multitude of fish at the Lord's word. This is not the work of human eloquence but the gift of a call from on high. Human arguments give way; the people believe by their own faith [?].

The nets break, yet no fish slips away. Their partners in the other boat are called to help. What is that other boat, if not perhaps Judea, from which John and James are chosen? For Judea became his sanctuary. So these men came over from the synagogue to Peter's boat, that is, to the Church, so that they might fill both boats. For at the name of Jesus every knee bends, whether Jew or Greek; Christ is all and in all. But I am wary of this heap, lest the boats nearly sink under their load. For there must also be heresies, so that the good may be proved.

Yet we may also take the other man's boat to be another church, for many churches are derived from the one. See here another worry of Peter's: he is now wary of his own catch. But the one who is perfect knows how to keep safe those he has stored away, since he knows how to catch those who are scattered. Those he catches by the word, he gives back to the Word. He disowns the catch as his own, he disowns the gift as his own.

"Depart from me, Lord," he says, "for I am a sinful man." For he marveled at God's gifts, and the more he had been granted, the less he presumed. You too should say: "Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinner," so that the Lord may answer you: "Do not be afraid." Do not be afraid to confess your sin to a forgiving Lord. Do not be afraid even to offer to the Lord what is yours, since he has given us what is his. He does not know how to envy, how to snatch away, or how to take back. You see how good the Lord is: he gives so much to men that they have the power to give life.
BOOK FIVE

And it came to pass, when he was in one of the cities, behold, a man full of leprosy; and he fell on his face and besought him, saying: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. And stretching out his hand he touched him, saying: I will; be clean. It is fitting that no particular place is named where the leper is cleansed, to show that it was not one people of some particular city but the peoples of all cities that were healed. It is fitting too that, according to Luke, this man is healed in the fourth sign after the Lord came to Capernaum. For if God lit up the fourth day with the sun and made it brighter than the other days when the elements of the world first began to shine, we ought to regard this work as brighter too. And according to Matthew, this man is presented as the first to be healed by the Lord after the Beatitudes. The Lord had said: I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it. So the man who was shut out by the law, trusting that he would be cleansed by the Lord's power, judged that the grace which could wash away the leper's stain came not from the law but stood above the law.

Indeed, just as the authority of power is shown in the Lord, so the steadfastness of faith is shown in this man. He fell on his face, a sign of humility and shame, so that each of us may blush for the stains of his own life; but his shame did not hold back his confession. He showed his wound and asked for the remedy, and the confession itself is full of piety and faith: If you will, he said, you can make me clean. He ascribed power to the Lord's will. And he did not hesitate about the Lord's will as one who doubted his mercy; rather, aware of his own filth, he did not presume upon it.

The Lord answered him with a kind of moral holiness: I will; be clean. And immediately the leprosy left him. For there is nothing between the work of God and his command, since the work is in the command. Thus, he spoke, and they were made. You see, then, that it cannot be doubted that God's will is power. If, then, his will is power, those who affirm that the Trinity is of one will surely affirm that it is of one power. So the leprosy left at once: that you might understand the healer's compassion, he added the reality of the deed.

Then again, according to Mark, the Lord had compassion on him, which is beautifully put. The evangelists set down many such things, wishing to ground us in both: they describe signs of power to lead us to faith, and they portray works of virtue for us to imitate. So he touches, not disdaining, and commands, not doubting; for this is a mark of power, that as one who has the power to heal and the authority to command he does not shrink from giving proof by the deed. So he says 'I will' because of Photinus, he commands because of Arius, he touches because of Mani.

Nor is the leprosy of one man alone cured, but that of all to whom it is said: You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. If, then, the word is the medicine for leprosy, contempt for the word is surely the leprosy of the mind. But so that the leprosy may not pass to the physician, let each of us follow the example of the Lord's humility and avoid boasting. For why is he commanded to tell no one, except to teach that our good deeds are not to be broadcast but kept hidden, so that we refrain not only from payment in money but even from payment in thanks? Or perhaps the reason for the command of silence was that he thought those better who believed out of spontaneous faith rather than in hope of benefits.

He is commanded to present himself to the priest according to the law, not so that he may bring something else, but so that he may offer himself to God as a spiritual sacrifice: wiped clean of the filth of his past deeds through the knowledge of faith and the discipline of wisdom, he is to be consecrated as an offering pleasing to God. For every victim shall be salted with salt. Hence Paul too says: I beseech you therefore, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God.

At the same time it is wonderful that he healed him in the very manner in which he had been entreated. If you will, you can make me clean. I will, he said; be clean. You have the will; you have also the effect of his mercy. And stretching out his hand he touched him. The law forbids lepers to be touched, but he who is Lord of the law does not obey the law; he makes the law. So he did not touch him because he could not cleanse him without touching, but to prove that he was not subject to the law and did not fear contagion as men do. Since he who set others free could not be defiled, the leprosy, which used to defile whoever touched it, was on the contrary put to flight by the Lord's touch.

He is commanded to show himself to the priest and to make an offering for his cleansing. In presenting himself to the priest, he would make the priest understand that he had been cured not by the order of the law but by the grace of God, which is above the law. And in ordering a sacrifice according to the precept of Moses, the Lord showed that he did not abolish the law but fulfilled it: walking according to the law, he was seen to heal, above the law, those whom the remedies of the law had not healed. And he rightly added: as Moses commanded. For the law is spiritual, and so it is seen to have ordered a spiritual sacrifice.

Then he added: that this may be a testimony to you. That is: if you believe God, if the leprosy of impiety departs, if the priest is one who knows hidden things, if he is a witness to a pure disposition. And who can better be seen to be a priest than he from whom hidden things are not concealed, to whom it is said: You are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek?

And behold, men carrying on a bed a man who was paralysed, seeking to bring him in and lay him before him; and finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and let him down through the tiles on his bed into the midst, before Jesus.

The healing of this paralytic is neither idle nor narrow in meaning, since we are first told that the Lord prayed—not, of course, to gain support, but to give an example; for he gave a model to imitate, not seeking to win a request. And while teachers of the law were gathering from all Galilee and Judaea and Jerusalem, the healing of this paralytic is described among the cures of the other sick. First of all, as we said before, every sick person ought to bring in others to plead for his healing, so that through them the loosened frame of our life and the lame steps of our actions may be restored by the remedy of the heavenly word. Let there be, then, some counsellors of the mind who will lift up to higher things the soul of a man, even when it lies numb because of the weakness of the outer body. Supported in turn by their help, and made ready both to raise himself up and to humble himself, let him be placed before Jesus, worthy to be seen by the Lord's gaze. For the Lord regards humility, since he has regarded the humility of his handmaid.

When he saw their faith, it says. Great is the Lord, who forgives some on account of the merit of others, and, while approving some, pardons the errors of others. Why, O man, should your fellow have no influence with you, when with the Lord a servant has both the merit to intercede and the right to obtain what he asks? You who judge, learn to forgive; you who are sick, learn to ask and obtain. If you despair of pardon for grave sins, bring in people to pray for you, bring in the Church to pray for you; out of regard for her the Lord pardons what he could have refused to you.

And although we must not set aside our trust in the history, so that we believe that the body of this paralytic was truly healed, still recognize the healing of the inner man, whose sins are forgiven. When the Jews assert that sins can be forgiven by the Lord alone, they surely confess him to be God and betray their own faithlessness by their own judgment, affirming the work while denying the person. So the Son of God received testimony to his work from them themselves, and he does not need the support of their word; for faithlessness can confess, but it cannot believe. So testimony is not lacking to his divinity; what is lacking is faith for salvation. For what the unwilling confess is all the stronger for faith, and what is denied by those refuted by their own assertions is all the more ruinous to their guilt. Great, then, is the madness of an unbelieving people: having confessed that it belongs to God alone to forgive sins, it does not believe God when he forgives sins. But the Lord, wishing to save sinners, shows that he is God both by his knowledge of hidden things and by the wonder of his deeds, adding: Which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven you,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'?

Here he displays the full image of the resurrection: healing the wounds of both mind and body, he forgives the sins of souls and drives out the weakness of the flesh; for this is to cure the whole man. Great as it is, then, to forgive men their sins—for who can forgive sins but God alone, who forgives also through those to whom he has granted the power of forgiving?—it is still far more divine to grant resurrection to bodies, since the Lord himself is the resurrection.

This bed that he is ordered to take up—what else does it mean but that the human body is ordered to be raised up? It is the bed that David washes every night, [as we read: Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears. This is] the bed of pain on which our soul lay sick under the heavy torment of conscience. But if anyone conducts himself according to Christ's commands, it is no longer a bed of pain but of rest. For by the Lord's mercy what was death has begun to be rest; he has turned for us the sleep of death into a gift of delight. And he is told not only to lift up his bed but also to return to his own house, that is, to go back to paradise. For that is the true house, which first received man and which was lost not by right but by fraud. Rightly, then, the house is restored, since he had come who would undo the bond of fraud and restore what was right.

No delay at all came before the healing: the word and the cure took a single moment. The unbelievers watch him rise, marvel as he goes away, and prefer to fear the miracles of a divine work rather than believe them. For if they had believed, they would surely not have feared but loved; for perfect love casts out fear. And so, because they did not love, they slandered. To the slanderers he says: Why do you think evil in your hearts? Who says this? The great High Priest. He saw the leprosy in the hearts of the Jews; he shows that they are worse than the leper. That man, once cleansed, was ordered to present himself to the priest; these the priest rejects, so that their leprosy may not defile others as well.

There follows the mystical calling of the tax collector, whom he bids follow him not with the step of the body but with the disposition of the mind. So this man, who had once greedily turned fees into profit and harshly squeezed gain from the labours and perils of sailors, when called by a word leaves his own possessions—he who used to seize those of others. And abandoning that paltry seat, he walks after the Lord with every step of his mind. He also lays on the preparations for a great feast; for whoever receives Christ into his inner dwelling is fed with the greatest delights of overflowing pleasures. And so the Lord gladly enters and reclines in the heart of the one who has believed.

But once again the envy of the faithless is kindled, and an image of future punishment is foreshadowed: while the faithful feast and recline in that kingdom of heaven, faithlessness will be tormented with hunger. At the same time it is shown how great the difference is between the partisans of the law and of grace: those who follow the law suffer the eternal hunger of a starving mind, while those who have received the Word into the depths of their soul, refreshed by the abundance of heavenly food and of the fountain, cannot hunger or thirst. And so those who were starving in spirit murmured, saying:

Why does he eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? This is the serpent's voice. Indeed, this was the first word the serpent uttered, saying to Eve: Has God really said, 'You shall not eat of every tree'? So those who say, 'Why does he really eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?' are spreading their father's poison. Hence the Lord, by eating with sinners, does not forbid us to share a meal even with Gentiles, saying: Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.

A new teacher has brought a new medicine. It did not spring from the earth; for all creation knew nothing of how it was compounded. Come, all you who have fallen into the various passions of sin, use this foreign medicine, by which the serpent's poison is driven out; it has not only removed the scar of the passions but has also cut away the cause of the dreadful wound. This medicine does not bring on hunger but supplies food for the soul; for the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say: He has a demon. And so our mind is not starving. Those are starving who lack Christ and are in want of the abundance of good merits. But he whose virtue is enough for his delight, who receives Christ into his house, lays on a great feast, that is, the spiritual feast of good works, which the rich people lacks and the poor feasts on. And so, he says, the sons of the bridegroom cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them.

But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them. What are those days in which Christ is taken away from us, especially since he himself said: I will be with you to the end of the world, and he himself said: I will not leave you orphans? For it is certain that if he leaves us, we cannot be saved. No one can take Christ away from you unless you take yourself away. Let not your boasting take you away, let not your arrogance take you away, and do not presume upon the law; for he did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.

How, then, has the Lord loved righteousness, and how did David never see the righteous forsaken? Or what justice is this, if the righteous man is abandoned and the sinner taken up—unless you understand that he calls righteous those who presume upon the law and do not seek the grace of the gospel? But no one is justified by the law; one is redeemed by grace. So there is righteousness in the law, but righteousness does not come through the law. For the Apostle himself, a Hebrew of Hebrews, as to the law a Pharisee, as to the righteousness that is in the law living blamelessly, one who could boast of the law, says: What things were gain to me, these I have counted loss for Christ. That is, he cast aside the righteousness and glory of the law; for the righteousness of the law without Christ is empty, since Christ is the fullness of the law. And so, although there is righteousness in the law, righteousness does not come through the law. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing; but Christ died in order to fulfil righteousness. Thus when John said: I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me? he answered: Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness. So Christ did not die for nothing; he died for us, so that the righteous might shine like the sun in the kingdom of his Father. But the Jews are not the righteous, to whom it is said: when you see the righteous entering the kingdom of heaven. These are the righteous: those who do not strike back at the one who strikes them, who love their enemy. If we do not take it this way, we find a contradiction:

I did not come to call the righteous—yet he does not call those who call themselves righteous; for, being ignorant of God and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God. So those who usurp righteousness are not called to grace; for if grace comes from repentance, surely whoever scorns repentance renounces grace. These are the ones who will be wounded, who sanctify themselves; from these the bridegroom is taken away. But from us neither Caiaphas nor Pilate has taken Christ away, and we cannot fast, because we have Christ and feast on Christ's flesh and blood. For how can one be said to fast who does not hunger, how can one be said to fast who does not thirst? And how can one who drinks Christ thirst, since he himself said: Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst? Finally, what follows will make clear that this was said of the fasting of the soul.
For he told them a parable: No one puts a patch from a new garment onto an old garment.

He had said that the sons of the bridegroom—that is, the sons of the Word, who through the washing of regeneration have been taken up into the right of divine sonship—cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them. This certainly does not set aside the fasting by which the flesh is subdued and bodily indulgence is chastised; for this fasting commends us to God. How could he forbid his disciples to fast when the Lord himself fasted, and when he said, finally, that the most wicked spirits are not usually overcome except by fasting and prayer? Then too, in this passage he called fasting an old garment, which the Apostle judged must be put off, saying: Strip off the old man with his deeds, so that we may put on the one who is renewed by the sanctification of baptism. So the sequence of precepts fits the same pattern: we are not to mix the deeds of the old and the new man. For the former, the bodily and outer man, does the works of the flesh, while the latter, the inner man who is reborn, ought not to wear a multicoloured appearance made of old and new deeds, but, of one colour with Christ, should imitate with the zeal of his mind the one to whom he was reborn in the washing. Away, then, with the discoloured coverings of the mind that displease the bridegroom; for he is displeased with one who does not have a wedding garment. And what can please the bridegroom but peace of soul, purity of heart, and love in the mind?

The Lord Jesus is a good bridegroom. By a new birth he has given nature a new beginning; she who is betrothed to him is set free from the corruptions of the flesh. He does not seek mortal children—he takes no delight in the pains of Eve—nor a husband liable to guilt, nor the inheritance of a condemned father. For she has seen the sores of the flesh she once desired and has noticed that a beauty that bears the deformity of vices is not true beauty. And so, woman, what have you to do with such a bridegroom? Search carefully, and you will find a scar on all his body. Come to know another, far better bridegroom, who is clothed with light, whose beauty cannot perish. Take him into your soul, consecrate him in your temple, carry him in your body, as it is written: Carry God in your body. Enter his new bridal chamber, gaze on his foreign beauty, put him on, see him at the right hand of the Father, and rejoice that you have such a bridegroom. He will clothe you with blessing, so that no tear of sin may harm you.

Let us keep, then, the garment with which the Lord clothed us as we came up out of the sacred font. A garment is quickly torn if our deeds do not match it; it is quickly worn away by the moths of the flesh and stained by the error of the old man. So here we are forbidden to join new to old, and in the Apostle we are forbidden even to put old over new; rather we must put off the old and put on the new, so that we may be found stripped, not naked. For we are stripped in order to put on better things, but we are made naked when our clothing is taken from us by another's fraud, not laid aside by our own will.

And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. The frailty of the human condition is laid bare when our bodies are compared to the hides of dead animals. And would that we could fulfil the use of good wineskins, so that we might keep safe the sacrament we have received! Care makes up for the damage if new wine is entrusted to renewed skins. And so we ought always to keep these skins full; for when empty they are quickly consumed by moth and rust, but grace preserves them when they are full.

Such precepts suit this work beautifully; for it is the sixth work, in which Levi is shaped in a new form. Man was made on the sixth day; so by Christ's sixth work he is re-formed, no longer an old but a new creature, a form from another world. And so, as a new creature, he lays on a feast for Christ, because Christ delighted in him and he deserved to have a share of delight with Christ. To shape him, then, the Lord gives precepts; for he was already following, glad, eager and exulting, saying: I am no longer a tax collector, I no longer bear the name of Levi. I put off Levi once I put on Christ. I hate my old kind, I flee my old life; I follow you alone, Lord Jesus, who heal my wounds. For who shall separate me from the love of God, which is in you? Shall tribulation, or distress, or famine? I am bound by faith as by nails, and fastened with the good fetters of love. I will keep every commandment of yours pressed into me like a cautery. Though the cautery of the commandment burns, it burns away the rotting parts of the flesh, so that the infection may not creep into the living tissue. Though the medicine stings, it takes away the disease of the sore. Cut away, then, Lord Jesus, with your mighty sword the rottenness of my sins. While you hold me bound with the chains of love, cut away whatever is diseased. Come quickly, lancing the hidden and secret passions of every kind; open the wound, so that the harmful fluid may not spread. Cleanse with your foreign washing all that is foul. Hear me, you men of earth, who carry thoughts drunk with your sins. I too, Levi, was wounded by such passions. I found a physician who dwells in heaven and scatters his medicines on earth. He alone can heal my wounds who has none of his own; he alone can take away the heart's pain and the soul's pallor who knows what is hidden.
Now it came to pass on the second-first sabbath, as he was going through the grain fields, that his disciples were plucking ears of grain and eating them, rubbing them in their hands.

The Lord Jesus begins to strip man of the observance of the old law and to clothe him in the new garment of grace not only by the words he speaks but also by the very practice and outward form of his deeds. So now he leads him through the sown fields on the sabbath, that is, he points him toward fruitful things [?]. What the sabbath means, what the crop means, what the ears of grain mean, is no small mystery. For the field is this whole world; the crop of the field, in the sowing of the human race, is the abundant fruitfulness of the saints; the ears of the field are the fruits of the Church, which the apostles rubbed out by their works and fed on, nourishing themselves on our progress.

So the fruitful crop of virtues was already standing with its ears sprouting, and our merits are compared to their fruit: for in the same way they either wither in the rain, or are scorched by the sun, or are soaked by showers, or are beaten down by storms, or are gathered by the reapers into the safe keeping of blessed barns. The earth, then, had already received the word of God, and the kindly field, sown with heavenly seed, had poured forth a rich yield. The disciples hungered for the salvation of men, and by the glorious miracles of their works they were drawing the fruit of minds out, as if from the husks of bodies, into the light of faith. But the Jews thought this was not lawful on the sabbath, whereas Christ, by the gift of the new grace, was showing that the rest of the law is the work of grace.

Nor do I think it is without a mystery that, in Matthew and Mark, the evangelist puts simply "sabbaths," because the sabbaths are the perpetual feast-days of the eternal resurrection. Whether, then, in this age, when the superstitions of the Jews are at rest and idle, or in the age to come, when we ourselves keep the feast-days in perpetual celebration, we shall eat the good things of the land, as it is written: "They shall eat, but you shall be hungry."

Yet it is remarkable that according to Luke he spoke of the "second-first" sabbath, not the "first-second" — for the Greek has deuteroproton — since what excels ought to be put first. It is "second" because the first, under the law, came before it, the one on which a penalty was also prescribed for anyone who worked; but it is "first" because that sabbath under the law, which had been first, was abolished, and this one, which was established second, became first. For since it is now lawful to work on the sabbath and there is no penalty for the one who works, not even the name of the sabbath under the law, whose force has been abolished, remained attached to it; yet the former may have been first in order, this one first in grace, and this one is no less for being second. For Adam too was first, yet he is not to be compared with the second Adam: for "the first Adam became a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit," and "the first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly." Clearly the second is preferred to the first, for the one was the cause of death, the other of life. So too the sabbath is called "second-first": second in number, first in the grace of what it accomplishes. For a sabbath on which impunity is granted is better than one on which a penalty is prescribed. The law came first, the gospel second; yet fear is inferior to grace. Or perhaps it is called "first" here with respect to the predetermination of the plan and "second" with respect to the enactment of the decree.

In this passage, too, the Lord rightly shows in the law a type of what was to come, and he convicts the defenders of the law of not knowing what belongs to the law, citing the example of David: when he and his companions were hungry, he entered the house of God, took the bread of the Presence, ate it, and gave it to those who were with him. It is a great and truly prophetic example, by which we are taught, first, that we should follow not the empty things of the law but the solid things of benefit; and second, that in David, fleeing with his companions from the face of King Saul, Christ is here prefigured in the law, who with his apostles hid from the prince of this world.

For how could that observer and defender of the law himself eat, and give to those who were with him, the loaves which it was lawful for none but the priests to eat, unless by that figure he wished to show that the priestly food would pass over to the use of the peoples — either because we all ought to imitate the priestly life, or because all the children of the Church are priests? For we are anointed into a holy priesthood, offering ourselves to God as spiritual sacrifices.

The teaching of Christ, then, now goes beyond the law; yet it does not abolish the law but fulfils it, since it does not abolish the sabbath either. For if the sabbath was made for man, and man's benefit required that hungry man, who had long been cut off from the fruits of the earth, should escape the fasting of his old famine, then the law is certainly not abolished but fulfilled. How, then, can something be charged against the Lord as a crime which is not held to be a crime in his servant?

And what could be plainer than this figure, which runs through the whole story? David entered the house of Ahimelech the priest; yet even with the danger of death set before him, the holy priest does not refuse his guest, nor does his spirit turn the exile away. So great is the grace of hospitality that we gladly take the dangers of others upon ourselves.

In the history this is a moral lesson; in the mystery it is prophetic: that devout priests would not shut that true David out from the hospitality of their minds, even when they foresaw that it would bring death upon them. And we are taught not only that Christ will find hospitality in the house of every prophet, but also that, under a figure, he will take the spoils and the weapons of spiritual wickedness; for whoever receives Christ as a guest strips that spiritual Goliath of his weapons.

And what is plainer than that in the house of Ahimelech David asked for five loaves and received one, the type showing that food would be prepared for the faithful no longer from the five books but from the body of Christ, so that Christ took on a body in order that none of the faithful should go hungry? Nor is the figure of Doeg without meaning, who was keeper of the mules, since none other than the keeper of a barren flock could fulfil the type of Judas the betrayer.

Then the fact that, because David had been received, Saul persecuted the whole house of Ahimelech except Abiathar, who was at that time chief of the priests, shows us by prophecy that no one can harm the true chief of the priests, who is Christ alone.

From here the Lord Jesus goes on to other things. For he who had resolved to make the whole man well was passing through each of his members in turn, so that he might truly say: "Are you angry with me because I made a whole man well on the sabbath?" So in this passage he watered with the healing juices of good deeds that hand which Adam stretched out to pluck the fruit of the forbidden tree, so that the hand which had withered through sin might be healed by good works. In this Christ refutes the Jews, who by their wrong interpretations violated the precepts of the law, supposing that on the sabbath one must rest even from good works, whereas the law in present things prefigured the form of things to come, in which there will surely be rest from evil works, not from good ones. For although worldly works cease, to rest in the praise of God is not an idle act but a good work.

You have heard, then, the words of the Lord saying: "Stretch out your hand." That is a common and universal remedy. And you who think you have a sound hand, beware lest it be shrunk by greed, beware lest it be shrunk by sacrilege. Stretch it out often: stretch it out to that poor man who begs of you; stretch it out to help your neighbour, to bring protection to the widow, to rescue from wrong the one you see subjected to unjust insult; stretch it out to God for your sins. This is how the hand is stretched out; this is how it is healed. So Jeroboam's hand shrank when he sacrificed to idols, and he stretched it out again when he prayed to God.

"Now it came to pass in those days that he went out to the mountain to pray, and he spent the night in prayer to God." Not everyone who prays goes up the mountain — for there is a prayer that becomes sin — but whoever prays well, advancing from earthly things to higher ones, climbs to the summit of lofty concern. The one who is anxious about the riches or the honours of this world does not go up the mountain; the one who covets the title to another's estate does not go up the mountain. He goes up who seeks God; he goes up who begs the Lord's help for his course. All the great, all the lofty, climb the mountain; for it is not to just anyone that the prophet says: "Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem." You are to climb this mountain not with bodily footsteps but with loftier deeds. Follow Christ, so that you yourself may become a mountain; for "the mountains are round about him." Search the Gospel: you will find that only the disciples went up the mountain with the Lord.

The Lord prays, then, not to make petition for himself but to obtain something for me; for although the Father has put all things into the Son's power, yet the Son, in order to fulfil the form of a man, thinks it right to entreat the Father for us, because he is our advocate. Do not open treacherous ears, so as to think that the Son asks as though he were weak, asking to obtain what he, the author of power, could not accomplish. The teacher of obedience instructs us by his own example in the precepts of virtue. "We have an advocate," it says, "with the Father." If he is an advocate, he must intercede for my sins. He entreats, then, not as one who is weak but as one who is loving. Do you want to know how fully he can do all that he wills? He is both advocate and judge: in the one is the office of love, in the other the mark of power.

"And he spent the night," it says, "in prayer to God." A pattern is given you, a model is set before you which you ought to imitate. What should you do for your own salvation, when Christ spends the night in prayer for you? What is it fitting for you to do when you wish to undertake some duty of devotion, when Christ, before sending out the apostles, first prayed, and prayed alone? Nor, if I am not mistaken, is he ever found anywhere praying with the apostles: everywhere he makes his petition alone. For human desires cannot grasp the counsel of God, and no one can share with Christ in his inmost things. Do you want to know how he prayed for me and not for himself?

"He called his disciples," it says, "and chose twelve of them," whom he was to appoint as sowers of the faith to spread the help of human salvation throughout the world. Notice at the same time the heavenly plan: he chose to send out not certain wise men, not rich men, not nobles, but fishermen and tax collectors, so that they should not seem to have won anyone over to his grace by cleverness, or bought them with riches, or drawn them by the authority of power and nobility, and so that the reason of truth, not the charm of argument, might prevail.

Judas too is chosen, not through want of foresight but through providence. How great is the truth, which not even a hostile minister weakens! How great the moral character of the Lord, who preferred to put his judgment rather than his affection at risk in our eyes! For he had taken on the frailty of man, and so he did not refuse even this part of human weakness. He willed to be deserted, he willed to be betrayed, he willed to be handed over by his own apostle, so that you, when deserted by a companion, betrayed by a companion, might bear with composure that your judgment has erred and your kindness has been wasted.

"And he came down with them," it says, "and stood on a level place." Note everything carefully: how he both goes up with the apostles and comes down to the crowds; for how could the crowd see Christ except in a low place? It does not follow him to the heights, it does not climb to lofty places. And so, where he comes down, he finds the sick; for on the heights there can be no sick. So Matthew too teaches that the infirm were healed in the lower places; for each one was healed first, so that, advancing gradually in virtue, he might be able to climb the mountain. And so he heals each one in the lower places, that is, he calls him back from lust, he takes away the injury of blindness, he comes down to our wounds, so that by a kind of familiarity and by the sharing of himself he may make us partakers of the heavenly nature. And he healed these, indeed, but left them in the lower places.

"But seeing the crowds," as you have read, "he went up the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came up to him."
