For when he is about to preach the gospel and bring forth the oracles of the beatitudes from the treasury of the Godhead, he begins to be loftier. Here, however, although he stood in a low place, he nevertheless lifted up his eyes. So too, when he raised Lazarus, he groaned in spirit; so too he raised his head when he forgave the adulterous woman her sins. For what is it to lift up the eyes but to open the inner light?

Then St Matthew says, "He opened his mouth": that is, he unlocked the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God, opening the inner sanctuary of his temple. So you too, open your mouth — but first pray that it may be opened. For if Paul prays for help in the opening of his mouth, how much more is it fitting for you to pray. The prophet also shows you the key of knowledge with which you should open your mouth, saying: "Open your mouth with the word of God." The word of God is the key of your mouth; the key of knowledge is the key of your mouth, by which the chains of silence are loosed and the bolts of ignorance are drawn back.

"Blessed are you poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst now, for they shall be satisfied. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. Blessed will you be when men hate you." St Luke gave only four of the Lord's beatitudes, but St Matthew eight. Yet the four are contained in the eight, and the eight in the four.

For the one embraced, as it were, the four cardinal virtues; the other in his eight unlocked a mystic number. For many psalms are inscribed "for the eighth," and you receive the command to give a portion to those eight — perhaps to the beatitudes; for just as the eighth is the perfection of our hope, so the eighth is the sum of the virtues. But let us look first at the fuller account. "Blessed," he says, "are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

Both evangelists placed this beatitude first, for it is first in order and is, so to speak, the parent and begetter of the virtues, since whoever has despised worldly things will himself deserve eternal ones; nor can anyone attain the merit of the heavenly kingdom who, possessed by desire for the world, has no means of rising out of it. The second beatitude: "Blessed," he says, "are the meek." The third: "Blessed are those who mourn." The fourth: "Blessed are those who hunger." The fifth: "Blessed are the merciful." The sixth: "Blessed are the pure in heart." The seventh: "Blessed are the peacemakers." And rightly the seventh, since on that day God rested from all the works of the world; for it is a day of rest and peace. The eighth: "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake."

Come, Lord Jesus, teach us the order of your beatitudes; for it was not without order that you said first, "Blessed are the poor in spirit," second, "Blessed are the meek," and third, "Blessed are those who mourn." Even if I know something, I know only in part. For if Paul knew in part, how much can I know, who am as inferior to Paul in speech as in life? For life demands and acquires speech, but speech without life is not the speech of God. How much wiser than I is Paul! He glories in dangers, I glory in successes; he glories that he is not puffed up by revelations, while I, if any revelations came to me, would glory in them. Yet God is able to raise up men from stones, to bring forth speech from what is shut, to draw a voice from the mute. And if he opened the eyes of a donkey so that it saw the angel, he is able to open our eyes too, so that we may see the mystery of God.

"Blessed," he says, "are the poor." Not all the poor are blessed; for poverty is neutral. The poor can be both good and bad — unless perhaps the blessed poor man is to be understood as the one the prophet described when he said that "a just poor man is better than a lying rich man." Blessed is the poor man who cried, and the Lord heard him; poor in crime, poor in vices, the poor man in whom the prince of this world found nothing, the poor man who imitates that Poor One who, though he was rich, became poor for our sakes. Hence Matthew made it fully plain when he said: "Blessed are the poor in spirit"; for the one who is poor in spirit is not puffed up, is not exalted by the mind of his flesh.

This, then, is the first beatitude: when I have laid aside all sin, stripped off all malice, and become content with simplicity, destitute of evils. It remains for me to temper my character. For what does it profit me to be without worldly goods unless I am gentle and meek? For whoever follows the right way surely follows him who said: "Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart." So lay aside what is wicked; be in want of vices according to the good poverty; soften your feelings, so that you do not grow angry, or at least, if angry, do not sin, as it is written: "Be angry and do not sin." For it is a fine thing to govern one's emotion by reason, and it is reckoned no less a virtue to restrain anger and check indignation than not to be angry at all, since the latter is generally judged the more sluggish, the former the braver.

When you have done this, remember that you are a sinner, and mourn your sins, mourn your offences. And it is fitting that the third beatitude belongs to the one who weeps over his sins, since it is the Trinity that forgives sins. Wash yourself, then, with your tears, cleanse yourself with your weeping. If you weep for yourself, another will not weep for you; for if Saul had wept over his sins, Samuel would not have wept over him. Each one has his own dead to weep for. We are dead when we sin, when we are filled with the bones of the dead. Dead is the evil word that comes out of the mouth, for it comes out of an evil tomb: "their throat is an open tomb." That is why the apostle says: "Be imitators of me." He wants us to remember our offences. Paul had nothing to mourn from the time he believed in Christ, and yet he wept over his former deeds, saying: "I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God." He, then, was a sinner before faith, but we still sin after faith. Let the one who is a sinner weep over himself and accuse himself, so that he may become righteous;

for the righteous man is his own accuser. Let us follow the order, then, for it is written: "Set love in order in me." I have laid aside sin, I have tempered my character, I have wept over my offences; I begin to hunger, and to hunger for righteousness. For a sick man, when he is gravely ill, does not hunger, because the pain of the illness drives out hunger. But what is this hunger for righteousness? What are these loaves the righteous man hungers for? Are they perhaps those of which it is said: "I have been young and now am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread"? Whoever hungers surely seeks an increase [?] of virtue. And what greater growth in virtue is there than the rule of righteousness?

After these, "Blessed," he says, "are the merciful"; for mercy follows righteousness. Hence it is said: "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever." But even the one who shows mercy loses his reward unless he shows mercy with a pure heart; for if he seeks display, there is no fruit. So cleanse the inner parts of your mind, and when you have carefully cleansed the secret places of your heart, have compassion on those who are under attack, and understand how many people, how many of your brothers, are seeking your help.

But unless you first empty your inner self of every stain of sin, so that no quarrels and strife issue from your feelings, you cannot bring healing to others. Begin peace, then, with yourself, so that when you yourself are a peacemaker you may bring peace to others. For how can you cleanse the hearts of others unless you have first cleansed your own?

You have helped others, then, and brought aid to many: hasten, press on to the end. Though there were many ways of leaving this life, one was fitting for the Lord; for what had been born according to the flesh had also to die according to the flesh. He chose the passion, so as to die for us; and you too should say, for all that he has rendered to you: "I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord" — that is, the passion. That is why he also said to those who wanted to sit at his right hand or his left: "Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?" He leads you to the end, he accompanies you all the way to martyrdom, and he sets up the palm of the beatitudes.

See, then, the order. You must become poor in spirit, for humility of spirit is the wealth of the virtues. Unless your mind is poor, you will not be able to be meek. The one who is meek can mourn present things; the one who mourns lower things can long for better ones; the one who seeks higher things shuns lower ones, so that he too may be helped from above; the one who shows mercy cleanses his heart. For what is it to cleanse the soul but to wipe away the filth of death? For almsgiving delivers from death, while patience is the perfection of love. And the one who suffers persecution, set in the final contest, is tested by adversity, so that, having competed according to the rules, he may be crowned. Some hold that these are certain steps of the virtues by which we may climb from the lowest to the higher.

Then too, just as the virtues increase, so do the rewards; for it is more to be a son of God than to possess the earth and to earn consolation. But since the first reward is the kingdom of heaven and the last reward is also the kingdom of heaven, is the reward the same for beginners and for the perfect? Or are we perhaps being taught in a mystical sense that the first kingdom of heaven is the one the apostle speaks of: “to depart [?] and be with Christ”? You have the first kingdom when the saints are caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; for many of those who sleep will rise, some to eternal life, others to disgrace. So the first kingdom of heaven is set before the saints when they are released from the body; the second kingdom of heaven is to be with Christ after the resurrection. Once you are in the kingdom of heaven, there is advancement through the dwelling places. Though the kingdom is one, there are different merits in the kingdom of heaven. After the resurrection, freed from death, you will begin to possess your earth. For the one to whom it is said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” does not possess his earth; one who does not gather its fruit cannot be its owner. So when you have been set free through the Lord's cross, provided you are found under the Lord's yoke, you will find consolation in that very possession. Delight follows consolation, and divine mercy follows delight. Those on whom the Lord has mercy he also calls. The one who is called sees the one who calls; the one who has seen God is taken up into the rights of divine sonship. Then at last, as a son of God, he delights in the riches of the heavenly kingdom. So the one is beginning, the other is being filled. For even in this world many people live within the Roman Empire, but those who are closer to the emperor receive greater favor in the empire.

Now let us explain how Saint Luke included the eight blessings in four. We know, of course, that there are four cardinal virtues: temperance, justice, prudence and fortitude. Whoever is poor in spirit is not greedy. Whoever weeps is not proud, but meek and peaceable. Whoever mourns is humbled. Whoever is just does not withhold what he knows has been given for everyone's common use. Whoever shows mercy gives of his own, and whoever gives what is his own does not seek what belongs to another or plot deceit against his neighbor.

So the virtues are connected and linked to one another, so that whoever has one is seen to have several. Each saint has one virtue that is especially his, but the more abundant that virtue has been, the more abundant its reward. How great was Abraham's hospitality, how great his humility, how great his holiness in rescuing his brother's son from the enemy, and how great his restraint in seeking nothing from the spoils! But because he excelled in faith, he earned the first place in faith above all others. So each person has many rewards, because there are many incentives to virtue; but whatever is more plentiful in someone's merit also overflows more richly in his reward.
“Blessed, then, are the poor in spirit.” Here you have temperance, which abstains from sin, tramples on the world, and does not seek what entices.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst.” For whoever hungers feels for the hungry; by feeling for them he gives; by giving he becomes just, because “his justice endures forever.” That is why in Matthew we understand a spiritual hunger and thirst, by which the food or drink of justice is desired. For this virtue is, as it were, the raw material of the virtues: it makes the just man put himself on an equal footing with those beneath him, shut out deceit, and seek the truth.

“Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.” Here you have prudence, whose task is to weep over passing things and seek those that are eternal, to mourn worldly things, which are at war with themselves, and to seek the God of peace, who chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and who destroys the things that are not, so that one may gain the things that are.

“Blessed will you be when people hate you.” Here you have fortitude, but the kind that does not earn hatred through crime and instead suffers persecution for the faith. For you reach the crown of suffering only if you disregard human favor and pursue God's. And so that you may know that suffering is the culmination of fortitude, he says, “This is how their fathers treated the prophets,” for the Jews persecuted the prophets even to the death of the body. It also belongs to fortitude to overcome anger and restrain indignation. In this way fortitude strengthens mind and body alike, and does not let them be disturbed by any fear or pain, which, like bad interpreters, often strike us down.
So temperance contains purity of heart and mind; justice contains mercy; prudence, peace; fortitude, meekness.

“Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation!” Although great wealth holds many allurements to sin, it also holds very many incentives to virtue. Virtue needs no resources, and a poor man's contribution is more commendable than a rich man's generosity. Even so, by the authority of the heavenly sentence he condemns not those who have riches but those who do not know how to use them. The poor man is more praiseworthy who gives with a ready heart, is not held back by the barrier of looming want, and does not think himself needy as long as he has what nature requires. In the same way the rich man is all the more guilty when he ought at least to have thanked God for what he received, and when he hides away unused the wealth that was given for common use and broods over treasures buried in the earth. So it is not wealth but the disposition of the heart that is at fault. The greedy mind keeps anxious watch all its life, guarding its wealth in misery, and there is no heavier punishment than this: to preserve with anxious fear what will only profit one's heirs. Yet since the pursuits of avarice and the desire to amass are fed by a certain empty pleasure, those who have had the consolation of the present life have lost the reward of the everlasting one.

Here, however, we can also understand the rich to be the Jewish people, or heretics, or certainly the philosophers of this world. Delighting in an abundance of words and a kind of inheritance of showy eloquence, they have gone beyond the simplicity of the true faith and stored up useless treasures. When you hear some heretic arguing about the Lord's begetting according to the ways of this world, does he not seem to you rich in words but poor in strength? He thinks he has abundant riches at present, but in the future he will recognize the poverty of his faith. Wasted away by an eternal fast from faith, he will know that the food of faithlessness he belched out in this present age is the cause of so great a punishment. And a time will come when those who laugh at our words now will mourn their laughter. To them it is fittingly said: “Woe to you when all people speak well of you!”

Does he not seem to you to be speaking to those who lately, at the Council of Rimini, became the authors of a faithless betrayal, and lost God's favor while pursuing the emperor's? In their eagerness to please the powerful they have put themselves under an everlasting curse.

So Saint Matthew called the peoples to virtue and faith by means of rewards, while Luke here also deterred them from crimes and sins by announcing future punishments. It was not without purpose that he first went through an account of many heavenly deeds and came later to the passage on the blessings. He wanted to teach peoples strengthened by divine miracles to advance in the footsteps of the virtues beyond the path of the law. In Matthew caution was needed, because the hearts of a still weak people were wavering; here virtue had to be roused by the blast of the trumpet. The language of this book shows this, both at its opening and as the account goes on. There, those who are weak are still given a kind of milk of the law to drink, and so are led along the path of the law to grace. They hear the things of the law so that, by following the law, they may advance beyond the law. Here the Church, more firmly founded, is not nourished on milk but feeds on solid food, for love is the stronger food. Indeed, among the three greatest things, hope, faith and love, the greatest is love.

Love, then, is set in order when it is said, “Love your enemies,” so that the Church's words quoted earlier may be fulfilled: “Set love in order in me.” For love is set in order when the precepts of love are laid down. See how he began from the higher things and put the law behind the blessing of the gospel. The law commands retaliation in kind; the gospel bestows love for enmity, kindness for hatred, prayers for curses, help for persecutors, patience for the hungry, and the grace of reward. How much more perfect is the athlete who does not feel the injury!

And so that the Lord would not seem to abolish the law, he keeps the rule of repayment in kindnesses, though he disregards it in injuries. Yet by saying, “Do to others just as you want them to do to you,” he makes the repayment itself more generous, since the deed is made to match one's own wishes. For virtue knows no limit in gratitude, nor is it content [?] to return what it has received; it wants to add to what it has been given, so as not to fall short in kindness even if it is equal in service. For kindnesses are weighed not only by their amount but by order and time, since where kindnesses are equal, the one who began first comes first. The benefactor is the one who began the favor; the debtor is the one who returned it. So being first to do a kindness is a further kindness. If someone has repaid money, he has not discharged the favor; he remains a debtor of gratitude, even if he no longer owes the money. Why should we think gratitude can be used up by returning it, when returning it testifies to a favor received rather than to a debt paid off?

So the Christian is trained by a good example: not content with the law of nature, he seeks its grace. For if loving in return is common to all, even to sinners, then one whose way of life is loftier should also have a richer zeal for virtue, and love even those who do not love him. Even if the lack of any reason [?] for loving rules out the practice of affection, it will not rule out the practice of virtue. With someone who loves you, it is shameful not to repay the favor, and through your wish to repay it you come to love someone you did not love before. In the same way, in someone who does not love you, you should love virtue, so that by loving virtue you begin to love the one you did not love. For the reward that comes from a lover is rare and fleeting, while the reward of virtue is everlasting.

What could be more wonderful than offering the other cheek to the one who strikes you? Is not every outburst of the angry man broken, and his anger calmed? Does not patience lead his own repentance to strike the striker harder than you could? In this way you both ward off the injury and win favor. And the strongest grounds for love often arise when insolence is repaid with patience and injury with kindness. Indeed, as I remember hearing, we consider that this alone humbles the haughtiness of philosophy. Philosophy thinks it has divided justice into three parts: one toward God, which is called piety; another toward parents and the rest of the human race; and a third toward the dead, so that they receive their due funeral rites. But the Lord Jesus went beyond the oracle of the law and the summit of philosophy, and extended the duty of piety even to those who have done us harm. If an enemy who has fought you with weapons in war lays down his arms and is granted mercy and spared, and this is often allowed out of regard for nature or by the very law of war, so that the conquered are given their lives, how much more should it be allowed out of the higher regard of religion! For if a fighter is not moved by the fact that his own life was attacked, how much less should a soldier of peace be moved?

So we see the apostle's saying, “Love is patient, love is kind, it does not envy, it is not puffed up,” brought to completion in these precepts. If love is patient, it owes patience to the one who strikes; if it is kind, it must not answer curses; if it does not seek its own, it must not resist the one who robs; if it does not envy, it must not hate its enemy. And yet the precepts of divine love go beyond the apostle's, for it is more to give than to yield, and more to love enemies than not to envy. The Lord both said and did all these things. When he was cursed, he did not curse in return; when he was struck, he did not strike back; when he was stripped, he did not resist; when he was crucified, he asked pardon for his very persecutors, saying, “Father, forgive them their sin, for they do not know what they are doing.” He excused his accusers from their crime.

They were preparing a cross; he was repaying them with salvation and grace. And yet, since even the pursuit of virtue grows sluggish without reward, he both gave us an example and promised a reward from heaven, promising that those who imitate him will be sons of God. Whoever hurries toward the reward must not disdain the example, for the more excellent the reward, the more earnest the duty. And how great is the reward of mercy, which is admitted into the rights of divine adoption! So follow mercy, that you may earn grace.

God's kindness reaches far and wide. He sends rain on the ungrateful; the fruitful earth does not deny its crops to the wicked; the same sun of the world shines on the sacrilegious and the devout alike. Or, to consider these things in a mystical sense: the Lord watered the Jewish people with the rains of the prophets and shone on them with the rays of the eternal sun, even though they did not deserve it. But since they were soaked only with earthly dew, the Church of God is admitted to the heavenly light. Even so, for them too the privilege of mercy is kept in reserve, if they believe.
He added that we must not judge rashly, so that, being aware of your own sin, you are not forced to pass sentence on another.

It is also a great lesson in virtue not to seek fruitful things from fruitless ones, or expect a rich harvest from untilled ground. Each thing bears fruit according to how it is cultivated. Among the thorns of this world that fig cannot be found. Because it excels in rich fruit, it is fittingly made a figure of the resurrection. Or it is because, as you have read, “the fig trees have put forth their green figs,” for an unripe, useless and falling fruit came first in the synagogue. Or it is because our life in the body is unripe, and will be ripe in the resurrection. And so we must cast far from us the cares of this world, which gnaw at the soul and scorch the mind, so that we may obtain the ripe fruits of careful cultivation, which we cannot find in the untilled places of this world: for “they do not gather figs from thorns or harvest grapes from thistles.” The one image refers to the world and the resurrection, the other to soul and body. Or it is because no one gains fruit for his soul through sins; like a grape lying close to the ground, the soul rots, but higher up it ripens. Or it is because no one can escape the condemnation of the flesh unless Christ has redeemed him, who hung like a grape upon the wood. So far from that flesh which was commanded to bring forth thistles for condemned man, let us lift up our spiritual eyes and stretch out our hands, so that we may gather in Christ as our harvest of grapes.

And he teaches that the foundation of all the virtues is obedience to the heavenly precepts. Through it this house of ours cannot be shaken by the flood of pleasures, the assault of spiritual wickedness, the rain of this world, or the cloudy arguments of heretics.

Fittingly, when he had finished giving his precepts, he shows the pattern for carrying them out. For immediately the servant of a gentile centurion is brought to the Lord to be healed. In him the people of the nations is portrayed, held in the chains of worldly slavery, sick with deadly passions, and about to be healed by the Lord's kindness. When the evangelist said the servant was about to die, he was not mistaken, for the servant would have died had he not been healed by Christ. So the one who loved his enemies so much that he snatched them from death and admitted them to the hope of everlasting salvation fulfilled the precept with heavenly love.

And what a great mark of divine humility it is that the Lord of heaven did not disdain to visit a centurion's lowly servant! Faith shines out in works, but humanity works even more through feeling. He certainly did not do this because he could not heal from a distance. He did it to give you a pattern of humility to imitate, teaching that deference must be shown alike to the lowly and to those of higher rank. Indeed, elsewhere he says to the royal official, “Go; your son lives,” so that you may know both the power of his divinity and the grace of his humility. There he chose not to go, so that he would not seem to have shown more deference to riches in the case of the official's son. Here he went himself, so that he would not seem to have despised the condition of a slave in the case of the centurion's servant. For all of us, slave and free, are one in Christ.

But see that faith comes before healing. Notice too that the gentile people itself has insight into the mystery. The Lord sets out; the centurion begs him not to trouble himself and, laying aside his military pride, takes on reverence, quick to believe and ready to show honor. And Luke rightly says that the centurion also sent friends to meet him. He did not want his own presence to seem to burden the Lord's modesty, or to seem to have provoked a courtesy with a courtesy. So much for the moral sense.

In the mystical sense, however, the people of the nations wants the one whom the Jewish people crucified to remain untouched by injury. As regards faith, it believed the word, judging that Christ gives health to human beings by the power of God and not of a man. As regards the mystery, it saw that Christ could not yet enter the hearts of the gentiles. And so the man, who had not yet washed away the stains of his former thinking, thought himself more burdened than helped by the Lord's condescension. In the same way the widow of Zarephath judged herself unworthy to give hospitality to the prophet. And so in this one man the Lord ranks the faith of the gentiles first.

Indeed, if you read it this way, “In no one in Israel have I found such faith,” the meaning is simple and easy. But if you follow the Greek, “Not even in Israel have I found such faith,” this man's faith is ranked even above that of the more chosen, who see God.

See how God orders things: the master's faith is proved and the servant's health is restored. So a master's merit can also help his servants, not only through the merit of his faith but also through his care to keep them well disciplined. Look also at another way in which the Lord's humility orders things: he does what he has not promised. For although he had not yet commanded the healing, the servants who had been sent found the young servant well.

Now as he drew near to the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow; and a large crowd was with her. When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion and said to her: Do not weep.

And he came up and touched the bier. This passage points to grace in two ways. First, it leads us to believe that God's mercy is quickly moved by the lament of a widowed mother, especially one broken by the suffering or death of an only son. Yet the crowd at the funeral also wins for her the merit of a widow's dignity. Second, it shows that this widow, surrounded by a crowd of peoples, appears to be more than a woman, since by her tears she earned the resurrection of her only son, a young man. For holy Church, through the sight of her own tears, calls the younger people back to life from the funeral procession and the last rites of the tomb. She is forbidden to weep for one to whom resurrection is due.

This dead man was being carried to the tomb on a bier by four material elements, but he had hope of rising again because he was carried on wood. That wood had not been of use to us before, but once Jesus touched it, it began to serve for life, as a sign that salvation would be poured back upon the people through the gibbet of the cross. So when they heard the word of God, those grim bearers of the funeral stood still, the ones who were pressing the human body onward by the deadly flux of material nature. For what else are we but lifeless bodies lying on a kind of bier, that is, the instrument of the last rites, when the fire of unbridled desire boils up, or cold moisture overflows, or the vigour of the soul is dulled by some sluggish condition of the body, or our spirit, clotted with defilement and empty of pure light, feeds the mind [?]? These are the bearers of our funeral.

But even when the last moments of death have wiped out every hope of life, and the bodies of the dead lie close to the grave, at the word of God corpses already about to perish rise again. The voice returns, the son is given back to his mother, he is called back from the grave, he is snatched from the tomb. What is this grave of yours but evil habits? Your grave is faithlessness, your tomb is your throat; for their throat is an open tomb, from which dead words come forth. From this tomb Christ sets you free; from this grave you will rise, if you hear the word of God.

Even if your sin is so grave that you cannot wash it away yourself with the tears of your repentance, let Mother Church weep for you. As a widowed mother she intercedes for each one as though for an only son, for she suffers with them by a kind of spiritual pain of nature when she sees her children driven toward death by deadly vices. We are the inmost parts of her inmost being; for there are spiritual inward parts too, which Paul has when he says: Yes, brother, let me have joy of you in the Lord; refresh my inmost being in Christ. We, then, are the inmost being of the Church, since we are members of her body, of her flesh and of her bones. So let the loving mother grieve, and let the crowd stand by her, and not just a crowd but a large one, sharing the suffering of the good parent. Then you will rise again from the funeral, then you will be set free from the tomb. Those ministers of your funeral will stand still, you will begin to speak words of life, and all will be afraid, for by the example of one, very many will be corrected. They will also praise God, who has granted us such great remedies for escaping death.
And John called two of his disciples and sent them to him, saying: Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?

Simple words do not have a simple meaning here; otherwise what came earlier would conflict with what is said now. For how can John fail to know here the one he recognized earlier when God the Father pointed him out? How could he there recognize the one he had not known before, and here not know the one he already knew? I did not know him, he says, but he who sent me to baptize said to me: He on whom you see the Holy Spirit descending from heaven. And he believed what was said, recognized the one who was pointed out, worshipped him when he was baptized, and prophesied his coming. Finally he says: I have seen and borne witness that this is the chosen one of God. What then? Could so great a prophet go so far astray that he still did not believe that the one of whom he had said, Behold the one who takes away the sins of the world, was the Son of God? For either it is presumption to ascribe divine things to someone you do not know, or it is faithlessness to have doubted the Son of God. So the suspicion of so great an error cannot fall on such a prophet.

Therefore, if the plain sense conflicts with itself, let us look for a spiritual figure. We have already said above that John is a type of the Law, which was the forerunner of Christ. It is fitting, then, that the Law cannot bring its witness to the Lord's dispensation to full completion without the confirmation of the Gospel. For the Law was held shut up, in a bodily way, in the hearts of the faithless as in prisons empty of eternal light, confined by inner chambers teeming with punishments and by the doors of madness.

The Law indeed prophesied the grace of baptism in Exodus through the cloud and the sea; it foretold spiritual food in the lamb, and pointed to a never-failing spring in the rock. In Leviticus it revealed the forgiveness of sins, in the Psalms it proclaimed the kingdom of heaven, and in Joshua son of Nun it declared most plainly the land of promise —

All these things agree with John's testimony as well. Yet it is held shut in by the tyrannical powers of this world, so that it cannot pour out the light of the Lord's resurrection. So John sends his disciples to Christ to gain what was lacking in their knowledge, since Christ is the fullness of the law. Words without deeds often waver, and faith is displayed more fully by the evidence of things done than by promises made in words. So the faith that was then wavering in the hearts of the Jews, as though the law had been bolted shut, was to be laid open by the very sight of the Lord's cross and by the full testimony of the resurrection.

And perhaps these disciples are the two peoples: one that believed from among the Jews, and the other from among the Gentiles, which believed because it heard. These, then, wanted to see, because of the saying: "But blessed are your eyes, which see, and your ears, which hear." Yet we too have seen in John; we have looked with our own eyes in the apostles, and we have examined with our own hands in the fingers of Thomas. For "that which was from the beginning, which we have heard and which we have seen, which we have looked upon with our eyes and our hands have examined, concerning the Word of life: and the life was made manifest." When was it made manifest? When we saw. It was not manifest in this way before it was seen. Thanks be to the Lord, then, who was crucified for our faith, crucified for our desires. My mind has been crucified in him.

So it is now too with those who study the Old Testament. Before they come to know the gospel, as they read what are like certain footprints of the Lord's body, they think he is still to come, and they ask whether he is the Christ, the Son of God, who is to come. And when they read of the time he spoke with Abraham, or when he showed himself as commander of the heavenly host, they certainly say: "Are you the one who is to come, or should we wait for another?" But when they come to the gospel and learn that the blind are given light, the lame walk, the deaf have heard, the lepers have been cleansed and the dead have risen, then they say: "We have seen him, and looked upon him with our eyes, and put our fingers into the marks of his nails." For we feel that we have seen the one we read about, that we have watched him hanging there, and have touched his wounds as the Spirit of the Church examined them. For if demons are cast out by the finger of God, faith too is found by the finger of the Church. Or perhaps, in a certain working part of our body, all of us seem to have traced out the course of the Lord's passion; for faith passes through a few to the many. So the law announces that Christ will come, and the scripture of the gospel confirms that he has come.

Some also understand John himself in this way: he was so great a prophet that he recognized Christ and announced the forgiveness of sins that was to come, yet not as one in doubt but as a devout prophet, he did not believe that the one whose coming he had believed in would die. So he doubted not from lack of faith but from devotion. Peter too doubted, saying: "Be merciful to yourself, Lord! This shall not happen." That leader in faith, who had believed Christ to be the Son of God before Christ had told him so, did not believe even Christ about Christ's death. That was the stumble of loving devotion, not of irreverence. Again, elsewhere he refuses to have his feet washed, because he does not recognize the mystery and is troubled at the Lord's service to him. So even the saints did not believe that Christ would die; for "what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, these things God has prepared for those who love him." So in devout people a stumble that comes from love does not hinder faith.

Then the Lord, knowing that no one can believe fully without the gospel, since faith begins in the Old Testament and is fulfilled in the New, when asked about himself, showed who he was not by any word but by deeds. "Go," he said, "tell John what you have seen and heard. The blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear, the lepers are cleansed, the dead rise, the poor have the gospel preached to them."

A full testimony indeed, by which the prophet might recognize the Lord. For it had been prophesied of him and of no other that "the Lord gives food to the hungry, the Lord raises up those who are bowed down, the Lord sets the prisoners free, the Lord gives light to the blind, the Lord loves the righteous, the Lord watches over strangers; he will uphold the orphan and the widow, and he will destroy the way of sinners." "The one who does these things," it says, "the Lord, will reign for ever." So these are the marks not of human but of divine power: to open the darkness of perpetual night for the blind and heal the wounds of sunken eyes by pouring in light; to bring hearing into the ears of the deaf; to restore loosened limbs by knitting their slack joints; and to call the dead back into the light by pouring the strength of life into them again.

Before the gospel such things were either rare or unknown. Granted, Tobit recovered his sight; but he is a single example, and that healing came from an angel, not a man. Granted, Elijah raised a dead man; but he prayed and wept, whereas Christ commanded. Granted, Elisha had a leper cleansed; but what worked there was not the authority of a command but the figure of a mystery. Granted, the flour multiplied at the prophet's word and did not run out as food for the starving widow; yet that flour kept only one widow alive, or rather, the figure of the sacrament prefigured in it kept her alive as well. Still, these are only small examples of the Lord's witness. The fullness of faith is the Lord's cross, his death and his burial. And that is why, after saying the things above, he added: "Blessed is the one who is not offended in me."

For the cross could be a stumbling block even to the chosen. Yet there is no greater testimony to his divine person than this, nothing that seems more beyond what is human, than that one man offered himself for the whole world. By this alone the Lord is fully declared. Indeed, this is how John pointed him out: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world." But this answer is given not to those two men, John's disciples, but to all of us, so that we may believe in Christ in this way: if the deeds fit. For one will come who usurps this name for himself; and though you cannot tell him apart by the name he bears, you may tell him apart by considering his deeds.

"What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind?" Having forewarned John's disciples that they must believe in the Lord's cross, when they had gone back he turned to the crowds and began to call the poor to virtue. He did not want them, proud of heart, unstable of mind and weak in judgment, to prefer the showy to the useful and the perishable to the eternal. Rather, in humility of spirit they should take up the cross instead of parading the trappings of this world, and, as the blessed poor who have nothing of the world to lose, gladly exchange the life of the body for immortal glory. So it is not without purpose that the person of Saint John is praised here, for he set aside his love of life and did not alter the pattern of righteousness even for fear of death.

"What did you go out into the desert to see?" This world seems to be compared to a desert: still untilled, still barren, still unfruitful. The Lord tells us not to go out into it in such a way that we regard as a model and an image to imitate men who are puffed up with a fleshly mind, empty of inner virtue, and who boast of the fragile heights of worldly glory. Exposed to the storms of this world and troubled by a shifting life, they are rightly compared to a reed. In them there is no fruit of solid righteousness; tufted with the trappings of public life, covered with knots, sounding with an empty rattle, of no use to themselves and often a cause of stumbling, they pursue things that are hollow within and showy without. We are reeds, grounded in no root of a sturdier nature; and if a light breeze of good fortune blows on us, we lash those nearest us with our restless swaying, powerless to help, quick to harm. Reeds love rivers, and we delight in the passing, perishable things of the world.

Yet if someone pulls this reed out of its bed in the earth and strips it of what is superfluous, putting off the old man with his deeds, and shapes it in the hand of a swift scribe, it begins to be no longer a reed but a pen, to imprint the commands of the heavenly scriptures on the depths of the mind and write them on the tablets of the heart. Of this pen you have the saying: "My tongue is the pen of a swift scribe," which some wish to refer to Christ. So in one passage we read of the word, the pen and the scribe. The word, because he came forth from the secret depths of the Father's womb: "My heart has poured forth a good word." The pen, because the flesh of Christ set out the course of the Father's will and fulfilled the commands of the divine tongue by pouring out his sacred blood. The scribe, because with his pen, split as it were into two, distinguishing the New and the Old Testament, or the divinity and the flesh, he revealed to us the mysteries of the Father's plan.

Imitate this pen by tempering your flesh. Dip this pen of yours, that is, your flesh, not in ink but in the Spirit of the living God, so that what you write may be eternal. With such a pen Paul wrote that letter of which he says: "You are our letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God." Dip your flesh in the blood of Christ, as it is written: "That your foot may be dipped in blood." So you too must dip the footstep of your soul and the walk of your mind in unwavering confession of the Lord's cross. You dip your flesh in the blood of Christ if you wash away vices, wipe out sins, and carry about the death of Christ in your flesh, as the Apostle taught, saying: "Carrying about in our body the dying of Jesus Christ." Do not bend toward earthly things, or you will break your reed. And so it was prophesied of Christ, since he was not to be bent toward earthly things: "A bruised reed he will not break," because by the power of the resurrection he made firm the flesh that sins had bruised. The flesh of Christ is a good reed, which nailed to the gibbet of the cross the head of the serpent, the devil, and the lures of worldly desire.

"But what did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing?" The Lord is not speaking here about clothes, although concern for softer clothing makes many effeminate. As if they could not bear the weight of wool, they sweep silk garments along the ground over their covered feet, and through habit make clothing a burden. But here he seems to be pointing to another kind of garment, and, unless I am mistaken, it is the human body, with which our soul is clothed. Indeed, Joseph's tunic too was stained with blood as a figure of the Lord's body; and what else does the Apostle's saying, "Stripping off the flesh, he made a show of all principalities and powers," show, except that the body served as a garment, which the Lord stripped off in his passion in such a way that his divinity remained free and untouched by injury? So this whole passage, by a prophetic example, urges us to the courage of undergoing suffering.

Then he added: "Behold, those who wear costly clothing are in the houses of kings." Soft garments are also luxurious habits and ways of life. That is why the Apostle urges us to put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, in whom there is no sweet allurement and wanton play, but the practice and fruit of labor. For the heavenly court by no means receives those made soft by tender care of the body, by luxury and by the desire for wantonness; one climbs up to it by the hard steps of laborious virtue. But those whose limbs are slack and loosened by pleasures are exiled from the heavenly kingdom and grow old within the dwellings of this world, and the rulers of this world and of darkness have received them as imitators of their own works; for these are the kings who hold sway with a kind of worldly power.

"But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet is this man." How then did they want to see John in the desert, when he was shut up in prison? The Lord sets him before us to imitate, since he prepared the way for the Lord not only by the order of his birth according to the flesh and by the announcement of faith, but also by going before him, as it were, in a glorious passion. A greater prophet indeed, in whom the prophets come to their end. A greater prophet, because many longed to see the one whom he foretold, whom he beheld, whom he baptized.

But surely he is not greater than that one of whom Moses said: "The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you," and of whom he said: "And every soul that does not listen to that prophet will be destroyed from among the people"? If, then, Christ is a prophet, how is this man greater than all? Do we deny that Christ is a prophet? On the contrary, I affirm that the Lord is a prophet, and I say that John is greater than all, but among those born of woman, not of a virgin. For he was greater than those with whom he could be equal by the lot of birth. That other is a different nature and is not to be compared with human generations. There can be no comparison between a man and God; each is ranked above his own kind. In fact, John could be so little compared with the Son of God that he is reckoned even below the angels.

"For the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven," he says, "is greater than he." Indeed, since he had called him an angel, he was rightly ranked above men; and since he had declared him the greatest among those born of women, he added: "For the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he," so that John would know he must give way to the angels. And John is rightly ranked above his equals, since from his days the kingdom of heaven is pressed. This seems a somewhat obscure expression, and so we thought it should be explained from another book of the Gospel. For if we follow the letter, surely the inferior is pressed by the stronger, and the kingdom of heaven surpasses human things. But since there are some things that are said to become dense by being pressed together, it is not absurd to say that the kingdom is pressed when it is thronged by many.

"And those who press it seize it." If we recall that saying of the Lord, written where the Son of God says, "The kingdom of God is within you," we see that the heavenly kingdom becomes firm within us when Christ, having driven out the kingdom of the prince of this world and put worldly pleasures to flight, reigns in the hidden depths of our souls. So force is applied to the human mind, which, soothed by various allurements, flees toil and seeks pleasure, when, restrained by fear of punishment or spurred by a reward, it strives to overcome itself and, as though its labors were already endured, struggles to snatch the palm that many adversaries try to take from it. For we snatch the palm of salvation out of this world, and with watchful labor we pick fruit guarded, as it were, by wakeful serpents, yet in such a way that it is not a stealthy theft but a triumphant seizing. There is also another kind of seizing, when we seize what was offered to others. We need not labor, then, to understand who these seizers are, since we know that we are descended from Benjamin, of the stock of the ravening wolf. John had gone before to make the Jewish people righteous; the Lord himself had come to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; he had appointed apostles to establish the faith of the Jewish people by argument or by signs and miracles. But when they shunned the gifts offered to them, tax collectors and sinners began to believe in God and to come together into the faith. In them, then, the kingdom of heaven is pressed by the preaching of the apostles and made firm by the breath of the faithful people.

The woman who suffered from a flow of blood seized the kingdom; for while the Lord was on his way to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, she took a foretaste of the remedy of healing by a stealthy touch. That Canaanite woman seized the kingdom, who came out from her own region crying: "Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is cruelly tormented by a demon." Truly she pressed the kingdom, persistent in her prayers, wise in her answers, faithful in her words. She calls him back as he passes by, she asks him though he is silent, she worships him as he excuses himself, she bends him when he refuses. Does she not seem to you to snatch it away, when she draws out what is refused and seizes first what was kept for others? For the Lord had said that the children's bread ought not to be given to dogs; but she agreed, and by agreeing she seized it, saying: "Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table."

You have learned how the heavenly kingdom is seized. Let us too, then, press it and seize it; for no one eats the Passover except in haste. But who is this woman who seizes the kingdom? Not shamelessness, not wantonness, not pleasure, but the one of whom it is said: "Great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish." See, she who obtained what she wanted, who wrested out what she asked for, has seized it. That widow too seized it, who by praying again and again wrests out a hearing, if not for her innocence, then at least for her persistence.

So the Church has seized the kingdom of the synagogue. My kingdom is Christ. I seize him, who was sent to the Jews under the law, born in the law, brought up according to the law, so that he might save me, who was without the law. Christ is seized when he is promised to some and predestined for others; Christ is seized when he is born for some and helps others; Christ is seized when he is killed by some and buried by us; he is seized from those lying in wait, he is seized from those asleep. You have a passage where they themselves confessed that we seized him, saying that they were asleep: "Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep." Rise, then, you who sleep, so that you too do not lose Christ while you sleep. "Rise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead." You see that those who sleep are dead. And so we do not envy others, but we take care for ourselves; for the dead [?] could not keep the Living One.

Let those who have slept rise, even if late, even those who have lost Christ. Christ is not lost in such a way that he does not return, provided he is sought; rather, he comes back to those who keep watch and is at hand for those who rise. Indeed, he is present to all, since he is always everywhere, because he fills all things. He fails no one; it is we who fail. He fails no one, I say; he overflows for all. For sin overflowed, so that grace might overflow. Christ is grace, Christ is life, Christ is the resurrection. So whoever rises finds that he is present.

So the kingdom of heaven is seized when Christ is denied by his own household and worshipped by the Gentiles; it is seized when he is rejected by them and honored by us; it is seized when he is not recognized through inheritance and is gained through adoption.
BOOK SIX

And all the people who heard, and the tax collectors, justified God, having been baptized with the baptism of John; but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves, not having been baptized. Saint Luke, by adding particulars, has made plain what Saint Matthew had left somewhat obscure by speaking in general terms; for Matthew says: And wisdom is justified by her children. First, we see expressed here what that wisdom is; for Luke says: they justified God. God, then, is wisdom, because the Son of God is wisdom, wisdom by nature, not by progress. The wisdom that is the power of God the Father is one thing; the wisdom that is a virtue of the soul is another. The former is begotten, the latter created. The one wisdom is the author of works; the other is a work, for it is a work of the mind to be wise with prudence and to perceive keenly. These are gifts of nature. But the one who works them is not a creature but the Creator; that is, not a gift of nature but the giver of nature's gifts.

So God himself is justified through baptism when people justify themselves by confessing their own sins, as it is written: Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified. And God is justified in this: he is not rejected out of stubbornness, but his gift is acknowledged out of righteousness, for the Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness. This, then, is God's justification: that he is seen to have bestowed his gifts not on the unworthy and the guilty but on those whom washing has made innocent and righteous. Let us therefore justify the Lord, so that we may be justified by the Lord.

Let us look more closely at what it means for God to be justified. The apostle says: Let God be true and every man a liar, as it is written: That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. David too says: Against you alone have I sinned and done evil before you, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. So whoever sins and confesses the sin to God justifies God, yielding to him as victor and hoping for grace from him. In baptism, then, God is justified, for in it there is both confession and the pardon of sins.

Let us not, then, despise the counsel of God as the Pharisees did. The counsel of God is in the baptism of John; who, then, could doubt that the counsel of God is in the washing of Christ? This is the counsel that the Angel of Great Counsel found, which no one knew; for who has known the mind of the Lord? No one despises a man's counsel; who would reject the counsel of God? So let us, as her children, justify our mother; let us follow our mother. We know that a mother exposes herself to danger for her children. Let us obey the counsel of our mother Wisdom, the command of our mother.

We sang to you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not weep. These words may not seem out of place in the mouths of children, who, not yet knowing the gravity of riper years, move their bodies lightly. Yet I venture to think they can be referred to a higher sense, since the Jews seem to have believed neither the psalms at first nor the prophets' lamentations afterward: by the psalms they were summoned to rewards, by the lamentations they were called back from error. David sang so that we might hang our instruments on the willows; he himself sang, and he danced before the ark of the Lord, not out of wantonness but out of devotion. What is meant, therefore, is not the leaping of a body twisting in an actor's movements, but the eager agility of the mind and the devout agility of the body. But the Jews were not corrected, neither in their triumphs nor in their destructions. Roused by the gifts of divine kindness, they ought to have lifted up their minds, raised up their bodies, forsaken earthly things and sought heavenly ones; and, worn down by the injuries of captivity, they ought to have wept for their sin, since it was guilt that had brought the injury upon them.

Wisdom, therefore, is justified by all her children. 'By all' is well said, because justice is kept in store for all, so that the faithful may be received and the faithless rejected. This is why most Greek copies read: Wisdom is justified by all her works, because it is the work of justice to keep due measure with regard to each person's merit. Rightly, then, he says: We sang to you, and you did not dance.

For Moses sang when, in the Red Sea, the waves stood stiff for the passage of the Jews, the water stood round about them, and the same water, flowing back, drowned the horses of the Egyptians and their riders. Isaiah sang the song of his beloved vineyard, signifying that the people, once fruitful in abundant virtues, would grow rough with crimes. The Hebrew youths sang when their footprints grew moist at the touch of a dewy flame, and, though everything within and without was burning, the fire licked them alone without harm and did not scorch them. Habakkuk too, taught to soothe the public grief with a song, prophesied that the Lord's passion would be sweet to the faithful. So the prophets sang, sounding forth in spiritual strains the oracles of public salvation; and the prophets wept, softening the hard hearts of the Jews with tearful lamentations.

Scripture has taught us to sing with gravity and to chant psalms spiritually; it has also taught us to dance wisely, when the Lord says to Ezekiel: Clap your hand and stamp your foot. For God, the censor of morals, would not demand the actor's movements of a loose body, nor command men to make unseemly clatter or the clapping of women, so as to lead so great a prophet down to the buffoonery of the stage and the effeminacies of women. The revealed mysteries of the resurrection do not agree with demands for the disgraces of dancing. Yet there is indeed, there is a certain applause proper to good actions and deeds, whose sound goes out into all the world, so that the glory of things well done resounds. There is an honourable dance, in which the mind [?] and the body is lifted up by good works, when we hang our instruments on the willows.

So the prophet is commanded to clap his hand and stamp his foot; he is commanded to sing psalms, because he already saw the wedding of the Bridegroom, in which the Church is betrothed and Christ is loved. And it is a good wedding when the soul is wedded to the Word, the flesh to the spirit. At this wedding the prophet David wished us to make merry; to it he invited us, because he was uniting his own descendants. And so, more joyful than the rest, as though he were present at the very ceremony of the wedding, he urges us to celebrate the festal gift, saying: Exult in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob. Take up a psalm and bring the timbrel, the pleasant psaltery with the harp. Do you not perceive here the action of the prophet dancing? And elsewhere: I will sing to you on the harp, Holy One of Israel. My lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and so will my soul, which you have redeemed. Do you hear the voices of the harpers? Do you hear the clatter of the dancers?

Believe in the wedding. You too, take up the harp, so that the strings of your inner veins, struck by the plectrum of the Spirit, may give back the sound of good works. Take up the psaltery, so that your words and deeds may sound together in harmony. Take up the timbrel, so that the spirit within may make music on the instrument of your body, and the sweet charm of your character may find expression in active deeds. So the prophet sang when he said: Come hither from Lebanon, my bride, come hither from Lebanon. This song the children sang, and they were not heard. Which children? Those of whom he says: Behold, I and the children whom you have given me. But this song was sung not in the marketplace, not in the streets, but in Jerusalem; for Jerusalem is the Lord's marketplace, where the laws of the heavenly precepts are laid down.

And behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner. At this point many seem troubled by a scruple and raise the question whether the two evangelists appear to have disagreed about the facts, or whether they rather wished to signify some difference of mystery by the difference in what they say.

For you have it in the Gospel according to Matthew that when Jesus had come to Bethany, into the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him with an alabaster jar of precious ointment and poured it on his head as he reclined at table. Moreover, here the Pharisee says within himself that if Jesus were a prophet, he would know the woman was a sinner and ought to avoid her and her ointment; there, when the ointment is poured out, the disciples complain. Both accounts, then, must be explained; but let whatever comes first in the order of the writers also take first place in the order of interpretation.

So the Lord Jesus came into the house of Simon the leper. The divine plan is plain: he does not flee the leper or avoid the unclean, so that he may wash away the stains of the human body. Now the leper's house was in Bethany, and Bethany, interpreted, means 'house of obedience.' So Bethany is the whole place, and the house of Simon a portion of the whole place. Does it not seem to you that Bethany is this world, in which we owe the service of obedient servitude, and the house of Simon the leper is the earth, which is a portion of the world? And the prince of this age is a kind of Simon the leper. So the Lord Jesus Christ came from those higher places into this world and descended to the earth. He was not in this world, but in obedient love he was sent into this world. He himself says: As you sent me into this world. So this woman heard that Christ had come, and she entered the house of Simon; for this woman could not have been healed unless Christ had come to earth. And perhaps she too enters the house of Simon because she bears the figure of some higher soul, or rather of the Church, which descends to earth in order to gather a people to herself by a good fragrance.

This woman, then, Matthew presents as pouring ointment on the head of Christ, and perhaps that is why he did not wish to call her a sinner; for according to Luke it was the sinful woman who poured ointment on Christ's feet. So she may not be the same woman, and then the evangelists cannot be thought to have contradicted each other. The question can also be resolved by a difference of merit and of time, so that the one is still a sinner and the other already more perfect. For even if the Church, or the soul, does not change its person, it does change in its progress. And so, if you picture a soul drawing near to God faithfully, not with foul and obscene sins but devoutly serving the word of God and having the confidence of unstained chastity, you will notice that it rises to the very head of Christ; and the head of Christ is God; and it spreads abroad the fragrance of its merits. For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God; indeed, the life of the righteous, fragrant with a good odour, honours God.

If you understand this, you will see that this woman is truly blessed: wherever this gospel is preached she is named, and her memory never fades, because she poured on the head of Christ the ointment of the fragrance of good conduct and righteous deeds. Whoever approaches the head does not know how to be puffed up, unlike that man who was vainly inflated by the mind of his flesh and did not hold fast to the head. But let whoever does not hold the head of Christ hold at least his feet, because the one body, joined together and supplied, grows with the growth that is from God.

The other woman, other either in person or in progress, is the one who is close to us, for we have not yet renounced our sins. Where are our tears, where our groans, where our weeping? Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and weep before the Lord who made us, so that we may at least come to the feet of Jesus. For we cannot yet come to the head: the sinner comes to the feet, the righteous to the head.

Yet she too who sinned has ointment. You too, bring me repentance after your sins. Wherever you hear that the Righteous One has come, whether into the house of an unworthy man or into the house of a Pharisee, hurry there, snatch the grace away from the host, snatch the kingdom of heaven; for from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. Wherever you hear the name of Christ, run there; whoever's inner house you learn that Jesus has entered, hasten there yourself. When you find Wisdom, when you find Righteousness reclining in someone's inner rooms, run to the feet; that is, seek even the furthest part of wisdom. Do not disdain the feet: that woman touched the hem and was healed. Confess your offences with tears, so that the heavenly Righteousness may say of you too: She has watered my feet with her tears and with her hair

has wiped them. And perhaps Christ did not wash his own feet so that we might wash them with our tears. Good tears, which can not only wash away our offence but also water the footsteps of the heavenly Word, so that his steps may abound in us! Good tears, in which there is not only the redemption of sinners but also the refreshment of the righteous! For this is the voice of the righteous man: My tears have been my bread.

Even if you cannot approach the head of Christ, let Christ touch your head with his feet. Both his hem heals and his feet heal. Spread out your hair; lay before him every honour of your body. It is no ordinary hair that can wipe the feet of Christ. He bears witness to this who could not be overcome as long as he had his hair. Moreover, it is not fitting for a woman to pray with her head shaved. Let her by all means have hair with which to wrap Christ's footsteps, with which to wipe his feet with the locks of her beauty and the comeliness of wisdom, so that they may be moistened at least by the last drops of the dew of divine power; let her press her kisses on the feet of Righteousness. This woman is of no ordinary merit.

Of her Wisdom can say: From the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet; so that she knows how to speak nothing but wisdom, to love nothing but righteousness, to taste nothing but chastity, to kiss nothing but purity. For a kiss is a sign of mutual love; a kiss is a pledge of charity.

Blessed is the one who can anoint the feet of Christ even with oil. Simon, indeed, had not yet anointed them. But more blessed is she who anoints them with ointment; for the charm of many flowers gathered into one spreads abroad a varied sweetness of fragrances. And perhaps no one but the Church alone could bring this ointment, for she has countless flowers of diverse scents; and she rightly takes on the figure of a sinful woman, because Christ too took on the form of a sinner.

And therefore no one can love as much as she who loves in many. Not even Peter himself, who said: Lord, you know that I love you; not even Peter himself, who was grieved because he was asked, Do you love me? For he did not want something manifest to be asked about as if it were unknown. So not even Peter himself, because the Church loved in Peter; nor Paul himself, because Paul too is a portion of her. You too, love very much, so that very much may be forgiven you. Paul sinned much, for he was even a persecutor, but he loved much, persevering even to martyrdom. His many sins were forgiven him because he too loved much, not sparing his own blood for the name of God.

See the divine plan: in the house of the Pharisee the sinful woman is glorified; in the house of the Law and the prophet, it is not the Pharisee but the Church that is justified; for the Pharisee did not believe, but she believed. In fact he said: If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him. Now the house of the Law is Judea, which is written not on stones but on the tablets of the heart. In this house the Church, now greater than the Law, is justified; for the Law knows no remission of sins, the Law does not have the mystery by which hidden things are cleansed, and so what is lacking in the Law is brought to completion in the Gospel.
There were two debtors, he says, who owed a certain moneylender: one owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty.

Who are these two debtors but two peoples, one from the Jews and the other from the Gentiles, both in debt to that lender of the heavenly treasure? One, he says, owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. This is no ordinary denarius: the king's image is formed on it, and the emperor's trophy is stamped on it. It is not material money that we owe this lender, but merits for the scales and the coin of virtues, whose worth is weighed out by the heaviness of their weight, the stamp of justice and the ring of confession. Woe to me if I do not have what I received! Or, since it is hard to find anyone who can pay this lender the whole debt, woe to me if I do not ask, "Forgive me my debt!" For the Lord would not have taught us to pray that our debts be forgiven unless he knew that hardly anyone would be able to pay what they owe.

But who is the people that owes more, if not we, to whom more has been entrusted? To them were entrusted the oracles of God; to us is entrusted the Virgin's giving birth. You have a talent, the Virgin's giving birth; you have the hundredfold fruit of faith. Emmanuel, God with us, has been entrusted to us; the Lord's cross, death and resurrection have been entrusted to us. Although Christ suffered for all, he suffered especially for us, because he suffered for the Church. So there is no doubt that whoever has received more owes more. By human reckoning, perhaps, the one who owed more has given more offence; but through the Lord's mercy the case is changed, so that the one who owed more loves more, if only he obtains grace. For gratitude belongs both to the one who repays and to the one who simply has it, since the one who has it pays by the very fact of having it. It is held by repaying, and it is repaid by holding.

And so, since there is nothing we can worthily return to God (for what could we return for the indignity of the flesh he took on, for the scourgings, for the cross, death and burial?), woe to me if I do not love! I dare to say that Peter did not repay, and therefore he loved more. Paul did not repay either. He did indeed repay death for death, but the rest he did not repay, because he owed much. Hear him saying that he did not repay: "Who has first given to him, that he should be repaid?" Even if we repay cross for cross and burial for burial, do we repay him from whom, through whom and in whom we have all things? Let us therefore repay love for the debt, charity for the gift, gratitude for the money; for the one to whom more is given loves more.

But let us return to that earlier woman. Even the apostles do not yet understand her purpose, which had been hidden in God from the ages; for who has known the mind of the Lord? So the disciples grumbled because the woman poured ointment on his head, and complained, saying, "Why is this being wasted like this? It could have been sold for a price and given to the poor." You cannot detect what exactly was wrong with their words unless you understand the mystery. To smell of ointment is the mark of a self-indulgent man, or rather of one who is no man. Even those who like to smell of it usually anoint themselves; they do not drench themselves. What is wrong, then, with saying, "This could have been sold for a price and given to the poor"? He himself had certainly said earlier, "Whatever you did to one of the least of these, you did to me." But he was offering his own death for the poor.

So this is no simple figure, and therefore the Word of God answered them, "Why do you trouble the woman? You always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me." You always have the poor with you, so do good. You must not put off the poor man just because he is always with you, since the prophet tells you, "Do not say to the poor man, 'Tomorrow I will give.'" But the prophet spoke only of mercy, whereas here he has put faith before mercy. Mercy has merit only if it is bestowed with faith going before it: "For in pouring this ointment on my body she did it for my burial." So it was not the ointment that the Lord

loved; he loved the charity, accepted the faith and approved the humility. You too, if you desire grace, must increase your charity. Pour onto the body of Jesus faith in the resurrection, the fragrance of the Church, the ointment of shared charity, and then go on to give to the poor. That money will profit you more if you do not hand it out as something you have in excess, but give it generously in Christ's name as something that will bear fruit, giving it to the poor in such a way that you offer it to Christ. So do not take the ointment poured on his head only according to the letter, for the letter kills, but according to the spirit, for the spirit is life.

What, then, is this woman's ointment? Who can hear this? Who has such ears that, when Jesus speaks the word he received from the Father (or rather, since he himself is the Word), he can grasp so lofty a mystery? Even the disciples understand in part, though they do not understand the whole. So some think that the disciples meant that the faith of the Gentiles ought to have been bought with the price of the ointment, when it could be bought only at the price of the Lord's blood. This seems likely. Indeed, John the evangelist records the words of Judas Iscariot, who valued that ointment at three hundred denarii, as you read: "It could have been sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor." Now the sum of three hundred signifies the cross. But the Lord does not look for a superficial foreknowledge of the mystery; he would rather that the faith of believers be buried together with him.

That, however, is how we understand the words of the other apostles. Judas, though, is condemned for avarice, because he preferred money to the Lord's burial. Even if he had some sense of the passion, he went wrong in setting so high a price. Christ wants to be valued cheaply, so that he may be bought by all and no poor person may be deterred. "Freely you have received," he says, "freely give." The depth of riches seeks not money but grace. He himself bought us with his precious blood; he did not sell us. We would say more about this if we did not remember having discussed it elsewhere.

Therefore, according to the words of the Lord, in whom are hidden the treasures of wisdom that no one could foresee, I must work at his burial. Then it will be believed that his flesh rested and did not see corruption, and the death of his body will fill our house with its fragrance, so that we believe that he committed his spirit into the Father's hands, and that his divinity, kept apart from death, did not share in the sufferings of the body.

Understand how the body of the Son smells of ointment. That body is the one that was laid aside, not the one that was lost. His body is the tradition of the Scriptures; his body is the Church. We are the fragrance of his body, and so it is fitting that we adorn the death of his body. It does not need our adornments, but the poor need them. I will adorn his body if I become a preacher of his words and can open the mystery of the cross to the Gentiles. He adorned it who said, "We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." The cross is adorned when what ignorance thinks foolish is judged through the gospel to be wiser, so that we can teach how the hostile power is destroyed through the Lord's cross. I have poured ointment on the Lord's body, and what was thought dead begins to breathe out fragrance.

So let each of us set about buying, by our own labour and the striving of the virtues, an alabaster jar of ointment. It should be nothing cheap and common, but precious ointment in alabaster, ointment of pure nard. For if anyone gathers the flowers of faith and preaches Jesus Christ crucified, he pours the ointment of his faith over the whole Church, which is the body of Christ, dead to the world and at rest in God. The whole house begins to smell of the Lord's passion, of his death and of his resurrection, so that each person in the number of this holy people can say to him, "But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." The fragrance breathes and the ointment smells in the body if anyone can confidently say (and would that I could!), "But to me the world is crucified." The world is crucified not to one who loves riches or the honours of this age, not to one who looks to his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, not to one who loves what is seen rather than what is unseen, not to one who is greedy for life. It is crucified to one who hastens to depart and be with Christ. For this is what it means to take up the cross and follow Christ: that we too die with him and are buried with him, so that we may give off the fragrance of the ointment this woman poured out for his burial. This is no ordinary ointment, for by it the name of Christ is spread far and wide. That is why it was also said prophetically, "Your name is ointment poured out." It was poured out so that faith might give off a stronger fragrance.

From this woman, then, we understand the meaning of the apostle's saying, "Sin abounded, so that grace might abound all the more."
