For if sin had not abounded in this woman, grace would not have abounded all the more; she recognized her sin and offered her gratitude. So the law is necessary, for through the law I came to know sin. If there had been no law, sin would lie hidden. By recognizing sin I ask for pardon. Through the law, then, I recognize the kinds of sins, including the crime of transgression; I run to repentance and obtain grace. The law, then, is the source of good, because it sends us to grace.

"My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it." The moral teacher makes himself an example to others; he gives the commands and also carries them out himself. He was about to lay down for others that whoever does not leave father and mother is not worthy of the Son of God, and so he is the first to submit himself to this rule. This is not because he rejects the dutiful service owed to a mother, since the commandment is his own: "Whoever does not honour father and mother shall surely die." It is because he recognizes that he owes more to his Father's mysteries than to his mother's affections. Nor are parents being wrongly rejected; rather, we are taught that the bonds of minds are holier than the bonds of bodies.

So those who wanted to see Christ ought not to have stood outside, for "the word is near, in your heart and in your mouth." The Word is within, then; the light is within. That is why it says, "Come to him and be enlightened." If even his own parents are not acknowledged when they stand outside (and perhaps they are not acknowledged in order to give us an example), how will we be acknowledged if we stand outside?

Let no one think that filial devotion is offended where the command of the law is being fulfilled. For if "a man will leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two will be one flesh," this sacrament is rightly kept in Christ and in the Church. So his parents should not have been preferred to his own body. Here, then, the mother is not disowned, as certain heretics claim, setting their traps, since he acknowledges her even from the cross. Rather, the pattern of the heavenly commands is preferred to bodily kinship. It is also reasonable to understand that, through the figure of his parents, he shows that the Church which believed is to be preferred to the Jews, from whom Christ came according to the flesh. So, understanding that he had come to earth for the sake of

the divine mystery and the gathering of the Church, he left his parents and went up into the boat. For no one could sail across this world without Christ, since a storm of worldly temptations often troubles even those with whom the Lord is present. The same plan is kept in the case of the apostles, so that you may notice that no one can leave this course of life without temptation, because temptation is the exercise of faith.

We are exposed, then, to the storms of spiritual wickedness; but like watchful sailors, let us wake the helmsman. Yet helmsmen themselves are often in danger. What helmsman, then, shall I look for? Surely the one who does not obey the winds but commands them, of whom it is written:

"But he rose and rebuked the wind." What does "rising" mean? He was at rest, but he rested in bodily sleep while his attention was on the mystery of his divinity. For where wisdom is, where the Word is, nothing is done without the Word and nothing without prudence.

Earlier you read that he spent the night in prayer, so how could he sleep here in a storm? But this shows the serenity of his power: while all were afraid, he alone rested undismayed. One who does not share the danger, then, does not share their nature. Even if the body sleeps, the divinity is at work, and faith is at work. So he says, "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?" And they are rightly rebuked for being afraid while Christ was present, since no one who clings to him can perish.

So he strengthened their faith, restored the calm and commanded the wind to cease. This was not the north wind or the south-west wind, but surely the one to whom the angel Michael said, in the Letter of Jude, "May the Lord rebuke you." That is why St Matthew too says, "He rebuked the wind and the sea." Would that he might deign to restrain its harsh blasts within us, so that calm may return to our storm-tossed life and take away the fear of shipwreck! Although he no longer sleeps with the sleep of his own body, let us take care that he does not sleep and rest within us through the sleep of our body.

It is enough to have touched briefly on what we outlined in an earlier place. In the book according to Matthew we learn that two men possessed by demons met Christ in the region of the Gerasenes, but here St Luke presents one, and him naked; for whoever has lost the covering of his nature and of virtue is naked. Why do the evangelists seem to disagree about the number? I think this should not be passed over idly but looked into. Although the number differs, the mystery agrees. This man who had a demon is a figure of the Gentile people: covered with vices, naked to error, exposed to crime. The two men are likewise a figure of the Gentile people. For although Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth, only Shem's family was taken into God's possession. From the other two sprang the peoples of the various nations. One of them was cursed because he did not cover his naked father. The other was blessed because, though he turned his face away so as not to take in the shame of his naked parent, piety led him to cover his father, and so he washed away the curse on his brother's descendants.

"For a long time," he says, "he had been driven about." He had been tormented from the flood until the Lord's coming, bursting the bonds of nature in his mad frenzy. St Matthew had good reason to note that they lived among the tombs, since the souls of such people seem to live in burial mounds. For what else are the bodies of the faithless but tombs of the dead, in which the words of God do not dwell? So he was driven into desert places, that is, places barren of spiritual virtues: a fugitive from the law, cut off from the prophets, far removed from grace.

He was afflicted not by one demon but by the assault of a whole legion. When the legion saw the Lord and recognized him, it knew in advance that at the time of the Lord's coming it was to be thrust into the abyss, and it began to beg for leave to enter the swine. First we should note the Lord's mercy: he condemns no one first, but each person brings his own punishment on himself. The demons are not sent into the swine; they ask for it themselves, because they could not bear the brightness of heavenly light. In the same way, people with sore eyes cannot bear the sun's rays, but seek out dark places and leave bright ones. So let the demons flee the splendour of eternal light and dread the torments that await them before their time. They are not foretelling the future; they are remembering what was prophesied. For Zechariah said, "And on that day the Lord will destroy the names of the idols from the earth, and they will be remembered no more; and I will burn the unclean spirit out of the earth." We are taught, then, that they will not remain for ever and that their malice cannot be everlasting. Now, fearing that punishment, they say, "You have come to destroy us." But because they still want to exist, they withdraw from human beings, on whose account they know they must undergo punishment, and ask to be sent into the swine.

Who are these swine, if not perhaps those of whom it was said, "Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, or they may trample them under their feet"? They are those who live like unclean animals, without speech or reason, and have defiled the ornaments of their natural virtues by the muddy conduct of their lives. They are carried headlong by impulse, since no consideration of any merit calls them back. Thrust, as it were, from higher to lower down the slope of wickedness, they are suffocated in the waters among the drifting things of this world, and they perish like men strangled, with their breath cut off. For those who are tossed uncertainly this way and that on the flowing tide of pleasures can have no life-giving exchange with any spirit.

We see, then, that a person brings his own misery upon himself. For if someone had not lived like a pig, the devil would never have gained power over him; or if he had gained it, it would have been to test him, not to destroy him. Or perhaps, since after the Lord's coming the devil could no longer corrupt the good, he seeks the ruin not of everyone but of the fickle. In the same way a robber lies in wait not for the armed but for the unarmed, and attacks the weak, knowing that he would be scorned by the strong or condemned by the powerful.

But someone says, "Why does God allow the devil to do this?" I answer: so that the good may be tested and the wicked punished, for this is the penalty of sin. Indeed, you read that the Lord sends fever and trembling, evil spirits and blindness and every kind of scourge, according to what sins deserve. But let us return to the reading.

"When the herdsmen saw this," he says, "they fled." For neither the teachers of philosophy nor the rulers of the synagogue can bring any cure to perishing peoples. Christ alone takes away the sins of peoples, provided they do not refuse to bear patiently with the healing. Otherwise he does not deign to cure the unwilling, and he quickly leaves the weak when he sees that his presence is a burden to them. So it was with the people of the Gerasenes. They came out of their city, in which the image of the synagogue seems to appear, and asked him to leave, because they were seized with great fear.
For a weak mind cannot take in the word of God or bear the weight of wisdom; it gives way and falls apart.

So he troubled them no longer, but went up and returned. He went up, that is, from lower to higher, from the synagogue to the Church. He returned across the lake, as Luke says here, or across the sea, as Matthew says; for between us and them lies a great sea. So no one passes from the Church to the synagogue without endangering his salvation. But anyone who wants to pass from the synagogue to the Church should take up his cross, so that he may escape the danger.

Why is the man who was set free not taken along, but told to return home? Surely so that any occasion for boasting may be avoided, and so that he may show unbelievers that this home is a natural dwelling place. So the man who had obtained the remedy of health is told to go back from the tombs and sepulchres to that spiritual home, so that where there had been a tomb of the mind, there may be a temple of God.

"And behold, there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. He fell at Jesus' feet and begged him to come to his house, because he had an only daughter about twelve years old, and she was dying." As we said, Christ had left the synagogue among the Gerasenes, and we, who were waiting for him, welcomed the one his own people had not received. So he was not long absent from us who were waiting for him, nor does he refuse to return to them if he is asked. This man, the ruler of the synagogue, who had an only daughter, was praying for the healing of the perishing synagogue, which was being driven towards death because Christ was leaving it. Whom are we to take as the ruler of the synagogue, if not the law? Out of regard for it the Lord did not abandon the synagogue completely, but kept the medicine of salvation in store for those who believe. So while the Word of God was hurrying to this ruler's daughter to save the children of Israel, the holy Church gathered from the Gentiles, which was perishing through falling into baser sins, seized first by faith the healing that had been prepared for others.

We have thought this passage sufficiently explained in its moral sense, so we will not go back over what has already been said, but wish to touch briefly on its mystical meaning. Did it not happen that when the Word of God came to the Jews, he was taken up by the Gentiles, and that those who had not believed under the law were the first to believe under grace?

For just as that woman had spent all her substance on physicians, so too the assembly of the Gentiles had lost all the gifts of nature and squandered its inheritance of life. It was holy, modest and devout, quicker in faith and more hesitant out of shame; for modesty and faith both mean acknowledging one's weakness and not despairing of pardon. So in her modesty she touched the fringe; in her faith she came near; in her devotion she believed; in her wisdom she knew that she had been healed. In the same way the holy people of the Gentiles, who believed God, blushed at its sin so as to forsake it, brought faith so as to believe, showed devotion so as to ask, and put on wisdom so as to perceive its own healing. It also took the confidence to confess that it had seized first what belonged to another.

But why is Christ touched from behind? Is it because it is written: "You shall walk after the Lord your God"? And what does it mean that the ruler's daughter, twelve years old, was dying, and that this woman had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, unless we are to understand that as long as the synagogue flourished, the Church was suffering? The failing of the one is the strength of the other, for "through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles"; and the end of the one is the beginning of the other, a beginning not of nature but of salvation, for "a partial blindness has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in." So the synagogue is older than the Church not in time but in the appearance of health, because as long as the one believed, the other did not believe, and lay sick and languishing through various afflictions of body and soul, with remedies that could not heal. She heard that the Jewish people were ailing; she began to hope for a remedy for her own salvation; she recognized that the time had come when the physician would be present from heaven; she rose to go and meet the Word, and saw that he was being pressed by the crowds. For those who press do not believe; those who touch believe. Christ is touched by faith, Christ is seen by faith; he is not touched by the body, he is not grasped by the eyes. For the one who sees without seeing does not see, the one who does not understand what he hears does not hear, and the one who does not touch in faith does not touch. And so, to bring out the faith of the one who touched him, he says: "Someone touched me;

for I perceived that power had gone out from me." This is clear evidence that the Godhead was not confined within the limits of the human condition, nor was Wisdom shut up within the enclosure of the body. It is not caught in bodily narrowness, it is not held fast, but the eternal power overflows beyond the bounds of our lowliness. For the Gentile people is not set free by human aid; the gathering of the nations is the gift of God, and even a small faith moves the eternal mercy to bend down. Now if we consider how great our faith is and understand how great the Son of God is, we see that compared with him we touch only the fringe, and cannot reach the upper part of his garment. If, then, we too want to be healed, let us touch the fringe of Christ by faith.

Whoever touches the fringe, whoever touches him from behind, is not hidden from him. For God does not need eyes in order to see, nor does he perceive in a bodily way; he holds within himself the knowledge of all things. Blessed, then, is the one who has touched even the outermost part of the Word; for who can grasp the whole?

But let us return to the girl who is still sick, so that she may not be thought to have died through our delay rather than through her own. Servants came, it says, and said to the ruler: "Do not trouble him; your daughter is dead."

First let us note that, when he was about to raise the dead girl, he first healed the woman with the flow of blood, to create faith. And so that you may know that the flow of blood was stopped as an example, the one woman is cured while the other is being sought. In the same way the temporal resurrection is celebrated at the Lord's passion, so that the eternal one may be believed. In the same way Mary is told that a barren woman will give birth, so that the virgin may believe that she will conceive. And indeed, Mary heard that Elizabeth would give birth, and did not doubt her own child-bearing.

Servants came, it says, and told the ruler: "Do not trouble him." These too still did not believe in the resurrection, which Jesus foretold in the Law and fulfilled in the Gospel. So when he came into the house, he brought in only a few witnesses of the resurrection that was to come, for many did not believe in the resurrection straight away.

Then, when the Lord said, "The girl is not dead but asleep," they laughed at him, it says. For whoever does not believe mocks. So let those who think their dead are dead weep for them. Where there is faith in the resurrection, what we see is not death but rest. Nor does this conflict with Matthew's statement that there were trumpeters and a noisy crowd in the ruler's house. Perhaps by ancient custom trumpeters were brought in to stir up and rouse the mourning. Or perhaps, because of the chant of the law and the letter, the synagogue could not grasp spiritual joy.

So Jesus held the girl's hand, healed her, and ordered that she be given something to eat. This is evidence of life, so that people would believe it was no phantom but reality. Blessed is the one whose hand Wisdom holds. Would that she might hold my deeds too! May justice hold my hand, may the word of God hold it, lead me into its inner rooms, turn away the spirit of error, turn me toward the spirit of salvation, and order that I be given something to eat! For the word of God is heavenly bread. Hence that Wisdom, who has filled the sacred altars of the divine body and blood with food, says: "Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you."

Yet why are the two cases so different? Earlier, the widow's son is raised in public. Here, most of the witnesses are sent out. But I think that the Lord's compassion is shown in the earlier case too. The widowed mother of an only son could not bear delay, and so he acted quickly, so that she would not suffer any longer. There is also a lesson of wisdom here. The widow's son shows that the Church will believe quickly. The daughter of the synagogue ruler shows that the Jews will indeed believe, but only a few out of many.

"And whoever does not receive you, when you leave that city, shake off even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them." The precepts of the Gospel describe what kind of man the preacher of the kingdom of God ought to be. He goes without staff, without bag, without shoes, without bread, without money. That is, he does not seek the props of worldly support, and being secure in faith, he should think that the less he seeks these things, the more readily they can be supplied to him. Those who wish may take these things in another sense, so that this passage seems to shape only a spiritual disposition. It would then describe someone who seems to have stripped off the body like a garment, not only by rejecting power and despising riches, but also by renouncing the allurements of the flesh itself.

First of all they are given a general command of peace and constancy: they are to bring peace, keep their constancy, and guard the rights of the bond of hospitality. For it is unfitting for a preacher of the heavenly kingdom to run about from house to house and break the rights of hospitality, which ought to be inviolable. But just as they are told to accept the kindness of hospitality, so too, if they are not received, they are commanded to shake off the dust and leave the city. This teaches that hospitality is rewarded with no small good. Not only do we bestow peace on our hosts, but if any faults of earthly fickleness cast a shadow over them, these are taken away when they receive the footsteps of apostolic preaching. Nor is it pointless that, according to Matthew, the apostles are told to choose the house they enter, so that they have no reason to change lodgings and violate the bond. Yet the one who gives hospitality is not given the same warning, lest hospitality itself be lessened while a guest is being chosen.

Taken literally, the form of this precept about the sacredness of hospitality deserves respect. But its heavenly meaning also smiles on us when we look at the mystery. For when a house is chosen, a worthy host is sought. Let us consider whether the Church and Christ are perhaps meant as the ones to be preferred. What house is more worthy to receive apostolic preaching than the holy Church? And who seems more worthy of preference than Christ? He is accustomed to wash his guests' feet, and he does not let anyone he has received into his house live there with polluted feet. Though they are stained by their former life, he still deigns to make their path clean for the future. He alone, then, is the one whom no one ought to desert or exchange for another, and to whom it is rightly said: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe." You see one who carried out the heavenly precepts. Because he did not change his lodging, he earned a share in the heavenly consecration.

We are commanded, then, to look first of all for faith in a church. If Christ is to dwell there, it should certainly be chosen. But if an unbelieving people or a heretical teacher defiles the dwelling, we are to avoid communion with heretics and flee the synagogue. The dust is to be shaken off the feet, lest the footprint of your mind be polluted by the barren drought of crumbling unbelief, as if by dry and sandy ground. The preacher of the gospel ought to take upon himself the bodily weaknesses of the faithful. As if with his own feet, he should lift up and wipe away their empty deeds, which are like dust, as it is written: "Who is weak, and I am not weak?" In the same way, if there is a church that rejects the faith and does not hold the foundations of apostolic preaching, it must be abandoned, so that it cannot spatter anyone with the stain of unbelief. The Apostle also stated this clearly when he said: "Avoid a heretic after one warning."

"But he said to them: You give them something to eat. And they said: We have no more than five loaves." Why is it that John's passion is described later, yet here Herod's words already show him dead? Perhaps it is because, after the law came to an end, the food of the gospel begins to feed the hungry hearts of the peoples [?]. And so, after the woman who stood as a type of the Church was healed of the flow of blood, and after the apostles were sent out to preach the kingdom of God, the food of heavenly grace is given. But notice to whom it is given. Not to the idle. Not to those sitting at ease in the city, as if in the synagogue or in worldly rank. It is given to those who seek Christ in the desert. Those who are not disdainful are themselves welcomed by Christ, and the Word of God speaks with them, not about worldly things but about the kingdom of heaven. And if any bear the sores of bodily suffering, he gladly grants them his medicine.

It followed, then, that those he had healed of the pain of their wounds he should also free from hunger with spiritual food. So no one receives Christ's food without first being healed, and those who are called to the supper are first healed by being called. If someone was lame, he received the power to walk so that he could come. If someone was deprived of the light of his eyes, he certainly could not enter the Lord's house unless his sight was restored.

Everywhere, then, the order of the mystery is kept. First, medicine is given to wounds through the forgiveness of sins. Afterwards, the food of the heavenly table is given in abundance. Even so, this crowd is not yet fed with stronger food, and hearts that hunger for a more solid faith are not yet nourished with the body and blood of Christ. "I gave you milk to drink," he says, "not solid food, for you were not yet able to take it. And even now you are not able." The five loaves are like milk. The more solid food is the body of Christ, and the stronger drink is the blood of the Lord. We do not feast on everything, or drink everything, straight away from the start. "Drink this first," it says. So there is a first thing to drink, and there is also a second. There is a first thing to eat, and there is also a second and a third. First there are five loaves, second there are seven, and third there is the very body of Christ.

Let us by no means desert such a Lord, then. He deigns to give us food according to each one's strength, so that stronger food does not overwhelm the weak and meager food does not leave the strong unsatisfied. For "let the one who is weak eat vegetables." And let the one who now seems to be escaping the snares of weakness eat of these five loaves and two fish. Certainly, if he is shy about asking for food, let him leave all his possessions and hurry to the word of God himself. As soon as he begins to listen, he begins to hunger. The apostles begin to see that he is hungry. Even if they do not yet understand what he hungers for, Christ understands. He knows that he hungers not for worldly food but for the food of Christ. He says: "I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way." The good Lord asks for eagerness and supplies the strength.

Lord Jesus, would that you were willing, together with me, not to send these people away hungry! Refresh them with the feast you give, so that, strengthened by your food, they may not fear the weakness of hunger. Would that you might also say of us: "I do not want to send them away hungry!" Tell me why you do not want to send them away hungry. But you have already told me: if you send anyone away hungry, he faints on the way. That is, he fails either during the course of this life or before he reaches the end of the road. He fails before he comes to the Father and understands that Christ is from the Father, that Christ is from heaven, and that the Christ who descended is the same one who ascended. Otherwise, when he learns that Christ was born of a virgin, he might begin to regard him as the power not of God but of a man.

So, lest they faint, he says: "You give them something to eat. And they said: We have no more than five loaves and two fish, unless we go and buy food for this whole crowd." The apostles had not yet understood that the food of a believing people is not for sale. Christ knew. He knew that it was rather we who had to be bought back, and that his own feast was free. So the disciples did not yet have the food that could redeem us. Yet they already had food that could satisfy us, food that could strengthen us, for "bread strengthens the heart of man." So the Lord has compassion, lest anyone faint on the way. If anyone does faint, then, he faints not because of the Lord Jesus but because of himself, and you have nothing to blame on the Lord, who prevails when he is judged. What could you say to him who gave you every support of strength? Did he not beget you? Did he not feed you himself? His food is strength, his food is courage. But if through your own negligence you have lost the strength you received, it was not the protection of heavenly food that failed you but that of your own mind. Indeed, just as the Lord sends rain on the just and the unjust, so he also feeds the unjust and the just.

When holy Elijah was already fainting on the way, did he not walk for forty days in the strength of food, and was it not an angel who gave him that food? But if Jesus feeds you and you keep the food you have received, you will walk not for forty days and forty nights, but (I dare to say it, relying on the examples of Scripture) for forty years. You will go out from the borders of Egypt until you reach a broad land, a land flowing with honey and milk, which the Lord swore he would give to our fathers. It is the strength of this land that you must seek. The meek possess it. I do not mean this land, which is dry, but the land that is strengthened by the food of Christ. Established under the rule of the eternal King, it is thronged with the homes of the saints.

So the Lord Jesus distributes food. He wants to give to all and refuses no one, for he is the steward of all. But when he breaks the loaves and gives them to the disciples, if you do not stretch out your hands to take food for yourself, you will faint on the way. Nor will you be able to lay your fault on him who has compassion and distributes. But he distributes to those who stay with him even in the desert, who do not leave on the first, second, or third day. For so you find elsewhere: "I have compassion on this crowd, because they have now stayed with me for three days." What graciousness, what kindness toward human beings is breathed out in him! He does not want to send them away hungry; he does not want them to faint on the way.

So do not fall away from God's discipline, and do not grow weary when he rebukes you. Do not grow weary now, so that you do not grow weary later. For what will you answer him, or how will you excuse yourself, if you lose the strength of the food he provides? You cannot say that he did not give you food, for he gives it to all. You cannot say that he did not want to make you good. He set good and evil before you, so that your goodness would be voluntary and not the result of necessity. There is a great difference between someone who does something unwillingly out of necessity and someone who chooses what is good of his own will. "For if I do this unwillingly, I am simply carrying out a stewardship entrusted to me; if willingly, I have a reward." Let us consider, then, that we shall stand before the judgment seat of Christ, and if our work is burned up, we shall have no excuse to offer. For he will say what he has already said through the prophet: "My people, what have I done to you, or how have I wearied you? Answer me." He will say to the one who has fainted on the way: "Why did you faint on the way? Did I not make loaves? Did I not bless them? Did I not order them to be given out? Why then were you unwilling to take them?"

How many even of those present will faint on the way, even after these sermons! The sermons are ours, yet they must be regarded as loaves, since no one says "Lord Jesus" except in the Holy Spirit. How many, I say, will faint, wander off into the ways of the Gentiles, and commit fornication on the byways! Would that it were one and not many! But even if someone faints, Jesus is not the cause of his fainting. For he distributes to all who follow him, whether they are five thousand or four thousand.

The number is not without meaning, nor the order, nor the leftovers of those who ate. Why are more people, five thousand, satisfied with five loaves, a smaller number, while fewer people, four thousand, are fed with seven loaves, a larger number? If we look only at the miracle of the deed, it seems more divine that more people had plenty from a smaller amount. Why, then, was the lesser miracle added to the greater one, as if it surpassed it? For we read that first five thousand were satisfied with five loaves, and afterwards four thousand with seven loaves.

Let us look, then, for the mystery, which surpasses the miracle. The five thousand, like the five bodily senses, seem to have received from Christ food still close to bodily things. The four thousand are still in the body and in this world, which consists of four elements. Yet with good reason they are said to have received the food of mystical rest, for they are already on a level with the world and are destined to be above it. Though they are in this world, those to whom the food of mystical rest is given are not within the world. For the world was made in six days, and on the seventh day there was rest, and the Lord sanctified it. Rest, then, lies beyond the world, and the fruit of rest lies beyond the world too. And so: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God." Since God is above the world, no one can see God unless he first rises above the world with spiritual sight. So the seventh beatitude belongs to the peacemakers, and seven baskets of fragments are left over from the four thousand. This bread of the sabbaths is no ordinary bread: it is sanctified bread, the bread of rest. And perhaps, if you have first eaten the five loaves in a way the senses can perceive, I will dare to say this: after the five loaves and the seven, the third time you will not eat bread on earth. Above the earth you will eat eight loaves, like those who are in heaven. For just as the seven loaves are loaves of rest, so the eight loaves are loaves of resurrection. So those who are fed with seven loaves stayed for three days, and perhaps they attained a complete faith in the future resurrection and constancy in it. Indeed, the saints say: "We will go three days' journey, to feast before the Lord our God." But those matters belong in their own place.

About the five loaves, holy John taught me something I did not know, which holy Matthew had not taught, nor holy Luke, for a different grace was given to each. He taught me, I say, that these five loaves were made of barley. So we were right to say that this food is suited to those who are still bodily. For why barley first? Because whoever comes to the faith must be nourished first with milk and then with solid food. For we were not yet able to take it, and perhaps many of us are still not able. Since there are quarrels and dissensions among us, are we not carnal and walking in a merely human way? Each kind of strength has its suitable food. So first barley, then wheat is given us as nourishment. To someone stronger, as to Elijah, bread of fine flour from the inner part of the grain is given. But which bread is there that does not defile sinners but feeds them? [?]

There is a difference not only in the bread and the number, but also in the way they recline. The first group sit down on the grass, while the second recline on the ground: the five thousand on grass, the four thousand on the ground. It is a greater thing to press the earth than to lie on grass. Those who still live by the bodily senses delight in softer things, and so they recline on the grass, for "all flesh is grass." But the others recline on the earth, which produces wheat, wine and the olive, and they attain the food of grace. The first group sit down, the second recline, for one who reclines enjoys a greater rest. There, there are two fish; here, no number is given. For this reason many have thought that the grace of the sevenfold Spirit is signified in the loaves, and that the fish are to be understood as a figure of the two Testaments.

It is no trouble, then, to suppose that the four thousand, gathered from the four quarters of the world, in which the Church is figured, receive the food of greater grace, as it is written: "For they will come from the east and the west, from the north and the south, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven." That is why here Christ gives thanks to the Father. It is not without reason that there was only a blessing in the first case, while here there is also thanksgiving. For the Lord is accustomed to give thanks to the Father for his Church, because what he hid from the wise he has revealed to little children. The blessing, then, is upon us who are lower, and the thanksgiving is upon those who have triumphed over the weaknesses of their bodies through sacred sufferings. We have already touched on this above. In the first case they are ordered to sit down in fifties, a number that is defined, even though it is sacred. Here, however, we seem to see the people of a more firmly founded Church, which reclines without any defined number.

It is also mystical that the people eat and are satisfied, while the apostles serve. Their satisfaction signifies that hunger has been driven away forever, since whoever has received Christ's food will not hunger. The apostles' ministry foreshadows the future distribution of the Lord's body and blood. And this is divine: the way five loaves overflowed for five thousand people. For it is clear that the people were satisfied not with a scanty amount of food but with food that had been multiplied.

You could have seen, through some incomprehensible flowing, pieces they had not broken multiplying between the hands of those who were distributing, and fragments untouched by the fingers of those who were breaking springing up of their own accord. Why should anyone who reads this marvel at the endless courses of waters or be amazed that streams pour continuously from clear springs, when even bread overflows and a more solid substance flows in abundance? These things were done so that through them we might also perceive the things we do not see. By them he clearly showed that the author of these things is also the creator of the whole material world. That world was not found ready-made, as the philosophers would have it, but made, and it supplies ever-flowing resources for the generation of all things.

It is indeed wonderful that whatever you draw from rivers leaves no sign of loss, and whatever you take from springs is restored by a flow that repays it with interest, as it were. But in rivers, though nothing seems to be lost, nothing seems to be added either. And in springs, just as the waters can be seen to rise, so it is plain to see when they go down. But this bread that Jesus breaks is, mystically, the word of God and the message about Christ, which increases as it is divided. For from a few words he has supplied nourishment in abundance for all peoples. He gave us words like loaves, which double in our mouths as we taste them. And visibly too, in an incredible way, this bread is heaped up as it is broken, divided and eaten, without any perceptible loss.

Nor should you wonder whether the food grows in the hands of those who serve or in the mouths of those who eat, since our own human work is always called on as evidence to strengthen belief. So too at the wedding, the water from the springs took on the color of wine while the servants did their work, and those who had filled the jars with water drew out wine that they had not brought. Grasp such great miracles, if you can! Here, as the people eat, the fragments grow by being used up, and from five loaves more is collected in leftovers than there was in total. There, the elements are turned into a different form. Nature suffers no loss of its own and does not recognize its own origin, yet it recognizes its proper uses. Indeed, the changed wine is better than wine produced in the natural way, because it lies in the Creator's will which uses to assign to natures, and which natures to give to things that come into being. See how many works he uses to establish this one work! While the servant pours in water, the fragrance passed into it makes one drunk, the changed color gives it form, and the taste, once drunk, adds to faith.

Let the pagans, if they like, compare with Christ's benefits the deeds of their gods, or rather their fictions. Their stories certainly tell of a king who turned to gold whatever he touched. But even his meals were deadly: the very napkins stiffened when his fingers grasped them, the food crackled in his mouth and brought him wounds instead of nourishment, and the drink stuck in his throat, neither going down easily nor coming back up. Benefits worthy of the prayer, gifts worthy of such a petitioner, generosity worthy of the giver! Such are the benefits of idols: when they seem to help, they do more harm. Christ's gifts, on the other hand, seem small and are very great. They were given not to one man but to whole peoples. The food grew in the mouths of those who ate it, and it seemed to be bodily nourishment, but what they received was eternal salvation.
Why, though, is more left over for five thousand people and less for four thousand? Because the four thousand had been with Christ for three days, and so they received more of the heavenly food.

It is not without purpose that the disciples gather what the crowds leave over, for you will find divine things more easily among the elect than among the multitudes. If only it might be granted to me to hear: “Gather up what is left over!” If I hear it and do it, I shall have much that the crowds could not eat, much that the children and women could not eat. Blessed is the one who can gather what is left over even by the learned.

Let us see how he gathers. The law said: “You shall not commit adultery.” Christ broke this bread and divided this word, adding nothing from elsewhere but sharing out what was already in it. “Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her,” he says, “has already committed adultery with her.” There you have one fragment of it. He added: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out.” There you have another; and: “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off”; and: “Whoever marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.” You see how many fragments come from one word. Moses says that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. Paul said: “These are the two covenants.” He divided this word and found a mystery. Blessed, then, is the one who gathers what Christ divides.

Why did Christ fill twelve baskets, unless it was to undo what was said of the Jewish people, “His hands served in the basket”? The people who once gathered clay in baskets now, through the cross of Christ, produce the food of heavenly life, and heap up the food of faith where before lay the filth of pagan unbelief. This gift is not for a few but for all. Through the twelve baskets the strengthening of faith overflows, as it were, to each of the tribes, for “bread strengthens the heart of man.”

And he said to them: “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered: “The Christ of God.” Even the crowd's opinion is not pointless: some thought he was Elijah, whose coming they expected; others John, though they knew he had been beheaded; others believed that one of the earlier prophets had risen. But to inquire into this is beyond us; it calls for another's judgment and another's wisdom. If it is enough for the apostle Paul to know nothing but Christ Jesus and him crucified, what more should I want to know than Christ? In this one name is expressed both his divinity and his incarnation, and faith in his passion. And so, although the other apostles knew it, it was Peter who answered ahead of the rest: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He embraced everything, for he expressed both the nature and the name, and in that lies the sum of all powers. Are we still to raise questions about God's begetting, when Paul judged that he knew nothing but Christ Jesus and him crucified, and Peter thought that nothing need be confessed except the Son of God? With the eyes of human weakness we pry into when and how he was born, and how great he is. Paul knew that such questions bring more stumbling and dispute than progress in building up, and so he decided to know nothing but Christ Jesus. Peter knew that all things are in the Son of God, for the Father has given all things to the Son. If he has given him all things, he has passed on to him the eternity and majesty that he has. But why do I wander further? The goal of my faith is Christ; the goal of my faith is the Son of God. I am not permitted to know the process of his begetting, but neither am I permitted to be ignorant of faith in his begetting.

Believe, then, as Peter believed, so that you too may be blessed and may deserve to hear: “For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” Flesh and blood can reveal only what is earthly; but whoever speaks mysteries in the Spirit rests not on the teaching of flesh and blood but on divine inspiration. So do not give in to flesh and blood, or you will drink in the precepts of flesh and blood and become blood and flesh yourself. For whoever clings to the flesh is flesh, and whoever clings to God is one spirit with him. “My Spirit,” he says, “shall not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh.”

If only those who hear were not flesh and blood! If only, set free from the desires of flesh and blood, each of them could say: “I will not fear what flesh can do to me!” For whoever has conquered the flesh is a foundation of the church, and even if he cannot equal Peter, he can imitate him. Great are the gifts of God, who not only restored to us what had been ours, but also granted us what is properly his own.

Still, it is worth asking what it means that the crowds took him for no one but Elijah or Jeremiah or John the Baptist. Elijah perhaps because he was taken up into heaven. But Christ is not Elijah. Elijah is carried up; Christ returns. Elijah is snatched up [?]; Christ did not count it robbery to be equal with God. Elijah is avenged by fire he called down; Christ chose to heal his persecutors rather than destroy them. Why did they think he was Jeremiah? Perhaps because Jeremiah was sanctified in the womb. But this is not Jeremiah. Jeremiah is sanctified; Christ sanctifies. Jeremiah's sanctification began with his body; Christ is the Holy One from the Holy One. And why do the people think he is John, unless perhaps because John, while still in his mother's womb, sensed the Lord's presence? But this is not John. John worshipped in the womb; Christ was worshipped. John baptized in water, Christ in the Spirit. John urged repentance; Christ forgave sins.

And so Peter did not wait for the people's opinion but brought out his own, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He who is, always is: he did not begin to be, and he does not cease to be. Great is the grace of Christ, who gave nearly all his names to his disciples. “I am the light of the world,” he says, and yet he granted his disciples the very name in which he glories, saying: “You are the light of the world.” “I am the living bread,” and: “We, though many, are one bread.” “I am the true vine,” and to you he says: “I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true.” Christ is the rock—“for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ”—and he did not refuse the grace of this name even to his disciple, so that he too should be Peter, the Rock, since from the rock he has steadfast solidity and firm faith.

Strive, then, to be a rock yourself. Look for the rock not outside yourself but within. Your rock is your conduct; your rock is your mind. On this rock your house is built, so that no storms of spiritual wickedness can batter it down. Your rock is faith, and faith is the foundation of the church. If you are a rock, you will be in the church, because the church stands upon the rock. If you are in the church, the gates of hell will not prevail against you. The gates of hell are the gates of death, and the gates of death cannot be the gates of the church.

And what are the gates of death, that is, the gates of hell, but each and every sin? If you commit fornication, you have entered the gates of death. If you violate faith, you have passed through the gates of hell. If you commit a mortal sin, you have gone in at the gates of death. But God is mighty to lift you up from the gates of death, so that you may declare all his praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion. The gates of the church are the gates of chastity, the gates of righteousness, which the righteous man habitually enters, saying: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, and when I have entered them I will give thanks to the Lord.” Just as the gate of death is the gate of hell, so the gate of righteousness is the gate of God: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter by it.” So flee from persisting in sin, so that the gates of hell cannot prevail against you; for if sin has gained dominion over you, the gate of death has prevailed. Flee, then, from quarrels, dissensions, the clamor and tumult of discord, so that you do not find your way in through the gates of death. For the Lord Jesus Christ did not wish to be proclaimed at first, so that no clamor should arise. He rebukes his disciples, telling them to say this to no one: that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the chief priests and elders and scribes, and be killed, and rise on the third day.

Perhaps he added this because the Lord knew that even the disciples would find it hard to believe in his passion and resurrection. So he preferred to be himself the one who bore witness to his passion and resurrection, so that faith might be born from the event rather than discord from hearsay. Christ, then, did not want glory but preferred to appear lowly, so that he might undergo his passion; and do you, born lowly, seek glory? You must walk the same road that Christ walked. This is how to know him, this is how to imitate him, through ill repute and good repute: to glory in the cross as he himself gloried in it. So Paul walked, and so he glories, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

But let us see why in Matthew we find the disciples warned to tell no one that he was the Christ, while here it is written that they were rebuked so that they should tell no one these things: that he was to suffer much and rise again. You see that everything is contained in the one name of Christ. He is the Christ who was born of a virgin; he is the one who worked wonders among the people; he is the one who died for our sins and rose from the dead. Take away any one of these and you have taken away your salvation. Even heretics appear to have Christ, for no one denies the name of Christ; but whoever does not confess all that belongs to Christ denies Christ. He orders the disciples to be silent, then, for many reasons: to deceive the prince of this world, to avoid boasting, to teach humility, and also so that the disciples, still untrained and imperfect, should not be crushed under the weight of so great a proclamation.

Now let us consider why he also orders the unclean spirits to be silent. Scripture has made this plain to us as well, for God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds?” It is so that no one, hearing him preach, should follow one who is astray. The devil is a dishonest teacher who often mixes the false with the true, so as to cloak his deceitful testimony with the appearance of truth.

Let us also consider whether this was the first time he commanded the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ, or whether he had commanded it earlier too, when he sent out the twelve apostles with the charge: “Do not go into the ways of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons”; and: “Find out who in it is worthy, and stay there.” So there too it appears they were not commanded to preach Christ as the Son of God.

The order of argument, then, is the order of teaching. So we too, when people from the Gentiles are called into the church, ought to arrange the sequence of instruction in this way. First we should teach that there is one God, the author of the world and of all things, in whom we live and are and move, whose offspring we also are, so that we should love him not only for the gifts of light and life but also because of a kind of family kinship. Next we should demolish the belief in idols, showing that material of gold and silver or wood cannot hold divine power within itself. When you have persuaded them that there is one God, you will then go on from that to establish that salvation has been given us through Christ. Begin with what he did in the body, and describe these works as divine, so that he may be seen to have been more than a man: death conquered by the power of one, a dead man raised from the underworld. Faith grows little by little, so that when he is seen to have been above man, he may be believed to be God. For unless you prove that he could not have done these things without divine power, how can you prove that divine power was in him?

But perhaps we are given too little authority and credence. Read, then, the apostle's speech at Athens. If he had set out to demolish the worship of idols from the start, the ears of the pagans would have rejected what he said. So he begins with the one God, the maker of the world, saying: “God, who made the world and everything in it.” They could not deny that there is one maker of the world, one God, one creator of all. He added that the Lord of heaven and earth does not deign to dwell in things made by hands, and then that it is not at all likely that human craftsmanship could shut up the power of the Godhead in empty material of gold and silver; and he taught that the remedy for error is earnest repentance. Then he came to Christ, and even then he chose to call him a man rather than God, saying: “by a man, through whom he has given assurance to all, raising him from the dead.” Whoever teaches must take account of his hearers, so as not to be laughed at before he is heard. When would the Athenians have believed that the Word became flesh and that a virgin conceived by the Spirit, when they mocked at hearing of the resurrection of the dead? Yet Dionysius the Areopagite believed, and others believed in the man so that they might come to believe in God. What does it matter in what order each person comes to believe? Perfection is not demanded at the beginning; from beginnings one arrives at what is perfect. This was the teaching with which he instructed the Athenians, and this is the order we must keep among the Gentiles.

When the apostles addressed Jews, however, they said that he was the very Christ promised to us by the oracles of the prophets. They did not at first, on their own authority, call him the Son of God, but a man approved, a righteous man, a man raised from the dead, the man of whom it was said in the prophets: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” So you too, for things that are hard to believe, call in the authority of the divine word. Show from the voice of the prophets that his coming was promised; teach from the testimony of the Scriptures that his resurrection was known long beforehand, and that it was not the ordinary resurrection shared with others, so that from the very affirmation of his risen body you may gain a testimony to his eternal divinity. For when you have shown that the bodies of others underwent corruption after death, you demonstrate that this one, of whom it is said, “You will not let your Holy One see corruption,” was free from human frailty; you prove that he rose above the deserts of the human condition and is to be compared with God rather than with men.

But if a catechumen is to be instructed [?] as he advances toward the sacraments of the faithful, he must be told that there is one God, from whom are all things, and one Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; that we must not speak of two Lords; that the Father is perfect and the Son is also perfect, but that the Father and the Son are of one substance; that the Son is the eternal Word of God, not a word that is uttered but one that acts, begotten of the Father, not produced by the voice. The apostles, then, are forbidden to proclaim him as the Son of God so that they might later proclaim him crucified. This is the glory of faith, if you truly understand the cross of Christ. Other crosses are of no profit to me; only the cross of Christ is useful to me, and truly useful, for through it the world is crucified to me and I to the world. If the world is crucified to me, I know that it is dead, and I do not love it; I know that it is passing away, and I do not covet it; I know that decay will consume this world, and so I avoid it as something foul, I guard against it as a plague, I leave it behind as something harmful.

But some cannot immediately believe that salvation was restored to the world through the cross. Show them, then, from the history of the Greeks that such a thing was possible. The apostle too sometimes persuades unbelievers in this way, and does not shy away from lines of the poets, so as to overturn the poets' fables. The histories of the Greeks claim that legions and great peoples were often set free by offering up the deaths of certain persons; they remember that a commander's daughter was summoned to be sacrificed so that the Greek armies could cross the sea; we may consider our own Scripture, that the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, when sprinkled, sanctify the defiled for the cleansing of the flesh, as is written in Hebrews; and it is claimed that a plague over whole regions, brought on by the sins of some men, was ended by the death of one person. Whether this held good by reason or took effect by divine arrangement, so that the Lord's cross might be believed more easily, if these things are recalled, those who cannot deny their own stories will readily confirm ours.

But no man could be great enough to take away the sins of the whole world: not Enoch, not Abraham, not Isaac, who, though he offered himself to death, was nevertheless spared, because he could not abolish all sins. For what man is so great that the sins of all could die in him? Therefore not one of the common people, not one of the crowd, but the Son of God was chosen by God the Father, so that, being above all, he could offer himself for all. He had to die so that, being stronger than death, he might set others free. He became free among the dead without help, that is, free from death without the aid of any man or of any creature; and rightly free, since he had thrust away the slavery of the passions and knew nothing of the chains of death.
BOOK SEVEN.

"But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God." The Lord always raises us toward the future rewards of the virtues and teaches that contempt for worldly things is profitable. In the same way he also supports the weakness of the human mind with rewards in the present. For it is hard to take up the cross, to expose one's life to dangers and one's body to death, to deny what you are when you want to be what you are not. And rarely does virtue, however lofty, exchange present things for future ones. People find it hard to buy hope at the price of dangers and to purchase the gain of the age to come with the loss of present things. So, because the allure of a sweet life soothes even a steadfast heart, the good teacher of morals promises the faithful that their life will go on uninterrupted, so that no one may be broken by despair or weariness. For consolations grow cold under the fear of death, and a great love of life finds it hard to set the charms of hope against the terror of losing the safety it longs for. You therefore have nothing to complain of and no excuse to offer. The judge of all has given both a reward to virtue and a remedy to weakness, so that weakness may be sustained by present things and virtue by future ones. If you are strong, despise death; if you are weak, flee it. But no one can flee death unless he follows life. Your life is Christ; he is the very life that cannot die.

So if we wish not to fear death, let us stand where Christ is, so that he may say of us too: "Truly there are some standing here who will not taste death." It is not enough to stand unless one stands where Christ is, for only those who can stand with Christ cannot taste death. From the nature of the word itself we may judge that those who seem to have deserved fellowship with Christ will not have even a faint sense of death. Bodily death is merely tasted, as one sips; the life of the soul is held as a possession.

But what does it mean to taste death? Could it be that, just as bread is life, so also bread may be death? For there are those who eat the bread of sorrow; there are also the peoples of the Ethiopians, who received the dragon as food. Far be it from us to devour the dragon's poison! For we have the true bread, that bread which came down from heaven. He eats that bread who keeps what is written. So there are some who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God. There are also some who will not see death, as it is written: "Who is the man who will live and not see death?"

But who is the man who does not die, since there can be no resurrection except of the dead? We have, it is true, heard of no bodily death for Enoch and Elijah, and the Lord said of John the evangelist, "If I want him to remain until I come." Yet since we do not think that John alone is meant here, but that this is a general statement about many, it is not the death of the body that is denied here, but the death of the soul. For there are those who live though dead, since there are those who are dead though living, like the woman who is dead while she lives; as it is written: "Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into hell." If, then, someone goes down alive into hell (for through sin one goes down into hell, the dwelling place of death), there are surely those for whom the course of life was not broken off even by the death of the body, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who we learn on the authority of the divine word are alive. For since he is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, he is certainly not the God of the dead, but of the living. So he speaks not of one, but of many. For Peter did not

die, against whom, according to the Lord's word, the gate of hell could not prevail; nor did James and John die, the sons of thunder, who have been taken up to serve heavenly glory, so that earthly things do not prevail over them but lie beneath them. Be a Peter yourself, then: devout, faithful, a peacemaker, so that you may open the gates of the Church and escape the gates of death. Be a son of thunder. You say: "How can I be a son of thunder?" You can be, if you recline not on the earth but on the breast of Christ. You can be a son of thunder if earthly things do not move you, but you instead shake earthly things by the strength of your mind. Let the earth tremble before you, not hold you captive; let the flesh fear the power of your soul and, shaken, submit. You will be a son of thunder if you are a son of the Church. Let Christ say to you too from the gibbet of the cross, "Behold your mother," and let him say to the Church, "Behold your son." For you will begin to be a son of the Church when you see Christ victorious on the cross. Whoever thinks the cross a stumbling block is a Jew, not a son of the Church; whoever thinks the cross foolishness is a Greek. But he is a son of the Church who thinks the cross a triumph, if he recognizes the voice of Christ triumphant.

So, that you may know that Peter, John and James did not taste death, they were found worthy to see the glory of the resurrection. For about eight days after these words he took these three alone and led them up a mountain. Why does he say, "eight days after these words"? Is it perhaps because whoever hears and believes the words of Christ will see the glory of Christ at the time of the resurrection? For the resurrection took place on the eighth day, which is why many psalms are also entitled "for the eighth." Or perhaps it was to show us that, when he had said that whoever loses his life for the sake of God's word will save it, he fulfills his promises in the resurrection.

But Matthew and Mark recorded that they were taken up after six days. We could say this means after six thousand years, since a thousand years in God's sight are like one day; but more than six thousand years are reckoned, and we prefer to understand the six days as a symbol, because the works of the world were created in six days, so that through the time we may understand the works, and through the works the world. And so it is shown that the resurrection will come when the times of the world are completed. Or else it is because whoever has ascended above the world and passed beyond the moments of this age will, as if set on high, await the eternal fruit of the resurrection to come.

Let us, then, pass beyond the works of the world, so that we may be able to see God face to face. "Go up on a mountain, you who bring good news to Zion." If he who brings good news to Zion goes up a mountain, how much more he who brings the good news of Christ, and of Christ rising in glory? Perhaps many may see him in the body; for many of us have known Christ according to the flesh, but now we no longer know him so.

Many of us have known him, because many of us have seen him ("we saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty"); but only three, and three chosen ones, are led to the mountain. I would have thought that the human race was mystically represented in the three, since the whole human race descended from the three sons of Noah, were it not that I see they were chosen. Or perhaps it is because only those who have confessed Christ will be found worthy to attain the grace of the resurrection, for the wicked do not rise to judgment, but are punished as though judgment had already been held. Three, then, are chosen to go up the mountain, and two are chosen to be seen with the Lord: on both sides a sacred number. And perhaps this is because no one can see the glory of the resurrection except one who has kept the whole mystery of the Trinity with the uncorrupted sincerity of faith. Peter goes up, who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven; John, to whom his mother was entrusted; James, who first ascended the priestly throne.

Then Moses and Elijah appear, that is, the Law and the Prophet together with the Word; for neither can the Law exist without the Word, nor is anyone a prophet unless he prophesied of the Son of God. Those sons of thunder, indeed, beheld Moses and Elijah too in bodily glory, but we also see Moses with the Son of God every day. For we see the Law in the Gospel when we read, "You shall love the Lord your God"; we see Elijah with the Word of God when we read, "Behold, a virgin shall conceive."

So Luke rightly added that they were speaking of his departure, which he was to accomplish in Jerusalem. For the mysteries teach you about his departure. Today too Moses teaches, today too Elijah speaks, and today we can see Moses in even greater glory. Who cannot, when even the Jewish people were able to see him, and in fact did see him? They saw the face of Moses in glory, but they received the veil; they did not go up the mountain, and so they went astray. Whoever saw Moses alone could not see the Word of God at the same time.

Let us, then, unveil our face, so that, beholding the glory of God with unveiled face, we may be transformed into the same image. Let us go up the mountain; let us pray the Word of God to appear to us in his splendor and beauty, to grow strong, go forth prosperously and reign. For these too are mysteries and have a deeper meaning. Indeed, the Word either diminishes or grows for you according to your capacity. Unless you climb the summit of higher wisdom, wisdom does not appear to you, the knowledge of the mysteries does not appear to you, nor how great the glory and the beauty in the Word of God. Instead the Word of God appears as though in a body, without its own form or beauty; he appears as a man stricken, able to bear our infirmities; he appears to you as a kind of speech born of a man, wrapped in the coverings of letters, not shining with the power of the Spirit. But if, while you consider him as a man, you believe that he was born of a virgin, and faith gradually breathes in you that he was born of the Spirit of God, you are beginning to climb the mountain. If you see him placed on the cross triumphing over death, not destroyed; if you see that the earth trembled, the sun fled, darkness was poured over the eyes of the faithless, the tombs were opened and the dead rose again, as a sign that the Gentile people, who had been dead to God, rose again when the tombs of their body were unsealed, as it were, and the light of the cross was poured in—if you see this mystery, you have climbed the high mountain, and you behold another glory of the Word.

His garments are some below, others above. And perhaps the garments of the Word are the discourses of the Scriptures, the garments, as it were, of divine understanding. For just as he appeared to Peter, John and James in another form and his clothing shone white, so the meaning of the divine readings is now growing white before the eyes of your mind. The divine words, then, become like snow, the garments of the Word exceedingly white, such as no fuller on earth can make them.

Let us seek this fuller; let us seek this snow. We read that Isaiah went up to the fuller's field. Who is this fuller, if not he who is accustomed to wash away our sins? Indeed, he himself said: "Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white as snow." Who is this fuller, if not he who washes away the bodily stains and is accustomed to present the garments of our understanding, the garments of the virtues, to the divine Sun?

I have also heard (to take an example from the opposing side in order to refute them) that [?] the eloquence of two wise men has been compared to snow and to bees. I have found too that David said: "How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!" And further on: "Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths." The word of God is light; the word of God is snow. The word of God is also beyond honey and the honeycomb, for speech sweeter than honey has flowed from the divine mouth, and words clear as snow fall with gentle meanings. Truly this speech alone is to be compared to snow, for, sent from heaven to earth, it has made fruitful the barren fields of our hearts. This is not presumptuously assumed but drawn from the sequence of the reading, as God himself testifies when he says: "Let my speech be awaited like rain, and let my words come down like dew, like a shower upon the grass and like snow upon the hay."

O Lord Jesus, may my mind grow green with the moisture of your rain! May you sprinkle my earth with the whiteness of this snow, so that the fields of my body may not run riot in the premature heat of spring, but rather that the seeds of the heavenly word, pressed down and kept warm by the snow, may bear fruit! When snow falls, the birds of the air have nowhere to dwell, and the harvest of wheat abounds more richly than usual.

Peter saw this grace, and so did those who were with him, even though they had been heavy with sleep. For the incomprehensible splendor of the Godhead overwhelms the senses of our body. If the sight of the body cannot bear a ray of the sun shining straight into the eyes of those who look at it, how could the corruption of human limbs bear the glory of God? And so in the resurrection the condition of the body is formed purer and finer, once the accretion of vices has been drained away. Perhaps they were heavy with sleep for this reason, that they might see the form of the resurrection after rest. And so, waking up, they saw his majesty; for no one sees the glory of Christ unless he is awake. Peter was delighted, and he whom the allurements of this world could not capture was drawn by the grace of the resurrection.

"It is good," he says, "for us to be here"—hence that other saying too: "to depart and be with Christ is far better." Not content with praising, he excelled not only in affection but also in the devotion of deeds, and like a tireless workman he offers the service of common obedience by building three tents. And although he did not know what he was saying, he still promised a service in which it was not thoughtless impudence but premature devotion that heaped up the fruits of piety. For what he did not know belonged to his condition; what he promised belonged to his devotion. But the human condition is not capable of making a tent for God in this corruptible, this mortal body. Whether in the soul or in the body or in any other place, avoid seeking what you may not know. If Peter did not know, how can you know? If he did not know, who made the promise and who through greatness of soul knew no bounds of the body, how can we know, shut up within the enclosure of the flesh by a certain sluggishness of mind? At any rate, such great devotion was pleasing to God.

"And while he was saying this, a cloud came and overshadowed them." This overshadowing is that of the divine Spirit, which does not darken human hearts but reveals hidden things. It is found in another passage too, when the angel says: "And the power of the Most High will overshadow you." Its effect is shown when the voice of God is heard saying: "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." That is:

"Not Elijah is the Son, not Moses is the Son, but this is the Son, whom alone you see." For they had withdrawn when the Lord began to be pointed out. You see that the perfect faith not only of beginners, but also of the perfect, and even of heavenly beings, is to know the Son of God. But since we have already said this above, understand that this cloud is not one formed from the misty moisture of smoking mountains, nor a pitch-black gloom of thickened air that covers the sky with the horror of darkness, but a bright cloud, which does not drench us with rainwater and a flood of wet showers, but from which, when the voice of almighty God was uttered, the dew of faith watered the minds of men.

"And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone." So, though there were three, they became one. Three are seen at the beginning, one at the end; for in perfect faith they are one. Indeed, the Lord also prays the Father for this, that we may all be one. And not only are Moses and Elijah one in Christ, but we too are the one body of Christ. So they too are, as it were, received into the body of Christ, since we too shall be one in Christ Jesus. Or perhaps it is because the Law and the Prophets come from the Word, and what began from the Word ends in the Word; for Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

"Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests where they may rest, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." It does not seem reasonable to consider this man simple and faithful, since he is rejected by the Lord's judgment even though he had promised the service of tireless discipleship. But the Lord does not look for an outward show of service; he looks for purity of heart. Earlier, indeed, he says: "Whoever receives this child in my name."

In this passage the Lord teaches that there must be simplicity without arrogance, love without envy, devotion without anger. For we are urged to receive a child's mind with the disposition of a mature person, since a child, claiming nothing for himself, carries out the pattern of virtue, and if he does not know reason, he knows nothing of guilt. Yet since to many people simplicity without reason seems not a virtue but a weakness, you are advised to receive the true kind, that is, to carry out by diligence the gift of nature.

And so he says: "Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me." For whoever receives an imitator of Christ receives Christ, and whoever receives the image of God receives God. But since we could not see the image of God, he became present to us through the incarnation of the Word, so that the Godhead, which is above us, might be reconciled to us.

As for John, who loved greatly and was therefore greatly loved in return, when out of an overeager zeal of love he thinks that one who does not follow with them should be shut out from the benefit, he is rightly not rebuked, but taught. He is not rebuked, because he acted out of love; he is taught, so that he may know the difference between the weak and the strong. And so the Lord, although he rewards the stronger, still does not shut out the weak.

"Let them be, and do not forbid them; for whoever is not against you is for you." Well said, Lord; for Joseph and Nicodemus too, though secret disciples for fear, did not in due time deny you their service. But since you said elsewhere, "Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters," explain it to us, lest it seem contradictory. I think that if one considers him who searches minds, one should not doubt that each person's deed is judged by his intention. Indeed, to one he says, "Follow me," to another, "Foxes have holes." The one is urged on, the other turned away, so that you may know that the devout is admitted and the undevout shut out.

His rebuke of the disciples for wanting fire to come down upon those who had not received Christ shows us that those who have sinned are not always to be punished. For sometimes clemency is of greater benefit: to you, for patience, and to the one who has fallen, for correction. Indeed, the Samaritans, from whom fire is here kept away, believed all the sooner. At the same time learn that he did not wish to be received by those whom he knew had not turned to him with a simple mind; for if he had wished, he would have made the undevout devout. But why they did not receive him the evangelist himself records, saying: "because his face was set toward Jerusalem." The disciples, however, were eager to be received within Samaria; but God calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes devout whom he wills. Nor do the disciples sin in following the Law, for they knew that Phinehas was reckoned righteous because he had killed the sacrilegious, and that fire came down from heaven at Elijah's prayer so that the wrong done to the prophet might be avenged. But let him who fears take vengeance; he who does not fear does not seek vengeance. At the same time it is shown to us that the apostles had the merits of the prophets, since they confidently claim for themselves, by right of asking, the same power that the great prophet earned. And they rightly presume that fire would come down from heaven at their word, since they are sons of thunder.

But the Lord does all things wonderfully. He neither receives the man who rashly offers himself, nor is he roused against those who undevoutly reject their own Lord. He did this to show that perfect virtue has no desire for revenge, that there is no anger where there is fullness of love, and that weakness is not to be shut out but helped. Far from the devout be indignation, far from the magnanimous the desire for revenge, far too from the prudent ill-considered association and incautious simplicity. Therefore it is also said to this man, "Foxes have holes," and the service of one whose sense of duty is not proven is not accepted. For the hospitality of faith ought to be circumspect, lest, while we open the inner rooms of our house to the faithless, we fall through careless credulity into the snares of another's treachery.
