But lest we seem to have carelessly passed over this question: why does he say here that those who can command unclean spirits by the laying on of hands in the name of Jesus are not to be forbidden, while according to Matthew he says to such people, "I do not know you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity"? We should note that there is no difference of meaning or disagreement of statements. Rather, it is to be judged in this way: not only offices are required in a cleric, but also works of virtue; and the name of Christ is so great that it helps even those who are not very holy for protection, even if it does not help them for grace. So no one should boast or claim for himself the credit for a man who has been cleansed, since it was the power of the eternal name that worked in him, not any ability of human frailty. For the devil is overcome not by your merit but by hatred of him.

Let a man do what he can: let him show sincere faith and keep the observance of the commandments with a devout mind, so that it may not be said to him, "Foxes have holes." For the fox is a deceitful animal, always bent on ambush, and practices fraudulent plunder. It allows nothing to be safe, nothing undisturbed, nothing secure, since it seeks its prey among the very dwellings of men.

He likens heretics to foxes. In short, when he calls the gentiles, he shuts out the heretics. The fox is an animal full of cunning: it digs itself a den and always wants to lie hidden in it. Heretics are like this. They do not know how to prepare a house for themselves, but they try to deceive others with their trickery. Jacob dwells in a house; the heretic is in a den, like the crafty fox always plotting against that hen of the Gospel, of whom it is written: “How often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were not willing! See, your house will be left to you desolate.” They rightly have dens, then, because they have lost the house they once had. This animal is never tamed, which is why the Apostle says, “Avoid a heretic after one rebuke.” Nor is it of any use or good for food, for it is not of this that Christ says, “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven.” Indeed, he banishes foxes from his fruits, saying, “Catch us the little foxes that ravage the vineyards,” that is, foxes that ravage the lesser vineyard, not the greater. And so Samson tied torches to their tails and let them loose into the crops of the Philistines, because heretics try to set fire to other people's fruits. They are more resonant in barking than refined in speech, for whoever denies the Word has no voice either. For the present their mouths are free, but their end is already bound for the future, and the torches on their tails signify the burning that will be their end.

The birds of the air, too, which are often taken as a figure of spiritual wickedness, build something like nests in the hearts of the wicked. And so, because iniquity has abounded, the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. For when cunning rules there is no room for simplicity, and the Godhead can have no possession in the affections of individuals. For the head of Christ is God. When he finds a mind innocent, he as it were lays the power of his majesty to rest upon it, and this seems to be a sign that a more abundant grace is planted in the hearts of the good.

So, that you may see that God spurns not worship but deceit, he who had rejected the deceitful man chooses the innocent one, saying, “Follow me.” But he says this to a man whose father he already knew to be dead, that father, surely, of whom it was said to him: “Forget your father's house.” See, then, that the Lord calls even the unwitting when he has mercy on them, and when the man asked leave to bury his father, he replied:

“Let the dead bury their own dead; but you go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” Since we have received burial as a religious duty, why is even the burial of one's father forbidden here, unless you are to understand that human things must give way to divine? It is a good concern, but a greater hindrance. For whoever divides his zeal diverts his affection, and whoever splits his care delays his progress. The greatest things, then, must be attended to first. For the apostles too, so that their zeal for preaching the word would not be taken up,

appointed ministers for the poor. And when they were sent out by the Lord, they were instructed to greet no one on the way, not because the duty of kindness displeased him, but because a purpose set on pursuing devotion pleased him more. But how can the dead bury the dead, unless you understand here a twofold death, one of nature and the other of guilt? There is also a third death, in which we die to sin and live to God, as Christ did, who died to sin; for the death he died, he died to sin once for all, but the life he lives, he lives to God.

There is, then, one death, by which the bond of body and soul is broken. It is not dreadful and not to be feared, since it seems to be a kind of departure of ourselves. It is not a punishment. The brave need not dread it; the wise should desire it, and the wretched seek it. Of this death it is said: “People will seek death and will not find it.”

There is another death, which brings the destruction of worldly pleasures, in which it is not our nature that dies but our sins. We undergo this death when we are buried with Christ in baptism and die with him to the elements of this world, when our former deeds pass into oblivion. Balaam, when he prophesied, wished to die this death so that he might live to God, and so he said: “Let my soul die among the souls of the righteous, and let my seed be like their seed.”

There is also a third death, when Christ, who is our life, is not known. But to know Christ is eternal life. The righteous have it now in shadow, but in the future they will have it face to face. For the breath of our face is Christ the Lord, of whom it is said: “Under his shadow we shall live among the nations.” In the shadow of his wings David hoped; in his shadow the Church longed to sit, and sat.

If your shadow, Lord Jesus, bestows so much, how much more will the truth itself bring! How shall we live when we are no longer in the shadow but in life itself? For now our life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, our life, appears, then, he says, we too will appear with him in glory. Sweet is that life which has no death. For this life of the body has death as the lot of its nature, and death is often even longed for. The soul itself, too, often has death through the stain of sin, for the soul that sins shall die. But when, strengthened by the firmness of blessedness, it begins to be no longer subject to sin, it will no longer be mortal but will enjoy eternal life.

Let us hasten to this life, brothers, sorrowful in this world because we are exiles from the Lord; for whoever is not away from the body is away from the Lord. It is far better to be released from the body and to cling to God, so that we too may be one with almighty God and may see the only-begotten Son of God. Then, taken up through the glory of the resurrection into the brightness of our nature, and joined by an inviolable harmony of souls in an everlasting covenant, we shall reflect the unity of lasting peace, and what the Son of God promised for us in his prayer to the Father will be fulfilled: “that they too may be one, as we are one.”

So it is not the burial of one's father that is forbidden. Rather, the devotion of divine religion is preferred to the ties of kinship: the one is left to kinsfolk, the other is enjoined on the chosen. Or else, because the throat of the ungodly is an open tomb, the command is that the memory of those whose merit perished together with their body should be blotted out. The son is not called away from his duty to his father; the believer is separated from fellowship with the unbeliever.

For there is a burial proper to the righteous, like the one of which it is said: “In pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it to prepare me for burial.” And so whoever in good faith buries Christ within himself, so as to rise with him, must not bury the faithlessness of the devil within himself.

There is also that prophetic burial, in which we place certain things upon the tombs of our forebears. You who read this recognize them, but the unbeliever ought not to understand. Food or drink is not what is commanded; rather, the venerable communion of the sacred offering is revealed. So it is not the gift that is forbidden. It is a mystery of religion that we are to have no communion with the heathen dead. For since the sacraments belong to the living, those who have life are not regarded as dead.

“See, I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.” He says this to the seventy disciples whom he appointed and sent in pairs ahead of him. Why did he send them in pairs? Because the animals were sent into the ark in pairs, that is, male with female. They were unclean by their number, but they were made clean by the sacrament of the Church. This was fulfilled by the oracle which holy Peter received when the Holy Spirit said to him: “What God has made clean, you must not call common.” And he understood that this was said of the gentiles, who followed the succession of bodily generation rather than that of spiritual grace. These the Lord made clean and made heirs of his passion.

So when he sent his disciples into his harvest, he said, “See, I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.” That harvest had been sown by the word of God, but it still needed the labour of cultivation and careful tending, so that the birds of the air would not scatter the seeds that had been sown.

These animals are opposed to each other, so that one devours the other. But the good shepherd does not know how to fear wolves for his flock, and so these disciples are sent out not to become prey but to bring grace. The care of the good shepherd ensures that the wolves can dare nothing against the lambs. He sends lambs among wolves, then, so that this might be fulfilled: “Then wolves and lambs shall feed together.”

Our recent discourse on the fox turned out not unwelcome to you. If I have found your judgment faithful regarding the figure of a tiny creature, I presume that with the support of your zeal I can open up the deep mysteries veiled under the form of wolves. We showed above that heretics are signified by foxes: in name they profess to follow Christ, but by their eagerness for deceit they forswear him. The Lord does not receive these, but keeps them away from his nest and shuts them out. Now we must consider what wolves seem to signify.

They are, of course, beasts that lie in wait for sheepfolds and prowl around the shepherds' huts. They do not dare to enter people's dwellings. They watch for the dogs to sleep and for the shepherd to be absent or careless, and they go for the sheep's throats so as to strangle them quickly. They are fierce and rapacious, and their bodies are so stiff by nature that they cannot easily turn, so they are carried along by their own rush and are therefore often tricked. Besides this, if they see a man first, some force of nature is said to make them rob him of his voice; but if the man sees them first, he is said to drive them off. So I must take care that if the grace of spiritual mysteries cannot shine out in today's discourse, people do not think the wolves saw me first and wrested from me the customary service of my voice.

Should not heretics be compared to these wolves? They lie in wait for Christ's sheepfolds and growl around the pens, more by night than by day. For it is always night for the faithless, who try to cover the light of Christ with the fogs of perverse interpretation and, as far as they can, to darken it. So they prowl around the pens, yet they do not dare to enter Christ's inn, and therefore they are not healed. For Christ does not wish to bring them into his inn, where that man was cared for who fell among robbers as he went down from Jerusalem. The Samaritan bound up his wounds, poured in oil and wine, set him on his own beast, brought him to the inn and left him with the innkeeper to be healed. Those who do not seek the physician do not receive the medicine; if they sought him, they would not disparage him.

They watch for the shepherd's absence, and so they strive either to kill the shepherds of the churches or to drive them into exile, because while the shepherds are present they cannot attack Christ's sheep. These plunderers try to despoil the Lord's flock. With a kind of bodily stubbornness of mind they are hard and stiff, and they are never wont to turn aside from their error. That is why the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretic after one rebuke, knowing that such a person is perverted.” Christ, the true interpreter of Scripture, outwits them, so that they pour out their empty rushes in vain and can do no harm.

If they get the better of anyone by the crafty trickery of their arguments, they strike him dumb. For he is mute who does not confess the Word of God with the glory that is his. Beware, then, lest the heretic take away your voice, if you have not caught him first. For his faithlessness creeps on while it lies hidden; but if you recognize the inventions of his impiety, you need not fear the loss of your devout voice. Beware, then, of the poisons of crafty argument: they go for the soul, they attack the throat, they fasten [?] on the vitals. Grievous are the bites of heretics, who are more savage and rapacious than the beasts themselves and know no limit to their greed and impiety.

Do not be misled because they seem to wear a human form: though outwardly a man is seen, inwardly a beast is growling. So there is no doubt that they are wolves, according to the divine sentence of the Lord Jesus, who says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. By their fruits you will know them.” If anyone is misled by appearance, then, let him examine the fruit. You hear someone called a bishop, and you know of his plundering: he has the clothing of a sheep but the deeds of a robber. Outwardly [?] he is a sheep, inwardly a wolf who knows no limit to his plundering, who, as though in the night, his limbs hardened by Scythian frost, prowls about with bloody jaws, seeking whom he may devour. Does he not seem to you a wolf, who, insatiable in his raw craving for human slaughter, longed to sate his rage with the death of faithful peoples?

He howls; he does not preach, this man who denies the author of speech and drowns it out with a bestial growl in sacrilegious words, who does not confess the Lord Jesus as the ruler of eternal life. We heard his howls when the sword was sent out through the world. He bared rough teeth and swollen jaws, and thought he had taken from everyone the voice that he alone had lost. And so, that we may escape these wolves, the Lord teaches us what to follow, saying:

“Carry no purse, no bag, no sandals.” What it means not to carry a purse he has explained clearly elsewhere, for Matthew wrote that the Lord said to his disciples: “Do not possess gold or silver.” If we are forbidden to possess gold, how can we seize it, how can we take it away? If you are commanded to give away what you have, how can you pile up what you do not have? You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who boast in the law, do you dishonour God by breaking the law? For the name of God is blasphemed because of you.

Not so the apostle Peter, who was the first to carry out the Lord's command, to show that the Lord's precepts had not been poured out in vain. When a poor man asked him to give him some money, he said, “Silver and gold I do not have.” He boasts that he has no silver and gold; are you ashamed to have still less than you desire? So there is a glorious poverty too, because poverty is also blessed, as it is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” Yet Peter boasts not so much that he has no silver and gold as that he keeps the command of the Lord, who directed: “Do not possess gold.” That is to say: “You see that I am a disciple of Christ, and you ask me for gold? He has given us something far more precious than gold, the power to work in his name. So I do not have what he did not give; but what he gave, I have: in the name of the Lord Jesus, rise and walk.”

So just as the man who wants to build barns to store up grain is rebuked by the authority of the Lord's sentence, so too the man who wants to get a purse for hoarding gold incurs the stain of reproach.

“No bag, no sandals.” Both are usually made from the hide of a dead animal, and the Lord Jesus wants nothing mortal in us. Accordingly he says to Moses: “Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” He is told to take off his mortal, earthly sandal when he is being sent to set the people free. The minister of this task must fear nothing and must not be held back from the duty he has taken on by the danger of death. For Moses had of his own accord taken up the defence of his brothers, that is, the Jews, but he was called back from what he had begun by fear of a false charge, and he fled from Egypt. And so the Lord, having approved his disposition but seen the weakness of his condition, judged that the footstep of his soul and mind should be stripped of its mortal bonds.

If anyone is puzzled why in Egypt they are told to eat the lamb with sandals on, while the apostles are sent out to preach the Gospel without sandals, he should consider this. One who is in Egypt must still beware the serpent's bite, for there are many poisons in Egypt, and the one who celebrates the Passover in figure can be exposed to a wound. But the minister of the truth blunts poisons and does not tremble. Indeed, a viper bit Paul on the island of Malta. When the people of that place saw the viper hanging from his hand, they thought he was going to die; but when they saw him standing unharmed, they said he was a god, since poison could not hurt him. And so that you may know this is true, the Lord himself says: “See, I have given you power to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will hurt you.”

The apostles are told not to take staffs in their hands, for so Matthew thought fit to write. What is a staff but a symbol of authority to be displayed and an instrument for avenging injury? So the disciples of a humble Lord (for in his humility his judgment was taken away), of a humble Lord, I say, carry out his command by the works of humility. He sent them to sow the faith, not to compel but to teach, not to exert the force of power but to exalt the teaching of humility. Here he thought patience too should be joined to humility, because he himself, as Peter testifies, when he was reviled did not revile in return, and when he was struck did not strike back. This, then, is what he means: “Be imitators of me. Lay aside the desire for revenge. Strike back at the insolence of those who strike you not by returning the injury but by the magnanimity of patience.” No one ought to imitate what he finds fault with in another. Gentleness inflicts heavier wounds on the stubborn. With this fist the Lord struck back at the one who strikes, saying: “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other as well.” For when a man notices that kindness has been returned to him for the injury he did, he condemns himself by his own judgment, and his feelings are pricked as if by a goad.

Yet he has apostles whom he sent even with a rod, as Paul testifies when he says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” The Apostle gave this rod to Timothy as well, saying, “Reprove, entreat, rebuke.” Or perhaps, before the Lord's passion, which strengthened the hearts of wavering peoples, gentleness alone was necessary, and after the passion, correction. Certainly, let the Lord soothe and Paul rebuke: let him persuade who can soften even hard hearts, and let him reprove who cannot persuade everyone. Paul, then, had taken up the rod from the teaching of the law. For he had read: “Whoever spares the rod hates his son.” He had also read that those eating the lamb were ordered by prophetic precept to hold a staff in their hands. And so in the Old Testament the Lord says: “I will punish their iniquities with the rod”; but in the New he offered himself so as to pardon all, saying: “If you are looking for me, let these men go.” And elsewhere you find that when the apostles wanted to call down fire from heaven to consume the Samaritans, who had refused to receive the Lord Jesus into their city, he turned and rebuked them, saying: “You do not know of what spirit you are; for the Son of Man did not come to destroy people's souls but to save them.”

So the more perfect are sent out without a rod, while the weaker eat with a staff. But even Paul, though he threatens the rod, visits wrongdoers in a spirit of gentleness. In fact, so that you may know he is a mild teacher, he consults the wishes of the very people he is reproving: “What do you want?” he says. “Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” He mentioned the rod once, but added milder things twice, joining gentleness to love. He threatened first, but he showed gentleness; for writing in his second letter to those same Corinthians he says: “I call God as witness against my soul that it was to spare you that I did not come to Corinth.” Hear why he thought he should spare them: “So that I might not come to you again in sorrow,” he says. He threw away the rod and took up the affection of love.

“And greet no one on the way.” Perhaps to some this may seem harsh and proud, and not in keeping with the precept of a gentle and humble Lord: that he who commanded us to give way even over a place at table should here instruct his disciples, “Greet no one on the way,” when this is a common courtesy. This is how inferiors usually win the favour of their superiors, and even gentiles share such exchanges of courtesy with Christians. How can the Lord do away with this humane custom?

But consider that he does not say only, “Greet no one,” and that “on the way” was not added for nothing. Elisha too, when he sent his servant to lay his staff on the body of the dead boy, ordered him not to greet anyone on the way. He told him to hurry so as to carry out the task of bringing about the resurrection, lest by chatting with someone he met he be turned aside from the task he had been given. So here too it is not the courtesy of greeting that is removed, but an obstacle that would hinder devotion, so that when divine things are commanded, human things are set aside for a while. Greeting is a fine thing, but finer is the prompt carrying out of divine commands, for delay has often brought offence. That is why even honourable things are forbidden: so that customary courtesy will not creep in and hinder the ministry of a duty

in which delay is a fault. Next comes another virtue: no one should move from house to house out of restless fickleness. In this way we keep constancy even in the affection of hospitality and do not lightly dissolve a bond of friendship once it has formed. We should bring a message of peace before us, so that our very first entrance is honoured with the blessing of peace. We ought to be content with the food and drink offered to us. The banners of faith must not be lowered, and the gospel of the heavenly kingdom must be preached. And we must shake the dust from our feet if anyone in a city thinks we should not be received with hospitality.

He also teaches that those who judge that the gospel need not be followed will be liable to a heavier penalty than those who judged that the law might be broken, because Tyre and Sidon, had they seen such great miracles of heavenly works, would not have despised the remedy of repentance. He teaches, too, that this worldly affluence or arrogance is neither to be compared with the heavenly gift nor, on the other hand, to be left without a remedy, since the help of repentance is available to everyone. Finally, he discloses a heavenly mystery: that it pleased God to reveal his grace to little ones rather than to the prudent of this world. The apostle Paul set this out more fully, saying: "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since, in the wisdom of God, this world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe."

Let us take as a little one, then, the person who does not know how to exalt himself or to show off the art of his own prudence with ornate speech, as most philosophers do. He was a little one who said: "Lord, my heart was not exalted, nor were my eyes lifted up, nor did I walk among great things, nor among wonders beyond me." And so that you might know that he was little not in age or in understanding but in his humility and a certain shunning of boastfulness, he added: "but I exalted my soul." Do you see how lofty this little one was, how high he stood on the summit of the virtues? Such little ones the apostle wants us to be when he says: "If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise; for the wisdom of this age is foolishness with God."

A most beautiful passage on the faith follows, when he says that all things have been handed over to him by his Father. When you read "all things," you recognize the Almighty, not of a lesser hue than the Father nor fallen short of him; when you read "handed over," you confess the Son, to whom all things belong by nature, by right of one substance, not conferred as a gift through grace. He added: "No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him."

I remember that this passage was not passed over in the books I wrote on the faith. But so that you may know that, just as the Son reveals the Father to whom he wishes, so the Father also reveals the Son to whom he wishes, hear the Lord Jesus himself, when he praised Peter for confessing him to be the Son of God: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven."

Joined to this is the reading in which those who think themselves experts in the law are exposed [?]: they hold to the words of the law but do not know its force. And from the very first chapter of the law he shows that they are ignorant of the law, proving that right at the beginning the law proclaimed both the Father and the Son, and also announced the mystery of the Lord's incarnation, saying: "You shall love the Lord your God" and "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."

Hence the Lord says to the expert in the law: "Do this and you will live." But he, who did not know his neighbor because he did not believe in Christ, replied: "Who is my neighbor?" So whoever does not know Christ does not know the law either. For how can anyone know the law while ignorant of the truth, when the law proclaims the truth?

A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. So that we may explain the passage set before us more plainly, let us recall the ancient history of the city of Jericho. We remember, then, that Jericho, as we read in the book entitled Joshua son of Nun, was a great city enclosed by fortified walls, which no iron could breach and no battering ram penetrate. In it lived Rahab the harlot, who took in as guests the spies whom Joshua had sent, devised a plan for them, answered the citizens who demanded them that they had gone, hid them on the roof, and, so that she might rescue herself and her family from the destruction of the city, tied a scarlet cord in her window. And the impregnable walls of that city collapsed at the sound of seven priestly trumpets and the harmonious shout of the people rejoicing.

See how each one keeps to his own duty: the spy to his watch, the harlot to the mystery, the victor to his faith, the priest to religion. The spies do not fear danger in the cause of glory; she does not betray those she has taken in, even in danger; he, more anxious to keep faith than to conquer, orders the harlot's safety before the destruction of the city; and the weapons of the priest are the emblems of religion. Now who would not think it full of wonder that from the whole city no one was saved except those whom the harlot set free? This is the truth of the plain history.

But if it is considered more deeply, it signifies wonderful mysteries. For Jericho is a figure of this world, into which Adam, cast out of paradise, that is, out of that heavenly Jerusalem, went down through the fall of his transgression, that is, passing from the realm of life to the underworld; and it was not a change of place but a change of conduct that sent his nature into exile. For he was greatly changed from the Adam who had enjoyed unblemished happiness, and when he turned aside into the sins of the world he fell among robbers, among whom he would not have fallen had he not, by straying from the heavenly command, made himself liable to them. Who are these robbers but the angels of night and darkness, who sometimes transform themselves into angels of light but cannot remain so? They first strip off the garments of spiritual grace that we have received, and then they are accustomed to inflict wounds; for if we keep unstained the garments we have put on, we cannot feel the blows of the robbers. Beware, then, of being stripped first, as Adam was first stripped: deprived of the protection of the heavenly command and stripped of the garment of faith, he then received a deadly wound, of which the whole human race would have died had not that Samaritan come down and healed his grievous wounds.

No ordinary man is this Samaritan, who did not himself despise the one whom the priest and the Levite had despised. Do not despise, because of the name of his sect, one whom you will admire for the meaning of that name; for the word "Samaritan" means "guardian." That is what the interpretation conveys. And who is the guardian but he of whom it was said: "The Lord guards the little ones"? So, just as one man is a Jew in the letter and another in the spirit, so too one is a Samaritan outwardly and another inwardly. This Samaritan, then, coming down (who is it that came down from heaven but he who ascended into heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven?), seeing the man half-dead, whom no one had been able to cure before, like the woman suffering from a flow of blood who had spent her whole fortune on physicians, came near him: that is, he became our neighbor by taking our sufferings upon himself, and drew close to us by bestowing mercy.

"And he bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine." This physician has many medicines with which he is accustomed to heal. His word is medicine. One word of his binds up wounds, another soothes with oil, another pours in wine: he binds up wounds with a sterner precept, soothes them with the forgiveness of sin, and stings them, as with wine, by the warning of judgment.

"And he set him," it says, "on his own beast." Hear how he sets you there. He bears our sins and suffers for us. And the shepherd laid the weary sheep on his shoulders. For man has become like the beasts, and so he set us upon his own beast, so that we might not be like the horse and the mule, and so that by taking on our body he might abolish the infirmities of our flesh. Then he led us, who were beasts, to the inn.
Now an inn is where those worn out by a long journey are accustomed to stop. So the Lord led him to the inn, he who raises the needy from the earth

and lifts the poor from the dunghill; and he took care that the sick man should not fail to keep the precepts he had received. But this Samaritan had no leisure to stay long on earth: he had to return to the place from which he had come down.

So on the next day (and what is this next day, if not perhaps the day of the Lord's resurrection, of which it was said: "This is the day that the Lord has made"?) he took out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said: "Take care of him."

What are these two denarii, if not perhaps the two Testaments, which bear stamped upon them the image of the eternal King, and at whose price our wounds are healed? For we have been redeemed at the price of blood, so that we might escape the sores of the final death.

These two denarii, then (though it is not absurd to see in them also the forms of the four books), the innkeeper received. Who is he? Perhaps the one who said, "And I count them as dung, so that I may gain Christ," so that he might take care of the wounded man. The innkeeper, then, is he who said: "Christ sent me to preach the gospel." The innkeepers are those to whom it is said: "Go into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature, and whoever believes and is baptized will be saved": saved, that is, from death, saved from the wound inflicted by the robbers.

Blessed is that innkeeper who can heal another's wounds; blessed is he to whom Jesus says: "Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return." A good steward is he who spends even more than was given. Paul is a good steward: his sermons and letters overflow, as it were, beyond the account he had received. He carried out the Lord's measured command with an almost measureless labor of mind and body, so as to relieve many of grave sickness by dispensing spiritual counsel. A good innkeeper, then, of that inn in which the ass recognized the manger of her master, and in which flocks of lambs are shut in, so that ravening wolves snarling at the folds may not easily break into the sheepfolds.

He promises, then, that he will pay the reward. When will you return, Lord, if not on the day of judgment? For although you are always everywhere, and although you stand in our midst unseen by us, there will nevertheless be a time when all flesh will behold you returning. Then you will repay what you owe. Blessed are those to whom God is a debtor! Would that we may be worthy debtors! Would that we may be able to repay what we have received, and that neither the office of the priesthood nor that of ministry may make us proud! How will you repay, Lord Jesus? You have indeed promised that the reward of the good is abundant in heaven; yet you will also repay when you say: "Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord."

Since, then, no one is more our neighbor than he who healed our wounds, let us love him as Lord, and let us also love him as neighbor; for nothing is so near as the head to the members. Let us love also the one who imitates Christ; let us love him who, through the unity of the body, suffers with another's need. For it is not kinship that makes a neighbor, but mercy, because mercy accords with nature; for nothing accords so much with nature as helping one who shares our nature.

Mercy, then, has been spoken of, but virtue has more than one form. There follows, in the example of Martha and Mary, the active devotion of the one in her works and the devout attention of the other's mind to the word of God; and this attention, if it accords with faith, is preferred even to works themselves, as it is written: "Mary has chosen the best part for herself, which will not be taken from her." Let us too, then, strive to have what no one can take from us, giving not a perfunctory but a diligent hearing; for even the seeds of the heavenly word itself are often taken away if they are sown along the road. Let the desire for wisdom drive you, as it drove Mary; for this is the greater work, this the more perfect. Do not let the cares of serving turn you away from knowledge of the heavenly word, and do not rebuke those you see devoting themselves to wisdom or judge them idle; for Solomon, that man of peace, took wisdom to himself to dwell with him.

Yet Martha is not rebuked for her good service; rather, Mary is preferred because she chose the better part for herself. For Jesus abounds in many things and bestows many things, and so the wiser woman chose what she perceived to be the chief thing. So too the apostles did not think it best to leave the word of God and serve tables. Yet both are offices of wisdom; for Stephen too, a man full of wisdom, was chosen as a minister. And so let the one who serves defer to the teacher, and let the teacher invite and encourage the one who serves; for the body of the Church is one, though its members are diverse, and each needs the other. The eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of your help," nor again the head to the feet, nor can the ear deny that it belongs to the body; for though some members are principal, others are necessary. Wisdom is in the head, action in the hands; for "the eyes of the wise man are in his head," since he is truly wise whose mind is in Christ and whose inner eye is lifted up to things above. And so the eyes of the wise man are in his head, but those of the fool are in his heel.

"Which of you has a friend, and will go to him at midnight and say to him: Friend, lend me three loaves?" This is another passage of precept: that prayer should be offered at every moment, not only by day but also by night. For you see that this man who went at midnight asking his friend for three loaves, and persisted in the very earnestness of his asking, is not cheated of what he asked for. What are these three loaves but the food of the heavenly mystery? If you love the Lord your God, you will be able to obtain it not only for yourself but also for others. And who is a better friend to us than he who gave up his body for us? David asked him for loaves at midnight and received them; for he asked when he said: "At midnight I rose to give thanks to you"; and so he earned these loaves, which he has set before us to eat. He asked when he says: "Every night I will wash my bed"; nor was he afraid of waking one asleep, for he knows that he is always awake and alert.

And so, mindful of what is written, let us persevere in prayer night and day and ask pardon for our sins. For if that man, so holy and occupied with the needs of a kingdom, praised the Lord seven times a day and was always intent on the morning and evening sacrifices, what ought we to do, who must ask all the more, the more often we sin through the frailty of flesh and mind, so that those who are weary from the road and sorely worn out by the course of this age and the windings of this life may never lack the bread of refreshment that strengthens the heart of man?

Nor does the Lord teach that we must keep watch only at midnight, but at almost every moment; for he comes in the evening, and in the second and third watch, and is accustomed to knock. Blessed, then, are those servants whom the Lord will find watching when he comes. If, then, you desire that the power of God should gird itself and serve you, you must always keep watch; for many are the snares laid for us, and the sleep of the body is heavy, and if the mind begins to sleep in it, it will lose the vigor of its strength. Shake off your sleep, then, so that you may knock at the door of Christ, which Paul too asks to have opened to him, begging to be helped not only by his own prayers but also by those of the people, so that a door may be opened to him to speak the mystery of Christ. And perhaps that is the door which John saw open; for he saw and said: "After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven, and the first voice that I had heard, like a trumpet, speaking with me and saying: Come up here, and I will show you what must take place." The door, then, was opened to John, the door was opened to Paul, so that he might receive loaves for us to eat. For he persevered in knocking at the door, in season and out of season, so that with the abundance of heavenly nourishment he might refresh the nations worn out by the toil of the world's road.

Here, then, is a passage that gives a precept to pray often, a hope of obtaining, and a way of persuading, first by precept and then by example. For whoever promises something ought to give hope of what is promised, so that obedience may be given to the admonitions and faith to the promises; and that faith, by considering human kindness, gains a greater hope of eternal kindness, provided, however, that what is asked is just, lest prayer be turned into sin. Nor was Paul ashamed to ask for something more than once, lest he should seem either to distrust the Lord's mercy or arrogantly to resent not having obtained something at his first request ("for this," he says, "I asked the Lord three times"); and he shows that God often does not grant what is asked of him because he judges useless the things we believe will profit us.

"Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste." The reason for this saying is that he was said to cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons; and so he showed that his kingdom is undivided and everlasting. Rightly, too, he answered Pilate: "My kingdom is not of this world." And therefore those who place their hope not in Christ but think that demons are cast out by the prince of demons he declares not to belong to an everlasting kingdom. This refers to the Jewish people, who in afflictions of this kind would summon a demon's help to cast out a demon. For how can a kingdom remain when it is divided, when faith is torn apart? For since the Jewish people live under the law, and Christ too according to the flesh was born of the law, how can the kingdom of the Jews, which comes from the law, be everlasting, when the people themselves divide the law, since Jesus, who is due from the law, is denied by the people of the law? So the faith of the Jewish people fights against itself in part, and by fighting is divided, and by being divided is dissolved. And therefore the kingdom of the Church will remain forever, because its faith is undivided and its body is one; for there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all.

What madness of sacrilegious frenzy is this! The Son of God took flesh to crush unclean spirits and to carry off the spoils of the prince of this world, and he gave to men too the power to destroy spiritual wickedness, dividing his spoils, which is the mark of one who triumphs; and yet some take to themselves the aid and protection of diabolical power, when demons are driven out by the finger of God, or indeed, according to Matthew, by the Spirit of God! From this we understand that the kingdom of the Godhead is, as it were, a single undivided body, since Christ is the right hand of God, while the Spirit, under the figure of a finger, seems to express the coherence of what is, so to speak, one body according to the Godhead. Does not the kingdom appear undivided, since it is like an undivided body? For, as you have read, the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ. This you certainly cannot deny of the Father, and you ought not to deny of the Spirit. Nor should you suppose, by comparison with our own members, that the power is to be divided into portions; for what is undivided cannot be divided, and so the name "finger" is to be referred to the form of unity, not to a distinction of power, since the right hand of God says: "I and the Father are one." But although the Godhead is undivided, the persons are distinct.

Yet when the Spirit is called a finger, a power that works is signified, because the Holy Spirit, like the Father and the Son, is the worker of divine works. For David says: "For I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers," and in the thirty-second psalm: "And by the Spirit of his mouth all their power." And Paul says: "All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills." And when he says:

"But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you," he shows at the same time that the Holy Spirit has a kind of imperial power, since in him is the kingdom of God, and that we too, in whom the Spirit dwells, are a royal house. Hence later on he also said: "The kingdom of God is within you." And therefore we must regard the Holy Spirit as sharing in the Godhead, the lordship and the imperial majesty, because the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

"When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it wanders through waterless places seeking rest, and finds none." There can be no doubt that this was said of the Jewish people, whom the Lord separated from his kingdom in the preceding passage. From this you are to understand that all heretics and schismatics too are separated from the kingdom of God and from the Church. And so it is perfectly clear that every assembly of schismatics and heretics belongs not to God but to the unclean spirit. So in one man is a figure of the whole Jewish people, from whom the unclean spirit had gone out through the law. But since it could not find rest among the nations and Gentiles because of faith in Christ (for Christ is a fire to unclean spirits, and he had quenched the fiery darts of the adversary in the hearts of the Gentiles, which before had been dry but afterward were moistened through baptism with the dew of the Spirit), it went back to the Jewish people, who, adorned with an outward and perfunctory show, remain more polluted in the inner mind. For they neither washed away nor quenched their burning in the stream of the sacred font; and rightly the unclean spirit returned to them, bringing with it seven spirits more wicked than itself, since with sacrilegious mind they sinned against the week of the law and the mystery of the eighth day. So, just as for us the grace of the sevenfold Spirit is multiplied, so for them every injury of unclean spirits is heaped up; for totality is sometimes expressed by this number, because God rested on the seventh day when the works of the world were completed. Hence also "the barren woman has borne seven, and she who had many children has grown feeble." Finally, so that you may know that the people of the synagogue is disfigured,

where the blessedness of the Church is praised, he went on: This generation is an evil generation; it seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so will the Son of Man be. Here too, while the people of the Jews is condemned, the mystery of the Church is plainly expressed. The Church is gathered from the ends of the whole world: in the Ninevites through repentance, and in the queen of the south through her eagerness to gain wisdom, so that she may come to know the words of the peaceable Solomon. A queen indeed, whose kingdom is undivided, rising up out of diverse and distant peoples into one body. And so that is a great sacrament concerning Christ and the Church; yet this one is greater, because that one went before in figure, whereas now the mystery is full in truth. There we had a type of Solomon; here we have Christ in his own body. The Church, then, is made up of two things: either you do not know how to sin, or you stop sinning. For repentance blots out sin, and wisdom guards against it. So much for the mystery.

Moreover, the sign of Jonah is a type of the Lord's passion, and it is equally a testimony to the grave sins the Jews committed. At the same time we may notice both an oracle of majesty and a token of mercy: through the example of the Ninevites a punishment is announced and a remedy is shown. Hence the Jews too ought not to despair of pardon, if they are willing to repent.

No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but on a lampstand. Having in the preceding passage set the Church above the synagogue, he now urges us to carry our faith over to the Church instead. For the lamp is faith, as it is written: Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord; and the word of God is our faith. The word of God is the light; faith is the lamp. That was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world. A lamp cannot shine unless it has received light from elsewhere. This is the lamp that is lit, namely the power of our mind and understanding, so that the coin that was lost may be found. Let no one, then, set faith under the law; for the law is within measure, grace beyond measure; the law overshadows, grace makes bright. So let no one shut his faith within the measure of the law, but let him bring it to the Church, in which the grace of the sevenfold Spirit shines out, the grace which that great High Priest illumines with the brightness of the divinity on high, so that the shadow of the law may not put it out.

Indeed, that lamp which the high priest used to light morning and evening according to the ancient rite of the Jews has vanished, as if set under the bushel of the law; and that Jerusalem which is on earth, which killed the prophets, lies hidden as though set in the valley of weeping. But that Jerusalem which is in heaven, in which our faith serves as a soldier, set upon that highest mountain of all, that is, in Christ, the Church, cannot be hidden by the darkness and ruins of this world; shining with the brightness of the eternal sun, it illumines us with the light of spiritual grace.

Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and the dish. You see that our bodies are signified by the image of earthly and fragile things, which shatter when they are thrown down by a brief slip. And the things the mind has willed within are easily betrayed through the senses and actions of the body, just as what a cup holds inside shows through on the outside. So too there is no doubt that further on the word "cup" denotes the passion of the body, when the Lord says: The cup which the Father has given me, do you not want me to drink it? For he drinks his own body who swallows up bodily frailty in spiritual affection and, as it were, pours it into mind and soul, so that the weakness of what is outward is drained away by what is inward. You see, then, that it is not the outside of this cup or dish that defiles us, but the inside. And so, like a good teacher, he taught how we ought to cleanse the defilement of our body, saying: Give alms, and behold, all things are clean to you.

Do you see how many remedies there are? Mercy cleanses us; the word of God cleanses us, as it is written: You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you. And you know how great a grace is expressed not only in this passage but in others too: For almsgiving delivers from death; and: Shut up alms in the heart of the poor, and it will plead for you in the evil day.

From here on, then, the whole of this most beautiful passage is directed to this end: since he invites us to the pursuit of simplicity, he condemns the superfluous and earthly practices of the Jews. Because they understand the things of the law according to the body, they are fittingly compared to glass and a dish on account of their own fragility. They observe things that are of no use to us and neglect the things in which the fruit of our hope lies, and so they commit a great sin in despising what is better. And yet even to that sin forgiveness is promised, if mercy follows.

He briefly touches on their many vices: they bend all their zeal to paying tithes on the cheaper produce, while they have no fear of the judgment to come and no love of God, though works without faith are vain. For they pass over the judgment and the love of God: judgment, because they do not refer all that they do to the judgment; love, because they do not love God from the heart.

But lest, on the other hand, he should make us zealous for faith and neglectful of works, he sums up in a brief saying the perfection of the faithful man, who is to be approved by both faith and works: These you ought to have done, and not to leave the others undone.

He also rebukes the arrogance and boastfulness of the Jews, who seek the first places at table in banquets. Against the experts in the law themselves, too, a sentence of condemnation is pronounced, for like hidden tombs they deceive by their appearance and mislead those who deal with them, so that while outwardly they promise something fair, inwardly they enclose things full of stench. This is what many teachers do who demand of others what they themselves cannot match. And therefore they are themselves tombs, as it is said elsewhere: Their throat is an open sepulchre.

This is also a fine passage against the utterly empty superstition of the Jews, who by building the tombs of the prophets condemned the deeds of their fathers, yet by imitating their fathers' crimes turned the sentence back upon themselves. For by building the prophets' tombs they convicted of crime those who had killed them, and by imitating similar deeds they declared themselves heirs of their fathers' wickedness as well. It is not the building, then, but the imitation that is counted as the crime. Nor can they be acquitted of inherited wickedness who, by crucifying the Son of God, added a heavier weight to the crimes of their fathers. And so he rightly added elsewhere: Fill up the measure of your fathers, since there is no sin they could commit graver than an outrage against God.
Therefore Wisdom sends to them apostles and prophets. Who is Wisdom but Christ? Indeed, in Matthew you have: Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men.

They are further rebuked under the name of Jews and declared liable to future punishment, because, while they claim for themselves the teaching of divine knowledge, they hinder others and do not themselves acknowledge what they profess.

Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before the Lord. Even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows. The Saviour has woven in here a most beautiful passage on holding to simplicity and striving after faith, so that we may not, after the manner of Jewish faithlessness, hold back one thing in our heart and feign another with our voice, since at the last time the hidden things of our thoughts, accusing or even defending us, will plainly lay open the secret of our mind. For what greater inducement to simplicity is there than for each person to know that there can be no hiding place for deceit?

But since the cause of faithlessness [?] is twofold, arising either from ingrained malice or from fear that befalls us, he added, so that no one terrified by fear of the authorities should be driven to deny the God whom he acknowledges in his heart, the fine teaching that only the punishment of the soul is to be dreaded, and that the penalty of the body is not to be feared. For death is the end of nature, not a punishment, and so death is the end of bodily punishment, whereas the penalty of the soul is everlasting. God alone is to be feared, for nature sets no bounds to his power but is itself subject to it. Death, on the other hand, is not to be dreaded, since immortality will redeem it with richer interest.

The Lord had breathed in the disposition of simplicity, he had raised up the strength of the mind; only faith was wavering. He rightly strengthened it by means of lesser things. For if God does not forget sparrows, how can he forget men? And if the majesty of God is so great and so eternal that not one sparrow, nor the number of our hairs, lies outside God's knowledge, how unworthy it is to think that the Lord either does not know or despises the hearts of the faithful, when he knows even lesser things!

Perhaps someone will say: How is it, then, that the Apostle said: Is it for oxen that God cares? For surely an ox is more valuable than a sparrow. But care is one thing, knowledge another. Indeed, the numbering of the hairs is to be understood not as an act of counting, but as ease of knowing. For God does not keep the anxious watch of one who counts; rather, to him who knows all things, all things are, as it were, numbered. Still, they are rightly said to be numbered, because we number the things we wish to keep.

We may, however, examine here some hidden meaning of spiritual understanding, especially since it seems absurd that men should be compared to sparrows rather than to men. These five sparrows, then, seem to be the five senses of the body: touch, smell, taste, sight and hearing. If, like sparrows, they poke about in the filth of earthly refuse and seek their food in wild and foul places, they are caught in the snares of their own sins and cannot fly back up to the fruits of higher works on which souls feast. For there is a certain snare of seductive pleasure which ties fetters to the footsteps of our souls, so that, once the sense of earthly matter has dulled the fiery vigour and purity of our nature, it sets the soul up for sale at a kind of auction of vices, made over for the price of worldly luxury.

There is even a kind of market for our sins. So, caught by the allurements of various pleasures, we are either sold under sin or redeemed from sin. Christ redeems us, the adversary sells us; the one auctions us off to death, the other redeems us to salvation. That is why Matthew rightly speaks of two sparrows, signifying body and soul, since the flesh too, if it consents to the law of God and strips itself of the law of sin, passes in purity of sense into the nature of the soul and is lifted up to heaven on spiritual wings. So we are taught that nature gave us the grace of flight and pleasure took it away, weighing down the soul with the food of evil things and bending it towards the nature of bodily mass.

And he rightly said that not one of them falls without the will of God; for what falls sinks to the earth, and what flies is carried up to the height of immortality. But so that no one might be in doubt about what Matthew said, Luke clearly settles it: the will of God means his knowledge. For it is not that whoever falls, falls by the will of God, but that one who has fallen under the weight of his sins cannot escape God's notice. Job, too, was tempted by God's will. He gave you an adversary, but he also set before you a reward. Do not plead your frailty: because you bear the image, you have received a defence. And this too serves your salvation, that you know the devil cannot do harm without God's permission, so that you may not fear the power of the devil more than offending the Godhead.

Now there is no doubt that the soul is compared to a sparrow, since you read: Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the fowlers. And elsewhere: How do you say to my soul: Flee to the mountains like a sparrow? We read too that man himself is compared to a sparrow, for it is written: But I am like a lone sparrow on the housetop, that is, made from two sparrows into one sparrow, formed into the fineness of spiritual substance by the joining of two wings in harmony. So there is a good sparrow, whose nature supplies it with the power to fly. There is also a bad sparrow, which has destroyed its use of flight through the vice of earthly defilement; such are these sparrows that are sold for two pennies.

In one place they are sold for a penny, in another for two pennies. How cheap sins are! For death is cheap, but virtue is precious. The adversary sells us off at a low valuation, like captive slaves; but the Lord, as one who knows how to value his own work, has redeemed us at a great price, as handsome servants whom he made in his own image and likeness. As the holy Apostle said: For you were bought at a great price. And rightly great, for it is reckoned not in money but in blood, since Christ died for us and set us free with his precious blood. Saint Peter also mentions this in his letter, writing to us: For you were redeemed from your vain way of life handed down by your fathers, not with perishable things, silver or gold, but with the precious blood, as of a lamb undefiled and spotless, Christ Jesus. And rightly precious, because it is the blood of a spotless body, because it is the blood of the Son of God, who redeemed us not only from the curse of the law but also from the everlasting death of ungodliness.

In sum, then, the meaning is this: if the Lord has provided for worthless birds and faithless men, whether in the rising sun or in the fruitfulness of the earth, if he bestows the gift of his mercy on all, there should be no doubt that regard for the merits of the faithful will count with him. And he has admirably woven this in, both sharpening faith and laying the foundations of the virtues beneath faith itself: for as faith is the spur of fortitude, so fortitude is the support of faith.

And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. By the Son of Man we of course understand Christ, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, since his only parent on earth is a virgin. Is the Holy Spirit, then, greater than Christ, so that those who sin against Christ obtain pardon, while those who offend against the Holy Spirit do not deserve to obtain forgiveness? But where there is unity of power, there is no question of comparison and no dispute about greatness, since the Lord is great and there can be no end to his greatness. If, then, as we believe, there is unity in the Trinity, the greatness is surely undivided, just as the working is undivided, as is shown in what follows. For whereas it is said elsewhere: The Father gives you what you are to speak, here he added:

For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that hour what you ought to say. If, then, the working is one, the insult is also one. But let us return to our subject. Some think that here we should understand Christ as both the Son of Man and the Holy Spirit, preserving the distinction of persons and the unity of substance, since the one Christ, both God and man, is likewise Spirit, as it is written: The Spirit before our face, Christ the Lord; and likewise holy, since just as the Father is God and the Son is God, and the Father is Lord and the Son is Lord, so the Father is holy, the Son is holy and the Spirit is holy. Indeed, the Cherubim and Seraphim cry out with unwearied voices: Holy, holy, holy, so that the Trinity is signified by the threefold repetition of the word. If, then, Christ is both, what is the difference, except that we should know we may not deny the divinity of Christ? For in persecution, what is demanded but that we deny that Christ is God? So whoever does not confess God in Christ, and Christ from God and in God, does not deserve pardon. But also every spirit that does not confess that Christ has come in the flesh is not from God; for whoever has denied the man has denied God, since Christ is God in man and man in God.
Most, however, hold that the unpardonable blasphemy is to say that Christ casts out demons by Beelzebub and not by divine power.

And someone in the crowd said: Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. But he said to him: Man, who appointed me a judge or divider over you? This whole passage is designed to prepare us to undergo suffering for confessing the Lord, whether through contempt for death, or hope of reward, or the warning of a lasting punishment for which pardon will never be granted. And since greed usually tests virtue, a precept and an example for getting rid of it are added as well, when the Lord says: Who appointed me a judge or divider over you? He who had come down for the sake of divine things rightly declines earthly ones, and he does not deign to be judge of lawsuits and arbiter of property, he who holds the judgment of the living and the dead and the assessment of their merits. You should consider, then, not what you ask for, but from whom you ask it; and do not think that a mind intent on greater things should be pestered with lesser ones. So this brother is deservedly rebuffed, for he wanted to busy the steward of heavenly things with perishable ones, when among brothers it is not a judge in the middle but family affection that ought to act as trustee in dividing the inheritance. Yet it is the inheritance of immortality, not of money, that men should seek. For he gathers wealth in vain who does not know whether he will use it, like the man who, when his full barns were bursting with new harvests, was preparing storehouses for his overflowing crops, not knowing for whom he was gathering them. For all the things of the world remain in the world, and whatever is gathered for heirs passes away from us; nor is anything ours that we cannot take away with us. Virtue alone accompanies the dead; mercy alone follows us, and, as guide and forerunner to the heavenly dwellings, it acquires for the dead eternal tabernacles at the interest of cheap money, as the commands of the Lord testify, who says to us: Make friends for yourselves of the unrighteous mammon, that they may receive you into their eternal tabernacles. This is therefore a good and saving precept, and one fit to stir even the greedy to strive to exchange perishable things for lasting ones, earthly things for divine. But since devotion of faith is often held back by weakness, and those ready to give away their inheritance are drawn back by thought of their own livelihood, the Lord added these words:

Do not be anxious for your life, what you will eat, nor for your body, what you will wear. The life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. For nothing is more instructive for producing faith that all things can be bestowed by God on those who believe than the fact that this airy breath, without any labour of ours, keeps in being the living union of soul and body joined in fellowship, and the wholesome use of food does not fail until the last day of death comes. Since, then, the soul is clothed with the garment of the body and the body is animated by the vigour of the soul, it is absurd for us to think that we shall lack an abundance of food, when we receive the continual substance of life itself.

Consider, he says, the birds of the air. A great example indeed, and one fit for us to follow in faith. For if divine providence grants unfailing nourishment to the birds of the air, which have no labour of cultivation and no yield from fruitful harvests, it seems true that the cause of our want is greed. The reason they have an abundance of food they did not toil for is that they do not know how to claim as their own private property the fruits given to them as common food. We have lost what is common by claiming what is our own; for nothing is one's own where nothing is permanent, nor is any abundance certain where the outcome is uncertain. Why should you prize your riches, when God has willed that even your food be shared with the other living creatures? The birds of the air claim nothing as their own, and therefore they do not know what it is to lack food, because they do not know how to envy others.

Consider the lilies, how they grow; and further on: But if God so clothes the grass, which is in the field today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. A good and edifying saying indeed, for by comparison with the flower and the grass the Lord's word has called us to faith in the mercy God will bestow, whether literally, since we cannot add anything to the stature of our body, or spiritually, since without God's favour we can add nothing beyond the measure of our stature. For what is so instructive and persuasive as to see that even things without reason are so clothed by God's providence that they lack nothing, whether for grace or adornment? How much more, then, should you believe that a rational man, if he places all his needs in God and does not violate his faith by a tendency to waver, can never be in want, since he has rightly put his trust in divine favour?

But let us weigh these words more deeply still. It does not seem idle that the flower is compared with a man, or indeed ranked above him, almost more than above other men, in the case of Solomon. He was so deserving that he both built a temple to God in visible form and, in a mystery, prefigured the Church of Christ. So it seems not out of place to think that the brightness of the flower's colour expresses the glory of the heavenly angels. They are truly the flowers of this world, because the world is adorned by their brightness, and they breathe out the sweet fragrance of holiness. Upheld by their protection we can say: “We are the sweet fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved.” Hindered by no anxiety and occupied by no labour, they keep within themselves the gift of God's generosity and the endowments of a heavenly nature. So it is fitting that Solomon is shown here clothed in his glory and elsewhere covered, because he clothed the weakness of his bodily nature with the glory of his works, as though covering it with a certain strength of mind. But the angels, whose more divine nature remains free from bodily harm, are rightly preferred even to so great a man, though only in view of the harm to which we are subject. Therefore, since through the resurrection people will be like the angels in heaven, the Lord, who also granted that glory to the angels, has commanded us too, following their example, to hope for an increase of heavenly glory until what is mortal is swallowed up by life. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality.

Many also think that this comparison suits better the nature of the flower and the habit of the plant it puts forward, because lilies need no yearly tending. Unlike the yield of other crops, the growth of this flower does not bring the farmer's toil round again in its circle for anxious farmers. However dry the field may be, everything in it that is nourished into flower is quickened by a kind of generative power from within itself and by a sap that always remains in it. So even when you see that the stalk with its young leaves has withered, the life of the flower still lives on, for its greenness is hidden, not lost. And when it has been coaxed out by the charms of spring, the plant's garment takes on again the foliage of the flower and the adornment of the lily. Since we recall that this topic has been treated more fully elsewhere, it is enough to have touched on it briefly here, so as not to go back over the same ground.

It is pleasing to notice that lilies grow not on rugged mountains or in wild woods, but in pleasant gardens. For there are gardens that bear the fruit of various virtues, as it is written: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride, a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.” For where there is purity, where there is chastity, where there is devotion, where there is faithful silence about secret things, where there is the brightness of the angels, there are the violets of the confessors, the lilies of virgins and the roses of martyrs. Nor should anyone think it unfitting that the angels are compared to lilies, since Christ himself called himself a lily, saying: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” And Christ is rightly called a lily, because where the blood of martyrs is, there Christ is. He is the lofty flower, spotless and harmless, in whom no sharp thorns give offence, but grace shines all around. Roses have thorns, for martyrs have torments. But the divine nature, which cannot be harmed and felt no torments, has no thorns.

So the lilies, or the angels, are clothed in more than human glory. Nor should we despair of God's mercy towards us, since through the grace of the resurrection the Lord promises us a form like that of the angels. In this passage he also seems to touch on the question that the apostle did not leave out either, since the peoples of this world ask how the dead rise and with what kind of body they come.

For when he says, “Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you,” he shows that grace will not fail the faithful, either now or in the future, as long as those who long for divine things do not seek earthly ones. It is unbecoming for people who serve as soldiers of the kingdom to worry about food. The King knows how to feed, nourish and clothe his household, and so it is said: “Cast your care upon God, and he will sustain you.”
I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish but that it be kindled already? I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!

In the preceding passage he wanted us to keep watch, constantly expecting the saving coming of the Lord. Otherwise someone might grow slack and careless, putting off his works from day to day, and then be overtaken by the day of the coming judgment or by his own death and lose the reward of his good standing. That precept was given as a general rule for everyone. But the example that follows seems to be aimed at the stewards, that is, at the priests, so that they may know that they will have to suffer a heavy punishment in the future if, intent on worldly pleasures, they neglect to govern the Lord's household and the people entrusted to them.

But to be called back from error by fear of punishment is slight progress and brings little merit. Charity and love carry a greater privilege. So the Lord sharpens our zeal to win his favor, and kindles in us a longing to gain divinity, when he says: I came to cast fire upon the earth. He certainly does not mean the fire that consumes good things, but the fire that produces good will. It refines the golden vessels of the Lord's house but consumes hay and straw. That divine fire burns up all worldly things that are bound up with the world's pleasure, and the work of the perishing flesh. It is the fire that blazed in the bones of the prophets, as holy Jeremiah says: For it became like a burning fire blazing in my bones. For there is a fire of the Lord, of which it is said: A fire shall burn before him. And the Lord himself is also fire, as he says: I am a burning fire and not a consuming one. For the fire of the Lord is eternal light. With this fire are lit those lamps of which he spoke above: Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning. And since the day of this life is night, a lamp is necessary. Ammaus and Cleopas also testify that this fire was sent into them by the Lord, when they say: Was not our heart burning on the way, when he opened the scriptures to us? So they clearly taught what the working of this fire is: it lights up the secret places of the heart. Perhaps this is why the Lord will come in fire: so that at the time of the resurrection he may consume all vices, fulfill the desires of each person by the sight of himself, and kindle the light of their merits and of the mysteries.

So great, then, is the Lord's condescension that he testifies he is eager to pour devotion into us, to bring perfection to completion in us, and to hasten his passion for our sake. Although there was nothing in himself that could grieve him, he was distressed by our troubles, and at the time of his death he showed a sorrow that he had taken on not out of fear of his own death but because of the delay of our redemption, as it is written: And how distressed I am until it is accomplished! Surely one who is distressed until the accomplishment is confident of the accomplishment. And elsewhere he says: My soul is sorrowful even unto death. The Lord is sorrowful not because of death but even unto death, because what troubled him was the condition of bodily feeling, not dread of death. For one who took on a body had to undergo everything that belongs to the body: to hunger, to thirst, to be distressed, to be saddened. But the divinity cannot be changed by these feelings. At the same time he shows that in the struggle of the passion the death of the body is a release from anxiety, not a piling up of pain.

Do you think that I came to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but division. For from now on five in one house will be divided, three against two and two against three. Father will be divided against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.

A spiritual meaning is at work in almost every passage of the Gospel. In the present passage above all, however, the train of thought must be tempered by spiritual depth, so that the harshness of a bare exposition does not offend anyone. This is especially so because our most holy religion, through its moral teachings and gentle examples of dutiful love, mercifully invites even those who are exiles from the faith to revere it. With the discipline of faith leading the way, its gentleness dissolves the hardness of superstitions and compels minds bound by error to believe by faith as well, minds which it was first able to soothe by its dutiful love. For when weak hearts cannot grasp the lofty things of faith, what is to be venerated is judged by what is commanded, so that just things bear witness to a just author, holy things to a holy one, and good things to the good author of his goods.

The Lord joined reverence for God and the grace of dutiful love in a single counsel when he said: You shall love the Lord your God, and you shall love your neighbor. Are we then to suppose that he has now changed so far as to abolish the names of kinship and shatter the affections of family love? Are we to believe that he commanded us to break with our dearest loved ones? How is he our peace, who made both one? How can he say: My peace I give you, my peace I leave you, if he came to separate parents from children and children from parents by breaking the bond of kinship? How can the one who does not honor his father be cursed, and the one who deserts him be devout?

But if we notice that religion comes first and family duty second, we shall find this question untangled as well, for you must put human things after divine ones. If duty must be shown to parents, how much more to the author of parents, to whom you owe thanks even for your parents! And if they do not acknowledge the Parent at all, how can you acknowledge them? So he does not say that we must renounce our loved ones, but that God must be preferred to all. Indeed, you have in another book: Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. You are not forbidden to love your parents, but to prefer them to God. The bonds of nature are the Lord's gifts, and no one ought to love the gift he has received more than God, by whom the gift received is preserved. So even according to the letter, a devout exposition is not lacking for those who understand piously. Yet there is something beneath it which leads us to think that this meaning should be carried higher, since he added: From now on five in one house will be divided,

three against two and two against three. But who are the five, when six persons seem to be listed: father and son, mother and daughter, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law? The same woman can, however, be taken as both mother and mother-in-law, for she who is the son's mother is his wife's mother-in-law. So even according to the letter the count is not absurd, and it is perfectly clear that faith is not bound by the chains of nature. For although they are bound by the duty of family love, they are nonetheless free in faith.
