It also seems fitting to untangle this meaning by a mystical interpretation. One house is one person, for each of us is a house either of God or of the devil. So the spiritual house is the spiritual person, as we have in the epistle of Peter: And you, like living stones, are built up as a spiritual house into a holy priesthood. In this house, then, two are divided against three and three against two. We often read of two, the soul and the body: If two agree on earth; and, He made both one. And elsewhere: I chastise my body and bring it into subjection.

What serves is one thing; what it is subject to is another. If we have recognized two, let us recognize three as well, which is easy to understand from those two. For the soul has three dispositions in the body: one rational, another desiring, the third spirited, that is, the logistikon, the epithymetikon and the thymikon. So it is not two against two, but two will be divided against three and three against two. For through the coming of Christ, man, who was irrational, was made rational. Before, we were like beasts that know no reason. We were carnal and earthly, according to the sentence: You are earth, and to earth you shall go. Then the Son of God came and sent his Spirit into our hearts, and we became spiritual sons.

We can also say that there are another five in this house: smell, touch, taste, sight and hearing. Suppose that, following what we hear or read, we set the senses of sight and hearing apart and shut out the superfluous pleasures of the body produced by taste, touch and smell. Then we divide two against three. The mind's disposition is not caught by the enticements of vice but, by striving after virtue, draws itself away from the allurements of pleasure. There is no single agreement among all of them to hurl it headlong into error; instead, by dividing, the heart's desires and the duties of virtue part from each other. Or if we take them as five bodily senses, then the vices of the body and its sins separate themselves. And perhaps these are the five whom the rich man of luxury in the Gospel calls his brothers. He is described as tormented in the underworld and asks that they be told to learn that delights must be renounced in this world, so that their pursuit of virtue may have rest after this world.

Flesh and soul can also be seen as separated from the smell, touch and taste of luxury, dividing themselves within one house against the vices that attack them. Flesh and soul submit themselves to the law of God and withdraw from the law of sin. Through the transgression of the first man their discord passed into nature, so that they never agreed with equal zeal for virtue. Yet through the Lord's saving cross, with both the enmities and the law of commandments made void, they have come together in the concord of fellowship. For Christ our peace came down from heaven and made both one. He broke down the dividing wall of partition and abolished in his flesh the enmity, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, so that he might create the two in himself into one new man, making peace, and reconcile both to God in one body. What are the two, if not the one inner and the other outer? The one concerns the vigor of the soul, the other belongs to the senses of the body. Yet they agree in the harmony of an inseparable affection when the flesh, subject to the better part, obeys its saving commands. This is not because the flesh passes into the nature of the soul, transformed by some refinement of its matter. It is because, having renounced delights and been purged of every stain of vice, it walks the path of heavenly life with obedient affection. It no longer fights against the law of the mind as before, but has been freed from the law of sin through the law of the mind and the Spirit of life. So the flesh becomes an appendage of the soul, no longer a procuress of vices but

a kind of imitator and, as it were, handmaid of virtue. Again, this happens when the soul does not connive at the body's enticements and is not overcome by delight in carnal pleasures. Instead the mind, pure and stripped of servitude to this world, entices the senses of the body and draws them into its own pleasures. Through hearing and reading it feasts on growth in virtue and, never to know hunger, is filled with the spiritual nourishment of an inner sap. For reason is the food of the mind and a splendid nourishment of sweetness. It does not burden the members or turn them into the shameful parts of nature, but into ornaments, when the wallowing-place of lusts is changed into a temple of God and the lodging-house of vices begins to be a sanctuary of virtues. This certainly happens when the flesh returns to its nature and recognizes the one who nurses its vigor. Laying aside its insolent daring, it is joined to the governance of the ruling soul. It becomes as it was when it received the hidden places of paradise to dwell in. That was before it was infected by the venom of the deadly serpent and came to know a sacrilegious hunger. It was before, in its eagerness to eat, it passed over the memory of the divine commandments that clung to the soul's senses.

From here, we are told, sin flowed forth, with body and soul as its parents, so to speak. While the nature of the body is tempted, the unsound soul suffers along with it. Had the soul reined in the body's appetite, the origin of sin would have been extinguished at its very birth. Instead, impregnated by the body's impulse as if by a male, the soul received that origin poured into it, and with its own vigor corrupted and heavy with another's burden, it brought it forth. For that more violent and stronger sex is carried along by a kind of powerful impulse, like the desire of a male, while she seeks to keep a reason that is gentle rather than vehement.

From these, then, the impulse of various desires grew up. But when the soul comes back to itself, confronted with shame at its misshapen offspring, it renounces its degenerate heirs, disinheriting those impulses and loathing sin. The flesh too is ruined by the principal of its heavy labors and wearied by the wretched interest of injury. When it grieves to find itself pierced by the desires it bore for itself, as by the thorns of the world, it hastens to strip off the old man and take itself away from itself, so that offspring doomed to perish may not bring ruin on their improvident parent. Again, the irrational impulse of desire, luring her with the allurements of pleasure as if with the painted beauty of some lovely form, took her to itself as if in the partnership of marriage. So pleasure, a kind of daughter-in-law of body and soul, marries the impulse of depraved desire.

So as long as an undivided and inseparable agreement remained in one house, with the vices conspiring together, there seemed to be no division. But then Christ sent upon the earth the fire with which to burn away the sins of the flesh, or the sword, which signifies the edge of drawn power and pierces the secret places of spirit and marrow. Then flesh and soul, renewed by the mysteries of regeneration, forget what they were and begin to be what they were not. They separate themselves from fellowship with the old vice, however dear it was to them before, and cast out the union, as it were, of a prodigal posterity. So the parents are divided against the children, while intemperate impulse is disowned by the temperance of the body, and the soul turns away from partnership in guilt. No place is left for that pleasure, alien and brought in from outside.

The children too are divided against the parents, while the old vices turn away from the aged strictness of the renewed man, and youthful pleasure flees the rule of devotion as the discipline of a serious household. It is also fitting to think that these too divide themselves so as to become better than their parents, especially since he said later: If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and children and brothers and sisters, and even his own soul, he cannot be my disciple. And so, according to the simple way of understanding, the son who follows Christ is preferred to gentile parents, for religion surpasses the duties of family devotion.

That passage may also be read in a higher sense. Sin is born of the flesh and works as if in the womb of the flesh; of this the apostle says: But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me. When the Lord's blood, poured out for the life of this world, has abolished the vices, offense is turned into grace, for sin abounded so that grace might abound all the more. And so repentance, born of sin, drives us to a change of purpose and to a longing for spiritual grace. Thus what was for me unto death will be unto salvation. So sin, washed in the flowing fountain, is separated from the flesh from which it was generated. And while each one longs to redeem his offense, so that out of the chain of guilt [?] a zeal for discipline.

The desire for evil things, too, and a certain more fervent impulse of craving are changed by the word of God into an appetite for divine charity and love. A different discipline arises in the same nature, and that appetite of body and soul gains for itself a far better pleasure than before, the pleasure of the heavenly mysteries. For the mind is nourished by the knowledge of things and, raised higher by learning the promise of things to come, disdains the old works of the natural life. For the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, since they are foolishness to him; but the spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one.

While you are going with your adversary to the magistrate, make an effort on the way to be freed from him, so that he does not condemn you before the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison. I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid even the last quadrans. Matthew also recorded this, but he did so in a particular sense and Luke in a general one. Matthew took it as said about restoring peace between brothers at odds, Luke about repentance and the amendment of every sin. Let us examine, then, who the adversary is, who the magistrate, who the judge and who the officer, and what we should take to be the quadrans which, unless it is paid, sends a person to prison.

According to Matthew, the adversary is the one with whom you seem to have been least at peace in this life, who may pursue you before the future judge of the dead and the living with the charge of lingering enmity. According to Luke, however, our adversary is above all the one who sows the enticements of sin, so that those he had as companions in error he may have as partners in punishment. That is why he seeks allies in guilt: to betray them as liable to punishment. The apostle Peter warns us to beware of him, saying: Your adversary the devil, like a ravening and roaring lion, seeks someone to devour.

According to Matthew, our adversary is every practice of virtue and the word of the apostles and prophets. This binds us to harsher precepts and to the lessons of a sterner life. We ought to agree with it and imitate it in our deeds, so that no stubbornness of ours may show that we have deserted it. According to Luke, however, no one is more our adversary than our own fall, which accuses us by the evidence of our life. This is not because the judge to come will need anyone to serve as accuser. It is because before the one who knows all things our own conduct accuses us, when it is found to be estranged from the practice of virtue and the precepts of the apostles.

So every practice of vice is our adversary. Lust is our adversary, greed is our adversary, every wickedness is our adversary, every unjust thought is our adversary; in short, so is every evil conscience, which both afflicts us here and will accuse and betray us hereafter. As the apostle testifies: their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts accusing or even defending them among themselves. If conscience betrays each of us, how much more is the work of our deeds present before God! It is imprinted on our body and will be reviewed at the last time, and the secrets of our thought, written in our hearts, will be read. Let us make an effort, then, while we are set on this course of life, to be freed from wicked action as from an evil adversary, so that while we are going with the adversary to the magistrate, he does not condemn our error on the way.

That is why he also says according to Matthew: Agree with your adversary while you are with him on the way. The Greek has eunoōn, that is, well-disposed. For if, while we are in this life, we free ourselves from the bonds of the devil, he will not be condemned on our account, and we shall be free of his bonds. That is also why Psalm 79 is headed For the Assyrian. You give good counsel to your adversary and act on behalf of that Assyrian, that is, the empty one, if you escape his snares and show him the goodwill of letting him escape the penalty for your fall and death. But if you remain caught in his bonds, he will hand you over to the magistrate as a defendant, being both your accuser and your betrayer.

Who is the magistrate, if not the one in whom all power resides, who claims for himself the sublime dignity of the full and perfect time? Relying on the conscience of good works and not fearing the adversary, the holy prophet hastens to him, saying: My soul has thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God? This magistrate will hand the defendant over to the judge, that is, to the one to whom he gave power over the living and the dead. He gave it by nature, not by grace, for the Son did not receive a power he did not have, but took it from the substance of the Father when he was begotten. The same apostle who pointed out the accuser shows you this magistrate and judge, and shows when he is to be revealed: On the day, he says, when God will judge the secrets of men according to my gospel through Jesus Christ our Lord. This, then, is the judge, Jesus Christ, through whom secrets are exposed and the punishment for wicked deeds is ordered.

Do you want to know that Christ is the judge who hands over to the officer and sends to prison? Ask him; or rather, read him in the Gospel, saying: Take him and cast him into the outer darkness. In another place he also pointed out his officers, where he says: So it will be at the end of the age: the angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

It now remains for us to understand what the figure of the quadrans means. The hidden spiritual sense seems to be expressed by the name of an everyday thing. Those who pay money pay back a debt, and the name of the loan is not cancelled until the whole sum of the principal has been paid, down to the last coin, by whatever kind of payment. In the same way, the penalty of sin is discharged by the compensation of charity and of other deeds, or by satisfaction of any kind.

Nor is it without reason that in this place he set down neither two coins, as elsewhere, nor an as, nor a denarius, but a quadrans. For exchange by the quadrans is a kind of compensation, in which one thing is paid and another is counted as settled. So here too either the injury is redeemed at the price of charity, or the penalty is remitted once the injury has been assessed.

We remember that a quadrans is usually given at the baths. By offering it, each person there receives the right to wash, and in the same way here each receives the right to be washed clean. For each person's sin is washed away under the kind of terms described above, when the guilty one is subjected to punishment until he has paid the penalty for the error he committed.

As for those Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices, this seems to be a figure touching those who, under the devil's compulsion, do not offer sacrifice purely. Their prayer becomes sin, as is written of Judas the betrayer, who was plotting the betrayal of the Lord's blood while he was present at the sacrifices.

A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard. What does it mean that the Lord so often brings in the parable of the fig tree in his Gospel? Elsewhere you find that at the Lord's command all the greenness of this leafy tree withered. From this you understand that he is the Creator of all, who can command natures either to wither suddenly or to grow green. Elsewhere he recalls that the coming of summer is usually inferred from the tenderness of this tree and its leaves. By both he signifies two things. First, the empty glory that the Jewish people displayed fell like a flower at the Lord's coming, because it remained fruitless in works. Second, the day of judgment, like the coming of summer, when the ripe fruits of all the lands are gathered in, is, by the fullness of the Church, into which the Jews too will come to believe,

to be measured. Here too, then, let us seek some secret of a higher sense. The fig tree is in a vineyard. Now the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts was the one he gave up to be plundered by the nations. So the one who let his vineyard be plundered also ordered the fig tree to be cut down. The comparison of this tree with the synagogue is apt. This tree abounds in leaves that fall, and disappoints its owner's hope with an empty expectation of the yield he hoped for. In the same way, in the synagogue the empty shadow of the law flourishes, while its teachers, barren in works, glory in words that abound like leaves. But the hope of a false yield, once looked into, mocks the prayers of the people who believe.

There is also something in the nature of this tree to make you believe all the more that the figure of the synagogue is expressed by comparison with it. If you inquire carefully, you will find that its natural habit differs from that of other trees. Others bear flowers before fruit and signal the fruit to come by a flower that announces it; this one alone puts forth fruit instead of flowers from the start. In others the flower is shed and the fruit is born; in this one fruits fall so that other fruits may follow. So those first fruits, empty of real fruit, appear in place of a flower. Thus, by a sort of premature birth, things that do not know nature's order cannot keep nature's benefit. For where a bud usually pushes out from the middle of the bark, there all the tiniest fruits of this kind burst forth. Of these we read in the Song of Songs: The fig tree puts forth its green figs. And so, while the other shrubs turn white in early spring, the fig alone does not grow white with a flower of its own, perhaps because no fruit ripens for use earlier than these. For when others follow, these are rejected as degenerate, and with their weak, withering root they are shed by the renewed fruits, whose sap is more useful. Yet some remain, a very few, and do not fall. These have had the good fortune to emerge from a short little knob bursting out between two twigs, so that, sheltered by a double protection, they grow as if in the lap of their parent nature, warmed by fuller sap. Stirred by the mildness of a gentler air and grown fuller over longer seasons, once they have shed the wild temper of their former sap, they are preferred to the rest in appearance and in the grace of ripeness.

Now look at the customs and minds of the Jews. As the first fruits of a poorly fruitful synagogue, they fell like the falling green fig, so that the fruits of our race, which will last beyond time, might follow. For the first people of the synagogue, weak as it were in the root of withering works, could not draw up the richness of natural wisdom, and so it fell like useless fruit. Then, as if from the same little shoots of the fruitful tree, the new people of the Church could emerge from the richness of the ancient religion. So the one that was ceased to be, so that the one that was not might begin. Yet the first of Israel, raised up by a branch of stronger nature, were colored by a twofold sap under the shade of the law and of the cross, in the lap of both. Like the ripening fig, they surpassed the rest in the grace of the most beautiful fruits. To them it is said: You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

Nor is it beside the point that Adam and Eve, the first parents of our race and likewise of our sin, who covered themselves with the leaves of this tree, deserved to be banished from paradise. Conscious of their transgression, they shrank from the presence of the Lord as he walked in the garden. This signified what was to come: in the last times, at the coming of the Lord our Saviour, who came to call them, the Jewish people would recognize that the devil's temptations had stripped them of their virtues. Dreading the uncovered shame of their conscience, straying from true religion and confounded by their transgression, they would withdraw from the Lord, covering the shameful parts of their deeds with flowing words as if with a veil of leaves.

So those who picked leaves from the fig tree, and not fruit, were shut out of God's kingdom, for they were made a living soul. The second Adam came, and he sought not leaves but fruit, for he was a life-giving spirit. It is in the spirit that the fruit of virtue is gained and the Lord is worshipped. Yet the Lord sought fruit not because he did not know that the fig tree had none, but to show in a figure that the synagogue ought by then to have borne fruit.

Then, from what follows, he teaches that he did not come before the time. He came over three years, for this is what you have: "Look, it is three years since I came seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down, then; why should it even take up the ground?"

He came to Abraham, he came to Moses, he came to Mary; that is, he came in the seal, he came in the law, he came in the body. We recognize his coming from his benefits: in one place there is purification, in another sanctification, in another justification. Circumcision purified, the law sanctified, grace justified: one in all, and all one. For no one can be cleansed except one who fears the Lord. No one deserves to receive the law unless he has been purified from guilt, and no one approaches grace unless he has known the law. So the Jewish people could not be purified, since their circumcision was of the body and not of the mind. Nor could they be sanctified, since they did not know the power of the law, following carnal things rather than spiritual ones (and the law is spiritual). Nor could they be justified, since they did not repent of their sins and therefore did not know grace.

Rightly, then, no fruit was found in the synagogue, and so it is ordered to be cut down. But the good vinedresser intervenes devoutly so that it may not be cut down. Perhaps this is the one on whom the church's foundation rests, who foresaw that another would be sent to the gentiles and he himself to those of the circumcision. Trusting in his own calling, he believed that even the Jewish people could be saved through the church, and so he says: "Leave it this year too, until I dig around it and put on a basket of manure."

How quickly he recognized that the hardness and pride of the Jews were the causes of their barrenness! So the one who knows how to detect faults also knows how to cultivate. He promises that the hard places of their hearts must be dug with apostolic hoes. In this way the twice-sharpened word may turn over the crust that long neglect has spread over the mind, break open the heart, and rouse a sense that already thrives on the breath of the air. So no heap of earth may smother and hide the root of wisdom. He also says that a basket of manure must be put on. Great indeed is the power of manure, so great that it makes the unfruitful fruitful, the withered green, the barren productive. Job sat on it when he was tempted, and he could not be overcome; and Paul counts things as dung so that he may gain Christ. Indeed, though Job had lost a great deal before, once he sat on the dunghill he had nothing left that the devil could take from him. Good, therefore, is the earth that is dug, and good the manure that is put on. So too the Lord raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dunghill.

So that good vinedresser expects that, through the exercise of spiritual understanding and a disposition of humility, even the Jews will bear fruit in the gospel of Christ. For he remembered that the Lord spoke through Haggai: "From the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day on which the temple of the Lord almighty was founded, the vine and the fig and the pomegranates and the olive trees, which do not bear fruit — from this day I will bless them." This reveals that at the very close of the declining year, that is, at the sunset of an age now growing old, the holy temple of God, which is the church, was to be built. By its grace, through the sanctification of the font, the peoples of the Jews and of the nations may have the fruit of their merits.

So the nature of the tree points to the form of the synagogue, which is fruitful in its later yields, for we come from the seed of the fathers. And the Jews are rightly compared to unripe figs that fall, because with a fattened heart and a very hard neck they cannot reach their own lasting maturity. But if they die and, as it were, fall away from this world, so that they are reborn into the inner man through the grace of the font, they will certainly be fruitful. The faithlessness of stubborn men, however, made the synagogue useless, and so it is ordered to be cut down as if barren.

I think that what was said of the Jews is a warning to everyone, and to us most of all, so that we do not occupy the fruitful ground of the church while empty of merits. Like pomegranates, we ought to bear blessed fruits within: fruits of modesty, fruits of union, fruits of mutual charity and love, enclosed within the one womb of mother church, so that no wind may harm them, no hail knock them down, no heat of desire scorch them, no shower of moisture crush them.

Some, however, think that this fig tree is an allegorical figure not of the synagogue but of malice and wickedness. These differ from us only in choosing the genus instead of the species. They say they avoid the other reading because the Lord said to the fig tree: "May no fruit ever grow from you again," while we know that very many of the Jews have believed and will believe. But whoever believes is no longer the fruit of the synagogue but of the church, and one who is reborn in the church is not born of the synagogue. There are those who went out from us but were not of us, for if they had been of us they would have remained with us. In the same way we say of the Jews who believe that if they had been of the synagogue they would remain in the synagogue; they went out from the synagogue precisely so that they might be believed never to have been of it. Besides, on their reading the vinedresser would be interceding for malice and saying that it should be cultivated so as to bear fruit, when the Lord came precisely to abolish the seeds of wickedness.
Now he was teaching in their synagogue on the sabbaths. And look, there was a woman who had had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, and she was bent over.

How quickly he showed that he was speaking of the synagogue! He shows that he had come to that very tree, since he was preaching in it. Next, the infirm woman follows as a figure of the church. When the church has fulfilled the measure of the law and of the resurrection, it will be raised up to the lofty summit in that everlasting rest and will no longer be able to feel the stoop of our infirmity. Nor could this woman have been healed unless she had fulfilled the law and grace: the law in the commandments, and grace in the font, through which we die to the world and rise again to Christ. For the perfection of the law lies in the ten words, and the fullness of the resurrection in the number eight. So the work done on the sabbath is a sign of the future: everyone who has fulfilled the law and grace will, through the mercy of Christ, be stripped of the troubles of bodily frailty. That is why sanctification was first set forth as a sign through Moses, as a training for the sanctification to come and for the spiritual observance of abstaining from worldly works. Indeed God too rested from the works of the world, though not from work as such, since his working is everlasting and unceasing, as the Son says: "My Father is working until now, and I am working." This was so that, in the likeness of God, our worldly works might cease, but not our religious ones.

But the ruler of the synagogue did not understand this and forbade anyone to be healed on the sabbath. Yet the sabbath is a type of the holidays to come, and so it is a rest not from good works but from evil ones. That is why it was prescribed that we should celebrate the sabbaths that are to come after death carrying no burden of sins and not empty of good works. So the Lord seems to answer in a spiritual sense when he says: "Hypocrites, does not each of you untie his ox or his donkey on the sabbath and lead it away to water?"

Why did he mention no other animal, except to show that, though the rulers of the synagogue opposed it, the Jewish and gentile peoples would nevertheless lay aside the body's thirst and the heat of this world through the abundance of the Lord's fountain? For the ox knew its owner, and the donkey its master's manger. So that people, which was formerly fed on cheap hay that withers before it is pulled up, received the bread that came down from heaven. And so he says that the church will be saved through the calling of the two peoples. When the time of the law had been fulfilled, in the age of the Lord's resurrection, the church received the time of its release. How merciful the Lord is, then, and how kind in both cases, whether he shows mercy or punishes! In the type of the synagogue he orders the tree to be cut down; in the type of the church he saves the woman. How sweet a parable! And the solution is easy. He compares bond with bond, so that the accusation of the Jews is refuted by their own practice. For while they themselves loosen the bonds of animals on the sabbath, they rebuke the Lord, who freed human beings from the bonds of sin.

What is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed which a man took and sowed in his garden; and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air rested in its branches.

The present reading teaches us that we must look at the nature of a comparison, not at outward appearance. So let us see why the lofty kingdom of heaven is compared to a grain of mustard seed. I remember reading of a grain of mustard seed in another place too, where it is compared to faith, as the Lord says: "If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain: Be lifted up and thrown into the sea." This is not a small faith but a great one, able to command a mountain to move. For the Lord does not demand a middling faith from the apostles, who he knows must contend against the height of spiritual wickedness that exalts itself. Do you want to know that great faith is required? Read in the Apostle: "And if I have all faith, so that I can move mountains."

So if the kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, and faith is like a grain of mustard seed, then faith is surely the kingdom of heaven, and the kingdom of heaven is faith. So whoever has faith has the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom is within us, and faith is within us, for we read: "The kingdom of God is within you," and elsewhere: "Have faith in yourselves." Indeed Peter, who had all faith, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven so that he might open it to others as well.

Now let us judge from the nature of mustard what the force of the comparison is. Its seed is certainly a cheap and simple thing, but once it begins to be ground, it pours out its strength. Faith too seems simple at first, but if it is ground by adversity, it pours out the grace of its power, so that it fills others too, those who hear or read, with its fragrance. Our martyrs Felix, Nabor and Victor are a grain of mustard seed. They had the fragrance of faith, but they lay hidden. Persecution came; they laid down their arms and bent their necks, and, crushed by the sword, they spread the grace of their martyrdom to the ends of the whole world, so that it may rightly be said:

"Their sound has gone out into all the earth." But faith is sometimes ground, sometimes pressed, sometimes sown. The Lord himself is a grain of mustard seed. He was untouched by injury, but the people did not know him, as one does not know a mustard seed one has not touched. He chose to be ground, so that we might say: "For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God." He chose to be pressed; so Peter too said: "The crowds are pressing upon you." He chose to be sown like a seed, which a man took and sowed in his garden. For it was in a garden that Christ was both seized and buried; in a garden he grew, where he also rose again; and he became a tree, as it is written: "As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my brother among the sons."

So you too must sow Christ in your garden. A garden is surely a place full of flowers and of many kinds of fruit, where the grace of your work may blossom and the manifold fragrance of varied virtue may breathe out. Let Christ be there, then, where the fruit is. Sow the Lord Jesus: he is a seed when he is seized, a tree when he rises again, a tree that overshadows the world; he is a seed when he is buried in the earth, a tree when he is lifted up to heaven.

Press faith too, together with Christ, and sow faith. Faith is pressed when we believe in Christ crucified. Paul pressed faith when he said: "And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come with eminence of speech or of wisdom, proclaiming to you the mystery of God; for I decided to know nothing among you except Christ Jesus, and him crucified." And since he taught us to press faith, he also taught us to raise it up, saying: "For now we no longer know Christ as crucified." We sow faith when, on the basis of the gospel and the readings from the apostles and prophets, we believe in the Lord's passion. We sow faith, then, when we cover it with the Lord's flesh as with softened and well-worked soil, so that faith may spread itself abroad as if by the warmth and pressure of the sacred body. For whoever believes that the Son of God was made man believes that he died for us and believes that he rose again for us. So I sow faith when I plant his burial within it.

Do you want to know that Christ is a seed and that Christ was sown? "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." So we have not erred, for we have said what he himself had already said. He is both a grain of wheat, because he strengthens the human heart, and a grain of mustard, because he sets the human heart on fire. And though both fit him in every respect, he seems to be a grain of wheat when his resurrection is discussed. For he is the bread of God that came down from heaven, since the word of God and the example of the resurrection nourish minds, sharpen hope and strengthen love. He is a grain of mustard because the word about the Lord's passion is more bitter and more pungent: more bitter to move us to weeping, more pungent to stir us. So when we hear and read that the Lord fasted, the Lord thirsted, the Lord wept, the Lord was scourged, and that at the time of his passion the Lord said: "Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation," we are rebuked as if by the juice of a more bitter word, and we temper the delights of bodily pleasures, which are sweeter than is right. So whoever sows a grain of mustard sows the kingdom of heaven.

Do not despise this grain of mustard. It is indeed the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it becomes greater than all the herbs. If Christ is the grain of mustard, how can Christ be the least, or how can he grow? It is not in his nature but in his appearance that he grows. Do you want to know that he is the least? "We saw him, and he had neither form nor comeliness." Learn that he is the greatest: "Fair in beauty beyond the sons of men." For he who had neither form nor comeliness was made more excellent than the angels, beyond all the glory of the prophets, whom weak Israel had eaten like herbs. For of the bread by which hearts are strengthened, Israel had rejected the one and not received the other.

Christ is a seed because he is the seed of Abraham, for the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one, "and to your seed," which is Christ. And Christ is not only a seed but even the least of all seeds, because he did not come in kingship, nor in riches, nor in the wisdom of this world. But suddenly, like a tree, he spread out the lofty crown of his power, so that we may say: "Under his shadow I longed to sit, and I sat." And often, I think, he was seen as tree and seed at the same time. He is a seed when it is said: "Is not this the son of Joseph the carpenter?" But amid these very words he suddenly grew, as the Jews themselves testify. As if they could not grasp the branches of a spreading tree, they said: "Where did this man get this wisdom?"

So the seed is his outward form, and the tree is wisdom. In its leafy branches now rest, in a safe dwelling, that night raven in the house, that solitary sparrow on the building, and he who was caught up into paradise and is yet to be caught up into the air and the clouds. The powers and angels of heaven also rest there, and all who have deserved to fly up by spiritual deeds. Saint John rested there when he reclined on Jesus' breast; indeed, he himself is stretched out like a branch by the sap of that tree. Peter is a branch; Paul is a branch, forgetting what lies behind and reaching for what lies ahead. We who were far off, we who have been gathered from the nations, whom the storm and whirlwind of spiritual wickedness long tossed through the emptiness of the world, take up the oars of the virtues and fly into their bosoms and into the hidden recesses of their teachings, so that the shade of the saints may shield us from the heat of this world, and we may flourish now in the security of a sure resting place,

because our soul, once bent down by grievous sins like that woman, has been snatched like a sparrow from the hunters' snare and has flown away to the branches and the mountains of the Lord. So we, who once flitted about, vain with needless observances and empty levity, now apply ourselves to good works through faith in Christ, our hands untied and free from the bonds of the sabbaths. Even at our meals we have freedom, but we shut out intemperance, so that we may not be free from the law only to become slaves to our desires. For the law bound people to itself in order to release them from their desires. Grace, which took away a lesser servitude, has commanded far weightier things: "All things are lawful for us, but not all things are expedient." For it is a grave thing to use your freedom in such a way that you fall back under another's power. Cease to be under the law, so that by virtue you may be above the law.
To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven which a woman took and hid in flour until the whole was leavened.

This comparison spreads so much uncertainty over the questions to be examined that it has given rise to a great many differing opinions. It was fitting, then, that above we called Christ the grain of wheat, since a spiritual leaven lay beneath for us; and for this reason many take Christ to be the leaven, because leaven raises up the power it has received. And just as leaven, though it comes from flour, surpasses its own kind in power, not in appearance, so Christ too, equal to the fathers in body, stood out as beyond compare in his divinity. Let holy Church, then, which is figured by that woman in the gospel and whose flour we are, hide the Lord of the laws [?] in the inner places of our mind, until the colour of heavenly wisdom spreads over the secret recesses of our soul.

And because we read in Matthew that the leaven was hidden in three measures, it seemed fitting for us to believe that the Son of God was hidden in the law, veiled in the prophets, and fulfilled in the preaching of the gospel. In this way he wins a perfect faith for us from all of them, and, formed in us, who are his body, by bringing the scriptures together, he is fulfilled as all in all. For he was the Word of God and the mystery that has been hidden from the ages and from the generations, and nothing could be said that bears clearer witness to his eternity than this. For he truly was: he was in such a way that, hidden from the sacrilegious and revealed in the saints, he was predestined before the ages and kept for glory. And this is glory, brothers: that we are able to search out the mystery hidden from the ages in God. What is in God is surely from God, for God cannot hold a nature foreign to himself.

I have no doubt that some think this was said of this world, which is leavened by the law, the prophets and the gospel until every tongue confesses the Lord. So let us examine everything and inquire more carefully. No one finds unless he has first sought. Let us build a tower; let us count the cost of the scriptures and gather the funds, so that no one may say of any of us: This man wanted to build and could not finish. Whoever builds must lay a good foundation. The good foundation is faith, the good foundation of the apostles and prophets. Our faith rises from the two testaments, and no one does it wrong who says that the measure of perfect faith is equal in both, since the Lord himself says: If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for in Moses too it was the Lord who spoke. Rightly, then, there is a perfect measure in both, because he is perfect in both, and the faith of both is one, since the oracle and its answer come from a single power and a single mind.

Yet I prefer to follow what the Lord himself taught, that the leaven of the Church is spiritual teaching. For since it is written, Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and the apostle has said, Not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, it is shown that teaching is leaven. But the leaven of tares is one thing and the leaven of wheat another. So we also agree with good authors in saying that the Church sanctifies the reborn man, who consists of body, soul and spirit, with a spiritual leaven. Body and soul are sanctified, and spiritual grace itself receives an increase of sanctification, when through the Church's work of leavening, as it were, and through the teaching of the scriptures, which grows as heavenly words are brought together in abundance, the practice of faith is poured into the whole man, mixed through him and takes root, so that they become one, the leaven included. This certainly happens when these three agree with one another, their desires weighed as if on an equal scale, and an equal harmony of wills breathes through them.

This work of the Church, then, is not hasty or haphazard. It is accomplished through long meditation, so that these three may be one, kept whole from the law of sin. For this view we have the apostle as our witness, who says: May the Lord himself sanctify you in all things, so that your spirit and soul and body may be kept whole and blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. Through the trials of the world this does not come about unless that woman in the gospel hides the leaven, to which the kingdom of heaven is compared, in three measures of flour until the whole is leavened. For the three measures, as I said, are those of flesh, soul and spirit. Yet the spirit by which all of us live while placed in this body is all the more truly spirit when the wantonness of the flesh does not overflow, when the soul is not bent by bodily errors, and when the measure of living is kept unimpaired in the whole man. But because this equality of the measures can hardly last without the help of the Church and of teaching, that woman, who bears the figure of the Church, keeps mixing the power of spiritual teaching into them until the whole inner man, the hidden man of the heart, is leavened and rises into the grace of heavenly bread. Rightly, then, is Christ's teaching called leaven, because Christ is bread, and the apostle says: Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body.

So they become one leaven when the flesh does not lust against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh, but we put to death the deeds of the flesh, and the soul, aware that it received the breath of life from the breathing of God, turns away from the earthly contagion of worldly ties. That is why the apostle commanded us to walk not in the flesh but in the spirit. Sanctified through the washing of regeneration, we put off the old man with his desires and put on the new man, who is created according to Christ, so that we may walk not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit. Thus the fellowship of body, soul and spirit may remain uncorrupted for us at the time of the resurrection, and even now we may obtain everything we ask. Many think the Lord also meant this when he says: If two of you agree on earth about anything you ask, it will be done for you by my Father who is in heaven.

So some take the two to be soul and body, and others soul and spirit. If soul and spirit agree on earth, that is, in the body, and do not fight against each other with conflicting desires, it seems that everything they pray for can be brought to fulfilment. This happens when both have become one: when their enmities are removed or dissolved and the two, soul and spirit, are formed into one new man, so that we pray with the spirit and pray with the mind as well. Many, however, take the two to be the two peoples, from Israel and from the Gentiles, who are to be gathered into one at the time of the resurrection, so that a perfection lasting forever may come about and what is in part may be done away. Many others take them to be husband and wife, agreeing with each other in the pursuit of love.

So if in this life the three measures remain in the same leaven until they are leavened and become one, so that no gap remains in their equality and we no longer appear to be made up of three different elements, then those who love Christ will have an uncorrupted fellowship in the future, and we will not remain composite. We who are now composite will be one and will be transformed into a single substance. For in the resurrection no part will be inferior to another, as now the weakness of the flesh is frail in us, and our bodily nature is open to wounds or exposed to injuries, or, pressed down by the weight of its own burden, cannot lift itself higher above the earth and raise its step. Instead we will be fashioned into the grace of a simple creature, when what John said is fulfilled: Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be; but we know that when it is revealed, we shall be like him. So since God's nature is simple, for God is spirit, we too will be fashioned into the same image, so that as the heavenly one is, so are the heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one, which our mind must put on.

That is why, at the very beginning of this passage, the man with dropsy is healed. In him an overflowing flux of the flesh weighed down the functions of the soul and quenched the ardour of the spirit. Next humility is taught, when at the wedding feast the craving for a higher place is checked. Yet this is done gently, so that the kindness of persuasion rules out the harshness of coercion, reason advances to the point of persuading, and correction amends the disposition. Joined to this, as on the next threshold, is generosity, which the Lord's saying defines by this mark: that it is bestowed on the poor and the weak. For to be hospitable to those who will repay you is the disposition of greed.

Finally, as to a man who has served out his time as a soldier, the pay prescribed is contempt for possessions. The one who, intent on lower pursuits, buys himself earthly estates cannot attain the kingdom of heaven, since the Lord says: Sell all you have and follow me. Nor can the one who buys oxen, since Elisha slaughtered the oxen he had and divided them among the people. And the one who takes a wife thinks about the things of the world, not the things of God. This is not said to condemn marriage, but because virginity is called to a greater honour, since the unmarried woman and the widow think about the things of the Lord, that they may be holy in body and spirit. For the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

But to make our peace now with married people, as we did above with widows, we do not shy away from the opinion that many hold, and we take it that three kinds of people are excluded from sharing in that great supper: Gentiles, Jews and heretics.

That is why the apostle says that greed must be shunned, so that we are not hindered, in the manner of the Gentiles, by iniquity, malice, impurity and greed, and so made unable to reach the kingdom of Christ. For every greedy or unclean person, which is idolatry, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

The Jews, on the other hand, place the yoke of the law on themselves through bodily observance. So, as the prophet says, let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us. For we have received Christ, who has laid the gentle yoke of his love upon our necks. The five yoke of oxen stand for the ten words, or for the five books of the old law, of which he seems to speak in the gospel when he says to the Samaritan woman: For you have had five husbands.

Heresy, however, like Eve, tries the firmness of faith with womanish feeling. Slipping away with easy looseness, it courts the charms of a false beauty and neglects the undefiled loveliness of truth. That is why they make excuses. Yet the kingdom is closed to no one except the one whom his own declaration has shut out. The Lord graciously invites everyone, but either our sloth or our error turns us away.

So the one who bought a farm is a stranger to the kingdom, for, as you have read, in the time of Noah the flood swallowed up those who were buying and selling. So is the one who chose the yoke of the law rather than the gift of grace, and so is the one who excuses himself because he is taking a wife. For it is written: If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife, he cannot be my disciple. Indeed, if for your sake the Lord renounces his own mother, saying, Who is my mother, or who are my brothers? why would you want to put her before your Lord? Yet the Lord does not command us to ignore nature or to be slaves to nature, but to indulge nature in such a way that you revere its Author and do not fall away from God out of love for your parents.

So after the haughty disdain of the rich, he turned to the Gentiles. He bids the good and the bad come in, to increase the good and to change the disposition of the bad for the better, so that what was read today might be fulfilled: Then wolves and lambs shall feed together. He invites the poor, the weak and the blind. This shows us either that no bodily weakness shuts anyone out of the kingdom, and that he sins more rarely who lacks the allurements of sin, or else that the weakness of sins is forgiven through the Lord's mercy, so that whoever is redeemed from guilt, not by works but by faith, may glory in the Lord if he glories at all.

So he sends out to the ends of the roads, for wisdom is sung at the gates. He sends to the streets, because he sent to sinners so that they might come from the broader ways to the narrow way that leads to life. He sends to the roads and along the hedges, because those are fit for the kingdom of heaven who, taken up with no present desires, hasten towards things to come, set on a path of good will. They are like a hedge, which separates cultivated land from uncultivated and keeps out the attacks of wild beasts: they know how to tell good from evil and to hold up the shield of faith against the temptations of spiritual wickedness. In fact the Lord, to show that his vineyard had been fortified, says: I put a hedge around it and dug around it. And the apostle says that the dividing wall of the hedge has been taken away, which had broken the continuity of the defence. So faith and reason are sought, and sought in the streets, that is, in the passages of the inner disposition, for it is written: Let waters be poured out in your streets,

your own waters. Yet even this is not enough, that someone should come when called, unless he has a wedding garment, that is, unless he has faith and love. So whoever has not brought peace and love to the altars of Christ will be taken up by hands and feet and cast into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there. What is the outer darkness? Are there some prisons and stone quarries to be endured there as well? Not at all. Rather, whoever stands outside the promises of the heavenly commandments is in the outer darkness, because God's commandments are light, and whoever is without Christ is in darkness, because Christ is the inner light.

So there is no gnashing of bodily teeth, no everlasting fire of bodily flames, and no bodily worm. These things are said because, just as fevers and worms arise from heavy indigestion, so if someone does not digest his sins through the sobriety of abstinence, but heaps sin upon sin and so brings on a kind of indigestion of old and new offences, he will be burned by his own fire and consumed by his own worms. That is why Isaiah says: Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled. The fire is the one that grief over offences produces. The worm is so called because the irrational sins of the soul sting the mind and senses of the guilty and gnaw at the inner parts of the conscience; they are born from each person like worms from the body of the sinner. Indeed the Lord declared this through Isaiah, saying: And they shall see the limbs of the men who transgressed against me; and their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched.
The gnashing of teeth also reveals the feeling of indignation, because each one repents too late, groans too late, and is angry with himself too late for having sinned with such stubborn wickedness.

Which of you, he says, having a hundred sheep, if one of them goes astray, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that went astray? In the preceding passages you had learned to put away negligence, to avoid arrogance, to take up devotion, not to be held fast by worldly occupations, and not to prefer what perishes to what lasts forever. But because human frailty cannot keep a firm footing on the slippery ground of this world, the good physician has shown you remedies even against going astray, and the merciful judge has not denied you hope of pardon. So it is not idly that St Luke set out three parables in a row: the sheep that was lost and found, the coin that was lost and found, and the son who was dead and came back to life, so that, spurred on by a threefold remedy, we might heal our wounds;

for a threefold cord is not broken. Who are these: the father, the shepherd, the woman? Are they not God the Father, Christ, and the Church? Christ carries you on his body, he who took your sins upon himself; the Church seeks; the Father welcomes. As a shepherd he carries back, as a mother she searches, as a father he clothes. The first is mercy, the second intercession, the third reconciliation. Each fits its own: the Redeemer comes to help, the Church intercedes, the Creator is reconciled. The mercy of the divine work is the same, but the grace differs according to our merits. The weary sheep is brought back by the shepherd, the lost coin is found, and the son returns to his father on his own feet, coming back full of repentance for the error he condemns. That is why it is well written: Men and beasts you will save, O Lord. Who are these beasts? The prophet spoke of the seed of Israel as the seed of men and of Judah as the seed of beasts. So Israel is saved as a man, and Judah is gathered as a sheep. I would rather be a son than a sheep, then, for a sheep is found by the shepherd, but a son is honoured by the father.

Let us rejoice, then, that the sheep that perished in Adam is lifted up in Christ. The shoulders of Christ are the arms of the cross. There I laid down my sins; on the neck of that noble gibbet I found rest. That sheep is one in kind, not one individual, for we are all one body, though many members. That is why it is written: You are the body of Christ, and members of his members. So the Son of Man came to save what was lost, that is, everyone, because just as in Adam all die, so in Christ all are made alive.

Rich, then, is the shepherd, of whose flock all of us are a hundredth part. He has countless flocks of angels, archangels, dominions, powers, thrones and others, whom he left on the mountains. Since they are rational beings, they rightly rejoice at the redemption of men. This should also spur us on to goodness, if each person believes that his conversion will please the companies of angels, whose protection he ought to seek and whose displeasure he ought to fear. So you too must be a joy to the angels; let them rejoice at your return.

Nor is it without meaning that the woman rejoices when the coin is found. This is no ordinary coin, for it bears the image of the prince. And so the image of the king is the wealth of the Church. We are sheep: let us pray that he may deign to settle us beside the waters of refreshment. Sheep, I say, we are: let us ask for pasture. We are coins: let us keep our value. We are sons: let us hurry to the Father.

Nor should we be afraid because we have squandered on earthly pleasures the inheritance of spiritual dignity we received. The treasure the father gave to the son he had, the wealth of faith, is never used up. Though he has given everything, he has everything still, for he does not lose what he has given. And do not fear that he will refuse to welcome you, for God takes no delight in the destruction of the living. Already running to meet you as you come, he will fall upon your neck, for the Lord raises up those who have been dashed down. He will give you a kiss, the pledge of his tenderness and love, and order a robe, a ring and sandals to be brought out. You still fear rebuke, but he restores your dignity; you dread punishment, but he offers a kiss; you fear reproach, but he prepares a feast. But now let us examine the parable itself.
A certain man had two sons, and the younger said to him: Give me my share of the property.

You see that the divine inheritance is given to those who ask for it. Do not think the father was at fault for giving it to the younger son. No age is too weak for the kingdom of God, and faith is not weighed down by years. He certainly judged himself fit, since he asked for it. And if only he had not left his father, he would never have felt the drawback of his youth. But after he went abroad (so he rightly squandered his inheritance, since he departed from the Church), after leaving home, it says, and abandoning his homeland, he set out abroad into a far country.

For what is farther away than to depart from oneself? It is to be separated not by regions but by ways of life, set apart by pursuits rather than by lands, and divorced in one's deeds, as though the tide of worldly luxury had flowed in between. For whoever separates himself from Christ is an exile from his homeland and a citizen of the world. But we are not strangers and sojourners; we are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household. For we who were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. Let us not begrudge those who return from a far country, for we too were in a far country, as Isaiah teaches. This is what you have: “Those who sat in the region of the shadow of death, on them a light has dawned.” The far country, then, is the shadow of death. But we, before whose face the Spirit is Christ the Lord, live in the shadow of Christ. And so the Church says: “In his shadow I longed, and I sat down.” So by living extravagantly he used up all the adornments of nature. Therefore you, who have received the image of God and bear his likeness, do not squander it in irrational foulness. You are God's work. Do not say to a piece of wood, “You are my father,” or you will take on the likeness of the wood, for it is written: “Let those who make them become like them.”

A famine came over that country. It was a famine not of feasts but of good works and virtues. What fasting is more pitiable? For whoever departs from the word of God goes hungry, because man does not live by bread alone but by every word of God. Whoever departs from the spring thirsts; whoever departs from the treasure is in want; whoever departs from wisdom grows dull; whoever departs from virtue falls apart. So this man rightly began to be in want, since he abandoned the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God and the depth of heavenly riches. He began to be in want and to suffer hunger because nothing is ever enough for prodigal pleasure. Whoever does not know how to be filled with everlasting food always suffers hunger [?].

So he went and attached himself to one of the citizens. Whoever attaches himself in this way is caught in a snare. This citizen seems to be the prince of this world. Then he is sent to that citizen's farm, the one bought by the man who excuses himself from the kingdom. There he feeds swine, surely the very swine into which the devil asks to enter, and which he hurls headlong into the sea of this world as they live in filth and stench.

“And he longed,” it says, “to fill his belly with the pods.” For the extravagant have no other concern than filling their belly, since their belly is their god. And what food suits such people better than one that is like a pod, empty inside and soft outside? It does not refresh the body but only stuffs it, so that it is more a burden than a benefit.

Some take the swine to mean herds of demons, and the pods to mean the feeble virtue of empty men and the boastfulness of their speeches. These can do no good. With an empty allurement of philosophy and a kind of applause for sonorous eloquence, they put on a show rather than offering anything useful. But such delights cannot last, and so no one gave him anything;

for he was in the country of one who has no one, because he does not possess those who truly exist. For all the nations are counted as nothing; there is only God, who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they were.

But he came to himself and said: “How many of my father's hired servants have bread in abundance!” It is right that he who had departed from himself returns to himself. For whoever goes back to the Lord restores himself to himself, and whoever departs from Christ disowns himself. And who are the hired servants but those who serve for wages? These are the ones from Israel, who do not pursue what is good out of zeal for uprightness and are moved not by the grace of virtue but by eagerness for gain. But the son, who has the pledge of the Holy Spirit in his heart, does not seek the petty gains of worldly wages; he keeps the right of an heir. There are also hired servants who are taken on for the vineyard. Peter, John and James were good hired servants, and to them it is said: “Come, I will make you fishers of men.” These have abundance not of pods but of bread. Indeed, they gathered twelve baskets of fragments. O Lord Jesus, if only you would take the pods away from us and give us bread, for you are the steward in your Father's house! O, if only you would deign to hire us too as your hired servants, though we come late! For you hire even at the eleventh hour, and you deign to pay an equal wage. It is an equal wage of life, not of glory, for the crown of righteousness is not laid up for everyone, but for the one who can say: “I have fought the good fight.”

I thought this should not be passed over, because I know that some say they are saving the grace of baptism, or penance, for their deathbed. First, how do you know that your soul will not be demanded of you this very night? Next, why do you think everything can be handed to you while you sit idle? Grant that there is one grace and one wage. Even so, the prize of victory differs. Paul did not strain toward that prize in vain: after receiving the wage of grace, he still pressed on to lay hold of the prize, because he knew that although the wage of grace was the same for all, the palm belonged to few.

And since we have come into the Lord's vineyard, let us not go away empty-handed, for it is pleasant to gather its fruit and to see his hired workers. Why are workers hired on a single day at different hours, unless because a thousand years in the eyes of the Lord are like yesterday that has passed, and like an hour in the night? What is the night but the one that went before, so that the day might draw near? And “an hour in the night” is rightly said, because a thousand years are like one day. The one who said, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever,” knew the force of this day. The one who wrote this also knew that the day has many parts: “This is the day of the generation of heaven and earth, when they were made; on the day God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field.” For after describing seven days earlier, he then gathered everything that was made into one day, showing that the whole time of the world is like a single day in the Lord's sight, because the form of this world came forth from what was formless and dark through the brightness of the divine work. So if the day is the whole time of the world, then it surely has its hours in the ages, or else the ages themselves are hours. Now the day has twelve hours. Fittingly, then, Christ in a mystery is the day, and his apostles are twelve, who shone with heavenly light, each with his own portion of grace.

So the master of the house came and hired workers at the first hour. These are perhaps those who were found worthy to be righteous from the beginning of the world until the flood, of whom he says: “I spoke to you before dawn, and I sent you my servants the prophets before dawn.” The third hour begins after the flood and covers the times of Noah and the others, who are assigned to the vineyard as good workers. That is why Noah became drunk, as if at the midday meal. The sixth hour and the ones after it are marked by the merits of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. At the ninth hour, when the age was already declining and the light of virtue was growing pale, the law and the prophets censured the faded morals of humankind. The eleventh hour, and whatever remains of the day, is brought in by the sacred coming. That is why he himself says in the gospel: “Walk while you have the light.”

But now let us return to the father. I do not fear that the example of this penitent will make us seem to have been absent for long, for we have never been absent: we were busy in the vineyard, and if he too had stayed there, he would not have left his father. Still, we must take care not to delay his reconciliation, since the father did not delay it. He is easily reconciled when he is earnestly entreated. So let us learn with what kind of plea the father should be approached. “Father,” he says. How merciful and how loving is the one who, even when offended, does not disdain to hear the name of father! “Father,” he says, “I have sinned against heaven and before you.”

This is the first confession, made before the author of nature, the guardian of mercy, the judge of guilt. Although God knows all things, he still waits to hear your confession. For confession is made with the mouth for salvation. Whoever takes the burden on himself lightens the weight of his wrongdoing, and whoever confesses before his accuser can speak removes the sting of accusation. For the righteous man accuses himself at the very beginning of his speech. It is useless to try to hide from one you cannot deceive in anything, and there is no danger in revealing what you know is already known. Confess instead, so that Christ, whom we have as our advocate with the Father, may intercede for you, the Church may pray for you, and the people may weep for you. And do not fear that you will fail to obtain it. The advocate pledges pardon, the patron promises grace, the defender assures you of reconciliation with your Father's love. Believe him, because he is truth; trust him, because he is power. He has reason to intercede for you, so that he may not have died for you in vain. The Father too has reason to forgive, because what the Son wills, the Father wills.

“I have sinned against heaven and before you.” This certainly does not mean the physical sky. Rather, it signifies that the heavenly gifts of the Spirit have been diminished by the sin of the soul. Or else it means that he ought not to have strayed from the bosom of that mother, the Jerusalem which is in heaven.
“I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” For one who has fallen low ought not to exalt himself, so that he may rightly be lifted up because of his humility.

“Treat me as one of your hired servants.” He knows that there is a difference between sons, friends, hired servants and slaves. One becomes a son through baptism, a friend through virtue, a hired servant through labor, and a slave through fear. But even slaves and hired servants can become friends, as it is written: “You are my friends if you do what I command you; I no longer call you slaves.”

He said this to himself, but saying it is not enough unless you come to the father. Where should you seek him, and where will you find him? First, get up: you who used to sit and sleep, rise. That is why the apostle says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead.” Iniquity sits on a talent of lead. But Moses too is told: “But you, stand here.” Christ chose those who stand. So rise up and run to the Church. Here is the Father, here is the Son, here is the Holy Spirit.

The one who hears you deliberating in the secret places of your mind runs out to meet you. While you are still far off, he sees you and runs to you. He sees into your heart; he runs so that no one may hold you back; and he embraces you. In his coming to meet you there is foreknowledge; in his embrace there is mercy and, as it were, the tenderness of a father's love. He falls upon your neck to raise you up as you lie there. You are weighed down by sins and bent toward earthly things, and he turns you back toward heaven, where you may seek your maker. Christ falls upon your neck to free it from the yoke of slavery and to lay his easy yoke upon it. Does it not seem to you that he fell upon John's neck when John was reclining on Jesus' breast with his head bent back? That is why John saw the Word with God: he was lifted up toward the things above. He falls upon your neck when he says: “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you; take my yoke upon you.” He falls upon you in this way, then, if you turn back.

And he orders the robe, the ring and the shoes to be brought out. The robe is the garment of wisdom, with which the apostles cover the body's nakedness, so that each person may wrap himself in it. So they receive the robe in order to clothe the weakness of the body with the power of spiritual wisdom. For it was said of wisdom: “He will wash his robe in wine.” The robe, then, is the spiritual clothing and the wedding garment. What is the ring but the seal of sincere faith and the impress of truth? And the shoe is the preaching of the gospel. So he received the first wisdom, for there is also another wisdom, which does not know the mystery. He received the seal of his words and deeds, and a safeguard for his good intention and his course, so that he would never strike his foot against a stone, be tripped up by the devil, and abandon the duty of preaching the Lord. This is the preparation of the gospel, which sets those who are prepared on the course toward heavenly things, so that we may walk not in the flesh but in the Spirit.

The fatted calf is also killed, so that he, restored to fellowship in the mysteries through the grace of the sacrament, may feast on the flesh of the Lord, rich in spiritual power. For no one ought to take part in the heavenly sacraments unless he has feared God, which is the beginning of wisdom; unless he has either kept or received the spiritual seal; and unless he has proclaimed the Lord. But whoever has the ring has the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. For God, whose image is Christ, has sealed us and has given us the Spirit as a pledge in our hearts, so that we may know that this is the seal of the ring placed on the hand. By it the inmost parts of our hearts and the service of our deeds are sealed. So we have been sealed, as we also read: “Having believed,” it says, “you were sealed with the Holy Spirit.” And it is fitting that the flesh is that of a calf, since the calf is the priestly victim that used to be offered for sins.

The Son portrays the father feasting on it to show that our salvation is the Father's food and that the redemption of our sins is the Father's joy. Here, if you apply it to the Father, the Father delights in the sinner's return, because the Son is the offering for sins. Earlier, the Son delights in the sheep that was found. So you may know that the Father and the Son share one delight and one work in founding the Church.

The father rejoices because his son was lost and is found, was dead and has come back to life. Only one who existed can perish, since one who never existed cannot perish. So the gentiles do not exist, but the Christian does, according to what was said above: God chose the things that are not, to destroy the things that are. Yet here too the one man can be taken to represent the whole human race. Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished. So humankind is formed anew in that very man who had perished, and he who was made in the likeness and image of God is restored by divine patience and generosity. What then does it mean that God chose the things that are not, to destroy the things that are? It means that he chose the people of the gentiles, which did not exist, to destroy the people of the Jews.

It can also be taken as said of the penitent, because no one dies except one who once lived. That is why the gentiles do not die but are already dead, for whoever has not believed in Christ is always dead. When the gentiles believe, they are brought to life through grace; but whoever has fallen away comes back to life through penance.

Next comes the passage teaching that we ought to welcome the forgiveness of sins after penance, so that we do not begrudge another's pardon and then fail to obtain it from the Lord ourselves. For who are you to contradict the Lord and stop him from forgiving the guilt of whomever he wills, when you pardon whomever you like? He wants to be asked; he wants to be entreated. If everyone were righteous, where would the grace of God be?

Who are you to begrudge God? That is why the brother is censured here, so much so that he is said to come in from the farm. This means he was busy with earthly works and ignorant of the things of the Spirit of God, so that he finally complains that not even a kid was ever killed for him. For the Lamb was sacrificed not for envy but for the forgiveness of the world. The envious man looks for a kid; the innocent man longs for a lamb to be sacrificed for him. That is also why he is called the elder: envy makes a person grow old quickly. That is why he stands outside: the malice of a jealous mind shuts him out. And that is why he cannot bear to hear the dancing and the music. This is not the theatrical kind that stirs up lewdness, nor the harmonies of the court, but the concord of the people singing together, which rings out with sweet joy over a sinner who has been saved.

Show me one of those who think themselves righteous, who do not see the beam in their own eye and cannot bear the speck of someone else's fault. How indignant such a man is when pardon is granted to someone who confesses his sin and has long wept and begged for forgiveness! How his ears cannot bear the people's spiritual symphony! For this is the symphony: when in the Church people of different ages and virtues sing a psalm together in undivided harmony, like various strings, when the response is made and the Amen is said. Paul also knew this symphony, and so he says: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind as well.” This is what we thought should be said about the present parable.

Nor do we object if anyone wishes to apply these two brothers to two peoples. Then the younger is the people from the gentiles, like Israel, whose elder brother begrudged him the gift of his father's blessing. The Jews did this when they complained that Christ ate with gentiles, and so they demanded a kid, a sacrifice with a foul smell. The Jew demands a kid, the Christian a lamb; and so Barabbas is released for them, while the Lamb is sacrificed for us. Hence among them there is the stench of crimes, and among us the forgiveness of sins, sweet in hope and delightful in its fruit. Whoever demands a kid is waiting for the Antichrist, for Christ is the victim with a pleasing fragrance.

The complaint about the kid may also mean that the Jews have lost the rite of the old sacrifice, or that no one's blood has helped them in the way that Christ's blood helps the Church, for the blood of the prophets could not redeem them. He is shameless, and like that Pharisee who justified himself in an arrogant prayer and thought he had never transgressed God's commandment because he kept the law according to the letter. He is also impious, because he accused his brother of squandering their father's property with prostitutes, when he ought to have noticed that it had been said to him: “Prostitutes and tax collectors are going into the kingdom

of heaven ahead of you.” He stands outside. He is not shut out, but he does not go in, because he does not know God's will concerning the calling of the gentiles; he has now become a slave instead of a son, and the slave does not know what his master is doing. When he learns of it, he is envious and tormented by the Church's blessings, and he stands outside. For Israel stands outside, hears the dancing and the music, and is angry, because here the people's gratitude sings in harmony and the jubilation of the people resounds as one.

But the good father wanted to save him too, and said: “You have always been with me.” He was with him either as a Jew under the law or as a righteous man in communion. And he added, provided that you stop envying: “and all that is
