mine is yours.” This applies either to the Jew, who possesses the sacraments of the Old Testament, or to the baptized, who possesses those of the New as well.

No servant can serve two masters. This is not because there are two, but because there is one Lord. For although there are people who serve mammon, mammon has no rights of lordship. They put the yoke of slavery on themselves, for this is not lawful authority but unjust servitude.

And so he says: “Make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous mammon,” so that by giving to the poor we may win for ourselves the favor of the angels and of the other saints. Nor is the steward blamed. Through him we learn that we are not owners ourselves, but rather stewards of another's wealth. So although he sinned, he is praised, because he used his master's leniency to secure help for himself for the future. He rightly called mammon unrighteous, because avarice used the various allurements of riches to tempt our desires, so that we would want to be slaves to riches.

That is why he says: “If you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?” Riches belong to another as far as we are concerned, because they are outside our nature: they are not born with us and they do not pass away with us. But Christ is ours, because he is life. Indeed, he came to his own, and his own did not receive him. So no one will give you what is yours, because you did not believe in what is yours and did not receive what is yours.

The Jews, then, seem to be convicted of both fraud and avarice. They were not faithful with their possessions. They knew those possessions belonged to another, since the Lord God gave the fruit of the earth to all for common use, and so they surely ought to have shared them with the poor. Therefore they did not deserve to receive Christ either, whereas Zacchaeus gave half of his goods in order to gain him.

So let us not serve what belongs to another, for we should know no master but Christ. For there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things. What then? Is the Father not Lord, or is the Son not God? But the Father is Lord too, for by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm; and the Son is God, who is God over all, blessed forever. Why, then, can no one serve two masters? Because there is one Lord, since there is one God. Indeed: “You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.” From this it is clear that the Father and the Son have one lordship. And it is one so long as it is not divided but is wholly in the Father and wholly in the Son. Therefore, since we hold that the Trinity has one Godhead and one lordship, we confess one God and one Lord. But those who speak of one power belonging to the Father, another to the Son and another to the Spirit bring many gods and many lords into the Church through the fault of pagan error.
BOOK EIGHT

"The law and the prophets were until John." This is not because the law failed, but because the preaching of the gospel begins; for lesser things seem to be completed when greater ones follow them. And therefore let us do violence to the kingdom of heaven; for everyone who does violence hurries on with eager zeal and does not grow slack through sluggish feeling. So there is a holy violence of faith, and sloth is a crime. The law granted many things in keeping with nature, so that by being more indulgent to natural desires it might call us to the pursuit of righteousness. Christ cut into nature, because he cuts away even natural pleasures. And therefore let us do violence to nature, so that it does not sink down to earthly things but lifts itself up to the things above.

"Everyone who puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman put away by her husband commits adultery." I think I should first speak about the law of marriage, so that afterwards we may discuss the prohibition of divorce. For some think that every marriage is from God, chiefly because it is written: "What God has joined, let no man separate." So if every marriage is from God, no marriage may be dissolved. How then did the apostle say: "But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart"? Here, in a wonderful way, he both refused to leave any ground for divorce among Christians and showed that not every marriage is from God. For Christian women are not joined to pagans by God's judgment, since the law forbids it. But that saying of Solomon confronts us:

"Fathers divide house and substance among their sons, but a wife will be prepared for a man by God." Whoever reads this in Greek does not think it a contradiction. For the Greek rightly says harmozetai, "is fitted together"; for "harmony" is the name for the fitting and apt joining together of all things. There is harmony when the pipes of an organ, joined in due order, keep the grace of a proper melody, and the fitting arrangement of the strings preserves concord. So a marriage does not have its harmony when a pagan woman is unlawfully joined to a Christian man. Where there is marriage, then, is there harmony? Where there is harmony, God joins; where there is no harmony, there is strife and discord, which is not from God, for God is love.

Do not, then, put away your wife, lest you deny that God is the author of your union. Indeed, if you ought to bear with and correct the ways of strangers, how much more the ways of your wife. Hear what the Lord said: "Whoever puts away his wife makes her commit adultery." For a woman who may not change her marriage while her husband lives may be crept upon by the desire to sin. So the one who causes the error is also guilty of the fault, when a woman who has borne children is sent away with her little ones, or is thrust out in old age with tottering step. It is harsh if you shut out the mother and keep the children, adding to the insult against love an injury to family affection as well; harsher still if, because of the mother, you drive out the children too, when the children should rather redeem their mother's fault in the eyes of their father. How dangerous, if you expose the fragile age of a young woman to error! How impious, if you abandon in her old age the woman whose youth you took in its flower! Shall an emperor, then, dismiss a veteran without glory, his service unrewarded, and thrust him out of the holding granted by the empire, and shall a farmer drive from his field the laborer worn out by his toil? Or is what is wrong toward subordinates right toward an equal?

So you put away your wife as if by right and without guilt, and you think it permitted to you because human law does not forbid it. But divine law forbids it. You who obey men, fear God. Hear the law of the Lord, which even those who make laws obey: "What God has joined, let no man separate."

But here it is not only a heavenly precept that is undone, but also a certain work of God. Will you endure, I ask you, that your children should live under a stepfather while you are alive, or under a stepmother while their mother is safe and well? Suppose the rejected wife does not remarry: ought she to have displeased you as her husband, when she keeps faith with you though you are an adulterer? Suppose she remarries: her necessity is your crime, and the marriage you think a marriage is adultery. For what difference does it make whether you commit adultery with an open confession of the crime or under the guise of a husband, except that it is more grievous to have made a law of the crime than to commit it by stealth?

But perhaps someone says: "Why then did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given and the wife put away?" Whoever says this is a Jew; whoever says this is not a Christian. And so, since he raises the objection that was raised to the Lord, let the Lord answer him: "Because of the hardness of your hearts," he says, "Moses permitted you to give a bill of divorce and to put away your wives; but from the beginning it was not so." Moses permitted it, he says; God did not command it. But from the beginning there is God's law. What is God's law? "A man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be in one flesh." So whoever puts away his wife tears his own flesh and divides his body.

This passage shows that what was written because of human frailty was not written by God. Hence the apostle too says: "I charge, not I but the Lord, that the wife should not depart from her husband," and further on: "To the rest I say, not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife and leaves her." So where the marriage is unequal, he added: "But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart." At the same time the same apostle denied that it belongs to divine law that any marriage whatever should be dissolved. He did not command it himself, nor did he give authority to the one who deserts; rather, he took away the guilt from the one who is abandoned.

So much for the moral sense. Yet since he set forth above that the kingdom of God is being preached, and after he had said that not one stroke of the law can fall, he added: "Everyone who puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery." Rightly does the apostle admonish us, saying that this is a great sacrament concerning Christ and the church. You find, then, a marriage that no one would doubt was joined by God, since he himself says: "No one comes to me unless my Father who sent me draws him"; for he alone could join this marriage. And therefore Solomon said in a mystery: "A wife will be prepared for a man by God." The man is Christ, the wife is the church: a wife in love, a virgin in integrity. So let persecution not separate the one whom God has drawn to the Son; let luxury not turn him away, let philosophy not plunder him, let the Manichee not defile him, the Arian not turn him aside, the Sabellian not taint him. God has joined; let the Jew not separate. All are adulterers who desire to adulterate the truth of faith and wisdom.

"What is this bill of divorce of your mother," he says, "by which I put her away?" You have heard of divorce; believe in marriage. You have heard what the husband himself says to the people of the Jews: "Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your sins I put away your mother." So stay in your father's house, stay with the bridegroom, strive to please your husband. O mind that has believed God, be a strong woman, like that one, whether the soul of a member of the church or the church itself, of whom Solomon says: "Who shall find a strong woman? She who is such is more precious than precious stones; her husband trusts in her." Let us see what she does for her husband, what her work is, what her service, and why Christ trusts in her.

A good wife clothes her husband. Let our faith clothe [?] him with its own body; let it clothe his flesh with the glory of his divinity, just as that woman made double garments for her husband, so that she might honor him both in the present age and in the age to come. No ordinary woman is she whose weaving is of this kind, whom her husband finds not plucking soft threads of wool but handling the spun portions of precious virtue; who lifts up her hands in the night, directs her work by the balance and weighs the weight of her conduct, and knows also how to keep measure in her deeds, weaving in the woof of glorious labor; anxious for the time when her husband will return, troubled and sighing and already longing to be with her husband, saying: "My husband delays his coming; I will hasten to him myself;

I will meet him face to face when he begins to come in his glory." Come, Lord Jesus, that you may find your bride not defiled, not adulterous, one who has not violated your house nor neglected your commands. Let her say to you: "I have found him whom my soul loved"; let her bring you into the house of wine (for wine gladdens the heart of man); let her be inebriated in the Spirit, recognize the mystery, and utter the oracle.

"There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple." This seems to be a narrative rather than a parable, since even the name is given. Not without purpose has the Lord here shown the rich man, who had enjoyed worldly delights, placed in the misery of perpetual hunger in hell. Not without reason does he have five brothers, that is, the five senses of the body, which seem to have been joined together by a kind of natural brotherhood and burned with immoderate and countless desires. But Lazarus he placed in Abraham's lap, as in a kind of bosom of rest and a retreat of holiness, so that we may not, enticed by present pleasure, remain in our vices, or, overcome by weariness of labor, flee from hardship. Whether, then, Lazarus is one poor in the world but rich toward God, or some apostolic man poor in speech but rich in faith (for not all poverty is holy, nor are riches criminal; but as luxury disgraces riches, so holiness commends poverty), whether, I say, he is an apostolic man who holds the true faith and does not seek the ornaments of words, the cosmetics of arguments, or the showy veils of fine phrases, he receives a reward with interest by fighting the heretics, Manichaeus, Marcion, Sabellius, Arius and Photinus (for these are nothing other than brothers of the Jews, bound to them by a brotherhood of faithlessness), and also by checking the desires of the flesh which, as I said, steam forth through those five senses. He receives, I say, a reward with interest, whose recompense is overflowing abundance and whose interest is everlastingness.

Nor do we think it out of place to suppose that this passage also treats of faith, which Lazarus gathers up when it is thrown away from the rich man's table. According to the letter, the fastidious rich man would certainly have shuddered at Lazarus's sores, and amid costly banquets and perfumed guests he would not have endured the stench of sores licked by dogs, he to whom the very smell of the air and nature itself were disgusting. Yet the insolence and swollen pride of the rich is expressed here by fitting signs: they are so forgetful of the human condition that, as if set above nature, they draw incentives for their pleasures from the miseries of the poor, laugh at the destitute, insult the needy, and take from those whom they ought to pity.

Let whoever wishes, then, gather up both, like Lazarus. To him I think that man was like who, beaten often by the Jews, offered the sores of his body to be licked by some, as if by dogs, for the patience of believers and the calling of the gentiles; for it is written: "They shall return at evening and suffer hunger like dogs." That Canaanite woman recognized this mystery. To her it is said: "No one takes the children's bread and throws it to the dogs." She recognized that this bread was not the bread that is seen but the bread that is understood, and so she answered: "Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters' table." These crumbs are from that bread. And since the bread is the word, and faith is of the word, the crumbs are, as it were, certain doctrines of the faith. Hence the Lord answered, to show that she had spoken faithfully: "O woman, great is your faith."

O happy sores, which shut out everlasting pain! O rich crumbs, which drive away eternal fasting and fill the poor man who gathers you with eternal food! The ruler of the synagogue threw you away from his table when he rejected the inner mysteries of the prophetic scriptures and of the law; for the crumbs are the words of the scriptures, of which it is said: "And you have cast my words behind you." The scribe threw you away, but Paul gathered you up most diligently, gathering a people amid his own injuries. Those licked his sores who saw him unafraid at the serpent's bite as he shook the serpent off, and who believed. That jailer licked them, who washed Paul's wounds and believed. Blessed are the dogs upon whom the moisture of such sores drips, filling their hearts and fattening their throats, so that they grow used to guarding the house, keeping the flock, and watching out for wolves.

Now set before your eyes the Arians, intent on worldly pursuits, who seek alliance with royal power so as to attack the truth of the church with military arms. Do they not seem to you to be lying on couches piled with a kind of purple and fine linen, men who defend counterfeits in place of the truth and abound in rich words, boasting that the earth trembled beneath the Lord's body, that the sky was covered with darkness, that the seas were stirred up or calmed by his word, yet denying that he is the true Son of God? Set before you also that poor man who, knowing that the kingdom of God is not in word but in power, expressed in few words what he believed, saying: "You are the Son of the living God." Do not those riches seem to you to be in want, and this poverty to overflow? Rich heresy composed many gospels; poor faith has kept this one gospel which it received. Rich philosophy made many gods for itself; the poor church knows one God.

Between this rich man and the poor man, then, there is a great chasm, because after death merits cannot be changed. And so the rich man is shown in hell longing to draw something of refreshing spirit from the poor man; for water is the refreshment of a soul in pain, of which Isaiah says: "And water shall leap up with delight from the fountains of salvation." But why is he tormented before the judgment? Because for a man of luxury, to be deprived of delights is itself punishment. For the Lord too says: "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth when you see Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of heaven."

Too late does this rich man begin to be a teacher, when the time he has now is for learning, not for teaching. In this place the Lord most clearly declares that the Old Testament is the foundation of faith, beating back the faithlessness of the Jews and shutting out the wickedness of heretics, by whom the weaker mind is tripped up; for they are the little ones who do not yet know growth in virtue.

One may notice that both in the earlier comparison of that steward and in the present one of this rich man there is an incentive to mercy. There, perhaps, he teaches giving to the saints, whom he calls friends and to whom he grants dwellings; here he teaches that we should give to the poor.

"If your brother sins against you, rebuke him." How well, after the rich man tormented in punishment, he added the precept of granting pardon, to those, that is, who turn back from their error, so that despair may not keep anyone from turning away from his fault! And how moderate he was, so that pardon is neither hard to obtain nor indulgence lax, lest harsh invective strike anyone down or connivance invite him to sin! So too elsewhere: "If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone." For friendly reproof does more good than stormy accusation: the one instills shame, the other stirs up indignation. Rather, let what the one being admonished fears may be exposed be kept secret. For it is good that the one reproved should believe you a friend rather than an enemy, since a man more readily accepts counsel than submits to injury. Hence the apostle too says: "Reprove him as a brother, that he may be ashamed; do not regard him as an enemy." For fear is a weak guardian of lasting conduct, but shame is a good teacher of duty. The one who fears is restrained but not amended; the one who is ashamed of doing wrong turns it into his nature.

He put it well: "if he sins against you"; for to sin against God and to sin against man are not the same case. Accordingly the apostle, the true interpreter of the divine oracle, says: "Avoid a heretic after one reproof," since faithlessness is not as pardonable as a fault. And since error often creeps in through ignorance, he commanded reproof, so that either obstinacy might be avoided or a lapse corrected.

But what does it mean: "If he turns to you seven times, forgive him"? Is a fixed number set for pardon? Or rather, since God rested on the seventh day from all his works, is a lasting rest promised us after the week of this world, so that, as the evils of this world will cease and keep holiday, so too the severity of punishment may come to rest? Now the sabbath is not only of days but also of months, and therefore on the tenth day of the seventh month there is the sabbath of sabbaths; and not only of months but also of years; and not of years only but also of generations; and finally of the world itself, of which the great sabbath is a type, just as in the law there is the seventh week, after which the year of jubilee is celebrated. This mystery the Lord willed to reveal to us when he says: "Not only seven times, but seventy times seven"; for in the seventh generation, as you have it according to Luke, Enoch was taken up, lest wickedness should change his heart, and in him the sting of pain came to rest. And in the seventy-seventh generation the Lord was born of Mary, taking upon himself the sins of the human race, and granted the remission of all offenses.

So although according to the letter you learn to forgive often and not to hold on to indignation (for nothing can offend one who is in the habit of forgiving), yet recognize the mystery. For it was not without purpose that the Lord said to the woman on the sabbath: "You are freed from your infirmity," showing his people, who were called to follow him as that woman was, that by his coming he had forgiven sins. Lamech, therefore, is condemned seventy-seven times, because one who commits a crime while punishing a crime sins more gravely. But the sacraments of baptism forgive every enormity of crime. Learn, then, to forgive the injuries done to you, since Christ pardoned his persecutors.

Nor is it without purpose that he suffered at the great sabbath, signifying that there would be a sabbath on which death would be destroyed by Christ. If the Jews celebrate the sabbath in such a way that they keep both a month and a whole year as a sabbath, how much more ought we to celebrate the Lord's resurrection! And therefore our forebears handed down to us that all the fifty days of Pentecost are to be celebrated like Easter, since Pentecost marks the beginning of the eighth week. Hence the apostle too, as a disciple of Christ who knew that seasons differ, writing to the Corinthians says: "Perhaps I will stay with you and spend the winter," and further on: "But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost; for a great door has been opened to me." So with the Corinthians, whose errors distressed him, he spends the winter, because their devotion to the worship of God had grown cold; with the Ephesians he celebrates Pentecost and hands on the mysteries to them, and relaxes his spirit, because he saw them burning with the ardor of faith. Therefore through these fifty days the church knows no fasting, just as on the Lord's day, on which the Lord rose; and all the days are like the Lord's day.

There will be another Lord's day too, on which the Lord's body will rise. Paul knew it, who says: "But you are the body of Christ, and members from members." For this body of the Lord, and the bones from his bones, will cleave to the head; and the head of the church is Christ. Then, therefore, fasting will cease, since in everlasting joy weariness, care and fatigue will cease. Then death will be destroyed; for death will be destroyed last. For though it ceased in Enoch and was not found in him, it was not destroyed; for he was taken up so as to escape, whereas Christ was sacrificed so as to destroy it. And so it is well said: "Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?" In this resurrection, then, Christ will rise again as in his own body. Blessed, therefore, is he who has a part in the first resurrection; for as Christ is the firstfruits of those who sleep, so then his saints will be the firstfruits of the church of those who rise.

Peter could not know this mystery. Perhaps he knew about Enoch; but who could grasp with a human mind the mystery hidden in God? Let the Lord, then, come into my soul, into my mind, and make it subject to himself, so that when my mind has been made subject I may say: "I will fear no evil, for you are with me."

"If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, 'Be uprooted and be thrown into the sea,' and it would obey you." The mustard seed was discussed above; now we must discuss the mulberry tree. I read "tree," yet I do not believe it is a tree. For what reason would there be, what profit to us, in a tree that bears fruit for toiling farmers being uprooted and cast into the sea? Although we judge it possible by the power of faith that insensible nature should obey the commands of sensible beings, what, after all, does this particular kind of tree mean? I have indeed read: "I was a goatherd, plucking mulberries," and I think the prophet signified to us that he himself, a sinner, had been converted from the flock of sinners. Yet it is also fitting that the future prophet of the gentiles should seem to have sought fruit among the brambles and dug food out of the brambles, as one who would settle the discolored and foul-smelling flocks of the gentiles, the peoples of the nations, in the pastures of his writings, so that they might grow fat on spiritual refreshment, while he himself would draw spiritual milk from the converted sinner.

But in another book of the gospel this is said of a mountain, whose appearance, bare of fruitful vines and empty of olives, barren of harvests, fit for the lairs of beasts and restless with the running of wild animals, seems to express the self-exalting height of spiritual wickedness, as it is written: "Behold, I am against you, corrupt mountain, which corrupts the whole earth." So it is fitting to suppose that in this place too it was said in the same sense, since faith shuts out the unclean spirit; especially since the nature of the tree agrees with this view. For its fruit is at first white in the flower, then, once formed, it turns red, and at ripeness it turns black. The devil too, cast down by his transgression from the white flower of angelic nature and the red glow of power, grew bristling with the foul stench of sin. Here you have the one who says to the mulberry tree: "Be uprooted and thrown into the sea," when he casts the legion out of a man and lets them pass into the swine, which, driven wild by the devilish spirit, plunged themselves into the sea.

This passage, then, is an exhortation to faith, teaching also in a moral sense that even things that have been made firm can be dissolved by faith. From faith comes love, from love comes hope, and they flow back into one another again in a kind of holy circle.

It follows that no one should boast of their works, since we rightly owe the Lord our service. For you do not say to a servant who is ploughing or keeping sheep, "Pass over and recline at table." Here we understand that no one reclines unless he has first passed over; indeed Moses too first passed over in order to see the great sight. So if you not only do not say to your servant, "Recline," but also demand some further service from him and do not thank him, then neither does the Lord allow you to be employed in only one work or labour, because as long as we live we must always be at work.

So recognize that you are a servant, bound by debt to a great many services. Do not exalt yourself because you are called a son of God; you must acknowledge the grace, but not forget your nature. Nor should you boast if you have served well, since you have only done what you ought to have done. The sun obeys, the moon submits, the angels serve. The vessel chosen by the Lord for the Gentiles says, "I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God." Then elsewhere, showing that he was aware of no fault in himself, he added, "But I am not justified by this." So let us not demand praise from ourselves, nor snatch away God's judgement and anticipate the Judge's sentence, but leave it to its own time and its own Judge. After this the ungrateful are rebuked, and so at last the text comes to treat of the judgement to come.
In that hour, whoever is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, must not come down to take them away; and likewise whoever is in the field must not turn back.

"Remember Lot's wife." When the disciples asked the Lord when the kingdom of God would come, he said: "The kingdom of God is within you", that is, through the truth of grace, not through the slavery of sin. So whoever wishes to be free, let him be a servant in the Lord, for in the measure that we share in this servitude we share also in the kingdom. So he said, "The kingdom of God is within you", but he would not say when it would come. Instead he said that the day of judgment would come, so as to

strike everyone with terror of the judgment hanging over them, and not give them the false security of delay. And so as not to seem to sadden the disciples by refusing them something, he says in another book: "But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son." He did well to place the Son in the middle. The same Son of Man is the Son of God, so we should rather take the saying as spoken of the Son of Man, since he knows the end of the times not through the nature of man but through the nature of God. Yet it is not foreign to the faith if you take it of the Son of God. For why would a good Father have hidden anything from the Son, to whom he gave all things? Or how could he have withheld knowledge of the time when he gave him the power of judgment itself? And how can the Son not know what the Father knows, since the Son is in the Father, and the Spirit searches even the depths of God, and the Son himself is the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God? But why he would not tell, he shows in another place: "It is not for you to know the times and years which the Father has set by his own authority."

Do you see where someone ends up who denies that the Trinity is of one power: there would then be something the Son does not know? Why would the Father hide it from his own Son? We are unwilling to disclose what we know to others either out of envy or for fear of being betrayed; but no suspicion of envy can fall on the Father, nor of treachery on the Son. So they are of one knowledge, because they are of one power. Further, he who knows the signs of the coming judgment surely knows the end as well.

For what could he not know who is like the flashing lightning, since he is the light, the Son of God, who illumines the inner depths of the heavenly mystery? "In that hour," he says. So he knows the hour too; but he knows it for himself, and for me he does not know it. And he rightly declares that the cause of the flood, of the fire and of the judgment arose from our sins, because God did not create evil; our own deserts found it for themselves.

"For they were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage." Not that marriage is condemned, any more than food is, since the one supports the succession of generations and the other supports nature; otherwise we would have to leave this world. But in all things moderation is sought, and whatever is in excess comes from evil. Let there be some agreement for a time, so that we may devote ourselves to prayer; between the cares of the world and the surfeit of intemperance let there be some sobriety of religion and some truce of chastity.

Since, then, because of the wicked, the good must suffer contrition of heart and mind in this age, so that they may receive a richer reward in the future, they are given remedies: those who are in Judea are to flee to the mountains. What is this Judea? For I know another Judea, according to the spirit and not according to the letter: "In Judea God is known." And what sort of mountains are these that could hold back the upheaval of the coming judgment, when it is written, "Trembling shall seize the mountains"? Heaven and earth will pass away: how will a portion of the earth remain untouched, or be able to protect me, when it cannot preserve even itself? Where then shall I hide from the wrath of him who stirs up the depths of the sea? If I ascend into heaven, he is there; if I descend into hell, he is present. He who is everywhere cannot be deceived, then, but he can be appeased.

So the day of judgment is at hand. If you do not want to be caught then, flee daily, daily. Do you ask where to flee? Go up onto the mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion, so that you may stand out on the summit of lofty merits; for God is the God of the mountains and not the God of the valleys. Go up to where Christ sits at the right hand of God, whose foundations are on the holy mountains, and mountains are round about him. Paul is your mountain, Peter is your mountain. Set the footstep of your mind upon their faith. Those who stand firm in the law of God and the inheritance of faith the day of judgment will find ready not for punishment but for glory.

And if anyone is on the housetop, that is, has climbed to the upper parts of his house and the summit of eminent virtues, let him not fall back to the earthly works of this world. For I know a roof on which Rahab, a harlot in figure but the Church in mystery, joined to the Gentile peoples by sharing in the sacraments, hid the spies whom Joshua sent. Had they gone down to the lower parts of the house, they would have been killed by the searchers sent out to seize them. The roof, then, is the work of a lofty mind and the summit of the soul, by which the naked weakness of the body is covered. That is why it seems to me that the paralytic who was let down from the roof by four young men was holy: with the support of four virtues, prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice, he laid himself at the feet of Christ by a kind of lofty reasoning. For nothing is loftier than humility, which, being as it were above, does not know how to be exalted, since no one aspires to what he judges to be beneath him.

But since we are dealing with the judgment, let us not leave the roof, lest we be caught while longing to carry off the vessels that are in the house. Not every house has vessels of gold and silver; most have wooden ones. Nor is every house full; there are empty ones too, which the prophet knew when he said: "What has happened to you now, that you have gone up to the empty houses? The city is filled with people crying out." And he added: "All your princes have fled; whoever was wounded in you has fallen from faith into faithlessness." Sabellius is wounded, Valentinus is wounded, Arius is wounded; for they were found in an empty house.

Do you want to see a full house? Follow Peter as he went up to the upper part of the house when he was hungry. There he recognized the mystery of the Church that was to be gathered, so that he would not judge unclean the Gentile people, whom faith could cleanse from every defilement. Now vessels are made of clay, so the vessel is the body. Beware, then, lest out of desire for the body you abandon the noble pursuits of the mind. If Peter did not receive the mystery while he was in the lower parts, how will you receive it? He received it because he went up, so that in preaching the Lord he would not fear the suffering of the body.

"So let him who is on the housetop not go down, and let him who is in the field not turn back." How am I to understand what the field is, unless Jesus himself teaches me when he says: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven"? The idle man sits at his country house; the hard worker sows in the field. The weak man is at the hearth, the strong man at the plough. Good is the smell of a field, for the smell of Jacob is the smell of a full field. The field is full of flowers, full of all kinds of fruit. Plough your field, then, if you want to be directed toward God's kingdom. Let a fruitful harvest of good merits flourish for you. Let there be an abundant vine on the sides of your house and young olive shoots around your table. Let your soul, now aware of its own fertility, sown with the word of God and ploughed with spiritual cultivation, say to Christ: "Come, my brother, let us go out into the field"; and let him answer: "I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh." For what vintage is better than the vintage of faith, in which the fruit of the resurrection is stored up and by which the fountain of everlasting joy is watered?

So since you are forbidden to look back, much more are you forbidden to go back and take your tunic; for you have learned that to anyone who asks for your tunic you should give up your cloak as well. So, once you are set on the way to God's kingdom, do not go looking for wealth and inheritance. I know of another tunic too, about which the apostle exhorts us: having stripped off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, we should not go looking for the tunic of our former error. That is why she too says: "By night I have put off my tunic; how shall I put it on again?" This means that you ought not only to renounce sins but also to wipe out all memory of your former conduct. Thus Paul, forgetting what lay behind, put off his guilt, but he did not give up penitence.

And so the Lord says, "Remember Lot's wife," who lost the gift of her nature because she looked back; for behind is Satan, behind is Sodom. So flee intemperance, shun luxury. And so that you may know that not all can flee to the mountain, remember that he who did not turn back to his old pursuits (for he had earlier chosen Sodom) escaped because he reached the mountain; while she, being weaker, because she looked back at what lay behind, could not reach the mountain even with her husband's help, but stayed behind.

"In that night there will be two in one bed; one will be taken and the other left." He rightly said "night", because the Antichrist is the hour of darkness: he pours darkness over the hearts of men when he says that he is Christ, while false prophets arise who claim now that he is living in the deserts [?], so as to delude people with the error of a wandering opinion, and now in inner chambers, so that those who hear may be bound by the name of a most exalted power. But Christ, like flashing lightning, scatters the rays of his light through the whole world. So he neither wanders in deserts nor is shut up in any places, because "I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord"; rather he shines with the light of his lightning, so that in that night we may see the glory of the resurrection. What then does he mean when he says:

"Two in one bed, and two women grinding, and two in the field; one will be taken and the other left"? Is God unjust, that he should make a distinction in rewarding the merits of people who are equal in their pursuits and their shared life, and indistinguishable in the quality of their deeds? Not so; rather the reward corresponds in kind to a person's deeds. Being joined as a couple, then, does not make people's merits equal. For father rises against son and son against father out of zeal for religion, because not all accomplish what they undertake, but "he who perseveres to the end will be saved." Moreover, the Lord searches out not outward compliance but the inner disposition; for if you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, the sacrifice is not acceptable to God. So from one bed (for there is a bed of human weakness, as it is written: "You have turned all his bed in his sickness") one is left and the other taken. The one who is taken is caught up to meet Christ in the air; the one who is left is rejected.

Two women grinding at the mill. The sense seems to be that this signifies those who seek nourishment from hidden things and bring it out from within into the open. Still, we must ask what these women are grinding, unless perhaps it is what we read in Isaiah: "If you bring fine flour, it is vain," so that the fine flour is what is offered by those who grind. Let us examine, then, who these grinders are, what they grind, and what the mill is. Perhaps the mill is this world; though I think it more fitting that it represents the form of the human body, in which our soul is shut up as in a bodily prison, to produce heavenly bread if it takes good counsel. In this mill, then, either the synagogue or the soul that is bound by sins, grinding wheat that is soaked and spoiled by heavy moisture, cannot separate the inner from the outer, and so it will be left, because its flour was displeasing. But the holy Church, or the soul stained by no defilement of sin, grinds wheat parched by the heat of the eternal sun, wheat which God clothed as he willed and which the angels have cleansed of every stain of refuse; and offering to God good flour from the inmost parts of man, it commends the offerings of its sacrifice.

And not only two women grinding, but also two men working will be in one field. Of these one will be taken: the good sower, who has sown not on the paths but on ploughed and cultivated soil, so that the earth may multiply fruit pressed down by humility, not scattered by boasting. But the sower of tares will be left, and from tares a flour fit only to be rejected is made. We can find out who these differing farmers are if we consider why the apostle said that there are two νοῦς, that is, two minds, in us. Perhaps it is because one belongs to the outer man and the other to the inner man, who is renewed through the sacraments. And perhaps the former is the worse, the one that is exalted, vainly puffed up by the mind of its flesh and not holding fast to the Head, because it turns away from keeping the saving commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ; for he who is the author of all things is the Head of all. The other is the better, the one that loves humility, seeks wisdom and does not neglect mercy: the good sower, that is, for "he has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever." This one, then, is spiritual, the other carnal. For just as we learn from the apostle's words that the seducer who exalts himself with a swollen spirit is puffed up by the mind of the flesh, so too we show that the holy man is renewed in the spirit of his mind, since the same apostle says: "Be renewed in the spirit of your mind." He thus shows that there are two minds: one that becomes the mind of the flesh when it is overcome by sin, and another that, joined to the spirit, renounces the allurements of the flesh.

And there are not only two minds but also two laws in us, both of which the apostle has explained to us when he says: "For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man, but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members." There is, then, a law of the inner man and also a law of the outer man: the one forbids sin, the other urges it; the one condemns error, the other suggests it; the one instructs the mind, the other tempts it. There are also two other, stronger laws in us, one of God and the other of sin, according to the same teacher, who says: "So then I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin." And this shows that when you speak of the mind alone, you show it to be opposed to the flesh. For when Paul says that he serves the law of God with his mind, he certainly shows that the mind in itself, unless it is overcome by the flesh, is good, and was so created by nature as to resist error. So when it is overcome, it is the mind of the flesh; it has its fall not from its nature but from the flesh, and, being conquered, it passes as it were into the name and character of its conqueror. By nature, however, it is opposed to the flesh. In short, with the mind we serve God, with the flesh sin. And the mind will be better if, working together with the Holy Spirit, it does not neglect its religious duty.

These, then, are the ones working in our field: one yields good fruit through diligence, the other loses it through neglect. This latter the lawgiver calls blood, when he says: "The soul of all flesh is its blood." Many also refer to this the text that is written: "You shall not eat flesh with its blood," so that we may not count as refreshment, rather than as bloodguilt, the pleasures of the body stained with the blood of the soul's wounds; for we ought to be refreshed by the word of God. There is, then, a food of refreshment and a food of blood; for as the Lord's flesh is truly food, so his blood is truly our drink. Let us therefore supply the Lord with good food from our works, so that when he comes again and, as with that fig tree, finds no fruit, he may not go hungry from the barrenness of our merits and turn away his purpose of mercy, saying to the soul he has found bare of fruit and stained with blood: "May no fruit ever grow from you again." So the soul of all flesh is its blood. But there is also a better soul, of which God said: "All souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine."

Nor should we pass over the interpretation that sees here two peoples: in this world, which is very often compared to a field, there are two peoples, one of believers and the other of those who do not believe, and each will receive the due return for its merits. So the one who is faithful is taken and the one who is unfaithful is left. The two women grinding are two souls, or else the Church and the synagogue; for in the divine Scriptures a figure is usually not single but manifold, so that one saying embraces several meanings. So the mind of the flesh, the soul of the flesh and the synagogue gather that wheat and grind that flour which are offered in vain; but the mind that is joined to the soul, and the soul that receives salvation, or the Church of God, cultivate and grind the spiritual fine flour of the true law. From it too are made the loaves of the presence, which only the priests eat, for they are commanded to eat a purer bread, namely the bread that came down from heaven. And we are all, if our merits allow, priests of righteousness, consecrated with the oil of gladness for kingship and priesthood.

So, since we have been entrusted with the task of this cultivation, let us work and till our field in such a way that in that Jerusalem above, where the keeping of the law is truly observed, we may have fine flour from our sheaves. Blessed are those who have been able to gather them, so that they may come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves. These, then, are the spiritual fruits and the happy yields of true labour, which are soaked by no useless rain; but the fruit of the flesh is subject to corruption, and so whoever sows carnal things will reap carnal things. As for the field, what need I say, since it is plain that praise or blame lies in the work of the farmer?

"And they answered and said: Where, Lord?" The disciples said this. But the Lord, having already warned them where and whither to flee, where to remain and what to beware of, summed it all up in a general statement, saying:

"Where the body is, there the eagles will gather." So let us first work out what the eagles are, so as to determine what the body is. The souls of the righteous are compared to eagles, because they seek the heights, leave lowly things behind, and are said to live a long life. That is why David says to his soul: "Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's." If, then, we have understood the eagles, we can no longer be in doubt about the body, especially if we remember that Joseph received the body from Pilate. Do not Mary the wife of Clopas, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of the Lord and the gathering of the apostles around the Lord's tomb seem to you to be eagles around the body? Do they not seem to you to be eagles around the body when the Son of Man comes with spiritual clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him?

There is also the body of which it was said: "My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink." Around this body are eagles that fly about it on spiritual wings. There are eagles around the body, too, who believe that Jesus has come in the flesh, because every spirit that confesses that [?] Christ has come in the flesh is from God. So where there is faith, there is the sacrament, there is the dwelling place of holiness. The Church too is a body, in which we are renewed in spirit through the grace of baptism, and what is declining with old age is restored to a youth come to life again.

"Let the children come to me, and do not forbid them; for to such belongs the kingdom of God." Yet this age is weak in strength, feeble in understanding, immature in judgment. So it is not one age that is preferred to another; otherwise it would be harmful to grow up. What need is there to pray for reaching mature years, if that maturity is going to take from me the merit of the heavenly kingdom? Did God, then, give the progress of life for the sake of vices, not for the growth of virtue? And why did he himself choose apostles not of childish years but of more advanced age? Why, then, does he say that children are fit for the kingdom of heaven? Perhaps because they know no malice, do not know how to cheat, do not dare to strike back, do not think to pry after wealth, and do not covet honour or ambition. But virtue lies not in being ignorant of these things but in despising them; and there is no praise for continence where purity comes from weakness. So what is meant is not childhood, but the goodness that emulates childlike simplicity. For virtue is not being unable to sin but being unwilling, and so holding to a persevering will that the will may imitate the nature of infancy [?]. Indeed, the Saviour himself expressed this when he said: "Unless you are converted and become like this child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven."

Who, then, is the child whom the apostles of Christ are to imitate? Is it one of the little ones? Would that be the virtue of the apostles? Who, then, is the child? Might it not be the one of whom Isaiah says: "A child is born to us, a son is given to us"? For this child said to you: "Take up your cross and follow me." And so that you may recognize the child: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he was struck, he did not strike back. This is perfect virtue. So in childhood there is a certain venerable maturity of character, and in old age an innocent childhood; for venerable old age is not that of long years, nor is it reckoned by the number of years, but understanding is grey hair for men, and a spotless life is ripe old age. Hence it is also written: "Praise the Lord, you children, praise the name of the Lord," because no one but the perfect praises the Lord; for no one says "Lord Jesus" except in the Holy Spirit.

This seems to have been prophesied of the people of the Church, which, though younger, has outstripped the older people of the Jews in the pursuit of virtue. Hence also the words: "Behold, I and my children whom you have given me." These are the children who, escorting the Lord as he rode upon the colt of an ass, with prophetic cries proclaimed that the redemption of the Gentiles had come. These are the children, or infants, who have drunk more deeply from those breasts of Christ that are better than wine; for "out of the mouths of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise."

Some may therefore think it harsh and unkind that the disciples kept little children from coming to the Lord, unless you understand either the mystery or the feeling behind it. They did not do it from any bitterness of mind or ill will toward the children. They were rendering the Lord the attentive service of servants, so that he would not be crushed by the crowds. Indeed, it is written elsewhere: “Master, the crowds are pressing upon you.” Our own advantage is certainly to be rejected where it brings an affront to the Godhead. Let us therefore flee pride and follow the simplicity of a child, for truth is the enemy of pride, while simplicity runs alongside truth and is lofty in its very humility. For God does not dwell in a base heart. Rather, as the prophets have handed down to us, “the throne of power is exalted”, that is, in the one whose wisdom is raised to the height of truth. Nor should anyone, like Cain, hide a murderer’s treachery under the appearance of a brother; let him be a brother outwardly and inwardly. So much for the feeling. As for the mystery, the disciples were eager that the Jewish people, from whom they had been born according to the flesh, should be saved first. Yet they also made supplication on behalf of the Canaanite woman. They knew the mystery, then, that the call was owed to both peoples, but perhaps they did not yet know the order.

Now pay attention to the difference in the words. Where he bids the infants come to him so that he might bless them, whether by prayer or by the laying on of hands, he calls them “children”; where he commands that they must not be made to stumble, he calls them “little ones”. For those whom Christ touches do not stumble, and those who draw near to Christ do not fall. The ones who fall are those made “little” not by smallness of age but by littleness of virtue. At the same time he teaches that the weak are not to be tempted, lest their sins be turned back upon us. Although they themselves are weak in the merits of virtue, their prayers are nevertheless carried up to the Lord under the patronage of angels. So let no one mock the poor, for he provokes the One who made him; let no one tempt the feeble, lest he wrong the angels; let no one cast down the weak, lest he undo the Redeemer’s gift.

And so he said: “Woe to this world because of stumbling blocks,” for many have judged the Lord’s cross to be a stumbling block, although the humility of the Lord’s passion is the sacrament of our salvation, so that we may be prompted [?] to the duty of virtue and take up an example of humility. Woe, then, to the one who does not believe in the Lord’s cross, at which the weak stumble: “It would be better for him that a millstone turned by an ass be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea.”

In the divine Scriptures, it is true, we ought to weigh not the sequence of the words but the weight of the matters, for a beastly display of punishment, of an unheard-of and hideous kind, does more to restrain sins. Still, so that no stumbling block may arise from this for any weak person, we do not think that the millstone turned by an ass, a man’s neck, and the depths of the sea have been set side by side without purpose. For since the Gentile people has taken on the figure of the ass, does it not seem to you to be turning an ass’s millstone, as it were, so long as it remains in the error of its ignorance? It is bound by the bonds of nature to grind out the word and to seek God, but it is so steeped in the blindness of a veiled mind that it does not know how to lift the face of the soul to God or to open the eyes of the heart. And so, with no eagerness in its course, its steps often circling back on themselves, it toils unwillingly for another’s use. Yet one who turns a millstone does at some point reach the end of the work and holds the hope of shedding his blindness. But who has the millstone hung around his neck? He carries a stone, because he refused to carry the yoke of the Lord. The ass, then, belongs to the millstone, the blind man to the stone, the Gentile to the rock, for he worships one whom he neither sees nor knows. God does not dwell in things made by hands, nor is he known in stone, but in the Spirit.

Both peoples, then, the Gentile and the Jew, are set forth through the imagery of this saying, but the heavier penalty is decreed against the Jews. The memory of the Gentiles will be overwhelmed by the waves of this age and blotted out by the mire of this world, for they chose to be among the things that are not, and, estranged from the knowledge of God, they have been sunk as it were into the depths of the sea. But the Jews, taken up through the patriarchs, marked by circumcision, and instructed through the law, will not perish as those who did not know; they will be punished as those guilty of sacrilege. For the God who was unknown to the Athenians was known in Judea, but not received. And so whoever does not know will not be known, and whoever transgresses will be condemned. The one who did not know his Maker is not freed from guilt, and the one who did not receive the Lord is shut out from pardon. Yet it is more bearable to have withheld faith from Christ than to have laid hands on him.
A certain ruler asked him, saying: “Good Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” And Jesus said to him: “Why do you call me good?

No one is good but God alone.” A crafty question, and therefore a shrewd answer. For this ruler, who was tempting him, called him “good teacher,” when he ought to have called him “good God.” For although there is goodness in divinity and divinity in goodness (for no one is good but God alone, and every man is a liar, and whatever is a liar is surely not good), yet by adding “Good Teacher” he called him good in part, not in totality; for God is good in totality, man only in part. Therefore the Lord says: Why do you call me good, when you deny that I am God? Why do you call me good, when no one is good but the one God? So he does not deny that he is good, but signals that he is God; for what is “good” but full of goodness? And when it is written: “There is none who does good, not even one,” it was surely said of men, not of God; for God is one, not one of a number. So too the Son of God is singled out as the only one, not as one of many; and he is only-begotten, not one of those who are begotten. And therefore “no one is good” passes no prior judgment on Christ, because no one judges Christ. For “no one” is said of us in common, but Christ has nothing in common with us.

But if anyone is troubled that no one is good but the one God, let him be troubled also by this: that no one is good but God. If the Son is not excluded from “God,” then surely Christ is not excluded from “good” either. But in God the Son is another in person yet one in power, for there is one God, from whom are all things, and one Lord, through whom are all things. And God and Lord are not two gods but one God, because the Lord your God is one Lord. Surely, then, since according to majesty God is one in both persons, there is also one good in both. For how could one born of the good not be good? A good tree bears good fruit. How could he not be good, when the substance of goodness taken from the Father has not degenerated in the Son, just as it has not degenerated in the Spirit? And therefore: “Your good Spirit will lead me in the right way.” If the Spirit, who received from the Son, is good, then surely he who gave is good as well. And since the Father is good, surely he too is good who has all things that the Father has. Or if you deny that the Son has goodness, you deny the Father as well.

Evident reasoning needs no examples; yet at least follow the authority of the Scriptures. For it is written: “The Lord is a good judge to the house of Israel.” Does it speak of the Son or of the Father? But the Father judges no one, for he has given all judgment to the Son. Therefore the good Lord is the Son. Take another. Those who come to baptism certainly confess the Trinity, since they are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; therefore they confess to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. So when it is said, “Confess to the Lord, for he is good,” surely the Father is good, the Son is good, and the Holy Spirit is good, but there is one God. And again: “For the Lord is good to those who wait for him.” Is he not good who grants good things to the soul that seeks him? Is he not good who satisfies your soul with good things? Is he not good who says: “I am the good shepherd”?

But you think God is good because he does not have judgment, which carries the need to punish. Although it has already been stated that the judge is good to the house of Israel, elsewhere you also have: “How good is the God of Israel to the upright of heart!” Of whom, then, do you think this is said, of the Father or of the Son? If of the Father, then he is not good to all. Why then do you detract from the Son? If of the Son, then confess that the Son too is good God; for he is the blessed God of Israel, because he has visited and brought about the redemption of his people. He is the King and God of Israel, to whom it is said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel.” So this is what he says here: Since you who tempt me cannot perceive that I am good, why do you call me good? I am indeed good, but to the upright of heart, to one whose goodness comes from nature, not from cunning. The Son, then, is good; for he is the brightness of eternal light and the spotless mirror of God's majesty and the image of his goodness. How then could he not be good who is the image of goodness? For just as the image of God is God, yet there is one God, so the image of divine goodness is good, yet there is one goodness. For my part, it is certainly profitable to believe that God is good, since I am to have him as the judge of my sins. Let those who will not believe him good see to it themselves. So, since this man who tempts him is an expert in the law, as is shown in another book, he rightly said: “No one is good but the one God,” to remind him that it is written, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God,” and so that he might rather confess to the Lord, for he is good.

Then he rebukes him repeatedly. For when the man boasted in the law that he had kept everything from his youth, Jesus, to expose his empty boasting, shows him that he still lacks what belongs to the law. And so he is led, sorrowful, to the commandment of mercy, and a saying drawn, as it were, from nature is pronounced against him.

It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. There is great force, great weight in these words. For by what other words could he more forcefully express that a rich man ought not to boast in his riches than by words such as these, which declare that a merciful rich man is contrary to nature? Away with the allurements and paint of words, which tend to weaken our meaning. This man, who spurned mercy, ought not to have been coaxed but broken. Yet there may be some who are delighted more by the ornaments of words than by a natural, manly bearing and form of meaning. Let them do what good suitors do in choosing a wife: they examine her character, not her beauty, and are not put off by her appearance when they are drawn by the strength of her mind. So let these, too, seek in the words the mystery, which is a kind of mind and soul of the words, and let them not pick at the words when there is a mystery.

The camel, then, is taken figuratively as the Gentile people, which that lion, seeking whom he may devour, drives laden with treasure into the desert, as the prophet saw it: “In tribulation and anguish, lion and lion's whelp, to the asps and the brood of flying asps, they carried their riches on asses and camels.” And the camel fittingly figures the Gentile people, because before the people of the nations believed, they had degenerated through the deformity of superstition and displayed the appearance of a beast's foulness, ungainly tracks and a hideous face. This sinner, therefore, entered more easily by the narrow way, which is the way of Christ (who, piercing the way of death like a needle by the passion of his own body, mended the torn garments of our nature), than did the people of the Jews, rich in the law, needy in faith, headlong in fury, shameful in crime.

You can also understand it morally, of every sinner and of the arrogant rich man. Does it not seem to you that the tax collector, burdened with the consciousness of his sins, who did not dare to lift his eyes to God, entered through the needle's eye like a camel, by the remedies of his confession, more easily than that Pharisee entered the kingdom of God? The Pharisee was arrogant in prayer, boastful of his innocence, presumptuous of glory, a reproacher of mercy, a herald of himself, an accuser of another, one who confronted the Lord rather than entreating him. If anyone, then, shudders at a camel, let him shudder at the man whose deeds are fouler than a camel.

Honor your father and mother. It is fitting that the opening of the law is read to me today, on the birthday of my priesthood; for every year the priesthood seems, as it were, to begin anew, when it is renewed with the turning of the seasons. It is good, too, that this is read: “Honor your father and mother”; for you are my parents, you who conferred the priesthood on me. You, I say, are both children and parents: children one by one, parents all together. For I would gladly call you mine, whether children or parents: children, you who hear the word of God and do it. For it is written: “Come, children, listen to me”; and parents, because the Lord himself said: “Who are my mother or my brothers? My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.”

Rightly, then, the law, having first said, “You shall love the Lord your God” and “You shall love your neighbor,” went on to say: “Honor your father and your mother.” For this is the first step of piety, since God willed that these should be the authors of your being. Honor them with dutiful service, so that you refrain from insulting them, since the reverence due to parents must not be wounded even by a look. But it is too little not to wound them, since the law has already seen to it that they suffer no wrong: “Whoever curses father or mother shall surely die.” You must honor them, that you may be good. The protection of the law is one thing, the duty of piety another. Honor your parents, because the Son of God honored his; for you have read: “And he was subject to them.” If God was subject to his servants, how much more should you be to your parents? Christ, then, honored Joseph and Mary not from any debt of nature but from the duty of piety. He also honored God the Father as no one else could honor him, by being obedient unto death. So you too, honor your parents.

Honor consists not only in respect but also in generosity. “Honor widows who are truly widows”; for to honor is to bestow according to merit. Feed your father, feed your mother. Even if you have fed your mother, you have not yet repaid the pains, you have not repaid the torments she suffered for you; you have not repaid the care with which she carried you; you have not repaid the nourishment she gave with tender, loving affection, pressing her breasts to your lips; you have not repaid the hunger she endured for you, so as not to eat anything harmful to you or drink anything that would spoil her milk. For you she fasted, for you she ate; for you she refused the food she wanted, for you she took the food she did not want; for you she kept watch, for you she wept. And will you let her go in want? O son, what judgment you bring upon yourself if you do not feed your parent! You owe what you have to her to whom you owe what you are. What a judgment, if the Church feeds those whom you refuse to feed! “If any believing man,” it says, “or believing woman has widows, let them provide for them, so that the Church may not be burdened, and may have enough for those who are truly widows.” This is said of strangers; what then of parents?

It was not idly that we spoke just now, for a mother's complaint has stung us; but we preferred to admonish publicly the one who behaves so rather than to restrain him privately. And if he is not betrayed by our voice, let him at least blush at his own feelings. Do not allow, son, that others' hunger should feed your parents; do not allow, son, that the fasting of the poor should provide food for your parents. If not for the sake of grace and salvation, then at least for shame's sake, feed them, son. Are you not ashamed if, as you enter the church, your aged mother stretches out her hands to strangers, and, passed over by her daughter, begs alms from strangers, while you pass by with your neck held high and your eyes flirting, trailing your robe, wearing earrings and bracelets and rings and the rest that Isaiah speaks of? What if she should turn her words against you, demanding back the debt of nature, the price of your nourishment, the service your hand owes to the one who bore you?

What will you answer? Will you give to others? What if they throw it back at you: “Go, first feed your mother”? For though they are poor, they do not seek an impious contribution. Have you not heard earlier that the rich man who reclined in fine linen and purple, from whose table Lazarus gathered crumbs, is tormented with eternal punishment because he did not share his food with the poor man? If it is a grave thing not to give to strangers, how much graver to shut out your parents! But you say you prefer to give to the Church what you would have given to your parents. God does not seek a gift drawn from the hunger of parents. Hence, when the Jews criticized the Lord's disciples for not washing their hands, the Lord answered: “Whoever says, ‘Whatever gift comes from me will benefit you,’ has not honored father or mother.”

That is why we have not unwisely turned aside to this obscure sense. For the Jews, while following the tradition of men, neglect that of God. The disciples, preferring the tradition of God, neglected that of men, so that they did not wash their hands when they ate bread, since he who has been washed all over has no need to wash his hands. Jesus had washed them; they sought no other washing, for by one baptism Christ did away with all baptisms. Thus one whom the Church has washed has no need to wash again. The disciples, then, attended to the mystery, seeking cleanness not of body but of soul. This the Jews criticized, but they are shrewdly refuted by the Lord for observing empty things and despising things that would profit them. And so he says to them: Why do you say to father or mother, whom the law commands to be honored, “Whatever gift comes from me will benefit you”? That is: when a needy father or mother asks the son for something toward their expenses, the Jew, fearing the law, looks for an excuse not to give, and is accustomed to say, “It is a gift that will benefit you from me,” so that the devout father is afraid to accept money dedicated to God. But this is the tradition of men who weave excuses for their own avarice; the tradition of God, on the other hand, is that you first feed your parents. For if, according to the divine oracle, an insult to a parent is atoned for by death, how much more is hunger, which is worse than death!

Here the Lord curbs arrogant boasting. For many, in order to be praised by men, give to the Church what they take from their own family, whereas mercy ought to begin from the duty of piety at home. Give first, then, to your parent; give also to the poor; give to that presbyter the earthly goods you have in abundance, so that you may receive from him the spiritual goods you lack; for he who honors will be honored. See, then, that when he receives he also gives, and he receives not as one in need but as one who will repay in greater measure. Give to the poor man for his rest, so that you too, by sharing what is yours with the needy, may obtain rest. But just as Scripture says that parents must be fed, so it also says that parents must be left for God's sake, if they hinder the affection of a devoted mind.

Now it came to pass, as he drew near to Jericho, that a certain blind man was sitting by the road. In the book according to Matthew two are introduced, here one; there as he was leaving Jericho, here as he was approaching. But there is no discrepancy. For since this one man is a type of the Gentile people, which by the Lord's sacrament recovered the brightness of the light it had lost, it makes no difference whether it receives healing in one man or in two. For that people, tracing its origin from Ham and Japheth, the sons of Noah, displayed in the two blind men the two founders of its race.

Luke too seems not to have left this out, when he goes on to Zacchaeus, who was small of stature, that is, raised up by no dignity of inborn nobility, slight in merits. Like the people of the nations, on hearing of the saving coming of the Lord, he desired to see the one whom his own people had not received. But no one sees Jesus easily; no one can see Jesus while standing on the earth. And since he had neither prophets nor kingdom as a grace of natural beauty, he climbed a sycamore, treading underfoot, that is, the vanity of the Jews and also correcting the errors of the former age; and therefore he received [?] into the hospitality of his inner house. And he fittingly climbed a tree, so that a good tree might bear good fruit, and so that, cut from the wild olive which was his by nature and grafted contrary to nature into the good olive, he might bring forth the fruit of the law. For the root is holy, even if the branches are useless; and the people of the Gentiles, by faith in the resurrection, as if by a kind of lifting up of the body, has risen above their fruitless glory.

And behold, a man named Zacchaeus. Zacchaeus in the sycamore, the blind man by the road. The Lord waits for the one in order to have mercy on him; the other he ennobles with the honor of staying in his house. The one he questions in order to heal him; with the other he invites himself without being invited. For he knew that his host's reward would be rich; and though he had not yet heard the voice of the one inviting him, he had heard his desire.

But lest we seem, like those who disdain the poor, to have quickly left that blind man and moved on to the rich man, let us wait for him, since the Lord also waited; let us question him, since Christ also questioned him. We question him because we do not know; he questioned because he knew. We question him so that we may know how this man was cured; he questioned him so that in one man many of us might learn how we may be worthy to see the Lord. For he questioned him so that we might believe that no one can be healed unless he confesses. And immediately, it says, he saw, and followed him, glorifying the Lord. And he was passing through Jericho.

For he would not otherwise see, unless he followed Christ, unless he proclaimed the Lord, unless he passed beyond the world. Let us also make our peace with the rich; for we do not wish to offend the rich, we who wish, if possible, to heal everyone. Stung by the comparison with the camel, and abandoned in Zacchaeus sooner than was proper, they should not be left with cause for just indignation.

Let them learn that guilt lies not in possessions but in those who do not know how to use their possessions. For riches, just as they are hindrances in the wicked, are aids to virtue in the good. Zacchaeus was certainly rich and chosen by Christ; but by giving half his goods to the poor, and also restoring fourfold what he had taken by fraud (for the one is not enough without the other, and generosity wins no favor if wrongdoing continues, since what is sought is gifts, not spoils), he received a richer reward than he gave.

And fittingly a chief tax collector is brought in. For who should despair of himself, when even this man, whose wealth came from fraud, reached salvation? And he was rich, it says, so that you may know that not all the rich are greedy.

Why is it that Scripture has described the stature of no one else but this man, saying that he was small of stature? Consider whether perhaps he was small in malice, or still small in faith; for when he climbed he had not yet made his promise, he had not yet seen Christ, so he was rightly still small. John, by contrast, was great, because he saw both Christ and the Spirit remaining upon Christ like a dove, as he himself says: “I saw the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him.”

And what is the crowd but the confusion of an untaught multitude, which could not see the summit of wisdom? So Zacchaeus, as long as he is in the crowd, does not see Christ; he climbed above the crowd and saw. That is, having risen above the ignorance of the common people, he was found worthy to behold the one he longed for.

And he finely added: because the Lord was going to pass that way, either where the sycamore was or where the man who would believe was, so that he might both preserve the mystery and sow grace. For he had come in such a way as to pass through the Jews to the Gentiles.

So he saw Zacchaeus up above; for already, by the loftiness of his faith, he stood out among the fruits of new works, as if on the height of a fruitful tree. And since we have turned from the type to moral matters, it is pleasant, amid the goodwill of so many believers, to relax the mind on the Lord's day and mingle in some festivity. Zacchaeus in the sycamore: a new fruit, that is, of a new season, so that in this too the saying might be fulfilled: “The fig tree has put forth its green figs.” For Christ came for this, that trees should bring forth not fruits but men. We read elsewhere: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” So Nathanael was under the tree, that is, upon the root, because he was righteous, for the root is holy; yet Nathanael was under the tree, because he was under the law, while Zacchaeus was above the tree, because he was above the law. The one was a hidden defender of the Lord, the other a public herald; the one was still seeking Christ from the law, the other, already above the law, was leaving his possessions and following the Lord.

Behold, your mina has gained ten minas. It is a good order that, when he was about to call the Gentiles and order the death of the Jews who did not want Christ to reign over them, he should first set out this comparison, so that no one could say: “He had given the Jewish people nothing by which they could become better,” or: “What is demanded of one who received nothing?” This is no ordinary mina. It is the one the woman in the Gospel, earlier, could not find: she lights a lamp, searches with the light brought close, and rejoices when it is found.

Then from one mina one servant made ten minas, another five. Perhaps the five stand for moral things, since there are five senses of the body, and the ten for twofold things, that is, the mystical things of the law and the moral things of uprightness. Hence Matthew too set down five talents and two talents: in the five talents the moral, in the two both the mystical and the moral. Thus what is lower in number is richer in substance. Here too we can understand the ten minas as the ten words, that is, the teaching of the law, and the five minas as the instructions of discipline. But I want the expert in the law to be perfect in all things; for the kingdom of God is not in word but in power.

And fittingly, since he is speaking of the Jews, only two bring back money that has been multiplied, not, of course, by interest on bronze coin but by the interest of discussion. For the interest from money lent at usury is one thing, the interest from heavenly doctrine another.
