Then, when the Lord says, “Why did you not put my money in the bank?”, he is seeking interest not on our money but on his own.

One says that he hid it in the earth, because through eagerness for pleasure he buried the reason given to us after the image and likeness of God, and hid it as in the pit of the flesh. Nothing is said of the others, who, like spendthrift debtors, lost what they had received. In those two are the few who were sent on two occasions to the tenants of the vineyard; in the rest are all the Jews. Matthew wished to apply this comparison to us as well: just as the rich man who does not share his money with the poor, so too the one who does not share the grace of his teaching with the unlearned, when he could teach them, is guilty of no slight fault. Since we have spoken about this in the books written On the Faith, it was better to pass over it quickly.

And what can the ten cities be, unless perhaps souls? Over these he is rightly set who has lent out at interest to the minds of men the Lord's money, those pure words tested like silver. For just as Jerusalem is said to be built as a city, so too are peaceful souls. And as angels rule over them, so too do those who have merited the life of the angels.
BOOK NINE.

And it came to pass, when he had drawn near to Bethphage and Bethany, to the mount called Olivet, he sent two disciples, saying: Go into the village opposite, where on entering you will find a colt of an ass tied up, on which no one has ever sat. Fittingly the Lord, leaving the Jews behind and about to dwell in the hearts of the Gentiles, goes up to the temple. For this is the true temple, in which the Lord is worshipped not in the letter but in the spirit; this is the temple of God, founded not by a structure of stones but by a course of faith. So those who hated are abandoned, and those who would love are chosen.

And so he came to the Mount of Olives, to plant young olive trees on the heights of virtue. Their mother is that Jerusalem which is above. On this mount is the heavenly husbandman, so that all who are planted in the house of God may each say: But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord. And perhaps the mount itself is Christ. For who else would bear such fruit—not olive trees bent under an abundance of berries, but Gentiles made fruitful by the fullness of the Spirit? He it is through whom we ascend and to whom we ascend. He is the door, he is the way; he is opened and he opens; he is knocked upon by those who would enter, and adored by those who have finished their service.

So the colt was in the village, and it was tied together with the ass. It could not be loosed except at the Lord's command. The apostolic hand loosed it: such was their conduct, such their life, such their grace. Be such that you too can loose those who are bound.

Now let us consider who they were who, when their error was exposed, were cast out of paradise and confined in a village. And you see how those whom death had driven out, life called back. And so in Matthew we read of both the ass and the colt, so that, since both sexes had been driven out in two human beings, both sexes might be called back in two animals. There, then, in the mother ass he figured, as it were, Eve, the mother of error; here, in the colt, he represented the whole body of the Gentile people.

And so the ass's colt is ridden. And rightly is it said, "on which no one has sat," because no one before Christ called the peoples of the nations into the Church. Indeed in Mark you have it thus: on which no man has yet sat. But it was held bound by the chains of faithlessness, made over to an unjust master, enslaved to error; yet that master could not rightfully claim lordship, since it was not nature but guilt that had made him lord. And so when "the Lord" is said, one alone is recognized—for there are many gods and many lords, but, speaking generally—one God and one Lord. Therefore, if the lord is not specified, he is identified no longer by the addition of a person but by the universality of his nature.

Mark, however, presents it tied before the door, because whoever is outside Christ is outside, in the road, but he who is in Christ is not outside. He added "in the street," where no one has any secure possession—no manger, no food, no stable. Wretched is the servitude whose rights wander; for he who does not have one master has many. Strangers bind in order to possess; he looses in order to hold, for he knows that gifts are stronger than chains.

Nor is it without purpose that two disciples are sent: Peter to Cornelius, Paul to the rest. And so he did not designate the persons but fixed the number. Yet if anyone insists on persons, he may think of Philip, whom the Spirit sent to Gaza, when he baptized the eunuch of Queen Candace and sowed the word of the Lord through all the cities from Azotus to Caesarea. Nor should we pass over the fact that he declares they will soon be sent back, because those who were to preach the Lord Jesus in the lands of the Gentiles had to be sent out.

So when those who had been sent loosed the colt, did they use words of their own? Not at all; they said just what Jesus had told them, so that you may recognize that it was not by their own speech but by the word of God, not in their own name but in Christ's, that they poured faith into the Gentile peoples, and that the hostile powers which claimed the homage of the nations for themselves gave way before the divine command.

Hence too the apostles spread their own garments under Christ, so that by their preaching of the gospel they might display the glory of the deed—for in the divine Scriptures garments often stand for virtues—virtues that might soften a little, by their own power, the hardness of the Gentiles, so that these might render with eager devotion the smooth, unstumbling service of a blessed ride. For it was not for outward show that the Lord of the world was pleased to be carried on the back of an ass, but so that by a hidden mystery he might saddle the inmost recesses of our mind, and the mystic rider might sit enthroned within, in the secret places of our souls, poured into them as into a kind of body of his divinity, guiding the steps of the mind, curbing the wantonness of the flesh, so as to tame, under the leading of piety, the habitual disposition of the Gentile people. Happy are they who have received such a rider in their inmost being; happy indeed are they whose mouths the rein of the heavenly Word has held in, so that they should not be loosed in much speaking!

What is this rein, brethren? Who will teach me how he either restrains or loosens the mouths of men? He showed me the rein who said: that speech may be given me in the opening of my mouth. The word, then, is a rein; the word is a goad; and so it is hard for you to kick against the goad. This man, then, taught us to open the heart, to endure the goad, to draw the yoke. Let another teach us also to bear the reins of the tongue; for the virtue of keeping silent is rarer than that of speaking. Let him teach us plainly who, like one mute, did not open his mouth in the face of treachery, ready for scourges and not refusing blows, so that there might be a devout seat for God.

Learn from this servant of God's household to carry Christ, since he first carried you, when as shepherd he brought back the straying sheep; learn to bend the back of your mind diligently beneath him; learn to be under Christ, so that you may be above the world. Not just anyone carries Christ easily, but he who can say: I am bowed down and greatly humbled; I roared with the groaning of my heart. If you wish not to be shaken, plant your washed foot on those garments of the saints. Beware of walking with muddy feet; beware lest by sidelong steps you abandon the paths of the prophetic ways that have been laid down for you. For to make the advance of the Gentiles who were to come safer, those who went before Jesus paved the way with their own clothing right up to the temple of God. That you may walk without stumbling, the Lord's disciples, stripping off the garment of their own bodies amid the hostility of the crowds, have spread the road for you with their martyrdom. Yet if anyone wishes to take it in this way, we do not object: that this colt was already treading upon the garments of the Jews.

But what the cut branches mean—which surely tend to entangle the steps of those who walk—I would certainly be in doubt, had not the good husbandman of the whole world taught me above that the axe is already laid to the roots of the trees, to cut down the barren ones at the coming of the saving Lord and to lay low on the ground the empty glory of the fruitless Gentiles, to be trampled by the feet of the faithful, so that the nations, by the spirit of a renewed mind, may spring up like shoots of young trees from old trunks.

So do not despise this little ass. For just as there are ravening wolves in sheep's clothing, so, conversely, the hidden man of the heart lies within, under the appearance of a beast; for beneath the outer covering of the body, which we have in common with the beasts, a mind full of God is quickened. That this refers figuratively to human beings, Saint John made clearer by adding that they took branches of palms; for the righteous will flourish like the palm. And so at the coming of Christ the banners of righteousness and the insignia of triumph were already being raised above men's shoulders. Why does the crowd marvel at what the mystery is accomplishing? Even if it does not know what it marvels at, it marvels nonetheless, because in that colt wisdom sits, power abides, righteousness holds fast.

Do not despise this ass either, which once saw the angel of God whom a man could not see. It saw, and gave way, and spoke, so that you might recognize that in later times, at the coming of the great Angel of God, those Gentiles who had formerly been asses would speak.

Fittingly, according to Luke, we read that the crowds praising God met him at the descent of the mount, to signify that the worker of the spiritual mystery had come to them from heaven. So the crowd recognizes God, calls him king, repeats the prophecy: Hosanna to the Son of David—that is, it declares that the Redeemer of the house of David has come, the long-awaited Son of David according to the flesh; and this from the very crowd that a short while later would crucify him. Truly a memorable mark of divine working, that testimony against themselves should be wrung from the unwilling, since in their hearts they deny the God whom they confess with their voices.

Hence also the Lord's saying: If these are silent, the stones will cry out. Nor is it any wonder if stones, against their nature, should echo the praises of the Lord, when his murderers, harder than rocks, proclaim him. Or perhaps it means that, when the Jews fell silent after the Lord's passion, there would be living stones, as Peter says, to cry out. So, though its own feelings fought against it, the crowd nevertheless leads God to his temple with praise.

But God wants his temple to be not a merchant's lodging-house but a dwelling of holiness, and he shapes the practice of the priestly ministry not as a religious office for sale but as freely given service. Consider, then, what the Lord's deeds prescribe for you as a pattern of life.

And he drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold doves. In general, then, he taught above that worldly business ought to be kept away from God's temple, but in particular he drove out the money-changers. Who are the money-changers but those who seek profit from the Lord's money and do not distinguish good from bad? For the Lord's money is divine Scripture. Indeed, when about to depart he distributed coins to his servants and divided out talents, and for the healing of the wounded man he left two coins with the innkeeper; for by the two Testaments our wounds are healed. But you, like a good money-changer, store up the words of the Lord—pure words, silver tried in the fire, refined by the sevenfold Spirit. Do not, by an impious exchange, accept a counterfeit image of the King—for Satan too transforms himself into an angel of light—nor mix into your treasury the debased likeness of your Prince through the fraud of Arian faithlessness; nor tempt the ears of the faithful with the sound of money, so that the jingle of bronze shuts out the hearing of the sacred Scriptures, or the craving for possessions is planted in devout hearts. Not all money-changers, then, are to be excluded, for there are good ones too. Indeed he says: You should have given my money to the money-changers, and on my return I would have received it back with interest. If the coin is that of the Scriptures, the interest is that of the Scriptures too.

But why he overturned the seats of those who sold doves I do not understand according to the letter; for dealers in birds could hardly claim for themselves the dignity of some seat of honour in the market. What prerogative of dignity is there in doves? Yet the pattern of the Lord's baptism, when the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, admonishes us that, as these merchants were cast out of the temple, so those who traffic in the grace of the Holy Spirit cannot have fellowship in the Church of God. For freely, he says, you have received; freely give. Indeed, to Simon, who thought that the gift of sanctifying could be conferred on him for a price, Peter replied: Your money perish with you, because you think you can obtain the grace of God with money. You have no part or share in this faith.

The sellers of sheep and oxen, too, I take to be those foul auctioneers who hunt out some kind of market from others' labour or simplicity. Or else, because the sheep and oxen are cast out and the doves ordered to be taken away, it is the Jewish people that seems to be shut out—for Ephraim is like a dove—because the Lord hated both their successions and their labours. The bronze is poured out so that grace may be gathered; the table of the money-changers is overturned so that the Lord's table may take its place; the altar is thrown down so that altars may be raised up.

And he did this not equipped with any armed band or wealth; with a whip of cords he struck the crowds, and no one dared resist. Now he uses a rod, now a whip—for a rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom—a rod to correct, a whip to persuade. The one is direct instruction; the other is moral instruction, bent as it were, by which the sinner's conscience is scourged as with a pliant lash. For the terrors of the prophets are one thing, the persuasions of the apostles another; yet in both there is the discipline of the one Word. And so he made a whip of cords, because, as it says, the lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; for what is mine is goodly to me. For "lines" are what surveyors use to mark out the boundaries of fields to be measured. And so, like a good surveyor, he was setting apart the boundaries of the synagogue and of the Church, and ordering the sacrilegious to leave the temple; for a new surveyor had come, a measurer of fruitful souls, who would measure out the kinds of fields, not their extent.

Fittingly, however, no measure of property is enclosed by stretched cords, nor are the limits of faith fixed as though it were some bounded thing; rather, with a whip that ranges freely without limit, the borders of the Church are extended, and the Jews are banished—not into any prescribed exile, but into one without end, so that no place for the synagogue should remain anywhere in the world.

A man planted a vineyard. Many draw various meanings from the term "vineyard," but Isaiah plainly stated that the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel. Who else but God established this vineyard? He, then, is the one who let it out and went abroad—not that the Lord, who is always everywhere, went from place to place, but because he is more present to those who love him and absent from the negligent. He was away for a long time, so that his demand should not seem overhasty; for the more indulgent the generosity, the less excusable the obstinacy.

Hence you rightly have in Matthew that he also set a hedge around it, that is, fortified it with the defence of divine protection, so that it should not easily lie open to the incursions of spiritual beasts. And he dug a winepress in it. How are we to understand what the winepress is, unless perhaps from the fact that certain psalms are entitled "for the winepresses," because in them the mysteries of the Lord's passion seethed more abundantly, like new wine, as the Holy Spirit of the prophets fermented within them? Indeed, those whom the Holy Spirit flooded were thought to be drunk. So here too he dug a winepress, into which the inner fruit of the rational grape might flow down through a spiritual outpouring. He built a tower, raising up, that is, the summit of the Law; and so he let out this vineyard, fortified, equipped and adorned, to the Jews.

And at the time of the fruits he sent his servants. He rightly said "the time" of the fruits, not "the yield"; for there was no fruit from the Jews, no yield from this vineyard, of which the Lord says: I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns. So the winepresses overflowed not with the wine of gladness, not with spiritual new wine, but with the gory blood of the prophets. Indeed, Jeremiah was cast into a pit; for these were by now the winepresses of the Jews, filled not with wine but with mire. And although the prophets in general seem to be meant, the reading nevertheless allows us to believe that the one who was stoned is Naboth. Though we have received no prophetic word of his, we have received a prophetic deed, because by his own blood he foretold that many would become martyrs for this vineyard. And who is the one wounded in the head? Surely Isaiah, whose bodily frame the saw divided more easily than it could bend his faith, wear down his constancy, or cut away the vigour of his mind.

So it came about that, after sending many others, whom the Jews sent away dishonoured and empty-handed, since they could gain nothing from them, last of all he sent even his only-begotten Son, whom the faithless, eager to get rid of him as the heir, killed by crucifying him and cast out by denying him.

How much, then, how many things in brief! First, that goodness is natural, and often trusts the unworthy; next, that Christ came as the last remedy for evils; then, that whoever denies the heir despairs of the author. But Christ is both heir and testator: heir, because he outlived his own death and receives in our progress, as if by inheritance, the benefits of the testaments which he himself made.

Fittingly, then, he asks them a question, so that they may condemn themselves by their own verdict. He says that the lord of the vineyard will come, because in the Son the Father's majesty is also present, or because in the last times he breathes more closely upon human hearts. So they pronounce sentence against themselves, that the wicked should perish and the vineyard be handed over to other tenants. Let us consider, then, who the tenants are and what the vineyard is.

The vineyard is a type of us, because the people of God, founded on the root of the eternal vine, rises above the earth and, covering the lowly soil, now ripens with budding blossom, now is clothed in spreading greenery, now takes on a gentle yoke, when it has grown with more mature arms like the shoots of a fruitful vine. The husbandman, indeed, is the almighty Father, the vine is Christ, and we are the branches, who, unless we bear fruit in Christ, are cut away by the pruning-knife of the eternal cultivator. Rightly, then, the people of Christ is called a vineyard, either because the sign of the cross is marked on its forehead, or because its fruit is gathered at the last season of the year, or because, as with all the rows of a vineyard, so for poor and rich, lowly and powerful, slaves and masters, there is in the Church of God an equal measure and no distinction. As the vine is wedded to trees, so the body is joined to the soul and the soul to the body. As the vine is raised up when it is yoked, as it is not diminished but increased when it is pruned, so the holy people is set free when it is bound, lifted up when it is humbled, crowned when it is cut down. Moreover, as a tender shoot cut from an old tree is grafted onto the stock of another root, so this holy people, the scars of the old shoot smoothed away, is nurtured on the wood of the cross as in the lap of a loving parent and grows into it; and the Holy Spirit, poured into this prison of the body as if let down into the deep trenches of the earth, washes away with the irrigation of saving water whatever is foul, and raises the disposition of our members to heavenly discipline.

This vineyard the careful husbandman is accustomed to dig, to stake, and to prune; and, clearing away the mounds of earthly bulk, to expose the hidden parts of our body now to the scorching sun, now to drenching rain. He is wont to weed the field, lest the bud be harmed by brambles, lest the shade of leaves grow rank and the fruitless boasting of words, overshadowing the virtues, hinder the ripening of our natural character. But far be it from us to fear any harm for this vineyard, which its ever-watchful guardian, the saving Lord, has fortified with the wall of eternal life against all the enticements of worldly wickedness. He has stretched out its branches to the sea; for the earth is the Lord's. Everywhere God the Father is worshipped, everywhere Christ the Lord is adored.

This is our vintage. Joyful, then, and secure, let some load their laps with clusters of mellow grapes; let others of us pour out heavenly gifts with our mouths; and let many of us, pressing out the fruit of the divine gift with the steps of good wills, stain our feet—bared, the buskins stripped off—in the flowing new wine. For the place where we stand is holy ground, and so our shoes must be loosed, so that the spiritual foot, as it mounts the tribunal of the sacred seat, may be freed from the ties of bodily bonds. For it is fitting that the vintage of the whole world should be here, where the vineyard of the whole world is.

Behold the acceptable time, when the year is not stiff with the wintry frosts of darkening faithlessness, nor does a shapeless crust of blasphemy congeal in deep snows under hardening ice; rather the earth, freed from the storms of sacrilege, is now in labour with new fruits and brings forth the old. For the storm of all dissensions has died down, and all the burning heats of worldly greed and every fever by which the people of Italy were scorched in the fires of perversity—once Jewish, lately Arian—are now tempered by a serene breeze. The storm is calmed, concord sets sail, faith breathes; eagerly the sailors seek again the harbours of faith they had left, and press sweet kisses on their native shores, rejoicing that they are freed from dangers and released from errors.

Hail, vineyard worthy of so great a guardian! Not the blood of one Naboth but that of countless prophets, and, what is more, the precious blood of the Lord has consecrated you. Naboth, it is true, was not so terrified by royal threats as to let fear crush his constancy, nor so enticed by lavish rewards as to sell his devout affection; resisting the king's desire that the vine be cut down and a bed of mallows be sown in his garden, when he could do nothing else, he quenched with his own blood the fires prepared for the vines—yet it was a temporal vineyard he was defending. You, however, the deaths of many martyrs have planted for us forever; you the cross of the apostles, emulating the Lord's passion, has spread to the ends of the whole world.

Whose image and inscription does it bear? In this place the Lord teaches us that we ought to be circumspect in answering heretics or Jews. Elsewhere he said: Be wise as serpents. Many take this passage to mean that, since the cross of Christ was foretold by the serpent that was lifted up, by which he would abolish the serpent's venom of spiritual wickedness, one ought to be wise as Christ is and simple as the Spirit is. Behold for you that serpent which always guards its head and wards off the deadly wound. When the Jews asked him whether he had received his power from heaven, he replied: The baptism of John, where is it from—from heaven or from men? So that, since they did not dare to deny that it was from heaven, they convicted themselves of madness in denying that its author was from heaven. When asked for the didrachma, he asks about the image; for the image of God is one thing, the image of the world another. Hence he too admonishes us: As we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.

Christ does not bear Caesar's image, because he is the image of God. Peter does not bear Caesar's image, because he said: "We have left everything and followed you." Caesar's image is not found in James or John, because they are sons of thunder; but it is found in the sea, where those dragons had their heads crushed upon the water, and the greater dragon himself was broken in pieces and his head given as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians. If, then, he did not bear Caesar's image, why did he pay the tax? He did not give from what was his own, but returned to the world what belonged to the world. And you, if you wish not to be liable to Caesar, do not keep the things that belong to the world. But you have riches: you are liable to Caesar. If you wish to owe nothing to an earthly king, leave all that you have and follow Christ.

And he rightly decrees that the things that are Caesar's must be rendered first; for no one can belong to the Lord unless he has first renounced the world. Yet we all renounce in words, not in our desires; for when we receive the sacraments, we renounce. How heavy a bond it is to promise something to God and not pay it! "It is better," Scripture says, "that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay." A contract of faith is greater than a contract of money. Pay what you have promised while you are in this body, before the collector comes and throws you into prison. "Truly I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid the last penny."

If a man's brother dies. The Sadducees, that is, the more detestable part of the Jews, test the Lord in this passage. Their foolishness is openly rebuked, while in a mystical sense the argument is turned back on them: what an example of chastity they offered from their own law, when, according to the letter, a woman is compelled to marry, even against her will, so that a brother may raise up offspring for the dead man! So the letter kills, like a procuress

[?] of vices, whereas the Spirit is the teacher of chastity. Let us consider, then, whether this woman who had seven husbands is not the synagogue, just as it is said to the Samaritan woman: "For you have had five husbands"; for the Samaritan woman follows only the five books of Moses, while the synagogue principally follows seven, and because of her unbelief she received from none of them the seed of an heir to carry on the line. And therefore she will not be able to have a share with her husbands in the resurrection, because she has twisted a spiritual precept to fit a carnal sense. For no brother in the flesh was appointed to raise up seed for his dead brother; rather, it was that Brother who would take to himself as wife, from the dead people of the Jews, the wisdom of divine worship, and from her raise up offspring in the apostles. They, like a remnant of the dead Jews, left still unformed in the womb of the synagogue, were found worthy, according to the election of grace, to be preserved by the mingling of the new seed.

Now the synagogue is often shown receiving the stole, which is the mark of marriage, as the source of the faithful; and she is also often shown as repudiated, because she is the mother of the unbelieving. For her the bodily law died, so that the spiritual law might rise again. Therefore the holy people of God, if they love the seven books of the law with a kind of conjugal love and obey them as they would a husband's commands, will have heavenly fellowship in the resurrection, not covered in the shame of bodily defilement but enriched with the gifts of divine grace.
BOOK TEN.

"The Lord said to my Lord" [?]. As he is about to complete his precepts, the Lord closes his testament with faith, which goes before the passion, and with mercy. Faith lies in our believing that Christ is both Lord and our God, and that he sits at the right hand of God. This does not mean that he who is everywhere sits there bodily. He is in the Father, because he is in the substance of God, because there is one power and one majesty. He is in the Father and the Father is in him, because the Word is in God and God is in the Word. He is in the Father and at the Father's right hand, because he shares with the Father and is second to none. He is sent by the Father, because he came down from heaven to fulfil the Father's will. Take away the disputes of unbelief, and religion is complete. He is not set above the Father because he sits at the right hand, nor is he wronged because he is sent. Where there is fullness of divinity, no one looks for degrees of rank.

We must also consider why he rebukes those who call Christ the Son of David. How, then, did that blind man earn healing by confessing him as the Son of David? How did the children who cried "Hosanna to the Son of David" give glory to God by their lofty proclamation? But the people here are not rebuked for confessing him as the Son of David. They are rebuked because they do not believe that he is the Son of God. True faith does not hold one of these and not the other; it holds both. At the beginning we resolved to know nothing but Christ [?] and him crucified. Yet now, being near the judgment, we no longer know Christ as the crucified one. We await him coming on the clouds. The unbeliever looks at the wounds; the believer is caught up into the air and runs to meet Christ.

Let us therefore believe that Christ is both God and man, one in both and not two persons. The Father subjects his enemies to him, not because his own power is weak, but because their nature is one, for each works in the other. The Son also subjects enemies to the Father, for he glorifies the Father on earth. And the Father gave the Son the name that is above every name. But the Son also says to the Father: "I have made your name known to the people you gave me." In giving the name that is above every name, the Father did not give more than he had; he gave all that he had. And he gave this name so that every tongue should confess to God that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.

Look, then, at each point in turn. The Father subjects things to the Son, and the Son subjects things to the Father. The Father raises the Son, and the Son raises himself. So he says: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again." The Father is Lord and the Son is Lord ("The Lord said to my Lord"), yet they are not two lords but one Lord. In the same way the Father is God and the Son is God, yet there is one God, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. There is one God because there is one Godhead: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the sceptre of your kingdom is a sceptre of uprightness. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you." Yet there is one God, and on this the teaching of the New and the Old Testaments agrees. In the Old Testament it is written: "You shall love the Lord your God," and "You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone." In the New: "One God and Father of all." So too the Father is Lord and the Son is Lord, but there is one Lord. That is why it is written: "Do not serve two masters." That is in the New Testament, while in the Old it is written: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord." The apostle wished neither to speak of two gods, nor to name two lords, nor to take anything away from either the Son or the Father. So he put it admirably: "There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things." For he who is God is also Lord, and he who is Lord is God. And so it is written: "Know that the Lord himself is our God."

Everything the Father has, therefore, the Son has too. The Father is God by reason of begetting; the Son is God by the oneness of the image. The Son is Lord because, although he could have subjected all things to himself by power, he subjected them by reason. The Father is Lord because he is the root of the Son. So for us the Father is distinguished from the Son by the definition of the persons and joined to him by the oneness of power. Each is in the other, and they are one in each other. It is the Father's glory that he has not fallen short in the Son, and the Son's grace that the Father is seen in Christ. He in whom the highest majesty of oneness dwells has not fallen short of his origin. He in whom the character proper to begetting expresses the truth is no stranger to the Father.

"There will not be left one stone upon another that will not be thrown down." The passage about the widow came next, but since we have already praised her in the book we wrote On Widows, we set it aside here. In keeping with the subject in hand, these words were truly spoken of the temple that Solomon built, which was to be overthrown first by the enemy at the time of judgment. Nothing made by hand is not either worn out by age, or pulled down by force, or burned up by fire. But there is another temple, built of beautiful stones and adorned with gifts, whose overthrow the Lord seems to point to: the synagogue of the Jews, whose old structure is dissolved as the Church rises. There is also a temple in each one of us, which falls when faith fails, above all when someone falsely puts forward the name of Christ to overpower the heart within.

There can also be an interpretation that profits me more. What good is it to me to know the day of judgment? Conscious as I am of so many sins, what good is it to me if the Lord comes, unless he comes into my soul and returns to my mind, unless Christ lives in me and Christ speaks in me? So Christ must come to me; his coming must happen for me. The Lord's second coming takes place when the world fails, when we can say: "The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world."

When the world fails in this way, suppose it finds such a man on the upper part of the house, so that his citizenship is in heaven. Then the bodily and visible temple will be destroyed, along with the bodily law, the bodily and visible Passover, and the bodily and visible unleavened bread. I dare to say that even a temporal Christ will be destroyed, such as Christ was to Paul before he believed, because in the one for whom the world fails, Christ is eternal. For such a person there is a spiritual temple, a spiritual law, and a spiritual Passover too, since Christ is slain once. He feasts on unleavened bread made not from the fruit of the earth but from the fruit of righteousness. For him, then, wisdom becomes present, and so do virtue, righteousness and redemption. Christ died once for the sins of the people, but he redeems the people's sins every day.

"But when you hear of wars and rumours of wars." When the Lord was asked when the destruction of the temple would happen and what the sign of his coming would be, he taught about the signs but did not think the time should be disclosed. Matthew adds a third question, so that the disciples ask about the time of the temple's destruction, the sign of his coming, and the end of the age. Luke thought that the end of the age would be known well enough if people learned about the Lord's coming.

No one bears better witness to these heavenly words than we do, whom the end of the world has overtaken. How many wars, and what rumours of wars, have we heard! The Huns have risen against the Alans, the Alans against the Goths, the Goths against the Taifali and the Sarmatians. The exile of the Goths has made us, too, exiles from our homeland in Illyricum, and the end is not yet. What famine everywhere, what plague among cattle, men and other livestock alike! Even those of us who did not suffer the war have been made equal to the conquered by pestilence. Since we are at the setting of the age, certain sicknesses of the world come first. Famine is a sickness of the world, pestilence is a sickness of the world, persecution is a sickness of the world.

There are other wars too, which the Christian man endures: battles of different desires and clashes of inclinations. Enemies within the house are far more dangerous than those outside. Now greed goads him, now lust inflames him, now fear terrifies him, now anger stirs him up, now ambition moves him, now the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places try to frighten him. So the shifting feelings of a wavering mind are pressed as if by battles and shaken as if by earthquakes.

But the stronger man says: "Though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war rise up against me, in this I will hope." He stands in the battle line and turns his breast to meet the enemy. Even if some cruel and towering Goliath rises up, while the others are afraid this humble man rises up like David. He casts away the arms of an earthly king and takes up the lighter weapons of faith. With a threefold cord he hurls the missile of pure confession and wounds the persecutor's shamelessness, scorning threats and disregarding the powers. He is fit to have Christ speak in him. In one place Christ speaks, in another the Father, in another the Spirit of the Father. These do not disagree but are in harmony. What one speaks, the three speak, because the Trinity has one voice. When such a victor has slain Goliath with his own sword, accepting death for Christ, and the foreigners have been put to flight, the young women come out to meet him (those, that is, who are like eagles), saying: "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands." This shows that the victors over the world are ranked above its princes. When kings are dead, the martyrs succeed for ever to the kingdom, honoured by heavenly grace. The kings become suppliants, and the martyrs their patrons.

There is another sword of Goliath, another weapon of the devil: the talk of heretics. The man who knows how to sing psalms seizes it to defeat the adversary. He hears of wars but does not suffer them. He is not unsettled or carried about by every wind of doctrine. He knows no famine of the word, for he is filled with the abundance of heavenly Scripture, and he is not afraid to challenge the heretic who resounds with empty words. Then let the one who is weak wait, so that by an unequal contest he does not prejudice the cause of the others. Let David come, whose mouth Christ opens to declare the mysteries. Let that Nazirite come whose hair does not fall, either because he has nothing superfluous that could fall, or because he will lose none of his higher virtues. He is whole in sobriety and strong in peace, and he guards all his thoughts and words to the end.

Let the gospel be preached, so that the age may be destroyed. The preaching of the gospel has already gone out into the whole world, and even the Goths and Armenians have believed, and so we see the end of the world. In the same way the gospel is preached by the spiritual man when he pursues every advance in wisdom and every virtue with a mind and spirit that sing psalms, destroying the last enemy, death. Then comes the end, when Christ hands over the kingdom in him to God the Father, and he is subjected to him who subjected all things to himself, so that God may be all in all. "And the gospel will be preached through all the cities," that is, the cities of Judah, for "in Judah God is known." The cities of Judah are built when the foundations of the virtues are laid.

"When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army." Jerusalem was in fact besieged and taken by the Roman army. So the Jews thought that the abomination of desolation came about then, because the Romans threw a pig's head into the temple to mock the Jewish ritual observance. I would not say that even if I were mad. For the abomination of desolation is the accursed coming of the antichrist, because with ill-omened sacrileges he defiles the inner parts of the mind. According to the literal history, he sits in the temple in order to claim for himself the throne of divine power. According to the spiritual interpretation, he is fittingly said to stand, because he wants to plant the footprint of his treachery firmly in the feelings of each person, arguing from the Scriptures that he is the Christ.

Then desolation will draw near, because many will fall from the true religion and go over to error. Then will come the day of the Lord. The apostle also explained this plainly when he said we must take care, as though the day of the Lord were at hand, that no one deceive us in any way, "for that day will not come unless the falling away comes first and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God," and so on.

So he will sit in the temple, in the inner temple of the Jews who will deny Christ. It is not an inviolable temple but one subject to corruption, which either the ruin of unbelief overwhelms, or the force of anger pulls down, or the fire of desires burns up. And it is well that the day of the Lord will come then and that the days will be shortened for the sake of the elect. The Lord's first coming was to redeem sins; his second will be to check offences, so that no more people fall into the error of unbelief.

Then come false prophets, then famine. Recall to me the times of Elijah, and you will find prophets of confusion then, and Jezebel, and famine, and the drought of the land. Why? Because iniquity had abounded and love had grown cold. And so the righteous man was in the desert and the wicked one on the throne.

There is also another antichrist, the author of this one: the devil. He strives to besiege my Jerusalem with the army of his legion, my soul, which is surely the soul of God, a peaceful soul. "For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world of darkness." The falling away happens when the soul deserts itself and then trembles and is troubled when it thinks of the Lord. While this antichrist holds sway, until he is taken out of the way, justice is exiled and iniquity reigns. Then faith is rare, as the Lord himself said, as though in doubt: "When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" That is, either in our own earth or in the whole world. So too elsewhere: "The Lord looked down on the children of men, to see if there was any who understood or sought God." This is not because God was in doubt, but because faith was so rare among men that, by human reckoning, it seemed a matter for doubt.

So when the devil is in the midst of the temple, there is the abomination of desolation, according to the prophet Daniel. But when the spiritual presence of Christ shines on each one who is struggling, the wicked one is taken out of the way, and righteousness begins to reign, which empties every rule of its power over the minds of the faithful.

There is also a third antichrist, Arius or Sabellius. In fact, all who lead us astray by false interpretation are antichrists. So "let the reader understand." Whoever understands is not led astray into believing falsehood instead of truth, as the Jews were. They denied the true Christ, and so it will follow that they believe in the one who is false. So too the Arians will not deny to the antichrist what they deny to Christ.

"Woe to those who are with child and to those who are nursing in those days!" Is conceiving a crime, then? Yet children are the rewards of marriage. And how did the Lord bless Sarah so that she gave birth? How did Hannah pray and bear a son? How was Rachel blessed so that she received sons? Were the prophets wrong? The Lord could not have been wrong. But the Lord spoke in the prophets too, and so they could not have been wrong either.

How then can the texts be reconciled when they disagree? Since there is war here, let us turn to the spirit of peace. Peace said: "When a woman is in labour she has sorrow, because her hour has come; but when she has given birth, she no longer remembers the sorrow." And he added: "So you also have sorrow now, but I will see you again and your heart will rejoice." He showed that the perfect rejoice, while the weak waver, as though still afraid of what is uncertain. But earlier in this passage too he said: "They ate and drank, they married and took wives," meaning that they bound themselves to this life and tied themselves down with worldly cares. These, surely, are the pregnant women to whom woe is spoken. They spread the fat of their flesh, and the steps of their inner minds grow sluggish. They are barren of virtues and pregnant with vices.

But even those pregnant women are not free from condemnation who have set about the work of good deeds yet have so far made no progress in the task they have taken on. There are some who conceive from the fear of God and say: "From your fear we have conceived and been in labour." But not all give birth, not all are perfect, not all can say: "We have brought forth the spirit of salvation on the earth." Not all are like Mary, conceiving Christ by the Holy Spirit and giving birth to the Word. Some cast out the Word as a miscarriage before they give birth. Some have Christ in the womb but have not yet formed him. To them it is said: "My little children, for whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you." So those who are still in the womb are being brought to birth as imperfect. Those to whom it is said, "I begot you through the gospel," are already more perfect.

There are many fathers through the gospel and many mothers who give birth to Christ. Who then will show me Christ's parents? He showed them himself, saying: "Who is my mother, or who are my brothers? Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother." Do the will of the Father, so that you may be the mother of Christ. Many have conceived Christ and not brought him to birth. The woman who brings forth righteousness brings forth Christ; the woman who brings forth wisdom brings forth Christ; the woman who is in labour with the Word is in labour with Christ.

There is also the woman who has been in labour with injustice and has given birth to iniquity. Woe to these pregnant women, who are heavy in body and slower to escape danger. Woe to those for whom the pain of the coming birth, which shakes the whole body, is still to be endured in full; for them the signs of the coming judgment are the beginning of their pains [?].

Moses also taught about a pregnant woman who quickly miscarries if two men quarrelling trample on her. So the good woman should flee strife and pursue peace, so that she can complete her delivery. She should not wait for nine months. The birth of the Word depends not on fullness of time but on fullness of diligence. "The righteous man, made perfect in a short time, fulfilled long years." On the other hand, the imperfect soul is quickly trampled and loses the Word it has conceived. But woe to him who causes one of these little ones to stumble, woe to him who tramples a pregnant woman! If he causes her to lose a child still unformed, the penalty is a fine. But if it was formed, he will give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand.

But why eye or hand, since the miscarried child who was already formed when he was struck out has both a hand and an eye? It is clear from this that each person is to be condemned according to the harm he has done. If a heretic or a schismatic strikes a catechumen out, as it were, from the womb of the soul or of the Church in labour, he is punished more lightly; if he strikes out a believer, more severely. So we must take care not to trample the Church by quarrelling with such people. "Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they breed quarrels"; through them the Church, as though in labour, is troubled by the trampling of the whole body.

So fill your womb quickly, so that you can give birth the sooner. Hear how you are to fill it, and with what: "A man has filled his belly with the fruit of his mouth, and he will be satisfied with the fruit of his lips."

Solomon's sublime judgment, and the dispute between those two women, have also taught me about those who nurse. Even when they are already freed from the pain of childbirth, they still waver in fear for the children who have yet to grow strong. Through drunkenness, sleep may creep over the nursing mother, and she may smother her little one, disown her own and seek another's. Even the woman who did not kill her son is in danger over her own, because she hangs on the uncertain outcome of the judgment.

So let us too hasten to wean our little ones, so that neither the day of judgment nor the day of death finds us parents, as it were, of imperfect works. Isaac, once weaned, was not exposed to his mother's sleep, and so Abraham held a great feast when he weaned his son. David, once weaned, hopes for the reward of his soul. For he is not, like the Corinthian at the beginning of faith, still too weak for food and given milk to drink [?]; he has already been strengthened with solid bread and has grown up to the fullness of mature age. So the care of begetting is not enough unless one has the means to nourish.

So let the Word of God grow in you as it did in Mary, and let it advance in wisdom and stature. This will happen if you keep all the words of righteousness in your heart and do not wait for old age. Betrothed in your early years to a righteous husband, conceive wisdom quickly without corruption of your body, give birth quickly, nurse quickly. Look at Paul: yesterday persecuting, today believing, tomorrow preaching.

"Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a sabbath." The Lord will come on the day of judgment, before which fire will blaze, and the force of fire is either always the same or burns more quickly in summer. Why, then, does he say we must pray that our flight not be in winter? Perhaps because the one who flees to the mountains must not fear the cold and ice, the storms and hail of sins, but should long for the clear light of summer, so that his weak steps do not slip on the slipperiness of the body.

So the soul, now secure in her progress and resting on firm roots, rejoices and says: "The winter is past, the time of pruning has come." In winter the wind strips the trees of their glory, and the bitter cold kills the tender leaves so that they look dead. But in spring the seeds rise again, and a new summer, as it were, grows up in green nature. Passover is in spring, when I was saved. Pentecost is in summer, when we celebrate the glory of the resurrection as a likeness of what is to come.

We must also pray that the Lord does not come and catch you on a sabbath, that is, idle and resting from works. So, as the law says, work day after day, be fervent in spirit and unwearying in labour. It is not without meaning that it is written, "On the sabbath you shall humble your soul," or that the people remained in captivity for seventy years. Then religion was violated, freedom crushed, chastity wounded. So you should depart from this life when the virtues are strong and the vices are captive. Do not depart when the soul is captive, when its vigour and virtue are idle and the sins of the body rule.

And there will be signs in the sun and the moon and the stars. This is both the true order of the prophecy and the full meaning of the mystery: the Jews too will be led captive a second time into Babylonia and Assyria. Those who denied Christ will be captives throughout the whole world. The visible Jerusalem will be trodden down by an enemy army, as the Jews fall by the edge of the sword. And all Judea will be made subject to the nations who are to believe, by the edge of the spiritual sword, which is the two-edged word. And various signs will appear in the sun and the moon and the stars.

These signs are set out more plainly in Matthew. "Then," he says, "the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall." When very many fall away from religion, the bright light of faith will be darkened by a cloud of unbelief, because for me that heavenly Sun grows dimmer or brighter according to my faith. When many people look at the rays of the sun of this world, the sun seems paler or brighter depending on how well each one can see. In the same way spiritual light is poured into each person according to the devotion of the believer. And the moon fades in its monthly courses, or when the earth comes between it and the sun as it stands opposite. In the same way the holy Church cannot borrow the brilliance of divine light from Christ's rays when the vices of the flesh block the heavenly light. For in times of persecution it is usually love of this life, and that alone, that shuts out the light of God.

The stars will fall. These are the ones who already gleam with the glory of the resurrection, the men who hold fast the word of life and shine like lights in the world. They are the men of whom it was said to Abraham that his seed would be like the heavens as they shine, and like the stars. So patriarchs will fall away from people, and prophets will fall away, if the bitterness of persecution grows strong. These things must happen until the Church's fullness of virtues is heaped up in all and in each. This is how the good are proven and how the weak are exposed. So the various storms of the mind will be so heavy that those whose consciences are burdened by many sins will fear the coming judgment, and in us the dew of the sacred fountain will dry up. For unbelief dries up, while faith brings dew.

For the powers in heaven will be shaken, and then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds. We await the Lord's coming, so that his presence may come about throughout the whole world, whether the world of mankind or the universe. That presence already comes about in each individual when you have received Christ with all your heart. Perhaps, in the same way, the powers of the heavens must also gain an increase of grace at the coming and return of the saving Lord, for he is the Lord of powers. Perhaps they too are moved as the fullness of the divinity pours itself into them more closely.

There are also powers of the heavens that tell the glory of God and that may be moved by a fuller pouring-in of Christ. These are spiritual powers, and they see Christ. David taught us how these powers are moved when he said: "Come to me and be enlightened." Paul too taught how you may see Christ:

"When you have turned to the Lord, the veil is taken away," and you see Christ. You see him in the clouds. I do not think, however, that Christ will come in dark gloom and dreary rain. Such clouds can be seen, and they certainly cover the sky in gloom and dreariness. If his coming were to be rainy, how could it be said that he has set his tabernacle in the sun?

But there are clouds that veil the brightness of the heavenly mystery, because it must be so. There are clouds that are moist with the dew of spiritual grace. Look at the cloud in the Old Testament: "In the pillar of cloud," it says, "he spoke to them." He spoke, of course, through Moses, and through Joshua son of Nun, who made the sun stand still so that he might receive the brightness of a fuller light. So Moses and Joshua son of Nun are clouds. See that holy men are clouds: "they fly like clouds, and like doves with their young." Above me there are clouds: Isaiah and Ezekiel, who show me the holiness of the divine Trinity through the Cherubim and the Seraphim. They are all clouds. In these clouds Christ comes. He comes in a cloud in the Song of Songs, a clear cloud, shining with the joy of the bridegroom. He comes also in a light cloud when he is made flesh from the Virgin, for the prophet saw something like a cloud coming from the east. He rightly called it a light cloud, because no earthly vices weighed it down. See the cloud on which the Holy Spirit came down and which the power of the Most High overshadowed.
So when Christ appears in the clouds, the tribes of the earth will beat themselves in mourning. For there is a certain order of crimes and chain of sins, and Christ's coming breaks it off.

Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they put forth fruit, you know that summer is near. The evangelists say this in different ways, yet their words seem to meet at one point. Matthew spoke of the fig tree alone, "when its branch is tender," while Luke here speaks of all the trees. There are two possible signs. First, when fruit grows green on all the trees and the fig tree, now fruitful, is in flower, so that every tongue confesses God and the Jewish people confess him too, then we should hope for the Lord's coming. At that coming the fruits of the resurrection will be reaped, as in summertime. Second, when the man of iniquity puts on light and flimsy boasting, as the branch of the synagogue puts on leaves, we should conclude that the judgment is drawing near. For the Lord is eager to reward faith and to put an end to sinning.

So the fig tree here is a figure with two meanings: either hard things grow soft, or sins run riot. Through the faith of believers, those that were withered before will flower. Through delight in their offences, sinners will boast. In the first case there is the fruit of faith; in the second, the wantonness of unbelief. The cultivation of the farmer in the Gospel promises me fruit from the fig tree. We must not despair if sinners have covered themselves with fig leaves, as with a garment of deceit, to hide their conscience. So leaves without fruit are suspect. Such are the garments worn by the exiles from paradise.

Behold, as you enter the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. It is good to consider where the Lord keeps the Passover. In Matthew you have: "Go into the city to a certain man." First notice the majesty of his divinity: he is speaking with the disciples, yet he already knows what is going to happen elsewhere. Then consider how he stoops to us. He does not choose a rich or powerful person. He seeks out a poor man, and he prefers the cramped lodging of a poor man to the spacious mansions of nobles. "Go," he says, "to a certain man." You knew this man's name, Lord, since you knew his service; and you knew his service, since you knew that he would meet them. But he is not named, so that he will be thought a man of no rank. Nothing here is contrived, since the reason is expressed and not the person. In Mark, however, he is carrying a flagon of water.

So the apostles are commanded to follow this man. And why is he called the master of the house? So that you may see that the term describes holiness, not wealth. Why does he have a furnished room upstairs? So that you may notice his great merit: the Lord and his disciples could rest in his house, delighting in his lofty virtues. If only it were given to me to carry a jar of water, to carry a flagon of water, as this master of the house carries it, who has a large furnished room upstairs! For what is a jar but a fuller measure, one that holds no small amount? "Good measure," says the Lord, "pressed down, shaken together and running over, will they give you."

And what shall I say of water? Before the very birth of the world, as you read, the Holy Spirit was moving over the water. O water, you washed the world when it was stained with human blood, so that a figure of our present baptism might go before! O water, you were found worthy to be the sacrament of Christ; you wash all things and are not yourself washed! You begin the mysteries and you complete them. From you is the beginning, in you is the end, or rather you make us know no end. Through you the stench of rotting flesh is removed, and with a sprinkling of salt, flesh that is perishing from decay is preserved for a long time. Through you a drink is poured into bodies parched with heat, sweet to delight, saving for life, pleasant to the taste. You gave a name to the prophets and the apostles, and you gave a name to the Saviour: they are the clouds of heaven, they are the salt of the earth, he is the fountain of life. When mountains press on you, you are not shut in. When you dash against rocks, you are not broken. When you are poured into the earth, you do not fail. You bubble up from the deepest veins. Shut in, you breathe out the breath of life; spread abroad, you supply fruitful moisture; poured over the land, you provide the watering it needs, so that the earth does not die with its life-giving parts dried up and refuse its yearly harvests. The substance of all the elements, sky, air, sea and earth, gives you back. The rock, struck by the touch of the prophet, poured you out to water the hearts of thirsty peoples. When you burst from the Saviour's side, those who struck him saw you and believed. And so you are one of the three witnesses to our rebirth. For there are three witnesses, the water, the blood and the Spirit: the water for washing, the blood for the price, the Spirit for the resurrection.

And I appoint for you a kingdom, as my Father appointed one for me. The kingdom of God is not of this world. So we are not to strive for man's equality with God, but for likeness to him. Christ alone is the full image of God, because the unity of the Father's brightness is expressed in him. A just man is made after the image of God if he imitates the likeness of the divine way of life. He does this by despising this world through knowledge of God, and by looking down on earthly pleasures through receiving the Word, by which we are fed for life. This is why we eat the body of Christ, so that we may share in eternal life. What is promised us as a reward and an honour is not food and drink but communion in heavenly grace and life. Nor are the twelve thrones some kind of bodily seats. Christ, as befits the divine likeness, judges by knowing hearts, not by examining deeds; he rewards virtue and condemns impiety. In the same way the apostles too are shaped for a spiritual judgment. They reward faith and curse unbelief, refute error by their virtue and pursue the sacrilegious with hatred.

Let us turn, then, and beware that no contest over who is first arises among us to our ruin. If the apostles contended, this is not offered to us as an excuse but set before us as a warning. Peter followed the Lord's very first call, and yet he is told that one day he will turn. Who, then, can claim to have turned quickly? So beware of boasting, beware of the world. The one who is told to strengthen his brothers is the one who said: "We have left everything and followed you."

Next we must consider that not every eagerness to show honour counts as humility. You can defer to someone to win worldly favour, out of fear of his power, or with an eye to your own advantage. What is sought is your own edification, not another person's honour. So one rule is given to everyone, that there should be no boasting about who is first but only a contest in humility, and for this reason the Lord sets himself before us as the one to imitate. We needed everything, he needed nothing, and yet he showed himself the author of humility when he served his disciples. He certainly did this not out of eagerness for advantage but as an exercise of virtue.

Peter, though eager in spirit, was still weak in his bodily feelings, and he is told that he will deny the Lord. He could not match the steadfastness of the divine purpose. The Lord's passion has imitators, but it has no equals. So I do not blame Peter for denying; I praise him for weeping. The denial belongs to the common human condition; the weeping is a special mark of virtue. And so he is taught to be on his guard, not forced to deny.

"Let him who has a purse," he says, "take it, and likewise a bag; and let him who has none sell his tunic and buy himself a sword." Why do you tell me to buy one, when you forbid me to strike [?]? Why do you command me to have what you forbid me to draw? Perhaps so that a defence may be ready, though vengeance is not needed, and so that you may be seen to have been able to avenge yourself but to have been unwilling. The law, however, does not forbid me to strike back. That is perhaps why, when Peter offers two swords, you say "It is enough," as though this were permitted until the Gospel. So the law gives teaching in fairness, and the Gospel gives the perfection of goodness.

To many this seems unjust. But the Lord is not unjust: though he could have avenged himself, he chose to be sacrificed. There is also a spiritual sword. With it you sell your inheritance and buy the word, which clothes the inner depths of the mind. There is also the sword of suffering. With it you strip off the body, and with the spoils of your sacrificed flesh you buy yourself the crown of holy martyrdom. You can learn this from the Lord's beatitudes, for he proclaimed the highest crown of all for anyone who suffers persecution for righteousness' sake. And so that you may know that he was speaking of the passion, and so as not to trouble the disciples' minds, he gave himself as the example, saying:

"For what is written must be fulfilled in me: 'And he was counted among the wicked.'" Still, it is puzzling that the disciples brought out two swords. Perhaps one is of the New Testament and one of the Old, and with them we are armed against the devil's snares. Then the Lord says, "It is enough," as though nothing is lacking to anyone whom the teaching of both Testaments has fortified.

Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me. Many stumble at this passage. They turn the Saviour's sadness into an argument that his weakness was ingrained from the beginning rather than taken on for a time, and they try to twist the natural sense of the words. I, however, not only think that it needs no excuse; nowhere do I marvel more at his love and his majesty. He would have given me less if he had not taken on my feelings. So he grieved for me, though he had nothing to grieve for himself. Setting aside the delight of his eternal divinity, he felt the weariness of my weakness. He took on my sadness so that he could give me his joy. He came down in our footsteps even to the misery of death, so that in his footsteps he might call us back to life. So I speak of his sadness with confidence, because I preach the cross. He took on not the appearance of a body but its reality. So he had to take on pain as well, in order to overcome sadness, not to shut it out. People who have felt numbness in their wounds rather than pain do not earn the praise due to courage. For it says, "a man in affliction, and knowing how to bear weakness."

He wanted to teach us. In Joseph we had learned not to fear prison; in Christ we were to learn to conquer death and, what is more, to conquer our sorrow at death to come. How could we imitate you, Lord Jesus, unless we followed you as a man, unless we believed that you died, unless we had seen your wounds? How would the disciples have believed that he was going to die, unless they had seen the sadness of a man about to die? Even so, they still sleep and do not know how to grieve, though it was for them that Christ was grieving. For we read that he bears our sins and grieves for us. So you grieve, Lord, not for your own wounds but for mine, not for your own death but for our weakness. We thought you were in pain, when you were grieving not for yourself but for me. You were made weak, but because of our sins. That weakness did not come to you from the Father; you took it on for my sake, because it was for my good that the chastisement that brings us peace should be upon you and that by your bruises you should heal our wounds.

But why be surprised that he grieved for all, when he wept for one? Why be surprised that he is weary when he is about to die for all, when he shed tears as he was about to raise Lazarus? There he was moved by the tears of a loving sister, because they touched his human mind. Here he acts out of deep feeling: since he was destroying our sins in his flesh, the grief of his soul was to do away with the sorrow of ours. And perhaps he is sad for this reason too: after Adam's fall we had to leave this world by such a passage that death was unavoidable. For God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living, and so he loathes what he himself did not make.

Then he says, "Take this cup from me." He speaks as a man refusing death and as God keeping his own sentence. For we must die to the world in order to rise to God. So, in keeping with the divine sentence, the law of the curse is undone when our nature comes to its end and is dissolved into the clay of the earth.

When he says, "Not my will but yours be done," he referred his own will to his humanity and the Father's will to the divinity. For the will of a man is temporal, while the will of the divinity is eternal. The Father does not have one will and the Son another; where there is one divinity there is one will. Learn, however, to be subject to God, so that you choose not what you want yourself but what you know will please God.

Next let us consider the exact meaning of the words themselves: "My soul is sorrowful," and elsewhere, "Now my soul is greatly troubled." So it is not the one who took on a soul who is troubled, but the soul that was taken on. The soul is subject to suffering; the divinity is free. Then: "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." It is not he himself who is sorrowful but his soul. Wisdom is not sorrowful, nor the divine substance, but the soul. For he took on my soul, he took on my body. He did not deceive me by being one thing and seeming another. He seemed sorrowful and he was sorrowful, not for his own passion but because we would be scattered. Then he says: "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered." He was sorrowful because he was leaving us behind as little children. As for the rest, Scripture shows how steadfastly he offered himself to death. He went out to meet those who were looking for him, strengthened those who were troubled, roused those who were afraid, and received the traitor, stooping to give him a kiss.

Nor is it far from the truth to say that he was sorrowful for his persecutors, because he knew they would pay the penalty for their sacrilege in torments. So he said, "Take this cup from me," not because the Son of God feared death, but because he did not want even the wicked to perish. Then he says, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them," so that his passion might bring salvation to all.

Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss? This is a great sign of divine power and a great lesson in virtue. The plan of betrayal is exposed, and yet patience is still not withheld. You showed, Lord, who was betraying you, since you bring hidden things to light. You showed also whom he was handing over, when you say "the Son of Man," because it is the flesh that is seized, not the divinity. Yet what refutes the ungrateful man even more is that he handed over one who, though he was the Son of God, had chosen for our sake to be the Son of Man. It is as if he said: "Ungrateful man, it was for your sake that I took on what you are betraying." Look at the hypocrisy! So I think the words should be read as a question, as though he rebukes the traitor with the feeling of one who loves him: "Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?" That is: Do you inflict a wound with the pledge of love? Do you shed blood with the gesture of affection? Do you bring death with the token of peace? Does a slave betray his master, a disciple his teacher, a chosen one his maker? This is the saying: "Better are the wounds of a friend than the willing kisses of an enemy." That is what is said to the traitor. But what is said to the one who loves peace?

"Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth." And he kissed Judas. He did not do it to teach us to pretend. He did it so that he would not seem to shrink from being betrayed, and so that he might move the traitor more deeply by not denying him the signs of love. For it is written: "With those who hated peace I was peaceable."

"And when the sign was given," it says, he is seized by those who had come with clubs. But it was mysteries, not weapons, that held the Lord of all. Then he spoke, and they fell backward. What need have I of legions of angels or a heavenly army? The Lord's voice alone terrifies more. The disciple who reclined on Christ's breast chose to record this as proof of his divine majesty. So the crowd lays hands on him, and he is willing; chains are fastened on him. O madmen! O faithless men! That is not how Wisdom is seized, nor how Justice is held.

Nor were the disciples lacking in zeal. Peter was learned in the law and quick in his love, and he knew that Phinehas was credited with righteousness for killing the sacrilegious. So he struck the servant of the high priest. But the Lord turned bloody wounds aside and put divine mysteries in their place. The man was a servant of the prince, the prince of this world: a slave of worldly powers not by the condition of his nature but by guilt. So he received a wound in his ear, because he had not listened to the words of wisdom. Moreover, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. "For your sins," it says, "you were sold." We were sold because of our sins, but our sins are redeemed because of God's goodness. Or, if Peter deliberately struck the ear, he taught that they ought not to have in outward form an ear that they did not have in the mystery. But the good Lord gives back hearing even to that man. In this way he shows, in keeping with the sayings of the prophets, that even those who were wounded in the Lord's passion can be healed if they turn, because every sin is washed away by the mysteries of faith.

So Peter cuts off the ear. Why Peter? Because he is the one who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. The one who condemns is also the one who absolves, since he received the power both to bind and to loose. He cuts off the ear of one who hears badly. With the spiritual sword he cuts off the inner ear of one who understands badly.

Let us beware that no one's ear is cut off. When the Lord's passion is read, if we attribute the weakness of his bodily suffering to his divinity, the ear is cut off. It is cut off by Peter, who did not allow Christ to be thought a mere prophet but taught that he should be acknowledged by faithful confession as the Son of God. So when we read that Jesus is held, let us beware of hearing anyone say, and of thinking ourselves, that he is held in his divinity, held against his will, held as though he were weak. He is indeed held, and, as John said, he is bound in the reality of his body. But woe to those who bind the Word! Those who think Christ only a man bind him. Those who do not believe he knew beforehand what would happen bind him. Those who do not confess him almighty bind him. Evil are the bonds of the Jews: with them they do not bind Christ but tie themselves up. He is bound not in the house of some pious and just man but in the house of Caiaphas, that is, in an impious house, where it is even prophesied that he will die for all. How mad, then, are those who acknowledge the benefits and persecute the one who gives them!

So they lose an ear because they have lost the benefit of hearing. Many who believe they have it do not have it. In the Church all have it; outside the Church they do not. Or perhaps he took away the ear so that those who could not keep what they heard would not go on sinning by hearing. In the same way the Lord once confused the languages of those building the tower, so that they could not understand one another and add to the work of their impiety.

Grasp, if you can, how at the touch of the saving right hand pain flees and wounds are healed, not by having medicine sprinkled on them but by being closed over at his touch. The clay recognizes its maker, and the flesh obeys the Lord's hand that made it, for the Creator restores his own work as he wills. So too, elsewhere, sight is restored to the blind man when mud is smeared on his eyes, as though nature itself were returning. He could have given a command, but he preferred to work with his hands, so that we might recognize that he is the one who formed the members of our body from the clay of the earth, fitted for their various tasks, and gave them life by pouring in the vigor of the mind.

So they came and seized him, doomed to perish all the more grievously by the fruit of their own zeal. The wretches did not understand the mystery, nor did they revere such gentle and loving kindness that he would not allow even his enemies to be wounded. They were bringing death to the righteous one, and he was healing the wounds of his persecutors.

But Peter followed at a distance. And rightly did he follow at a distance, since he was already close to denying him; for he could not have denied him if he had kept close to Christ. Yet perhaps in this very thing he deserves our deepest admiration and reverence, that he did not abandon the Lord even when he was afraid. Fear belongs to nature; concern belongs to devotion. His fear was not truly his own; what was his own was that he did not run away. That he follows comes from devotion; that he denies comes from being caught off guard. Slipping is common to all; repenting belongs to faith. Already a fire was burning in the house of the high priest. Peter came near to warm himself, because with the Lord shut away the warmth of his mind had grown cold even in him.

What does it mean that a maidservant is the first to give him away, when men surely could have recognized him more readily? Is it not so that this sex too might be seen to have sinned in the Lord's death, and so that this sex too might be redeemed through the Lord's passion? And so a woman was the first to receive the mystery of the resurrection, and she keeps its commands, so that she might wipe out the ancient error of transgression.

So Peter, once exposed, denies. Let us grant that Peter denied, since the Lord said, "You will deny me three times"; and I would rather that Peter denied than that the Lord was mistaken. What did he deny? What he had rashly promised. He thought about his devotion but did not take account of his condition, and he was punished for it, because he said he would lay down his life, which belongs not to human weakness but to divine power. If he paid so heavy a penalty for an imprudent word, how great is the penalty for faithlessness!

And where does Peter deny? Not on the mountain, not in the temple, not in his own house, but in the praetorium of the Jews, in the house of the high priest. He denies where the truth is not; he denies where Christ was seized, where Jesus was bound.
