Why should he not go astray, when it was a doorkeeper who let him in and a doorkeeper of the Jews who questioned him? Eve did ill to lead Adam on, and a woman did ill to bring Peter in. But Adam fell in paradise, where the fault was not pardonable; Peter fell in the praetorium of the Jews, where innocence is hard to keep. For Adam the fall was forbidden; for Peter the error was foretold. Adam's fall, once committed, prejudged Peter's; Peter's undid Adam's.

Let us also consider in what condition he denies. It was cold where Jesus was not recognized, where there was no one to see the light, where the consuming fire was denied. So the cold was of the mind, not of the body. That is why Peter stood by the coals: he was chilled in his affections. An evil flame is the Jewish flame: it burns but does not warm. An evil hearth it is, which sprinkles a kind of soot of error even on the minds of the saints; beside it even Peter's inner eyes grew dim, not the eyes of flesh and blood, but the eyes of the mind with which he saw Christ.

Someone says, "Do you condemn even the elements of the Jews?" I do not condemn the elements, for they do not belong to the Jews. What I condemn is something else: the flame of faithlessness. I condemn this flame of the Jews by following the divine oracles, for the Lord says, "Your silver is rejected silver." If the silver of the Jews is rejected, the hearth of the Jews is rejected too. Indeed it was by the hearth and the gold of the Jews that the calf's head was fashioned, that is, the chief seat of sacrilege.

But let us look at the course of the denial, which I see is told differently among the evangelists. It was so new a thing that Peter could sin that even the evangelists could not grasp his sin in one consistent account. Matthew writes that when the maidservant gave Peter away as one of those who were with Jesus the Galilean, his first words in reply were, "I do not know what you are saying." Mark says the same, and he was a follower of Peter and could learn it more accurately from Peter himself. This is the first utterance of Peter's denial, and yet in it he seems not to deny the Lord but to distance himself from the woman's accusation.

Yet consider what he denied: that he was one of those who were with Jesus the Galilean, or, as Mark puts it, with Jesus the Nazarene. Did he deny that he had been with the Son of God? It is as if he said, "I do not know a Galilean, I do not know a Nazarene; I know him as the Son of God." Let men be called by the names of places; no homeland can give a name to the Son of God, whose majesty no place can contain. And so that you may know this is true, it is also proved by an example. For elsewhere, when the Lord asked his disciples, "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?", some said Elijah, others Jeremiah or one of the prophets, but Peter said, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." [?] Did he deny there too, because he chose to confess Christ as the Son not of man but of God? Surely we cannot think something doubtful here that even Christ approved?

Consider another point. When Peter was asked, "Are you too one of those who were with Jesus the Galilean?", he shrank from a word that belongs to eternity (for those who had begun to exist did not truly "exist"). That is, only he "was" who was in the beginning.

So he says, "I am not"; for "to be" belongs to him who always is. Hence Moses too says, "He who is has sent me." Again, when he was pressed about being one of them, according to Mark he denied it, so that you may know the evangelist gave more weight to truth than to favor. Yet he denied that he was one of them; he did not deny Christ. He may have denied fellowship with men, but not the grace of God. He may have denied that he was one of those who were with the Galilean, but he did not deny being with the Son of God.

Then, according to Matthew, when he was exposed as having been with Jesus the Nazarene, he said, "I do not know the man." Both the evangelists we have cited also record that at the third question he answered with an oath that he did not know the man. And rightly did he deny the man, whom he knew to be God. Indeed, where there is an oath, the answer is cautious. For although Peter denied, he still did not swear falsely, since the Lord had not said that he would swear falsely. But if there is doubt in Peter's case, how dangerous an oath is!

John, however, writes that when Peter was asked by the maidservant whether he was one of that man's disciples, his first answer was, "I am not." For he who was the apostle of Christ was not the apostle of a man. So too Paul denied that he was an apostle of man, saying, "Paul, an apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father." But so that he might not seem to cast any doubt on the incarnation, he added, "who raised him from the dead," so that you may believe him to be man as well, having first believed him to be God. He keeps to the same pattern elsewhere too, where he says, "For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." He named him mediator of God before mediator of men; for it is not enough to believe both unless the order of faith is preserved.

So the answer agrees everywhere. For it was fitting that one who had said, "I do not know the man," should say, when asked whether he was one of the man's disciples, "I am not." Thus he did not deny that he was a disciple of Christ, but denied that he was a disciple of a man. So both Peter and Paul denied the man whom they confessed to be the Son of God. What Peter perceived, Paul expressed; and from this Paul too gained. Peter's error is the teaching of the righteous, and Peter's stumbling is the rock of all. On the waves he stumbles, yet he stretches out his right hand to Christ; on the mountain he falls, yet he is raised up by Christ. This same Peter stumbled on the sea, yet he walked. Peter's stumbling is firmer than our firmness. He falls where no one has climbed; he wavers where no one walks. And yet, though he stumbles among the waves, he does not slip; he wavers but does not fall; he is tossed about but not plunged under. And if he fell, at least he fell on the mountain; and he fell more happily than

others stood. He fell more happily, for Christ raised him up. John wrote that when he was asked a second time whether he was one of his disciples, he denied it. And rightly did he deny it, since he was said to be one of the disciples of the one whom they had called a man in the earlier questions.
For the third time too he denied that he had been seen with him, and this also follows from what came before: "I was not with the one you call a man, but I have not departed from the Son of God."

Luke too wrote that Peter, asked whether he was one of them, answered at first, "I do not know him." And he spoke well. For it would have been rash to say that he knew him whom the human mind cannot comprehend; for no one knows the Son except the Father. Again, at the second question, according to Luke, the same Peter said, "I am not"; clearly he preferred to deny himself rather than Christ. Or, since he seemed to deny fellowship with Christ, he certainly denied himself. Surely, when he denies concerning the man, he sinned against the Son of Man, so that it might be forgiven him, and not against the Holy Spirit. Asked a third time, he said, "I do not know what you are saying," that is, "I know nothing of your sacrileges."

But we make excuses for him; he made none for himself. For an evasive answer is not enough for one who confesses Jesus; open confession is needed. What use is it to wrap words in ambiguity if you want to be seen to have denied? And so Peter is not portrayed as having answered in this way by design, since afterwards he remembered, and yet he wept. He preferred to accuse his own sin, so as to be justified by confessing rather than burdened by denying, for the righteous man is the first to accuse himself; and so he wept. Why did he weep? Because a fault had crept up on him. I usually weep when I am deprived of a fault, that is, when I cannot avenge myself, when I cannot get what I wickedly crave; Peter grieved and wept because he had erred as a man. I do not find what he said; I find that he wept. I read of his tears; I do not read of any apology. But what cannot be [?] can be washed away. Let tears wash away the offense that shame keeps the voice from confessing. Weeping provides both for pardon and for modesty. Tears speak of guilt without dread; tears confess a crime without offending modesty; tears do not ask for pardon, yet they earn it. I have found why Peter kept silent: so that asking for pardon so soon might not give greater offense. First one must weep, and then pray.

Good are the tears that wash away guilt. Indeed, those on whom Jesus looks weep. Peter denied the first time and did not weep, because the Lord had not looked at him. He denied a second time and did not weep, because the Lord had still not looked at him. He denied a third time: Jesus looked at him, and he wept most bitterly. Look on us, Lord Jesus, so that we may learn to weep for our sin. Hence even the falls of the saints are useful. Peter's denial did me no harm; his amendment did me good. I have learned to beware of conversation with the faithless. Peter denied among the Jews; Solomon, led astray by living with Gentiles, went wrong.

So Peter wept, and wept most bitterly; he wept so that he could wash away his offense with tears. You too, if you wish to earn pardon, wash away your guilt with tears; at that same moment, at that same time, Christ looks on you. If perhaps you slip in some matter, then since he stands by as witness of your secrets, he looks on you so that you may remember and confess your error. Imitate Peter, who elsewhere says three times, "Lord, you know that I love you." For since he had denied three times, he confesses three times; but he denied in the night, and he confesses in the day.

These things were written so that we may know that no one ought to boast. For if Peter fell because he said, "Even if the others fall away, I will not fall away," who else can rightly presume on himself? So too David, because he had said, "I said in my abundance, I shall never be moved," confesses that this boasting did him harm, saying, "You turned your face from me, and I was troubled."

Where shall I call you forth from, Peter, so that you may teach me what you were thinking as you wept? Where, I say, shall I call you forth from? From heaven, where you have already joined the choir of angels, or even from the tomb, since you do not think it an indignity to be there too, where the Lord rose from? Teach us what good your tears did you. But you taught us at once: for you who fell before you wept were chosen after you wept to rule others, you who before had not ruled yourself.

So Peter had tears, which he shed out of loving devotion. The betrayer had no weeping with which to wash away his guilt, only the torments of conscience by which he confessed his sacrilege. Thus, while the guilty man was condemned by his own judgment and the crime expiated by a self-inflicted punishment, the Lord's goodness was proved, since he would not avenge himself, and so was his divinity, since by an invisible power he

was questioning the man's conscience. "I have sinned," he said, "in betraying innocent blood." Although the betrayer's repentance is fruitless, since he sinned against the Holy Spirit, there is still some shame in a criminal acknowledging his guilt. And though he is not absolved, the shamelessness of the Jews is nonetheless refuted. Even though the seller's admission convicts them, the wicked men still claim the rights of the contract for themselves and believe they are free of guilt, saying, "What is that to us? See to it yourself." Plainly mad are they, who think they are released rather than bound by the crime of the one who carried it out. In money matters, when the price is paid back the obligation is dissolved; these men take back the price yet press on with their sacrilege, and with stubborn zeal claim for themselves the deadly purchase of blood, even when the seller was paying back the wages of sacrilege.

So it is clear that, when the price of blood is kept apart from the treasury of the Jews, and the potter's field is bought with the money for which Christ was sold, and when that place is set aside for burying the remains of strangers, both the oracle of prophecy is fulfilled and the mystery of the rising Church is revealed. For according to the divine teachings, the field is this whole world, and the potter is the one who formed us from clay, of whom you read in the Old Testament that God fashioned man from the clay of the earth; he has the power, as he wills, to form us by nature and to re-form us by grace. For even if we collapse through our own vices, yet through his mercy, once the spirit of our mind is restored, we are re-formed, according to the oracles of Jeremiah.

The price of blood, too, is the price of the Lord's passion. So by the price of blood the world is bought by Christ; for he came so that the world might be saved through him, to whom it belongs [?] as the work of its maker and by right. He came, then, to keep for the grace of eternity those buried with Christ through baptism and dead with him. But not everyone without distinction has a place for burial; for although the world encloses all, it does not keep all. Though the dwelling is shared, the lawful burial belongs to those who are now members of God's household through faith, but who under the law were strangers. Who are these, if not those of whom it is said, "Remember that you were once Gentiles, who in the flesh were alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise"? But these are now no longer aliens and strangers, since by right of faith they have earned citizenship with the saints.

There follows a remarkable passage, by which the moral virtue of patience in bearing injuries calmly is poured into human hearts. The Lord is accused and is silent. And rightly is he silent who has no need of defense: let those seek to be defended who fear being defeated. So by keeping silent he does not confirm the accusation; he scorns it by not refuting it. For what should he fear who was not seeking his own safety? The salvation of all gives up his own in order to win that of all. But why speak of God? Susanna kept silent and won; for that cause is better which is proved without being defended. Here too Pilate acquitted him; but he acquitted him by his verdict and crucified him by a mystery. This, however, is peculiar to Christ; the other is human: that before unjust judges he should seem to have been unwilling rather than unable to defend himself.

Why the Lord kept silent he himself explained beforehand, saying, "If I tell you, you will not believe me; if I question you, you will not answer me." Yet the most striking thing is that he preferred to prove himself a king rather than say so, so that those who admitted the very thing they charged him with could have no grounds for condemning him.

When Herod wanted to see him perform some miracles, he kept silent and did nothing, because Herod's cruelty did not deserve to see divine things, and the Lord shunned display. And perhaps Herod is a type of all the impious, who, if they have not believed the law and the prophets, cannot see Christ's wonderful works in the gospel either.

He is sent to Herod and sent back to Pilate. Though neither pronounces him guilty, both yield to the cruel zeal of others. Pilate did wash his hands, but he did not wash away his deeds; for a judge ought to give way neither to ill will nor to fear so as to hand over innocent blood. His wife warned him, grace shone in the night, the divinity stood out clearly; even so he did not hold back from his sacrilegious sentence.

Here too, I think, a type was set forth beforehand of all the judges who would condemn those they judged innocent. Yet the figure of Pilate set beside them shows that the Gentiles are more tolerable than the Jews and more readily moved to faith by divine works. But what sort of men were those who crucified the Lord of majesty!

Fittingly do they ask for the release of a murderer, who were demanding the death of an innocent man. Such are the laws of iniquity: it hates innocence and loves crime. Here, though, the meaning of the name gives the outline of a figure; for Barabbas in Latin means "son of the father." So those to whom it is said, "You are of your father the devil," are shown to be about to prefer to the true Son of God the son of their own father, the Antichrist.

"And he dressed him in a white robe and sent him back." It is not without meaning that he is clothed in a white robe by Herod, who thereby gives signs of an unstained passion, because the spotless Lamb of God was taking up the sins of the world in glory. In the type of Herod and Pilate, too, who from enemies became friends through Jesus Christ, there is preserved a figure of the people of Israel and the Gentile people: through the Lord's passion there would come to be concord between the two, but in such a way that the people of the nations would first receive the word of God and then pass it on to the people of the Jews by the devotion of their faith, so that they too might clothe with the glory of their majesty the body of Christ, whom they had once despised.

By the soldiers he is clothed in a scarlet cloak and a purple tunic: the one signifies the palms of the martyrs, the other the insignia of royal power, because his flesh would take upon itself for us the blood shed throughout the whole world, and his passion would bring forth a kingdom out of us.

The crown of thorns fastened on his head, too, what does it show but the gift of the divine work, namely that triumphal glory would be won for God from the sinners of the world, as from the thorns of this age? The scourges also have meaning, because he was scourged so that we would not be scourged; for, a man under the lash and knowing how to bear infirmities, he suffers for us, turning the scourges away from us who had once fled from God, the Lord so patient that he offered his own hands to the chains of runaways and his own body to the lashes of runaways. So with a detestable intent the Jews nonetheless display an honored death; for in piercing him they crown him, in mocking him they worship him. Though they do not believe in their hearts, they confess the one they put to death. They may have lacked the disposition for a good work, yet God did not lack his due honor: he is hailed as king, crowned as victor, worshiped as God and Lord.

The reed too, according to Matthew, is put into his hand, so that human frailty might no longer be shaken like a reed by the wind but be made firm by the works of Christ and established, and so that, with the bond that stood against us nailed to the cross, the ancient sentence might cease. Or, according to Mark, it strikes his head, so that our condition, made solid by the touch of the divinity, may not waver.

But now let the victor raise up his trophy. The cross is placed on his shoulders as a trophy. Whether Simon carried it or he himself, both Christ carried it in the man and the man carried it in Christ. The accounts of the evangelists do not conflict, since the mystery agrees; and it is a good order for our progress that he should first raise up the trophy of his cross himself and then hand it on to the martyrs to raise. It is not a Jew who carries the cross but a foreigner and stranger, and he does not go in front but follows, as it is written: "Take up your cross and follow me." For it was not his own cross that Christ mounted, but ours. Nor was that death the death of the divinity, but of him as man. That is why he himself says, "God, my God,

look upon me! Why have you forsaken me?" Fittingly, when he was about to mount the cross, he laid aside the royal garments, so that you may know that he suffered as man, not as God the King; for though Christ is both, it was as man, not as God, that he was fastened to the cross. Yet it is the soldiers, not the Jews, who know at what time and what kind of garments befit Christ. At the judgment he stands as a victor; to the passion he comes as a humble defendant.

Now that we have seen the trophy, let the victor mount his chariot. Let him hang the captive spoils of the world on his triumphal gibbet, not hang plunder taken from a mortal enemy on tree trunks or four-horse wagons. Here we do not see nations with their arms bound behind their backs, or images of razed cities and likenesses of captured towns. We do not gaze in wonder at the bowed necks of captive kings, the usual sight in human triumphs, and we do not see the bounds of victory marked off by the borders of a region. Instead we see rejoicing peoples of the nations, won not for punishment but for reward. We see kings worshipping with free affection and cities surrendered by their own willing zeal. We see images of towns reformed for the better, portrayed by no paint but coloured by the devotion of faith. We see arms and the rights of victory running through the whole world, the prince of this world taken captive, and the spiritual hosts of wickedness in the heavenly places obeying the command of a human voice. We see dominions subdued and the forms of various powers, shining not in silks but in conduct. Chastity gleams, faith shines, and devotion, clothed in the spoils of death, now rises again in strength. One triumph of God, the cross of the Lord, has made nearly all people triumph. So it matters to consider how he mounts it.

I see him naked. Let the one who prepares to conquer the world mount the cross like this, so that he does not seek the world's aids. Adam, who sought clothing, was conquered. He who laid aside his coverings conquered. He mounted it just as nature, with God as its author, formed us. So the first man had lived in paradise, and so the second man entered paradise. And so that he might conquer not for himself alone but for all, he stretched out his hands to draw all things to himself. Freed from the knot of death and hung upon the yoke of faith, he joined to heavenly things the things that before had been earthly.

A title is also written. A procession usually goes before victors, but before the Lord's triumphal chariot went the good procession of the dead rising again. A title also usually shows the number of nations subdued. In those other triumphs, let the wretched and shameful captivity of conquered and perishing nations be set out in its order. Here the grace of redeemed nations blossoms like spring. The steeds yoked to so great a triumph are worthy of it, so that heaven, earth, the seas and the underworld are changed from corruption to grace.

The title is written and placed above the cross, not below it, because the principality is upon his shoulders. And what is this principality, this beginning, but his eternal power and divinity? So when he himself was asked, "Who are you?" he answered, "The Beginning, who also speak to you." Let us read this title: "Jesus," it says, "of Nazareth, King of the Jews."

The title is rightly above the cross, because the kingdom Christ holds belongs not to the human body but to divine power. The title is rightly above the cross, because although the Lord Jesus was on the cross, above the cross he shone with a king's majesty. A worm on the cross, a beetle on the cross. He was a good worm, clinging to the wood, and a good beetle, crying out from the wood. What did he cry? "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." He cried to the thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise." He cried out like a beetle, "My God, my God, look upon me! Why have you forsaken me?" He was a good beetle, rolling along in the footsteps of the virtues the mud of our body, which before was shapeless and sluggish. He was a good beetle, who raises the poor from the dung heap. He raised Paul, who counted things as dung, and he raised Job, who sat on the dung heap.

So the title is no ordinary one. The place of the cross itself was either in the middle, so that all could see it, or above the grave of Adam, as the Hebrews maintain. It was indeed fitting that the firstfruits of our life should be set where the beginnings of death had been.

The garments are divided, and different things fall by lot to different men. The Spirit of God is not grasped by human opinion but glides in as if by some unexpected chance. Perhaps these soldiers bear the figure of the four evangelists, who wrote the title for all of us to read. I read the title of the King of the Jews when I read, "My kingdom is not of this world." I read Christ's charge written above his head when I read, "And the Word was God," for the head of Christ is God.

So these men kept guard over [?], and they keep guard today, so that he does not slip away from anyone and does not come down from his passion for anyone, as the Jewish people demanded. For my part, let Christ indeed die in his passion, so that after his passion he may rise again. He would not come down for his own sake, so that he might die for mine. So Christ is now kept for us, and his garments are divided for our sake. Individuals cannot have everything, and so lots are cast for the tunic, because the Holy Spirit is not distributed according to human will. There are divisions of graces, but it is the Spirit who works, distributing to each as he wills.

Look now at Christ's divided garments. Where shall I look for them? Look in Matthew: with him alone you will find the scarlet cloak. With John you will find the purple robe, with Mark only the purple, and with Luke the white robe, for he was content with this alone as his share. How many, then, Christ clothed with his garment! But I think he clothed not just four soldiers but all of them, and had plenty for all. But let us return to the evangelists.

So these four parts seem to me to be not parts of garments but qualities of virtues. One wrote more loftily about the kingdom, another more fully about his formation as a man. Luke chose for himself the brightness of the priestly vestment. Mark did not want a woven fabric of words. John, finally, wove in certain sayings, as it were, to clothe our faith. Does this not seem woven to you: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him"? Mark, on the other hand, as if content with the brilliance of purple, says without any weaving of words, "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God."

So the garments of Christ that were divided are either his deeds or his grace. The tunic could not be divided. This tunic is faith, which belongs to all by common right, not to each by individual share. What is not divided among individuals remains whole.

And it was rightly woven from the top. The faith of Christ is woven so that it comes down from divine things to human, because he who was born of God before the ages took on flesh at a later time. This shows us that faith must not be torn but must remain whole.

"Truly, truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." This is a most beautiful example of conversion to strive for. Pardon is granted to the thief so quickly, and the grace is richer than the prayer, for the Lord always gives more than he is asked. The thief asked the Lord to remember him when he came into his kingdom, but the Lord said, "Truly, truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." To be with Christ is life, because where Christ is, there is the kingdom.

So the Lord forgives quickly, because the thief turns quickly. This also seems to resolve the difficulty that the other evangelists bring in two thieves reviling him, while Luke has one reviling and one asking. Perhaps this one also reviled him at first but was suddenly converted. Nor is it surprising that he forgave the guilt of a converted man, since he granted pardon to those who mocked him. He could also have spoken of one man in the plural, as in the verse "The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together." In the Acts of the Apostles, Peter declares that only King Herod and the governor Pilate conspired against Christ. So too in Hebrews you have, "They went about in goatskins, they were sawn in two, and they stopped the jaws of lions." Yet we are told that Elijah alone had a sheepskin, Isaiah alone was sawn in two, and Daniel alone remained untouched by lions.

How detestable was the wickedness of the Jews in this deed, crucifying the Redeemer of all as though he were a robber! Yet in mystery the thief is good, for he lay in wait for the devil to carry off his goods. Mystically, the two thieves signify two sinful peoples who are to be crucified with Christ through baptism. Their disagreement marks the differences among those who equally believe. One was on the left and the other on the right. The rebuke also reveals that the cross would become a stumbling block even among believers.

And the Jews offered vinegar. To bring all things to completion, the corruption of what was pure is fittingly drunk up as well, so that everything that had been spoiled might be nailed to the cross. So the vinegar is drunk, but the wine mixed with gall is not. This is not because of the gall, but because bitterness mixed with wine is refused. He certainly took on the bitterness of our life, in keeping with the condition of the body. Indeed he himself says, "They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." But bitterness ought not to be mixed with what is pure, to show that the future immortality of those who rise again will be without bitterness. That immortality had turned sour in the human vessel, and it is restored in Christ. So the vinegar is drunk: the flaw of the immortality corrupted through Adam is abolished on the reed, so that it might be drawn out of the human body. Let us too pour into Christ our vices, hardened through the carelessness of mind and body. Let us pour them out through baptism, so that we may be crucified in Christ. Let us pour them out through penance, so that he may pour back into us the uncorrupted purity of heavenly wine and blood.

Then, when he had drunk the vinegar, he said, "All is finished." The whole mystery of the mortality he had taken on had been fulfilled, and with every vice drained away, only the joy of immortality remained.

So he says, "Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit." The spirit is rightly commended, because it is kept safe, and what is entrusted is certainly not lost. The spirit, then, is a good pledge, a good deposit. So the Apostle also says, "O Timothy, guard the good deposit." The spirit is entrusted to the Father, and so he says, "For you will not abandon my soul in hell." But see a great mystery. At one moment he commends his spirit into the Father's hands, at another he sits in the Father's bosom, because no one else can hold the whole Christ. Indeed he says, "I am in the Father and the Father in me." So the spirit is commended to the Father. But while it is in the regions above, it also lights up the regions below, so that all things may be redeemed. For Christ is all, and all things are in Christ, even though Christ works in each individual. The flesh dies so that it may rise again. The spirit is commended to the Father so that heavenly things too might be freed from the bond of wickedness, and peace might be made in heaven for earthly things to follow.

"And having said this, he gave up his spirit." He rightly gave it up, because he did not lose it unwillingly. Indeed Matthew says, "He sent forth his spirit," for what is sent forth is sent willingly, while what is lost is lost by necessity. That is why he added, "with a loud voice." This is either a glorious profession that he had come down even to death for our sins, so that I too will not blush to confess what Christ did not blush to profess with a loud voice. Or it is a clear sign of God bearing witness to the parting of the divinity from the body. For you have this: "Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, 'My God, my God, look upon me! Why have you forsaken me?'" The man cried out as he was about to die through the separation of the divinity. Since the divinity is free of death, death certainly could not happen unless life departed, because the divinity is life.

What follows now shows that the end of the world will come because of human impiety. So the Lord's passion signifies that present things will pass away so that future things may arise. Darkness was cast over the eyes of the faithless so that the light of faith might rise again. The sun set for the sacrilegious, or fled, to cast a shadow over the spectacle of a deadly crime. The rocks were split. The broken stones showed in figure what was to come: the power of the Word would pierce hard hearts, so that the hunters Jeremiah foretold might more easily hunt for the Lord out of the clefts of the rocks. And the opening of the tombs, with the bars of death broken, signifies nothing other than the resurrection of the dead. Their appearing shows faith, and their coming out is a type. By going into the holy city, they declared under the figure of present things the future everlasting dwelling of those who rise again in the Jerusalem that is in heaven. The veil too is torn, which declares either the division of the two peoples or the profaning of the synagogue's mysteries. So the old veil is torn so that the new Church may hang up the veils of its faith. The covering of the synagogue is taken away so that we may behold the inner mysteries of religion with the unveiled gaze of the mind. Then even the centurion confesses that the one he had crucified is the Son of God. O hearts of the Jews, harder than the rocks [?]! The rocks are split, but their hearts are hardened. The judge rebukes them, the servant believes, the traitor condemns his crime by his own death, the elements flee, the earth quakes, the tombs are opened. Yet while the world is shaken, the hardness of the Jews remains unmoved.

The women stood watching these things, and his mother also stood there, setting her own dangers aside out of devoted love. And the Lord, hanging on the cross and disregarding his own dangers, commended his mother with a son's devoted affection. John had good reason to set this out at greater length. The others described the world shaken, the sky covered in darkness, and the sun fleeing. Matthew and Mark, who dealt more fully with human and moral matters, added, "My God, my God, look upon me! Why have you forsaken me?" They did this so that we would believe that his taking on of the human condition reached as far as the cross of Christ. Luke clearly states that it was fitting for pardon to be granted to the thief through priestly intercession, and for forgiveness to be asked by the same grace for the Jews who persecuted him.

So John, who entered more fully into the divine mysteries, rightly took pains to declare that she who had given birth to God remained a virgin. He alone teaches me what the others did not: how Christ, set upon the cross, spoke to his mother. He thought it of greater worth that, as victor over torments and punishments and victor over the devil, he was assigning the duties of filial love than that he was granting a heavenly kingdom. If it is a holy thing that the Lord grants pardon to the thief, it is much holier that the son honours his mother.

Let no one think it out of order that I wrote about the thief's absolution before the words to the mother. Since he came to save sinners, it is not absurd if in my writing he first fulfils the task he took on of redeeming the sinner's salvation. Indeed he himself says, "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" because he had not come to call the righteous but sinners. But that was said to suit the occasion. Here, even on the cross, not forgetting his mother, he speaks to her, saying, "Behold your son," and to John, "Behold your mother." Christ was making his testament from the cross, and John was sealing it, a witness worthy of so great a testator. It is a good testament, a testament not of money but of life, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. "My tongue is the pen of a scribe who writes swiftly."

Mary, too, behaved in a way that befitted the mother of Christ. When the apostles fled, she stood before the cross and looked with loving eyes at her son's wounds, because she was waiting not for the death of her child but for the salvation of the world. Or perhaps, because she knew that the world would be redeemed through her son's death, she, the royal hall, thought that by her own death she might add something to the gift given for all. But Jesus needed no helper to redeem all, for he said, "I have become like a man without help, free among the dead." He accepted his mother's affection, but he did not seek a human being's help. So we have a teacher of devoted love. The reading teaches what a mother's love should imitate and what children's reverence should follow. Mothers should offer themselves when their children are in danger, and children should be grieved more by their mother being left alone than by sorrow at their own death.

This passage gives the richest testimony to Mary's virginity. A wife is not taken away from her husband, since it is written, "What God has joined together, let no one separate." But she who had put forward marriage as a veil for the sake of the mystery no longer needed marriage once the mysteries were fulfilled. Or, if we follow the moral sense, chastity is required in time of mourning.

Yet there is a mystery in her being entrusted to John, younger than the rest, and we must not hear it with idle ears. Union with a young man and the beauty of youth are dangerous for women. Some woman might be curious about the example but care nothing for the mystery. Wanting to indulge herself in Christ's name, she might hold up Mary as a pretext without imitating her love, just as the common sort of women now have a bad name for leaving an older husband to follow a younger man. So let her learn [?] that here is the mystery of the Church. The Church was joined to the older people in appearance, not in practice. After she had brought forth the Word and sown it, through faith in the cross and the burial of the Lord's body, in human bodies and minds, she chose by God's command to join the younger people.

I also ask why we do not find that he was pierced before his death, but only after it. Perhaps it was to teach that his departure was willing rather than forced, and so that we might know the mystical order: not the sacraments of the altar before baptism, but first baptism and then the cup. It was also so that we might notice that, although his body was mortal by nature and alike in quality, it was unlike in grace. After death the blood in our bodies congeals, but from his body, incorrupt though dead, flowed the life of all. Water and blood came out, the one to wash and the other to redeem. So let us drink our ransom, so that by drinking we may be redeemed.

What does it mean, too, that Christ was buried not by the apostles but by Joseph and Nicodemus? One was just and steadfast, the other a man in whom there was no guile. Such is the burial of Christ: it has no fraud or wickedness in it. So there is no room left for evasion, and the Jews are refuted by witnesses from their own household. If the apostles had buried him, the Jews would surely say that he had not been buried at all, since they claimed he had been stolen.

The just man covers Christ's body with a linen cloth, and the innocent man anoints it with ointment. We find that this distinction is not idle, because justice clothes the Church and innocence supplies grace. So you too, clothe the Lord's body with its own glory, so that you too may be just. Even if you believe it to be dead, cover it with the fullness of his divinity. Anoint it with myrrh and aloes, so that you may be the good fragrance of Christ. That just man Joseph sent a good linen cloth, perhaps the one Peter saw let down to him from heaven. In it were kinds of four-footed creatures, wild beasts and birds, representing the Gentiles. So with that mystical ointment of faith the Church, which has united the diversity of peoples in the communion of its faith, is buried with him.

I find in John alone that this Joseph came secretly to Pilate for fear of the Jews. How could a just man seek a hiding place out of fear of danger? But I think he asked secretly in order to obtain the body, not to avoid danger. And yet what wonder is it if a just man hid himself, when even the apostles, the teachers of the just, were hiding? You come too. Whether you come late or at night, at whatever hour, you will find Jesus ready to receive you, and he pays no smaller wage to those who come later. The one who came at the sixth hour was not cheated of his wage, and the one who came at the eleventh received the full wage. Nicodemus too came by night. It was night because the resurrection had not yet happened. Then Christ rose, and the just man said, "The night is far gone, the day has drawn near."

Luke called this Joseph just, and Matthew called him rich. He is rightly called rich here, where he received the body of Christ, for by receiving the Rich One he knew no poverty of faith. So the just man is rich, and therefore he wraps him in a linen cloth. The Israelite, for his part, mixes various fragrances of virtues and brings about a hundred pounds of aloes, that is, the full measure of perfect faith. And they bound the body of Jesus according to the custom of the spiritual Jews, not with the knots of unbelief but with the bonds of faith. They laid it in a garden, to which the Church is often compared, since she has the fruits of different merits and the flowers of the virtues.

It is not for nothing that one evangelist called it a new tomb and another called it Joseph's tomb. So Christ had no tomb of his own. A tomb is prepared for those who are under the law of death, and the victor over death has no tomb of his own. What fellowship can a tomb have with God? Indeed Ecclesiastes says of the one who meditates on good things, "And he has no burial." So Christ's death is special, beyond the common death of all. That is why he is not buried with others but is shut alone in a tomb. The Lord's incarnation had everything in the likeness of human beings, but it was a likeness with a difference in nature. He was born of a virgin: like us in birth, unlike us in conception. He healed the sick, but by his command. John baptized with water, he with the Spirit. So Christ's death too is common in the nature of the body and special in its power.

Who is this Joseph in whose tomb he is laid? Surely that just man. So Christ is fittingly entrusted to the tomb of a just man, so that the Son of Man might have a place to lay his head and might rest in the dwelling of justice. It was fitting, too, that the tomb was new. In the literal sense, this was so that the faithless could not say someone else had been raised. In the mystical sense, what can we understand, unless perhaps what we read: "Their throat is an open sepulchre"? So the human throat is an open sepulchre, where deadly unbelief and dead words are laid, and it crumbles and falls apart through age and the attacks of beasts. In contrast, there is a tomb in the secret places of the human heart. The just man hews it out for himself with the piercing word in hearts hardened by paganism, and polishes it by the works of faith and teaching, so that the power of Christ might spread among the nations.

A stone was very fittingly rolled against this tomb so that it would not lie open. Whoever has buried Christ well within himself should guard him carefully, so as not to lose him and so that unbelief may find no way in. For you see that Peter and John were the first who were found worthy to enter. And indeed John himself did not go in before he believed.

And it is rightly said to have been hewn out of rock, that is, in the firm foundation of faith, from which the true Israelites sucked the sweetness of honey and spiritual oil. For it was a just man and one who saw God who buried Christ; none bury Christ except those who believe God.

Not everyone can bury Christ. Indeed, the devout women stand far off; yet because they are devout, they carefully note the place, so that they may bring ointments and pour them over him. In their anxiety they are both the last to leave the tomb and the first to return to it. Though they lack constancy, they do not lack diligence.

Their sex wavers; their devotion burns. Indeed, at the time of the resurrection they are at hand, and while the men had been put to flight, they alone are told by the angel not to be afraid. They call Peter: they are ahead of him in eagerness but behind him in confidence. And indeed he comes without fear, and he who had arrived later is the first to go in, and goes in boldly,

as one who had received the keys of the kingdom in order to open it to others. The earthquake, moreover, means resurrection to the faithful and fear to the ignorant: to the former, because the sluggish body is stirring itself from the sleep of death; to the latter, because, unsettled by the trembling of the body and the instability of earthly things, they fall away from faith and belief in the resurrection.

Early on the morning of the sabbath, at a very early hour, they came to the tomb. At this point a great question arises for many. Although the evangelists do not appear to have said contradictory things, they have nevertheless said different things. Here it says that the women came to the tomb “early, at a very early hour”; Mark says “very early”; Matthew, “in the evening of the sabbath”; John, “on the first day of the week, while it was still dark.” Then this evangelist records that two men were seen, Mark one young man sitting in white, Matthew one angel, John two angels sitting in white. Finally, and this seems almost impossible to untangle, John wrote that Mary Magdalene was told, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father”; while Matthew wrote that the Lord met Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, and set out in the clearest possible account that they came up, took hold of his feet and worshiped him.

How then is this to be resolved, unless you suppose that the four evangelists spoke of four different times, so that you may infer different women and different visions? Indeed, some come with ointment on the first day of the week, others without ointment in the evening of the sabbath. The names of the one group are given; the others are described as women who had followed the Lord from Galilee.

At this point, so that no one may be put off by the harshness of a thorny interpretation at the end, where perhaps something pleasant was expected, consider that we are already lowering the sails to bring our discourse to a close. For we have come to harbor, and a ship that has crossed the seas at a swift pace, when it begins to approach the shore, grazes hidden rocks once its course is checked. So, lest my discourse run aground on the sands of the shore as though under a sluggish helmsman, I think the way should be taken slowly rather than in haste, as if picking a path through hidden shallows, so that our speech may not spring leaks and break apart.

First, then, we must consider what is meant by what is written: that the Lord rose “in the evening of the sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week.” For this is what you have: “In the evening of the sabbath Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake.” He did not rise on the sabbath day, for they rested on the sabbath according to the commandment, but after the sabbath day, and certainly at night. Indeed, the women who came in the morning, though at a very early hour, nevertheless learned that the Lord had already risen.

So it must be understood in such a way that the resurrection is not believed to have taken place either on the morning of the Lord's day, which is the first day after the sabbath, or on the sabbath. Otherwise how are the three days completed? So he rose not as the day was turning to evening, but in the late hours of the night. Indeed, the Greek says “late,” that is, opse. Now “late” both marks the hour at the close of the day and signifies the lateness of anything at all, as when you say, “It was suggested to me late,” that is, tardily; or “he came late,” that is, he arrived after the appointed time. Even if he came on the morning of the following day, it is still late when the time for acting has passed. “Late” is also the depth of night, as when you say, “I got up late to work by lamplight,” that is, I got up not in the evening but in the depth of the night.

This is also why the women are able to approach the tomb, since the guards were certainly already asleep, and why the guards themselves are all the more terrified, as commonly happens to those roused from sleep. Finally, the chief priests too, gathered with the elders, confirm that this happened at night, when they say to the guards: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep.” For they seize on the time they learned from the guards as a pretext for their deceit. John, too, indicates that Mary Magdalene came to him and to Peter in the morning, while it was still dark, and yet he presents her as unaware that the resurrection had taken place. Surely, if it had happened as the day was turning to evening, it could have become known at once.

It is morning, and still Peter does not know, John does not know. Would the Lord have allowed his disciples to be tormented any longer by uncertainty about his death, when the angel at once, and the Lord at once, sent the women to them to announce what had happened? And so that you may know that it happened at night: some of the women do not know, others do. Those who kept watch night and day know; those who had gone away do not. One Mary Magdalene does not know, according to John; another Mary Magdalene knows, according to Matthew. For the same woman could not have known earlier and then not known later. So if there were several Marys, perhaps there were also several Magdalenes, since the one is a personal name, the other a name taken from a place.

Indeed, recognize that she is a different woman. The one is allowed to hold the Lord's feet; this one is forbidden to touch the Lord. The one was found worthy to see an angel; this one, when she first came, saw no one. The one announced to the disciples that the Lord had risen; this one reports that he has been taken away. The one rejoices; this one weeps. Christ, already in his glory, comes to meet the one; this one is still looking for him as dead. The one saw the Lord and believed; this one could not recognize him even when she saw him. The one worshiped in spirit with a faithful heart; this one was saddened by doubting feelings.

It is no wonder, then, that she is rightly forbidden to touch the Lord, for we touch Christ not by bodily touch but by faith. “For I have not yet ascended,” he says, “to my Father,” that is: I have not yet ascended for you, who are looking for the living among the dead. And so she is sent to those who are stronger, so that she may learn to believe from their example, and so that they may preach the resurrection.

For just as in the beginning the woman was the author of sin for the man and the man the one who carried out the error, so now she who had first tasted death was the first to see the resurrection: first in the order of sin, first also in the remedy. And so that she, who had passed sin on to the man, might not bear among men the reproach of perpetual guilt, she passed on grace as well, and made up for the misery of the ancient fall by announcing the resurrection. Through a woman's mouth death had once gone forth; through a woman's mouth life is restored.

But because she is less steadfast for preaching, and her sex weaker for carrying things through, the office of proclaiming the gospel is entrusted to men. For just as in the case of the woman [?] not only is sin undone but grace is also multiplied, so that she who had once deceived one man might persuade many, so too the man, who had once believed rashly, had to recover the gift with interest, so that he who had been unsteady in believing for himself might become fit to preach to others.

But let us attend to the very words of the command: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.” How had you not ascended, Lord Jesus? In what way were you absent, you who had commended your spirit into the Father's hands? Or when can you be absent, you who are always in the Father and always with the Father? Indeed, you yourself said: “If I go down to hell, you are there; if I take my wings before dawn and dwell in the farthest part of the sea, even there your hand will lead me.” Or how do you ascend, you who are always everywhere?

You did indeed descend as the Son of Man, and when you descended you were not absent from the Father; but you descended for us, so that we might see you with our eyes and our minds, so that we might believe in you. So you also ascended for us, so that we might follow with our minds you whom we cannot see with our eyes. You ascended for the apostles, to whom you said: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” Indeed, John knew where to look for you. He sought you with the Father and found you, and that is why he says: “And the Word was with God.” You ascended for Paul too, who, not content to follow you by himself, also taught us how we should follow you and where we can find you, saying: “If then you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.” And so that we would not think this a task for the eyes rather than for the soul, he added: “Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth.”

So if we wish to find you, we must not seek you on the earth, nor in the earth, nor according to the flesh; for now we no longer know Christ according to the flesh. Indeed, Stephen did not seek you on earth, and he saw you standing at the right hand of God; but Mary, who was seeking on earth, could not touch you. Stephen touched you because he sought you in heaven. Stephen, among the Jews, saw you when you were absent; Mary, among the angels, did not see you when you were present. But why she could not touch you the evangelist himself has taught us, saying that when she saw you, she did not know that it was you. For this is what you have: “She turned around and saw Jesus standing, and did not know that it was Jesus.” Rightly could she not touch him whom she had not been able to see; for whoever sees, touches.

So Scripture marks the difference between that Mary and this one. The one runs to meet Jesus in order to see him; this one turns around. The one is greeted; this one is rebuked. Indeed, this is what you have: “Jesus said to her: Woman.” She who does not believe is a woman, and is still designated by the name of her bodily sex; for she who believes attains to perfect manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, now free of a worldly name, of bodily sex, of the unsteadiness of youth and the garrulousness of old age. So Jesus says: “Woman, why are you weeping?” As if to say: God requires not bare tears but faith. Tears are good if you recognize Christ. “Whom are you looking for?” he says; for the Lord condemns belated efforts. But he did well to add “whom,” not because he is unsure whom she is looking for, but because she does not know whom she is seeking; for she is not seeking Christ, since she thinks he has been carried off. Christ is present: in what sense is he being sought? So the one who is sought is unknown, since he is not recognized when he is seen.

Indeed, she was looking at Christ and thought he was the gardener. For this is what you have: “She, supposing him to be the gardener, said to him: Lord, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.” Though uncertain in her faith, she is not careless in her speech; though she thought him the gardener, she nevertheless pointed to the Son of God; though she does not yet believe, she is still reaching toward belief. For he who raised the body himself carried it away. So the woman's mistake is pardonable: although she ought not to have doubted that Christ's body had been taken up through the glory of the resurrection, she still longs to be taught by Christ. And in her devotion she already pledges her faith, so that she too may now lift it from the earth and seek it at the right hand of God.

Indeed, after these words she is no longer called “woman” but “Mary”; for the common name shared with the crowd is one thing, the personal name of one who follows Christ is another. And she is sent to the disciples as a messenger, though not yet as a judge of full faith. But she is forbidden to touch him because she had not yet grasped, as Paul had, that the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ; she had not yet rid herself of the unsteadiness of the world and the uncertainty of the flesh; she had not yet lived the life of Christ. Indeed, she neither worships the Lord nor holds his feet, as that other Mary did; and in her what is signified is not so much an act of bodily homage as the disposition of full faith, which believes Christ to be both man and God. For it is God who is worshiped and man who is held.

So the Lord does not disdain to be touched by a woman (Mary even anointed his feet with ointment), nor does he scorn her touch; rather, he is teaching progress, because not all who touched Christ while he lived in this life and in the body can touch him as he rises. Whoever wishes

to touch Christ must put his members to death and, to become like the one who is to rise, put on a heart of mercy and not hesitate to renounce earthly things. What then does “Do not touch me” mean? Do not lay your hand on greater things, but go to my brothers, that is, to those who are more perfect (for whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother), because the resurrection cannot easily be grasped except by the more perfect; the privilege of this faith is reserved for those more firmly grounded. “But I do not permit women to teach in church; let them ask their husbands at home.” So she is sent to those who belong to the household, and she has received the commands laid down for her.

Nor have I failed to notice that some have held here that Christ did not wish to be touched because he had not yet received back the form [?] that he had commended to the Father, as though she ought not to touch him yet.

“I am ascending to your Father, to my God and your God.” He made the distinction well, because he was speaking to a woman; for we have no nature in common with Christ except that of the human condition. He is Father to him by his own generation, to us by willing adoption; to him by nature, to us by grace. He is God to him by the unity of the mystery, to us by heavenly power.

Someone says: How then did Thomas touch Christ while he still did not believe? But he seems to have doubted not the Lord's resurrection but the nature of the resurrection, and by his touch he had to teach me, just as Paul also taught: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality,” so that the unbeliever might believe and the hesitant could no longer doubt; for we more easily believe what we see. Thomas, moreover, had reason to marvel when he saw that, with everything shut, a body had entered through barriers impassable to bodies, without any breach in their structure. And so it was a wonder how a bodily nature had poured itself through an impenetrable body, by an invisible entrance yet in visible form: easy to touch, hard to comprehend.

Indeed, the disciples were troubled and thought they were seeing a spirit, and so the Lord, to show us the form of the resurrection, said: “Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.” So it was not by an incorporeal nature but by the quality of a risen body that he passed through what was closed and normally impassable. For what is touched is a body, and what is handled is a body; and it is in a body that we rise. For “it is sown a natural body, it rises a spiritual body”; but the latter is finer, the former coarser, since it is still compounded with the quality of earthly corruption.

For how was it not a body, when the marks of the wounds and the traces of the scars remained in it, which the Lord offered to be handled? In this he not only strengthens our faith but also sharpens our devotion, for he chose to bring into heaven the wounds he received for us rather than to erase them, so that he might show God the Father the price of our freedom. Such is the one whom the Father places at his right hand, embracing the trophies of our salvation; such, by the crown of his scars, has he shown us the martyrs there to be.

And since our discourse has come to this point, let us consider why, according to John, the apostles believed and rejoiced, while according to Luke they are rebuked as unbelieving; why there they received the Holy Spirit, while here they are told to stay in the city until they are clothed with power from on high. It seems to me that the apostle John touched on the greater and loftier matters, while Luke treated what followed and what lies closer to human experience: the one used the expansive method of a historian, the other a summary. For there can be no doubt about the one who bears witness to things at which he himself was present, and his testimony is true; and it is only right to clear the other too, who was found worthy to be an evangelist, of any suspicion of carelessness or falsehood. And so we hold that both are true, and are not divided by any difference of meaning or of persons. For although Luke says at first that they did not believe, he afterward shows that they did. If we consider the first part, the accounts are contrary; if we consider what follows, it is certain that they agree. Let us then consider the very words of Scripture.

John says this: “And the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. So he said to them again: Peace be with you; as the Father has sent me, so I send you. And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said: Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained.” But Luke says: “and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread. While they were saying these things, he himself stood in their midst and said to them: Peace be to you; it is I, do not be afraid. But they were troubled and terrified, and thought they were seeing a spirit.” And there might seem to have been more people present here. But because here too it was late on the day of the resurrection (for the two who had gone in to stay with the Lord when the day was already turning to evening are said to have returned to the disciples at the very hour when he suddenly withdrew from them, and it was then that he offered himself to be handled), and because according to John he is presented as appearing to the disciples late on that day, the first day of the week, and offering his wounds to be handled, we thought this should be examined more carefully, so that it would not create any ambiguity.

For he seems to have shown himself separately to these eleven, just as he had already shown himself apart to Ammaon and Cleopas in the evening; and just as those two could come together, so the eleven too seem to have been able to gather in order to strengthen the rest. Indeed, they were also troubled, as you have it in Luke, and so he opened their minds so that they might understand what was written. There is no doubt that one evangelist wrote more fully and the other more briefly. For how could they say that he had appeared to Cephas alone, if he had been seen by everyone? But just as among the women he was seen by Mary and the other Mary Magdalene, so among the men he was seen by Peter early in the morning. And Paul says this: “For I delivered to you first of all that Christ died according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas.” And that is why Mark specifically introduces a young man telling the women to say to Peter and the disciples that the Lord had risen.

So Peter alone saw the Lord. For his devotion, always ready and eager, believed, and so he was keen to gather ever more signs of faith. Sometimes with John, sometimes alone, he runs tirelessly everywhere, everywhere either alone or first. Not content with having seen what he had seen, he goes back to look at it again, and, fired with love for seeking the Lord, he never has his fill of seeing. He sees alone, he sees with the eleven, he sees with the seventy, he sees when Thomas came to believe, he sees while fishing. But not content with having seen, impatient in his longing, heedless of his catch, unmindful of danger, yet not unmindful of reverence, when he saw the Lord on the shore he wrapped his garment about him, thinking it too late to arrive with the others by boat. So too, when the Lord was walking on the sea, he forgot his own nature and ran to meet him over the waves; so, when the Lord was seized by the Jews, he alone drew his sword against the crowds; and so now, when the Lord stood on the shore, he hastened to pay his devout homage by a dangerous shortcut.

There is no doubt, then, that Peter believed, and believed because he loved, and loved because he believed. That is also why he is saddened at being asked a third time, “Do you love me?” For one is questioned when there is doubt about him; but the Lord had no doubt. He asked not to learn but to teach whom he was leaving us, as he was about to be lifted up into heaven, as a kind of vicar of his love. For this is what you have: “Simon, son of John, do you cherish me?” “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.” Jesus says to him: “Feed my lambs.” Well aware of himself, Peter testifies to an affection not taken up for the moment but long since known to God. For who else is there who could readily profess this of himself? And so, because he alone of all professes it, he is placed above all; for love is greater than all.

This too should be examined more carefully: why, when the Lord said, “Do you cherish me?”, Peter answered, “You know, Lord, that I love you.” Here it seems to me that cherishing involves the charity of the mind, while love is a kind of heat kindled by the ardor of body and mind; and I think Peter is indicating that not only his mind but also his body was burning for the worship of God. Indeed, the third time the Lord asked not “Do you cherish me?” but “Do you love me?”, and he is now told to feed not lambs, as the first time, who are nourished on milk, so to speak, nor little sheep, as the second time, but sheep, the more perfect, so that he, being more perfect, might govern them.

And so, as to one perfect in all things, whom the flesh could no longer call back from the glory of martyrdom, a crown is decreed. “When you were younger,” he says, “you girded yourself and walked wherever you wished; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” Good is the old age that is not made feeble for use by length of life, but prepared for martyrdom by ripeness of virtue; that curbs the wantonness of bodily pleasures and does not indulge desires, that turns away from everything sweet and does not crave what is attractive. For the flesh lusts against the spirit, and finds for itself byways of diverse pleasures by which to go wherever it wishes. But good is the old age of the mind, which chooses not what is pleasant to the body but what it judges useful to the mind, and is not taken captive by the willful appetite of the body, but is held back, as if against its will, by a restraint that resists.

So Peter too, though he was ready in spirit to undergo martyrdom, still bent in his firmness of mind when the danger came; for we are held captive by the sweetness of enjoying its heavenly gift. Who would not choose martyrdom, if he could die gladly? So Peter too seems unwilling, yet he prepares to conquer. And what wonder if Peter is unwilling, when the Lord says, “Father, if it can be, take this cup away from me; yet not my will, but yours be done”? Finally, after his presumption had been put to the test, Peter no longer dares to promise that his will would hold firm, but looks for the companionship of another, as if for his own comfort.

Led, then, by so many examples of virtue, we believe that Peter could not [?] have doubted. It is clear too that John believed when he saw the Saviour; indeed he had already believed back then, after he saw the empty tomb. Why, then, does Luke present them as having been troubled? First of all, because the judgement of the greater part takes in the opinion of the few. Secondly, because even if Peter had believed in the resurrection, he could still be troubled when he saw that the Lord, with his body, suddenly poured himself into a place shut in by barred doors and enclosed by built walls. Luke, then, followed up each detail as a historian: John looked to the end, Luke to the sequence. For certainly, in saying, “Then he opened their minds, so that they might understand what is written,” he too declares that the disciples believed.

As for the Holy Spirit, either he breathed him on those eleven as the more perfect, and promises that he will be granted to the rest later; or he breathed him on the same men in the one place and promised him in the other. Nor does this seem contradictory, since there are different kinds of gifts: “to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the gift of healings; to another kinds of tongues.” So in the one place he breathed one working, and in the other he promises another. For there the grace of forgiving sins was granted, which seems the more exalted, and so it is breathed by Christ, so that you may believe that the Spirit is Christ's and believe that the Spirit is from God; for God alone forgives sins. Luke, on the other hand, describes the grace of tongues poured out. Thus in the one place you have: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they will be forgiven.” But in the Acts of the Apostles you have this: “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Spirit gave them to speak.”

The variety of the visions, moreover, signifies the throng of ministering angels, just as the Lord himself had promised, saying, “And you will see the angels descending and ascending upon the Son of Man.” And would that our discourse too might close with the end of the Gospel!

Why, according to Matthew and Mark, does he command the disciples, “I will go ahead of you into Galilee; there you will see me,” while according to Luke and John he even showed himself to be seen inside a room? Indeed, that he often showed himself to be seen—to more than five hundred brothers, to Peter and to James—we have proved by the testimony of the Apostle as well; and Luke taught in the Acts of the Apostles that he showed the disciples he was alive after his passion by many proofs, appearing to them and speaking of the kingdom of God. Therefore, since he appeared quite often and to different people, and since Scripture by no means marked out a prescribed and fixed time for when he was seen in Galilee, while for when he showed himself in Jerusalem it stated both the day and the hour, the more fearful were visited inside rooms, and the braver gathered at the mountain.

Thus John presents the disciples gathered inside a room with the doors shut for fear of the Jews, and Luke wrote that these were not eleven but more. Matthew, however, did not pass over the fact that these eleven alone gathered in Galilee. For this is what you have: “But the eleven disciples went away into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them, and when they saw him they worshipped him, but some doubted.” To them he gave the power to teach and to baptize. Mark too writes at the end that he appeared to the eleven disciples as they reclined at table, when he likewise commands them with the duty of preaching throughout the whole world.

Hence I think it more fitting to hold that the Lord did command the disciples to see him in Galilee, but that he first showed himself to them while they were staying inside a room out of fear, and that afterwards, once their spirits had been strengthened, those eleven made for Galilee. Or certainly—and I find that this view too has pleased careful writers—nothing stands in the way if we say that there were fewer in the room, and a good many more on the mountain.
